Some in the Serbian diaspora were made to vote in the middle of the night after authorities tied voting hours to local Serbian time.

Recent Serbian elections had been marred by irregularities and the EU was closely watching the conduct of Sunday’s vote in a candidate nation for the bloc’s membership.

Independent election monitors reported dozens of cases of irregularities on Sunday such as photographing of ballots that suggested pressure on voters and attempted vote buying.

Both international and local election monitors had expressed concern about the safety and fairness of an election campaign marked by detentions, near-total government control over the media and reports of surveillance and cyberattacks against activists.

Local elections earlier this year in 10 municipalities in Serbia saw violent attacks on journalists and activists. The previous parliamentary vote in 2023 was followed by opposition protests alleging fraud.

World.title: Kamala Harris responds to her critics and Democrats who don’t want her to run again
World.content:
Clarksdale, Mississippi —

“Nice to meet you, Madam President,” Kamala Harris said, shaking hands with the Coahoma Community College student body representative on her surprise stop by the campus on Thursday afternoon.

Harris likes that disarming joke. She was the biggest political figure to come across this underfunded school in the Mississippi Delta, the grass so dry it crunched as she walked with a gathering of stunned students for a group picture.

“You don’t know how many people this uplifts,” said Don Green, who followed Harris that afternoon from the college to a rural health clinic in Clarksdale, most famous for being the site of the legendary Crossroads of the Blues.

Mike Cavanaugh, a sophomore at the University of Mississippi and president of the campus’ College Democrats, spoke ahead of Harris at a rally that day and answered her questions about voter registration during his brief chat with her on the photo line. “Young people are very excited,” he said.

“It didn’t have to be this way,” is one of the lines Harris used several times on the stump in Mississippi as she campaigned for Democrat Scott Colom, whose challenge to Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is drawing a new burst of national attention and outside money.

“There are so many people who were devastated with the outcome of that election — for good reason, for really good reason,” Harris told CNN backstage before her speech at the rally and two days after her 62nd birthday. “That pain, it lingers, because every day we are witnessing events that we know didn’t have to happen. Could have been different.”

After the interview ended, Harris asked to go back on the record.

“The American people want leaders who aren’t just occupied with looking in the mirror. They want leaders who are looking at the people, you know?” she said. “And they can tell the difference.”

Much of the political insider world has been clear in not wanting Harris to run for president in 2028, or really not wanting to hear from her again, ever. Even before Democrats’ horror year of Joe Biden’s collapse, the contortions over Gaza that she’s still struggling with and Donald Trump’s return, Harris was never good about cultivating donors or keeping aides from fleeing her overly cautious style and the constant infighting that followed.

Yet with her stops in Mississippi and across the country, she’s hearing from many Democratic campaigns who believe having her around helps — and lots of voters who are turning out to show they agree. All told, she’ll end the midterms with more campaign appearances than Barack Obama, and after a late flurry that includes Wisconsin and Georgia this week, more than almost any potential top-tier 2028 candidate.

Several close to the former vice president and 2024 presidential nominee told CNN they believe when she keeps saying she’s thinking about running again, what that means is that after months of soaking up the superfans who bought tickets to her book tour, she hasn’t ruled it out.

But not killing the option is different from pursuing it, whether lining up staff or crafting a new agenda, and Harris acknowledged that her time-treading answers about not having made up her mind can only go on so long. But asked if that means six months or even a year, she said, “I don’t know.”

“I go back and forth. I honestly go back and forth,” Harris said of which way she’s leaning. “There’s so many factors.”

What Harris does know, two years after losing, is that she’s less interested in the game of inches that presidential primaries tend to be.

“I’ll be very specific,” she said. “If I run, my motivation is not to beat other Democrats. It’s to actually do the job.”

Privately, she’s been known to do her wry stare at comments from other Democrats who say she shouldn’t run – convenient, she says, since that would mean they didn’t have to run against her.

“I’m sure there are many who think that I should just sit at home and eat bonbons and cook Doug’s favorite foods,” she said, brushing off the Wall Street Journal article reporting that her husband, Doug Emhoff, had privately told some people that he preferred she didn’t run. “I could cook Doug’s favorite foods and do this.”

Harris said Emhoff was upset at his feelings being portrayed inaccurately. According to one person who has spoken directly with him, his more precise feeling is that the moves the two of them have been making were not done with a plan to run again.

“I feel so strongly and therefore am compelled, and maybe propelled, into doing this, because I know that I can help,” she added. “And how can I sit at home in the comfort of my home when I know there are things I can do to help? I don’t know any other life but that – that’s my point. I don’t know any life that is not about, ‘There’s a problem, what can I do to fix it?’”

Other Democrats could start campaigns in the next several weeks

When Harris talks about “turning pain into purpose,” that means one thing to frustrated voters in the final days of these midterm campaigns, like the retired plumber who shouted “You told us so!” as she ripped Trump’s record in the gym at Columbus High School.

It can mean another to the woman who was herself the candidate Trump beat, even as she kept up the smiles pouring drinks behind the bar at another stop in New Hampshire on Saturday. Around this time two years ago, Harris was calling around to make sure old friends would be with her to celebrate back on the quad at Howard University. She stopped her remarks on Thursday to call back to the man, “Yes, brother, I did.”

Supporters listen as Democratic presidential nominee US Vice President Kamala Harris delivers remarks, conceding the 2024 US presidential election to President-elect Donald Trump, at Howard University in Washington, on November 6, 2024. Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters

Harris did not, like Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, hit the Hamptons fundraising circuit this summer. She has not, as had been proposed in an internal memo circulated among her advisers, launched an extensive engagement tour championing Black voting rights in the wake of the Supreme Court’s Callais decision.

She spent much of the last year on an extended book tour that took her to 27 states and made her millions more than expected. She sold one of the X accounts she controlled to a partnership that netted her more money.

Yet she kept working the phones, whether calling a range of advocates and asking what she could have done differently in her abbreviated presidential run, or checking in with candidates like Texas Senate Democratic nominee James Talarico, to whom she offered some advice over how to manage the ongoing criticism from his former primary opponent, Rep. Jasmine Crockett, whom she endorsed before he won.

Her prospective opponents aren’t waiting on her.

Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear has discussed a plan to launch his campaign shortly after the December meeting of the Democratic Governors Association, when he’ll officially wrap up his stint as its chair. After months of public denials while maintaining a national travel schedule, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore has started telling people that after November he’s going to take another look at running for president.

Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg have been all over the country stumping for candidates, including in early states, as aides make sure to remind reporters each time they add more stops. New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker has quietly banked $20 million and started thinking through a South Carolina and Super Tuesday-focused strategy.

Operatives associated with multiple likely contenders are assembling opposition research files on expected opponents and asking around for suggestions of staff to hire. Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, her former running mate, is already saying his advice for the future of the Democratic Party is “pick Pete Buttigieg” (which Harris said she hadn’t seen).

Harris’ motorcade is now just two cars, no sirens. She flies commercial. She pays for staff and security out of the limited fundraising she’s still doing off her old campaign email list, which left her and advisers having to pick between stops she was asked to make and forcing her to stack several virtual appearances into a day she’ll spend this week holed up in a hotel room with a computer instead.

“I have more access, you know? It’s like, the bubble is smaller, and that’s nice. Or there’s not a bubble,” she said.

As for candidates like Rob Sand, running for governor in Iowa, or Adam Hamilton, running for Senate in Kansas, who’ve said they don’t want her to come, Harris says she doesn’t take that personally.

“Oh, I want them to do whatever they need to do to win. I mean that sincerely,” Harris told CNN. “I have run for local, state, and national office. I am not naïve. And I want to win, and I respect whatever decisions they need to make in order to do that.”

Nor was she interested in drawing a line against candidates like Angie Nixon, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Florida who said she joined the Democratic Socialists of America specifically as part of launching her campaign, and who will be part of one of Harris’s virtual events this week.

Asked how big of a role the DSA should have in Democrats’ future, Harris said, “We are, as we say, a big tent, and I don’t think anybody should be kicked out.”

The lessons of Mississippi

Mississippi won’t be an early stop on the 2028 presidential calendar. But its electorate could offer a preview of what might await Harris in South Carolina, which is set to host the first Democratic primary again and where Black voters are critical.

“The conventional wisdom,” she said in Mississippi, is, “‘Those are red states, we can’t win there, therefore we won’t go there,’ as opposed to reconditioning ourselves to think about the fact that there are a lot of people who live here who actually care about the things we care about and deserve to be heard and deserve to have us spend our time and resources sitting with them and listening to them.”

Harris first connected with Colom in January, after Rep. Bennie Thompson, the lone Democrat sent to Washington from Mississippi, got them on the phone when she brought her book tour to Jackson. Colom’s campaign to unseat Hyde-Smith, in a state Harris lost to Trump by 23 points, has drawn increasing buzz and now outside spending from both Democratic- and GOP-aligned groups.

Still several Colom consultants initially opposed having Harris join campaign events, worried about nationalizing the race and bringing in a candidate known for losing. With some encouragement, Colom overruled them and called her directly to ask.

Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, who told CNN that he’s considering a presidential run and for months was a main engine of getting Democrats to focus on Colom’s race, drew 100 people when he came to the state two weeks ago. Harris had over 1,000 on their feet in the gym, with an RSVP list that had to be closed because of the fire marshal – even after a sudden decision to bar holding the event at a local college forced a last-minute venue change.

“In this community, it transcends the fact that she lost the last election,” Thompson told CNN while waiting for her to arrive at the community college.

Former US Vice President Kamala Harris speaks during a special lecture titled “American Leadership and the Future of Alliances” at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies in Seoul, South Korea, on October 14. Ahn Young-joon/AP

Black maternal mortality was a top issue for Harris when she was vice president. But when he’s campaigning with a focus on 400,000 people in the state without health insurance, rural hospitals closing and mothers dying waiting for a limited number of ambulances to be able to get them, Colom said he saw enormous value having Harris help draw a dozen reporters from across the state to a maternal health care clinic that’s struggling to cover costs.

“The question is: why does Vice President Harris care more about healthcare in our hospitals than our junior senator? If she cares more than our junior senator, I want to bring attention to that issue because that matters,” Colom told CNN after the rally. “You see how many people showed up, you see the excitement. People care about folks that are going to fight for the people.”

In Mississippi, as in Harris’ other stops, the memory of her loss cuts two ways.

“There’s people that think that she got the raw end of the deal,” said Chris Miller, the former chair of the Clark County Democrats in Nevada, who was an early supporter of her 2020 presidential campaign and attended the rally she did with the powerful Culinary Workers Union on behalf of her longtime supporter, state Attorney General Aaron Ford, running for governor. “There’s a feeling that if she wants to run, she should run.”

Patrick Gaspard, who was Obama’s first political director at the White House and has recently been informally advising a number of rising new voices in the Democratic Party including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, was part of the Colom kitchen cabinet encouraging him to bring Harris in.

Videoing the crowd’s reaction to her on stage on his iPhone in Columbus on Thursday night, Gaspard said that has to be factored into any 2028 math, especially at a moment when voters around the country are making clear that they feel abandoned by the people who read tipsheets in green rooms.

“When Muhammad Ali was trying to regain the heavyweight crown, there were a lot of people who were saying they didn’t want him fighting again, they didn’t want him in the ring,” Gaspard told CNN. “They were saying that not because they were worried that Muhammad Ali would fall flat on his face — they were worried he would win.”

The story headline has been updated.

World.title: ‘He can barely walk’: Russians tell how vulnerable men are being targeted and coerced into signing up
World.content:
“They put him in the car and forced him to sign a contract…”

“Now he’s listed as missing… I haven’t fully accepted that he is most likely already dead.”

“It’s a paralyzing fear.”

All of these are quotes from people who say they have personal experience of forced military recruitment in Russia.

Their stories, told directly to CNN and backed up by human rights groups and a growing body of accounts from individuals and social media, paint a picture of a quiet shift underway in Russia’s war recruitment machine, now in its fifth year. We are obscuring their identities over their fear of reprisals.

Since a mass mobilization drive in 2022, which sparked a panicked exodus across its borders, Russia has relied mostly on large financial incentives to lure soldiers to fight. Evidence suggests that is now slowly giving way to coercion and deception.

Russia has repeatedly dismissed Ukrainian claims it is planning a new wave of mass mobilization, despite rising frontline casualties and falling recruitment numbers. And yet, as Russia escalates attacks, this “creeping mobilization” – as some are calling it – threatens to erode public acceptance of the war, just as the Kremlin needs it most.

Vulnerable targets

“I have (or rather I had) an uncle,” reads the message to CNN. “He is an old sick man, he has vascular problems and alcoholism, he can barely walk.”

In July, the person said, their uncle, an employee at a state defense company in his late 50s, was approached outside his apartment block by several men in civilian clothes and taken away in a car. They didn’t know where he was taken, but said that day “they slipped him a document to sign, supposedly a ‘notification that they were there.’ It turned out to be a contract (to join the military).”

The story, from a town in western Russia, fits an all-too-familiar pattern, said Artem Klyga, a Russian military lawyer based in Berlin, who advises Russians on their rights when it comes to military service. Since the start of the summer, he said, he has seen a surge in people reaching out to him about this kind of incident. “Now it’s a day-to-day practice,” he told CNN. Most cases he sees involve vulnerable men, often in debt or with health or alcohol problems. “They simply do not have a chance to say no, simply do not know their rights.”

“Call to Conscience,” a coalition of lawyers helping conscripts and reservists in Russia with advice around conscientious objection, told CNN they had seen a surge in reports of forced recruitment in July and August, with tactics “getting harsher by the day.”

In this case, after signing the document, the uncle returned home, his relative said, but a week later he disappeared. A few days after that he called to say he was at a training ground in Luhansk, in Russian-controlled eastern Ukraine. In late September came the news he was missing in action.

“I have trouble falling asleep, sometimes I have nightmares that they catch me,” the relative told CNN.

Ukrainian servicemen fire a Panzerhaubitze 2000 self-propelled howitzer towards Russian troops at a position in the Donetsk region on September 18. Anatolii Stepanov/Reuters

Another Russian who contacted CNN via a human-rights group said their brother was “detained” in mid-July “in a state of alcoholic intoxication, by unknown employees” – the relative’s assumption being that they worked for the local military recruitment office.

In this case, CNN has seen the military contract the brother ended up signing, as well as a video of what appears to be his last goodbye to his tearful mother before he gets into a white van. The relative also shared the written response from the local military prosecutor’s office to the family’s petition for the man to be released. It concludes he appeared at the recruitment office “of his own free will, without any coercion,” adding that “the contrary has neither been proven nor documented.”

Less than a month later came the news that he, too, was missing in action.

“He had a very difficult life, problems with alcohol,” the relative told CNN.

I am psychologically devastated; I always knew that rights in the Russian Federation are systematically violated, but I did not fully grasp what it is like to experience it.” Message to CNN from relative of recruit into Russian army

In June, Russia’s Penza region, about 375 miles south of Moscow, emerged as a particular hotspot for forced recruitment, according to social media accounts and human rights groups. Videos and accounts surfaced online of individuals being forcefully recruited off the streets.

In one video from June which CNN has geolocated to a military recruitment center in Penza, women crowd around a bus demanding the men inside be released. One woman points inside the bus: “What do you think, did they sign voluntarily or not?” she shouts at the camera. One of the men inside the bus seems to shake his head. “They forced you, they beat you,” shouts another woman. The Russian Ministry of Defense dismissed the reports of forced mobilization in Penza as fake.

Reports of violence in cases of forced recruitment are common, as is a disregard for medical exemptions. “The contract was signed under physical and moral pressure,” wrote one relative, who told CNN their uncle was taken in August. At the time he had a broken rib, they said.

‘Bring a friend’ bonuses

Another common feature of many of these stories: the individuals taking men on the street are not clearly identified, and are often in civilian clothes. This has raised concerns that they could be ordinary people trying to cash in on another type of military bonus – paid to anyone helping recruit new soldiers. One relative described them as “bounty hunters.”

“The recruiters know they are sending people to probable death for a reward, they have no compassion for either the contract soldiers or their relatives.” Message to CNN from relative of recruit into Russian army

CNN has not been able to verify this in specific cases, but regional authorities are making no attempt to hide the fact these payments exist.

“We will encourage those who provide assistance in attracting citizens to sign contracts,” announced Pavel Malkov, the governor of Russia’s Ryazan region, last August in a session of the regional parliament.

“We will provide a financial payment for each contract soldier. The bonus sum will vary from 50,000 to 300,000 rubles ($590 to $3,500), this is after tax.”

Staff at a recruitment stand for military contract service are pictured in a shopping mall in Moscow on October 10. Getty Images

CNN has found evidence of these official payments in multiple regions, as well as dozens of job ads offering recruiters large sums for each candidate who signs a military contract, with payouts varying by region.

“It’s literally a ‘bring a friend’ kind of promotion, where you just find someone – anyone, in any state; in other words, it could be a drunk, a homeless person, or just about anyone – you drag them to the enlistment office, force them to sign a contract, and get your money,” said the founders of New Alternative Route, an anti-war organization set up this spring.

Founded by Russian IT professionals in self-exile, it works to collate information on forced mobilization practices and advise people trying to leave Russia. Its representatives also spoke anonymously to CNN, out of fear for their families still in Russia.

“It infuriates me that poverty has so dehumanized people that they are willing to send others to their deaths for pennies.” Message to CNN from relative of recruit into Russian army

‘I panicked a bit’

Russia has for years tried to differentiate itself from Ukraine, where conscription is mandatory from the age of 25 to 60 for men who are fit, and where reports have surfaced of incidents of press-ganging: violent or coercive mobilization.

“We see every day on the television and on the internet how in Ukraine they catch people, like homeless dogs, and drag them forcefully to the front, said Russian President Vladimir Putin in early September. “Here people go voluntarily, as you know, and sign contracts.”

With Russia’s military recruitment managed at a regional level via quotas, this rise in coercive tactics is unlikely to be directed by the Kremlin, said Janis Kluge, head of the Eastern Europe and Eurasia Division at the German Institute for International and Security affairs, and yet it may be seen as a convenient solution to Russia’s manpower problem.

“The system where essentially the recruiters are doing the dirty work… is at least tolerated,” by those at the top, he told CNN. “It could be, in the eyes of the authorities, part of the solution.” Russia’s Ministry of Defense has not responded to CNN’s request for comment.

A view of the Alley of Fame, a burial place for Russian servicemen killed in Ukraine, at a local cemetery in the town of Istra in Moscow region, Russia, on February 7, 2025. AFP/Getty Images

And yet, in the eyes of some Russians, it’s a tipping point. Rights groups told CNN that inquiries about how to emigrate are rising.

Igor, a 21-year-old from central Russia for whom CNN is using a pseudonym over fears for his family’s safety, left the country three months ago, after years of planning to escape what he calls the “totalitarian madness.”

In the year before he left, he said he had been pressured twice to sign military contracts – once by his university, and then on a visit to his local military recruitment office to update his medical exemption. “I panicked a bit,” he told CNN. “I worried that someone might sign on my behalf. I wouldn’t have been able to do anything about it.”

The fear of a new wave of mass mobilization also brought urgent practical concerns. “I was afraid they’d close the border and I’d never be able to leave,” he told CNN.

“I don’t think we’re going to see a scenario where we suddenly recruit 300,000 people tomorrow,” the founders of the New Alternative Route told CNN.

Instead, they predict “a quiet, creeping mobilization driven by coercive measures. In other words, what happened in Penza… it’s all preparation.”

World.title: AI is exposing how fragile the web really is. What you can do to stay safe
World.content:
The vulnerabilities were around for years — more than a decade — but researchers were only able to understand how hackers could take advantage of them with the help of AI.

The vulnerability, called P2PShell, impacts a coding language that powers 70 percent of the world’s websites, enabling hackers to remotely execute code or gain access to information stored on servers. That sent websites into a scramble to update their systems, with some government websites in Europe going offline temporarily this past week until they could install the fix.

The discovery is yet another reminder of the fragile infrastructure of the internet. And with AI supercharging the abilities of both researchers and bad actors to discover flaws, it likely won’t be the last time a discovery like this is made.

“A lot of the internet and a lot of global IT infrastructure runs on technology that’s quite old, or is based on things that are very old in terms of computers, and likely have similar vulnerabilities,” said Patrick Fussell, IBM’s global head of adversary simulation.

With a vulnerability like P2PShell, there isn’t much that users can do to protect themselves. It’s up to organizations, businesses and governments to update their services with the latest security patches.

But it does underscore the importance of being smart about your digital habits. The age-old advice of keeping your passwords secure and being wary of suspicious emails is more important than ever as hackers gain more sophisticated tools and use AI to find more of the internet’s weak points.

Don’t ignore those software update notifications on your laptop or phone. Many of these updates include critical security fixes, and installing them as quickly as possible shortens the amount of time hackers have to take advantage of bugs.

“Users still need to do their parts in terms of installing those updates and maintaining a good security hygiene to put them in a slightly better position,” said Gang Wang, associate professor of computer science at the University of Illinois.

Most smartphones now support software updates for roughly seven years following their release. If you have an older phone, you should check if it’s still compatible with new software versions. You can find information about software compatibility on Apple, Google and Samsung’s websites.

Update screen is seen displayed on a phone screen in this illustration photo taken in Krakow, Poland, on September 17, 2025. (Photo by Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images) Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images

Watch out for phishing attacks

Pay attention to the URLs of websites you’re visiting and links you’re clicking, especially if you’ve received the link in an email or text claiming to be your bank or credit card company. Never share personal data, email addresses, passwords, banking information or credit card numbers unless you’re certain the website is legitimate.

AI has enabled attackers to create sophisticated phishing attacks that are more difficult to spot and may lack the key red flags of a scam.

“The traditional way of determining a phishing attack was, ‘Hey, it didn’t sound right. It used wrong language. It had spelling errors, grammar errors,’” Jud Dressler, head of the risk operations center at cyber insurance firm Resilience, previously told CNN. “All of that stuff, the AI is going to take care of that.”

AI can also help attackers conduct deeper research on potential targets to create more personalized and convincing messages, Dressler added.

The best way to avoid phishing scams is to log into your account or call the company or person you’ve received a suspicious message from, rather than clicking links.

Also, remember that smaller businesses may be slower to patch their systems in the event of an attack or data breach compared to large companies.

Brush up on your passwords

Never reuse passwords. Instead, try a password manager that creates long, unique passwords for all your online accounts.

Simply put: Computers are better than humans at making passwords that are hard to guess.

“We know humans, when they make decisions, they tend to make the same decisions as other people,” Rachel Tobac, CEO of cybersecurity and training company SocialProof Security, told CNN’s Terms of Service podcast with Clare Duffy in 2024. “So, you know, they make a password for their work. It has the work’s name in it. It’s got a capital letter in the first position to satisfy the capitalization requirement.”

Tobac recommended password managers like Bitwarden, 1Password and Dashlane. The most important thing to look for is whether a password manager offers encryption, which keeps your passwords safe and unreadable to hackers.

Other tips for staying safe online

Use passkeys instead of passwords: Passkeys are digital credentials that let you sign into online services using your fingerprint, face scan or PIN instead of a typed password. Passkeys are generally thought to be more secure than passwords since they’re tied to biometric data stored on your device that can’t be as easily stolen or spoofed. Apple, Google and Microsoft’s operating systems all support passkeys.

Use two-factor authentication: Enable two-factor verification on any service that offers it. Two-factor authentication sends a login code via text, email or phone call as an extra layer of protection in addition to your password. Some experts prefer app-based code generators like Google Authenticator since text messages can be vulnerable to hackers.

Monitor all your important accounts: Keep an eye on all important accounts for suspicious changes. Many offer automatic email or text alerts.

Freeze your credit report: Freezing your credit file with the three main agencies — Experian, Transunion and Equifax — is an easy way to prevent nefarious actors from trying to open new accounts in your name.

Create a family code word: If you get a suspicious call or message from someone who sounds like a loved one asking for information, call them back yourself, or call people close to them if you can’t get a hold of them. A code word shared between you and your loved ones can confirm their identity.

While AI is making it easier for even novice hackers to execute more advanced campaigns, bad actors are still trying to take advantage of humans at the end of the day.

“It’s still kind of a familiar attack method,” said Dressler. “It’s just using essentially AI to make it more believable and more effective.”

World.title: Spiritual leader Sri Sri Ravi Shankar guides meditation and cultural program across Egypt
World.content:
World-renowned Indian spiritual leader and humanitarian Sri Sri Ravi Shankar—affectionately known to millions as Gurudev—embarks on a four-day cultural and spiritual journey across Egypt from October 25 to 28.

Titled “A Journey to Egypt with Gurudev,” this unique retreat weaves together historical exploration and inner reflection, guiding participants through the awe-inspiring Pyramids of Giza, the historic temples of Luxor, and a scenic voyage along the Nile.

Beyond admiring Egypt’s ancient heritage, the program offers a sanctuary for deep meditation, music, and thought-provoking discussions focused on cultivating daily tranquility and fostering deep human connection.

As the founder of the Art of Living Foundation, established in 1981, Ravi Shankar has spent over four decades championing global peace and self-discovery.

What began as a singular vision has expanded into an international educational and non-profit powerhouse active across more than 180 countries.

The foundation pairs breathwork and meditation courses with wide-reaching community development and humanitarian relief.

Its extensive scope includes expanding access to children’s education, supporting women’s empowerment, rehabilitating prison inmates, and delivering crucial aid to regions ravaged by natural disasters and armed conflict.

Environmental stewardship forms another core pillar of its mission, driving major initiatives in river restoration and sustainable agricultural practices.

Beyond his educational endeavors, Ravi Shankar’s personal commitment to peace-building has positioned him as a vital mediator in conflict zones worldwide – foremost being facilitating peace and reconciliation dialogues in Colombia.

In recognition of his distinguished service to humanity, he was awarded the Padma Vibhushan in 2016, India’s second-highest civilian honor.

His official biography reflects the vast reach of his work: he has personally designed over 50 meditation and self-development programs, trained upwards of 41,000 certified instructors, and touched the lives of more than one billion people globally, backed by an online community exceeding 26 million followers.

Following his four days in Egypt, the global spiritual figure heads to Munich, Germany, from October 30 to November 3 to host a series of live breathing and meditation workshops culminating in a Happiness Festival.

World.title: Prime Minister attends opening of IWWI 2026 International Water, Waste and Infrastructure Exhibition & Conference
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly took part on Monday, October 26, 2026, in the opening of the IWWI 2026 International Water, Waste and Infrastructure Exhibition & Conference.

The exhibition and conference serve as a specialized platform for showcasing the latest technologies and solutions in water and wastewater management, desalination and water reuse, as well as waste treatment and recycling.

The event also provides an opportunity to exchange expertise and explore technological advances in water resource management and improving water-use efficiency.

A number of organizations and companies operating in the water, wastewater and environmental technology sectors are participating in the conference to showcase solutions and technologies aimed at developing infrastructure and improving water services, amid challenges related to rationalizing consumption and promoting sustainability.

World.title: Egyptian, Algerian and Tunisian Foreign Ministers reject all forms of foreign interference in Libya’s internal affairs
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty participated in a ministerial meeting of the Tripartite Mechanism of Libya’s Neighboring Countries, held in Algeria on Sunday, October 25, 2026.

Algerian Minister of State and Minister of Foreign Affairs, National Community Abroad and African Affairs Ahmed Attaf and Tunisian Minister of Foreign Affairs, Migration and Tunisians Abroad Mohamed Ali Nafti also took part in the meeting.

The meeting was held as part of the ongoing work of the tripartite mechanism and aimed to strengthen consultations among the three countries on developments in Libya.

Foreign Ministry Spokesman Nader Zaki said on Monday, October 26, 2026, that the meeting focused on coordinating the positions of Libya’s immediate neighbors regarding developments in the country.

During the meeting, Abdelatty reaffirmed the fundamental principles underpinning Egypt’s position, particularly the need to preserve Libya’s territorial integrity and sovereignty.

He stressed that Libya’s security is an integral part of Egyptian and Arab national security.

In this regard, Abdelatty categorically rejected any external dictates, emphasizing that a Libyan-led and Libyan-owned solution is the only foundation for ensuring lasting stability and achieving a comprehensive settlement.

He underscored the importance of reaching a Libyan-owned political settlement that would preserve the country’s unity, ensure the unification of its institutions, and create favorable conditions for holding simultaneous presidential and parliamentary elections as soon as possible.

He also stressed the need for the immediate withdrawal of all foreign forces, mercenaries and foreign fighters from Libyan territory, in accordance with relevant international resolutions.

The three Foreign Ministers emphasized the importance of adopting a comprehensive approach that addresses not only the security and political dimensions of the crisis but also its economic and social aspects, with a view to tackling its root causes.

The meeting’s final communiqué stated that the gathering was held within the framework of the tripartite mechanism to follow up on developments in the Libyan crisis and explore prospects for resolving it.

In the communiqué, the Foreign Ministers reaffirmed the historical responsibility and central role of the neighboring countries’ mechanism, under United Nations auspices, in supporting Libya’s political process and backing all serious efforts aimed at ending the crisis.

They stressed the importance of recognizing the mechanism’s pivotal role, noting that its member states are more directly concerned than others with developments in their neighboring and brotherly country, have a deeper understanding of the crisis’s complexities and repercussions, and are particularly committed to accelerating efforts to achieve a comprehensive and lasting settlement.

The Foreign Ministers also expressed their full support for United Nations (UN) efforts and international initiatives aimed at facilitating the political process and organizing simultaneous, free and fair presidential and parliamentary elections under an agreed constitutional and legal framework.

They said the elections should bring an end to the successive transitional phases that have become entrenched and contributed to the deepening of the crisis. They added that the elections should lead to the establishment of legitimate, unified, strong and stable constitutional institutions capable of ending the current institutional division.

The Foreign Ministers stressed the need to coordinate and integrate regional and international efforts in support of an inclusive Libyan political process facilitated by the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL).

They further emphasized that the political process must be Libyan-led and Libyan-owned, and that a political solution must reflect the will of the Libyan people and their national consensus while guaranteeing the unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Libyan state.

They stressed the need for mercenaries, foreign fighters and foreign forces to withdraw from all Libyan territory to preserve the gains achieved under the ceasefire agreement and accelerate the unification of all Libyan institutions, including military and security institutions.

The Foreign Ministers underscored the importance of safeguarding Libya’s resources and using them to serve the interests of its people and promote development and prosperity.

They also highlighted the need to protect Libya’s financial assets frozen abroad, preserve their value, and ensure their proper management by the international financial institutions holding them, in accordance with relevant UN Security Council resolutions.

The Foreign Ministers agreed that the next meeting of the tripartite mechanism would be held in Tunisia on a date to be agreed upon later.

World.title: GUEA-USA: Egypt Forum recommendations open new horizons for strengthening Egyptians’ ties with their homeland
World.content:
Vice President of the General Union of Egyptians Abroad in the United States (GUEA-USA) Essam Eddin Bassiouni said on Monday, October 26, 2026, that the outcomes of the Egypt Forum 2026 and the initiatives proposed during the event represent an opportunity to deepen ties between Egyptians living abroad and their homeland, translate their demands and proposals into practical steps, facilitate their lives, and strengthen their participation in development efforts.

In an exclusive interview with Nile News TV, the union’s Vice President noted that issues concerning Egyptians abroad received considerable attention during the five-day forum. Participants’ demands and proposals were heard and documented, helping shape a number of outcomes and recommendations aimed at improving the services provided to them and strengthening their ties with Egypt.

Bassiouni explained that the forum’s sessions addressed a number of important issues affecting Egyptians abroad and resulted in decisions concerning consular and housing initiatives, including the “Beit Al-Watan” and “Housing for All Egyptians” programs, alongside other issues that will undergo further study and discussion in the coming period.

He said the proposed initiatives include the “Speak Arabic” initiative, which seeks to preserve the Arabic language and national identity among the children of Egyptians living abroad, particularly those residing in European countries. Other initiatives include programs related to “Your Insurance in Egypt.”

Bassiouni stressed the importance of continuing to develop initiatives and services for Egyptians abroad in ways that respond to their needs, strengthen their ties with their homeland, and create greater opportunities for their participation in development efforts.

World.title: Liberia: MOVEE Vows To Appeal Mixed Verdict In Saudi Rice Case, Alleges Political Persecution OF Kemayah
World.content:
Party maintains confidence in former Foreign Minister’s innocence, calls for due process, equal application of anti-corruption laws, and stronger safeguards for humanitarian aid

By: Willie N. Tokpah

Monrovia-The Movement for Economic Empowerment, MOVEE, has reaffirmed its confidence in the innocence of its political leader, former Foreign Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah Sr., following the mixed verdicts returned by a jury of Criminal Court “C” in the Saudi-donated rice case, while signaling support for a possible appeal to the Supreme Court of Liberia.



In a statement issued by the party’s National Executive Committee, MOVEE said the October 9, 2026, verdicts involving 13 former officials of the Congress for Democratic Change, CDC-led government and other co-defendants do not represent the final determination of the case, arguing that the defendants retain the right to pursue legal remedies available under Liberian law.

The party’s response places renewed attention on a case involving humanitarian assistance intended for disaster victims and vulnerable communities, raising broader questions about public accountability, the administration of donated relief supplies, and the need to ensure that corruption prosecutions are conducted transparently and without political interference.

MOVEE said it fully supports Kemayah’s defense counsel in taking the appropriate legal steps to challenge the verdicts before the Supreme Court, should counsel consider an appeal warranted.

“The Movement for Economic Empowerment hereby makes it clear that it has absolute and unshaken confidence in the innocence of its Political Leader and Standard Bearer,” the party declared in a statement.

However, the party’s position represents its assessment of the proceedings and its political leader’s conduct.

The legal implications of the jury’s verdicts, including the precise findings against individual defendants and any subsequent appeals, must be determined from the court record and applicable law.

MOVEE disputes allegations against Kemayah

At the center of MOVEE’s defense is its assertion that the evidence presented during the trial did not establish that Kemayah personally diverted, misappropriated, or otherwise improperly benefited fro Saudi-donated rice.

The party cited testimony attributed to former General Services Agency Director-General Mary T. Broh, former Internal Affairs Minister Varney A. Sirleaf, and former Deputy Internal Affairs Minister for Administration Momolu S. Johnson.

According to MOVEE, the testimony of these former officials supports its position that Kemayah neither personally took any of the rice nor authorized, requested, or recommended its distribution to any individual, group, or institution.

The party further maintained that Kemayah did not ask for any portion of the donated rice for himself.

Those assertions, however, should be assessed against the complete trial record, the specific charges against Kemayah, the jury’s individual findings, and any judicial rulings that may follow.

The fact that a defendant did not personally take relief supplies would not, by itself, resolve every possible question of legal responsibility; the applicable charges and evidence remain central to any such determination.

Party alleges political persecution

MOVEE also used its statement to renew allegations that the former foreign minister has been subjected to political persecution and a sustained political witch hunt since 2024.

The party linked what it described as a campaign against Kemayah to objections by the current government to his proposed appointment as ECOWAS ambassador to Sierra Leone.

MOVEE characterized those objections and the subsequent developments involving its leader as politically motivated, alleging that the pattern has continued to the present.

The statement did not provide independent evidence establishing that the prosecution in the Saudi rice case was initiated for political reasons.

The allegation nevertheless adds a political dimension to a case that has drawn attention because of its connection to public officials and humanitarian relief.

The government’s position on the allegation, along with the prosecution’s account of the evidence and the court’s detailed findings, would be important to establishing a fuller picture of the dispute.

Beyond the verdict

The accountability question

While defending its political leader, MOVEE said it supports the fight against corruption but argues that anti-corruption enforcement must not be selective, vindictive, or designed to damage the reputations of individuals.

The party’s statement highlights a fundamental challenge for Liberia’s justice system, where maintaining public confidence that allegations of corruption are investigated and prosecuted on the strength of evidence, regardless of the political affiliation or public standing of those involved.

For the public, the central issue extends beyond the political contest surrounding the defendants.

The Saudi-donated rice was humanitarian assistance intended to support disaster victims and vulnerable people. Ensuring that such resources reach their intended beneficiaries is a matter of public trust, effective relief administration, and responsible stewardship of donated resources.

The case presents an opportunity to examine not only individual criminal responsibility but also the administrative procedures governing the receipt, storage, allocation, distribution, and monitoring of humanitarian donations.

A solution-based path forward

A credible resolution of the controversy required more than competing political statements. It requires transparent legal processes, accessible records, clear accountability mechanisms, and practical reforms that reduce the risk of future disputes over relief supplies.

First, the court record should clearly establish the charges, the evidence presented against each defendant, and the jury’s findings on each count. Where an appeal is filed, the relevant legal questions should be resolved through the established judicial process, without political pressure or premature declarations of guilt or innocence, also, government agencies responsible for humanitarian assistance should strengthen documentation and oversight. Publicly available records of donated goods, inventory receipts, warehouse movements, distribution authorizations, beneficiary lists where appropriate, and final delivery reports would make it easier to trace relief supplies from arrival to distribution and independent audits and risk-based monitoring should be incorporated into the management of large humanitarian donations.

These safeguards would help identify discrepancies early, protect intended beneficiaries, and distinguish administrative failures from conduct that may warrant criminal investigation.

Anti-corruption institutions should apply consistent, evidence-based standards.

Similar allegations should receive comparable investigative attention, while every accused person should have a meaningful opportunity to challenge the evidence and exercise the rights guaranteed by law and at the same time, government, political parties, civil society organizations, and development partners should avoid turning corruption cases into instruments of political mobilization.

Public criticism and scrutiny are legitimate, but conclusions about criminal liability should rest on evidence and judicial determinations rather than party loyalty or political rivalry.

These measures would help ensure that accountability is not merely punitive but preventive, protecting public resources, strengthening institutions, and improving the delivery of assistance to people in need.

MOVEE urges calm, reaffirms solidarity

As the case moves through its remaining legal stages, MOVEE called on its supporters in Liberia and the diaspora to remain calm, prayerful, resolute, and law-abiding.

The party reaffirmed its support for Kemayah, describing him as a leader whose integrity and character it continues to defend.

It also expressed appreciation to individuals and institutions, that it said had supported evidence-based anti-corruption efforts, justice, and the rule of law.

MOVEE separately lauded the government and people of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for donating rice intended for disaster victims and vulnerable communities in Liberia.

World.title: Liberia: Low Inflation, High Cost of Living: Senator Konneh Raises Alarm Over Rising Fuel and Commodity Prices, High Interest Rates Squeezing Liberian Small Businesses
World.content:
Monrovia- The Chairman of the Senate Committee on Public Accounts and Audit Amara Konneh has observed that the increase in macro-economic stability in Liberia, low inflation and the execution of the over US$1billion budget have not positively impacted the lives of ordinary Liberians across the country.

By Obediah Johnson

Senator Konneh is representing the people of Gbarpolu county in the 55th National Legislature. He previously served as a Minister of Finance and Development Planning during the administration of ex-Liberian President Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf.



According to him, the decline in the exchange rate between the United States and Liberian dollars is not bringing any relieve to ordinary Liberians.

He made these comments during the confirmation hearing of the Central Bank of Liberia (CBL) Deputy Governor for Economic Policy-designate Euphemia Sweh Monmia

Senator Konneh stressed that despite Liberia’s current low inflation rate of 4.6%, the prices of basic commodities, including rice, cement remain high across the country.

He put the cost of a 25kg bag of rice in some parts of Gbarpolu county at US$22, US$15 for a bag of cement, which are far above the US$17 and US$8 they are being sold in Monrovia.

Currently, Senator Konneh claimed that the cost of a gallon of fuel in the county is also sold for L$1,500.

He maintained that the more than 87% increment in the prices of basic commodities in western Liberia cannot easily transition citizens from mud to bricks houses.

He said present hike in the cost of petroleum products are negatively contributing to the increase in basic commodities citizens need for survival.

Growth inflation dynamics

Senator Konneh noted that despite efforts being applied by the economic management team of Liberia to improve the country’s economy, inflation remains higher than growth.

“The economy is more stable now; the interest is that macro environment is stable and growth is expected to be more than 5% this year. We’ve worked hard from December 2024 to present to bring down inflation. However, inflation is still higher than growth. So, that dynamics is contributing to the legitimate noise amongst citizens.”

He said Liberians are not feeling the impact of the decline in inflation as the prices of goods and tuition fees for students continue to increase.

“Our money, the Liberian dollars is stronger here today against the US dollar. But with all of that we should see some relieve (on our people) technically. Eventhough inflation is 4.6% real on paper, but in Bopolu, Gbarpolu county, Kinjor in Cape Mount closed to where the biggest mining company in our country is operating today, and Tubmanburg, the prices are still high. The people are not feeling the impact of this impressive number. Prices are rising higher on top of an already price flow.”

He observed that the current situation is strangulating growth in real income.

Senator Konneh wondered why the prices of major goods are not reducing, despite the appreciation of the local currency.

He further alarmed over the unproductive capacity of both the mining and agriculture sectors, with manufacturing only contributing to 8% growth in the economy.

He maintained that though 87% of Liberians are in the informal sector, they are not captured in the Liberian economy.

Senator Konneh said government should intensify efforts to accelerate growth and decelerate inflation.

On US$1billion budget

He further observed that despite the passage of the US$1.25billion national budget, students of the Monrovia Consolidated School System (MCSS) were constrained to stage protests for the return of their teachers to the classrooms over unpaid salaries.

He added that many public schools are in deplorable conditions, while the University of Liberia remains closed.

Senator Konneh indicated that citizens would only celebrate the execution of the US$1.25billion budget, if it impact their lives positively.

“We keep announcing low inflation, but inflation should be reflected in the consumer price index on the ground.This US$1billion budget should be celebrated because it is felt.”

High importation of fuel

Senator Konneh disclosed that 30% of Liberia’s economy runs on imported fuel.

He accused the Liberia Petroleum and Refining Company (LPRC) and the Ministry of Commerce of using March last year exchange rate circular to set the price of petroleum products for May without consulting the CBL.

He added that consumers were unknowingly paying the price at various filling stations as a result of the blunder from the two agencies.

Meanwhile, Senator Konneh has underscored the need for the executive to regulate and supervise price control to help alleviate some of the constraints citizens are experiencing.

He stressed that inter-agency coordination would address most of the problems confronting Liberians.

High petroleum Taxes

Senator Konneh pointed out that additional two levy fees being charged petroleum importers to the already existing including Goods and Services Tax (GST) and road fund are contributing to the increase in the prices of petroleum and diesel on the Liberian market.

He said the Economic Management Team (EMT) must sit with the relevant authorities to address the situation as lawmakers do not intend to take arbitrary actions to affect the smooth execution of the national budget.

“Our people are paying for the price at the pump through the transportation cost and the prices rice they eat. The importers are getting wealthier; the government is getting fatter US$1.3billion budget-about 80% goes to recurrent cost and we in the government are getting fatter everyday and the skinning man out there is paying for the price.”

He maintained that government should consider providing a “tax holiday” to importers to alleviate sufferings they are encountering on a daily basis.

Senator Konneh observed that Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) are the engine of growth of the Liberian economy.

He said CBL monetary policy alone cannot fix the supply and pricing.

He noted that a shorter pay-back period for loan credited from commercial banks is strangulating the growth of many SMEs in Liberia.

Senator Konneh called on the CBL to be intentional towards ensuring low interest rate for SMEs and the reduction of risks to the sustenance of their businesses.

He said steps should be taken by the bank towards the publication of the daily exchange rate and the setting of a variation interest rate for both SMEs and large businesses.

He observed that despite the passage of the Small Business Empowerment Act of 2016, no single Liberian company has benefited.

Amongst other things, the Act calls for at least 25% of public procurement and contracts for goods and services to be allocated to Liberian owned Micro, Small and Medium-sized (MSMEs),

Senator Konneh said government must be deliberate to provide support to MSMEs operating in the country, adding that, “the interest rate is killing our people.”

World.title: Liberia: The New Era of DStv Starts Now
World.content:
Monrovia – The completion of CANAL+’s acquisition of MultiChoice last year marks the beginning of a new era for African entertainment, creating greater opportunities to invest in content, innovation, and customer experiences across the continent. Reflecting this ambition, MultiChoice Group, a CANAL+ Company, introduces its most significant product update in years, bringing more of Africa’s greatest entertainment live to subscribers from 5 November.

The new package line-up is designed around how customers watch today, with clearer choices, more accessible content, and greater value across the portfolio.

With a focus on giving subscribers better value and access to the entertainment they love, DStv is focusing on its strength with African entertainment, leading international content and unrivalled live sport in one place. Our new packages are reimagined to reflect how customers watch today, with tailored options specifically for general entertainment and sports fans.



More Entertainment for More Subscribers

For the first time, some of DStv’s biggest channels will be available at significantly more accessible price points.

• DStv Access becomes DStv Starter ($7/month): Adding more channels than its predecessor, including the brand-new SuperSport KICKOFF channel, Premier League Match of the Week, La Liga, M-Net Legends, and Star Life.

• DStv Family becomes DStv Select ($13/month): Offering a wide variety of entertainment for the whole family across a broad selection of channels. Subscribers will enjoy all movie channels (including M-Net Movies+), African and international series (Novelas+, Telemundo, Serie A, Betway PSL), as well as top kids’ channels like Nickelodeon.

• Refreshed Movie Line-up: Refreshed with M-Net Movies+, M-Net Stars, and M-Net Legends, bringing more blockbuster movies, faster access to new releases, and fewer repeats.

More Sport Across the Line-Up

• DStv Compact becomes DStv Sports ($24/month): DStv’s first package built specifically for sports fans, covering every Premier League and UEFA Champions League match, cricket, selected international club rugby, WWE, and UFC.

Alongside this extensive sporting offering, DStv Sports includes all the general entertainment channels available on DStv Select, proving that Expect More is not simply a new brand tagline, but a tangible promise delivered through DStv’s refreshed content offering.

• DStv Compact Plus & Premium become DStv Ultimate ($37/month): DStv’s most comprehensive all-in-one package, combining everything available on DStv Sports with additional premium sport—including Formula 1, MotoGP, ATP Tennis, and PGA Golf majors—as well as flagship M-Net entertainment.

More African Stories, Backed by CANAL+

As part of the MultiChoice Group’s integration with CANAL+, the business is able to draw on CANAL+’s global scale, content relationships, and more than 30 years of experience across Africa to further enhance its offering to customers.

At the same time, MultiChoice remains firmly committed to investing in local content and telling authentic African stories. The business continues to expand its portfolio of original productions across markets, ensuring audiences can enjoy a rich mix of locally relevant entertainment alongside the very best international content. Over the next few months, viewers in Liberia can look forward to rich West African storytelling, hit Nollywood blockbusters, and flagship regional productions across MultiChoice’s local channels.

“MultiChoice has built an extraordinary connection with African audiences and a deep understanding of the stories they love to watch,” said Nomsa Philiso, EVP Content, CANAL+ Africa. “Not only does CANAL+ share that passion and commitment, but it is also investing in African storytelling through increased production and global distribution opportunities.”

Get Connected for Less

To make premium entertainment and sport more accessible to households across Liberia, DStv will launch a special hardware promotion. During this period, customers will be able to purchase selected decoders and hardware bundles at promotional prices, making it easier and more affordable to get connected and enjoy an unmatched range of local and international content.

The promotion reinforces MultiChoice’s commitment to delivering greater value, wider access to quality entertainment, and more opportunities for customers to experience the very best of DStv.

For more information on the new packages, migration, and local decoder promotions:

• Visit: www.dstv.com

• Customer Support: call 0886 510 000 / 0777 510 753

• Office: Consolidated Group Incorporated, Monrovia, Liberia

World.title: Liberia: LMTI and LiMA Strengthen Maritime Regulatory Capacity Through Port State Control Training
World.content:
MARSHALL, Margibi County – The Liberia Maritime Training Institute (LMTI), in collaboration with the Liberia Maritime Authority (LiMA), today concluded a five-day Basic Port State Control (PSC) Training Course aimed at strengthening Liberia’s maritime regulatory capacity and enhancing the professional competencies of maritime personnel.

Held from October 19 to 23, 2026, at LMTI’s campus in Marshall, the training brought together 25 participants nominated by the Liberia Maritime Authority and provided them with foundational knowledge of Port State Control principles, vessel inspection procedures, and international maritime regulatory requirements. Participants were awarded certificates during a formal certification ceremony marking the successful completion of the program.

Port State Control is a critical component of the international maritime safety and environmental protection framework. It enables competent authorities to inspect foreign-flagged vessels calling at national ports and assess their compliance with international conventions relating to vessel safety, seafarer welfare, security standards, and environmental protection.



The training forms part of ongoing efforts to strengthen Liberia’s maritime administration, improve regulatory oversight, and support compliance with international maritime standards.

LiMA Reaffirms Commitment to Professional Development

Representing the Liberia Maritime Authority at the certification ceremony was Mr. Joel O. Dickerson, Director of Training, who underscored the importance of continuous capacity building and professional development within Liberia’s maritime sector.

Speaking during the program, Mr. Dickerson commended the partnership between LiMA and LMTI and emphasized the value of investing in human capital as a cornerstone of maritime development.

“The continued development of maritime professionals is essential to maintaining Liberia’s reputation and effectiveness as a leading maritime nation. Port State Control is a vital regulatory tool that helps safeguard maritime safety, protect the marine environment, and ensure compliance with international standards. We are pleased to see participants successfully complete this training and acquire knowledge that will contribute meaningfully to the advancement of the maritime sector.”

Mr. Dickerson further encouraged the participants to remain focused, disciplined, and determined as they continue their professional development journeys. He reminded them that the knowledge and skills gained through the training come with a significant responsibility, noting that they are not only representing their respective institutions but also representing Liberia on the international maritime stage.

“As maritime professionals, you carry the responsibility of upholding the highest standards of professionalism and competence. Stay focused and determined in your pursuit of excellence, because the work you do reflects not only on yourselves but on Liberia as a maritime nation. You represent your country, and your commitment to quality and integrity will help strengthen Liberia’s standing within the global maritime community.”

Mr. Dickerson also noted that collaboration between LiMA and LMTI remains important in building a skilled workforce capable of meeting the evolving demands of the global maritime industry.

Building National Maritime Expertise

As one of the world’s foremost maritime registries, Liberia recognizes the importance of strengthening local maritime expertise to support safer shipping operations, identify substandard vessels, and promote compliance with international maritime conventions.

The Basic Port State Control Training Course provided participants with practical exposure to internationally recognized inspection procedures and regulatory frameworks, establishing a solid foundation for continued professional growth in this specialized field.

By investing in maritime education and training, Liberia continues to strengthen its institutional capacity, enhance regulatory effectiveness, and support the sustainable development of the maritime sector.

Advancing Maritime Education and Institutional Cooperation

For LMTI, the successful delivery of the training reflects its commitment to providing industry-relevant maritime education and professional development opportunities that contribute to the growth of a highly skilled Liberian maritime workforce.

The Institute remains committed to working closely with national and international partners to advance maritime knowledge, foster professional excellence, and support a safer, more secure, and environmentally responsible maritime industry.

About the Liberia Maritime Training Institute (LMTI)

The Liberia Maritime Training Institute (LMTI) is Liberia’s premier maritime education and training institution dedicated to developing competent maritime professionals through quality education, practical training, and industry-focused capacity-building programs that support national and international maritime development.

World.title: Liberia: How One President Could Shape Liberia’s Supreme Court for a Generation
World.content:
Monrovia – Few Liberian presidents have been in a position to remake the Supreme Court from top to bottom. President Joseph Nyuma Boakai is on course to do exactly that. If the justices retire as the Constitution requires, every seat on the five-member bench will have been filled by Mr. Boakai by the time Liberians vote in the October 2029 general elections, or shortly after.

By Rodney D. Sieh

The arithmetic is set by Article 72(b) of the 1986 Constitution, which requires the Chief Justice and Associate Justices to retire at 70. They may stay on only to finish cases they began hearing before that birthday. Justices are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate.



Three down, two to go

Mr. Boakai, who took office in January 2024, has already made three appointments.

In July 2024, the Senate unanimously confirmed Judge Ceaineh D. Clinton-Johnson, his nominee, to replace the late Associate Justice Joseph Nagbe. She was the first nominee confirmed under a new Senate rule requiring a two-thirds vote, or 20 senators, for tenured presidential nominees.

A year later, Chief Justice Sie-A-Nyene Yuoh reached the mandatory retirement age. Mr. Boakai nominated Associate Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay, Sr. to succeed her. Mr. Gbeisay had joined the Court as an associate justice in October 2022, under former President George Weah. He was confirmed as Chief Justice in July 2025.

To fill Mr. Gbeisay’s former seat, the President nominated Cllr. Boakai N. Kanneh, chairman of the Law Reform Commission. Mr. Kanneh is a former deputy foreign minister for legal affairs and public defender, and has taught at the Louis Arthur Grimes School of Law. He is also the brother of Gbarpolu County Senator Botoe Kanneh, a family tie that has drawn political attention.

The retirement calendar

The remaining seats will open on a predictable schedule:

• 2027: Associate Justice Jamesetta Howard Wolokolie, the longest-serving member of the bench, appointed in 2007 under President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf.

• 2028: Associate Justice Yussif D. Kaba, born July 19, 1958, appointed under President Weah in 2019.

• 2029: Chief Justice Yarmin Quiqui Gbeisay, born May 3, 1959, turns 70 in May 2029, five months before the election.

• 2029: Associate Justice Clinton-Johnson, a Boakai appointee, is also due to retire in 2029.

• 2041: Associate Justice Kanneh, the youngest member of the Court.

By 2028, the last two justices appointed by earlier presidents, Ms. Wolokolie and Mr. Kaba, will have left. Mr. Boakai will then fill the Chief Justice’s seat and Ms. Clinton-Johnson’s seat in 2029, in the middle of an election year. If all of these appointments are made and confirmed, the full bench will be his.

Why it matters

In most democracies, the makeup of the highest court is decided gradually, by several presidents. That spread is one of the quiet protections of judicial independence. No single administration owns the bench, and justices are less likely to be seen as one leader’s choices.

Liberia’s fixed retirement age makes turnover predictable, but it can also cluster vacancies. That is what is happening now. A Court made up entirely of one president’s nominees is not illegal or improper by itself. Whether it becomes a problem depends on who is chosen and how they rule.

Concerns have already been raised. When Mr. Gbeisay was nominated as Chief Justice in 2025, a veteran lawyer told allAfrica that three Supreme Court appointments in less than two years signaled growing executive influence over the judiciary. The lawyer also questioned Mr. Gbeisay’s firmness, pointing to his lone dissent in the Court’s December 6, 2024 ruling on the House speakership crisis.

That crisis shows why the Court’s independence matters. In November 2024, a majority bloc of lawmakers declared the Speaker’s seat vacant and elected Rep. Richard Koon outside a formal session. Speaker J. Fonati Koffa refused to step down. The Executive began recognizing Mr. Koon after a Ministry of Justice opinion in favor of the bloc. In April 2025, the Supreme Court declared Mr. Koffa the constitutional Speaker, but he resigned weeks later and Mr. Koon took the gavel.

The tension has not gone away. This week the Court reserved its ruling in former Rep. Yekeh Kolubah’s appeal against his April 2026 expulsion. The House voted to expel him a day after Justice Kaba ordered it to halt the proceedings. These cases put the Court at the center of disputes between the Legislature, the Executive and individual lawmakers. A future bench will decide many more.

The 2029 election

The timing of the final vacancies raises its own questions. Two seats are due to open in 2029, the year Liberians choose a president. A bench appointed entirely by the sitting president could be asked to rule on election disputes, including challenges involving that president or his party. Liberia’s Supreme Court is the final arbiter of electoral disputes. Its rulings in 2017 and 2023 helped settle contested results peacefully.

The Senate’s two-thirds confirmation rule gives senators a real check. Nominees now need broad support, not just a governing majority. How the Senate uses that power in 2028 and 2029, in the heat of a campaign, will be closely watched.

There is also a longer-term effect. Justices appointed in their fifties will serve into the 2040s. The next president, whether it is Mr. Boakai in a second term or someone else, may inherit a bench with few scheduled vacancies. Mr. Kanneh alone is set to serve until 2041. Unless justices die, resign, or are removed through impeachment, a new president could serve a full six-year term without appointing anyone.

Is there room for young lawyers?

The Constitution sets a low floor. Under Article 68 and Section 2.4 of the Judiciary Law, a justice must be a Liberian citizen for at least 10 years, at least 30 years old, a Counsellor-at-Law of the Supreme Court Bar, and engaged in active practice of law for at least seven years before appointment.

In practice, the path is long. A Liberian lawyer usually earns an undergraduate degree before law school, then a law degree, typically from the Louis Arthur Grimes School of Law. After passing the bar, the graduate is admitted as an Attorney-at-Law. Only after years of active practice can an attorney petition the Supreme Court to be admitted as a Counsellor-at-Law. The Court has cited a five-year practice requirement for that petition. Candidates are then examined by committees of senior lawyers.

Can someone be a Counsellor-at-Law at 30? On paper, yes, but only with an unusually early start. A lawyer who finishes a first degree at 21, completes law school by 24 and is admitted to the bar at 25 could, after five years of practice, petition at about 30. Most Liberian lawyers reach that point in their mid-thirties or later.

Because of the seven-year practice requirement, the earliest realistic age for appointment to the Supreme Court is the early-to-mid thirties. No Liberian president has come close. Liberia’s justices have generally been appointed in their fifties or sixties, after long careers as judges, government lawyers or senior practitioners. Mr. Kanneh, the youngest on the current bench, will serve until 2041, which suggests he was appointed in his early fifties.

So for lawyers aged 30 to 45, the honest answer is: not soon. With the bench likely to be filled by 2029, the next wave of scheduled vacancies may not come until the late 2030s and 2040s. Today’s young counsellors who build strong careers as judges, scholars or advocates may be the leading candidates then. A president could choose to appoint a younger justice sooner, but that would break with long practice, and the Senate would have to agree.

A test of institutions, not just appointments

Mr. Boakai did not create this calendar; the Constitution and the birthdates of sitting justices did. How he uses it is a choice. He can pick nominees known for independence and legal skill, from a range of backgrounds and regions, and give the Senate time for real scrutiny. Or the appointments can be seen as political rewards. The first path would strengthen a Court that Liberians and Liberia’s international partners increasingly rely on to settle political disputes.

For a country that rebuilt its institutions after 14 years of civil war, the Supreme Court is one of its most important achievements. The next five appointments, more than any single ruling, will decide whether the Court stays a check on power or becomes an extension of it.
