World.title: Liberia: Inside the Peter Bon Jallah verdict, and the questions Criminal Court “E” has yet to answer
World.content:
MONROVIA – A 63-year-old resident of Monrovia’s Airfield area will spend the coming weeks in the Monrovia Central Prison awaiting sentence. On Friday, Criminal Court “E” found him guilty of statutory rape and kidnapping of a 16-year-old boy who, according to the indictment, ran errands and did domestic work at his home.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh, Sr., sitting without a jury at the defendant’s own request, found Peter Bon Jallah guilty of statutory rape and kidnapping. He acquitted Jallah of gang rape, the most serious-sounding charge in the three-count indictment. The court ordered the Bureau of Probation Services at the Ministry of Justice to prepare a pre-sentence report “as soon as possible,” and suspended the matter until then.



The verdict closes one chapter of a case that has moved slowly through the system since the boy was found by the roadside in Sinkor on the night of January 3, 2026. It also raises questions about how such cases are prosecuted, what the split verdict means, and why a ruling of this weight was issued with its legal reasoning still unwritten.

What the State Alleged

According to the indictment returned by the Montserrado County Grand Jury in its February 2026 term, the abuse began in late 2025. Prosecutors alleged that on November 29 and December 24, 2025, Jallah lured the boy to his residence and sexually abused him there.

The indictment says the most serious episode began on New Year’s Day. Prosecutors alleged that after the boy played in a community football match, Jallah met him outside his fence and offered to take him to buy football boots. He told the boy to go home, bathe and come back. The boy returned and got into Jallah’s car.

Instead of a shopping trip, the indictment alleges, the boy was taken to a building in the Camp Johnson Road area. He was held there for three days, given noodles that made him dizzy, and abused repeatedly. Prosecutors alleged that two unidentified men took part.

On the night of January 3, the indictment says, the boy was hidden in the back of Jallah’s vehicle and left on the roadside on 15th Street, Sinkor. Private security guards found him and alerted his family. His mother and relatives took him to the John F. Kennedy Medical Center for examination.

Why Gang Rape Fell Away

The court’s ruling does not explain why Jallah was acquitted of gang rape. The two men named alongside him in the indictment were never identified, never arrested and never brought before the court. Jallah was severed from them and tried alone.

Gang rape by definition requires proof that more than one person took part. With the alleged accomplices still unknown, the prosecution may simply have been unable to prove their involvement to the court’s satisfaction. That is an inference, not a finding. The court has not yet said why. Each of the three findings ends with the same note: “legal citations are pending.”

That phrase matters. The public, the defense and any appellate court now have the outcome without the reasoning. Until the full opinion is filed, it is impossible to say which evidence the judge found credible and which he set aside.

A Long Road to Trial

The case was first filed before Criminal Assizes Court “A” before being transferred to Court “E.” Court “E” is Liberia’s specialized court for sexual and gender-based violence. Jallah was arraigned on June 18, 2026, pleaded not guilty, and chose a bench trial.

The trial then stalled. The prosecution’s motion for a change of venue was denied. Prosecutors went to the Supreme Court seeking a writ of certiorari, which the Justice in Chambers also denied, and the case was ordered to proceed. It stalled again when the court’s regular term expired before evidence could be taken. Hearings finally began on August 5 under a reassigned judge.

The record shows a heavily contested trial. The prosecution called 13 witnesses, including the boy himself and police officers, plus six rebuttal witnesses. The defense called eight witnesses, including Jallah himself. It also subpoenaed three institutions: the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, the mobile operator Orange, and the JFK Medical Center. The Orange subpoena suggests phone records were part of the defense’s case.

The Wider Picture

The case is unusual in one important way: the victim is a boy. Liberia’s 2005 rape law amendment made rape gender-neutral. Advocates nonetheless say sexual abuse of boys remains heavily under-reported, shadowed by stigma and the assumption that only girls are at risk. A conviction in a case involving a male child, especially one in which the accused held a position of trust and patronage over the victim, is rare in Liberia’s courts.

It also shows a familiar pattern. Prosecutors alleged that Jallah had small, everyday power over the boy, as an employer for errands and the man who could buy him football boots. Child-protection workers say that kind of power is often the doorway to abuse.

What Comes Next

Jallah is remanded until the probation report is ready, after which the court will hand down its sentence. Under Liberian law, rape of a minor by an adult is a first-degree felony that can carry a sentence of up to life imprisonment. The defense is expected to have the right to appeal to the Supreme Court once judgment is entered.

For now, the boy’s family has a verdict. What it does not yet have, and what the public is owed, is the court’s written explanation of how it got there.

World.title: Liberia: New executive order prepares the ground for a permanent railway regulator, four years after the idea was first launched by decree
World.content:
MONROVIA – Liberia’s President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has issued a new executive order setting out how the country’s interim railway office will finish its work and hand over to a permanent, legally established railway authority. The move comes as two global mining companies prepare to share the country’s only major rail line to export iron ore.

By Rodney D Sieh

Executive Order No. 169, signed on October 22, 2026, renews the Liaison Office for the Establishment of the Liberia National Railway Authority (LNRA). For the first time, it also sets out a timetable for winding the office down. Once the Legislature passes a law creating the authority, the office will have 90 days to hand over its records, studies, staff and equipment. It will then be dissolved.



The order matters well beyond Liberia’s borders. The railway between the Nimba mountains and the port of Buchanan is becoming one of West Africa’s most important export routes for iron ore. It carries ore from Liberia and, soon, from neighbouring Guinea, to steel mills in Europe, Asia and the United States.

The order also comes as Liberia hosts the Liberia International Mining and Energy Conference and Exhibition (LIMEC 2026) in Monrovia this week. The conference is organised by the Ministry of Mines and Energy, the Liberia Chamber of Mines and AME Trade Ltd., and will bring together investors, mining companies and government officials. Its agenda includes iron ore expansion and the planned rail and port corridor linking Guinea’s Nimba region to Buchanan. Organisers expect current and planned projects to attract more than $3 billion in new investment.

One Track, Two Giants

The line is currently operated by ArcelorMittal Liberia, a subsidiary of the world’s second-largest steelmaker. In January, the company and the government extended their mineral development agreement to 2050, with a right to renew for another 25 years. ArcelorMittal agreed to pay $200 million for the extension and for reserved rail capacity. It is completing a $1.8 billion expansion expected to lift its shipments from about 5 million tonnes a year to 20 million.

Under that deal, President Boakai said the railway would become independently operated from October 2030.

The second user is Ivanhoe Atlantic, a company linked to mining billionaire Robert Friedland. In December 2025, the Legislature ratified its $1.8 billion rail access and concession agreement. The deal allows Ivanhoe to move high-grade ore from its Kon Kweni mines in Guinea across the border and down the Liberian line to Buchanan. It is the first project carried out under a 2019 treaty between Liberia and Guinea. Liberia is expected to earn more than $1 billion in rail access fees over the life of the project.

Until now, there has been no independent body to referee the arrangement. That is the gap the LNRA is meant to fill.

What the Order Does

Executive Order 169 keeps the Liaison Office under the supervision of the Minister of State for Presidential Affairs. It directs the office to complete a U.S. Trade and Development Agency-funded study of the condition and capacity of the Tokadeh–Buchanan corridor. The office must also finalise a draft LNRA Act with the Law Reform Commission and submit it to the Legislature through the Ministry of State.

The office is further tasked with preparing staffing plans, budgets and funding models for the future authority, including public-private partnerships, along with draft safety and regulatory rules. It must continue engaging mining companies, local communities, ECOWAS and neighbouring countries on regional rail development.

The order is careful about the limits of its own power. It bars the Liaison Office from adopting any regulations or commitments that must await the law. Any rules the office drafts for the future authority will take effect only after the Act is in force. The order’s preamble says the aim is to wind down the office “without creating gaps or extending executive powers beyond the lawful transition period.”

Four Years of Decrees

That caution reflects a long-standing criticism. That caution reflects a long-standing criticism. Liberia’s railway authority has existed only through a chain of executive orders since October 2022, when former President George Weah first created it. President Boakai renewed it in 2024 and again in October 2025 with Executive Order 153, which brought in international technical advisers and provided for a liaison officer.

Rail workers have grown impatient. In February, the National Association for Railway Workers of Liberia petitioned the Legislature to pass a law creating an autonomous authority, separate from the Ministry of Transport. The workers also asked that rail assets left behind by defunct mining companies be placed under the authority’s control.

The new order does not set a deadline for introducing the bill. Instead, it says the bill’s introduction will trigger the transition, and that the office will continue until the law passes or the President revokes the order. Any extension beyond “a reasonable transition period” must be justified in writing and approved by a separate executive order. The order does not define how long that period is.

What It Could Mean for the Sector

For investors, a statutory regulator would offer something executive orders cannot: permanence. An executive order can be amended or revoked by any president. A law passed by the Legislature carries more weight with lenders and with companies making 25-year commitments.

A permanent authority could also settle questions that remain open as traffic on the line grows. These include who sets and enforces the terms on which new users gain access to the track, who inspects a railway carrying heavier and more frequent trains, who decides when the line needs new capacity and who pays for it, and who resolves disputes between companies sharing the track.

The order commits the government to “multi-user, open-access” governance that is fair and transparent to all users. It does not say how disputes between users would be settled. Those details are likely to sit in the draft Act, which has not been made public.

Timing is also a factor. If the railway is to be independently operated by October 2030, as the government has said, a regulator will need to be in place well before then, with staff, rules and a budget of its own.

The Road Ahead

The order lays out a path from preparation through legislative consideration to handover. It requires the liaison officer to submit a final report to both the President and the Legislature before the office is dissolved. Staff will move into the new authority unless they choose to return to their previous posts.

What the order cannot do is pass the law. That decision now rests with the Legislature. Lawmakers moved quickly to ratify the Ivanhoe deal last year. Whether they move as quickly on the body meant to regulate such deals may shape how well Liberia manages its rail boom.

As investors gather in Monrovia this week, the question of who will regulate Liberia’s busiest railway, and when, is likely to be on many of their minds.

World.title: A Former Security Chief’s Vision for Liberia’s Immigration Service Finally Plays
World.content:
MONROVIA – C. Clarence Massaquoi once commanded Liberia’s national police and led the unit that guarded the head of state. On Friday, he stood before a group of young cadets holding trumpets and drums and described himself as something else: a father who had come home.

By Jaheim T Tumu

“I stand before you today not just as a Guest Speaker, but as a proud father returning home,” Massaquoi told the pioneer graduating class of the Liberia Immigration Service (LIS) Basic Military Band Training. The Armed Forces of Liberia Band Unit ran the program.



For Massaquoi, the day closed something he had left unfinished. He had first proposed a marching band for the immigration service years earlier, when he was Commissioner of what was then the Bureau of Immigration and Naturalization (BIN).

A Vision Interrupted

Massaquoi has held several of the most sensitive security jobs in Liberia. He directed the Special Security Service, the presidential protection detail now called the Executive Protection Service (EPS). He was Commissioner of BIN. He later led the Liberia National Police, and served as its Inspector General until September 2016, when President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf named Col. Gregory Coleman to replace him. Sirleaf said at the time that the government still had confidence in him and would need his skills in another role. Massaquoi has also served as National Security Advisor.

He said his goal at BIN had been to turn the agency “from a checkpoint institution into a full-fledged, disciplined, paramilitary service worthy of its place in the Joint Security Architecture of Liberia.” That is the framework of agencies, led by the army and police, that has protected the country since its civil wars ended in 2003.

He considered a marching band central to that plan. “We started the process; we identified talent, we began consultations,” he said. “But before the first drum could be beaten, I was reappointed by the President to head the Liberia National Police Service. I left with an unfinished agenda in my heart.”

He told the cadets they had finished that work. He thanked the current leadership of the service for “keeping the dream alive.”

More Than Music

A brass band may look like ceremony with little to do with protecting a border. Massaquoi made the opposite case. He said the band training holds lessons a security officer needs in the field.

“You did not just learn music. You went through basic military training. You learned discipline, endurance, teamwork, and precision,” he said. “In a band, if one man is out of step, the whole parade is spoiled. If one trumpet is out of tune, the whole melody is lost. You have learned the greatest lesson of our profession: We succeed together, or we fail together.”

Bands have been part of military life for centuries, and he placed the new unit in that tradition. “The world over, the band is the commander’s voice,” he said. “It sets the pace, it announces his arrival, it comforts troops on long patrols.”

He said the habits learned on the band square, “punctuality, practice, perfection,” would follow the graduates to border posts in Lofa, Grand Cape Mount, Ganta and Maryland. Liberia shares these frontiers with Sierra Leone, Guinea and Côte d’Ivoire, and they are long and porous.

Ending the Silence

He also spoke about the agency’s pride. The LIS is part of the Joint Security, but he said that “for too long, at national parades and state functions, we marched in silence, or to the drums of another institution.”

He said that ends now. The LIS will march to its own music on July 26, Liberia’s Independence Day. It will greet visiting heads of state at Roberts International Airport with its own band, and honor fallen colleagues the same way. “That builds esprit de corps that money cannot buy,” he said.

He listed five benefits of the band:

• Identity and morale

• Discipline and command

• A stronger place in the Joint Security alongside the army and police

• Community trust

• Recruitment for the future

Soft Power at the Border

His strongest argument was about how the public sees the service. He described the band as a tool of soft power.

“An immigration officer is the first and last Liberian a visitor meets,” he said. When the band plays in schools, border towns and county programs, he said, it changes how people see the LIS, “from an enforcement body to a people’s institution. And in modern border management, community trust is our best intelligence.”

Many border agencies around the world have learned the same thing: people living near a frontier are often the first to notice smuggling, trafficking or unusual movement. Massaquoi said that kind of trust “is more powerful than any fence.”

He also pointed to the next generation. “You are the First Notes of a new LIS anthem,” he told the graduates. “The child who hears you play in Bo Waterside today will want to wear this uniform tomorrow.” Bo Waterside is the main crossing into Sierra Leone.

Arms and Accountability

Massaquoi also spoke about a more sensitive reform he had pushed: arming immigration officers.

He said many Liberians had worried about giving guns to a semi-military service in a country still recovering from years of civil war. He said the service has since answered those fears. He cited Bo Waterside, Roberts International Airport, the Ganta border and central Monrovia, and said “there have been no reports of misuse, intimidation, accidental discharge, or harassment of citizens with LIS weapons anywhere.”

He praised officers for “discipline and restraint in carrying arms,” courtesy toward travelers and residents, and professionalism at checkpoints. He warned that being armed brings “a heightened responsibility.” Officers who carry weapons, he said, must “consistently demonstrate professionalism and humility.”

He asked the service to use the new band to build ties with communities at every border point.

A Charge and an Appeal

He gave the graduates a direct charge: “Guard this legacy jealously. Practice every day. Respect your instruments. Teach others. Never let these drums gather dust.”

He then asked LIS Commissioner General Elijah F. Rufus to make the band a permanent unit, with a bandmaster, its own budget line, a home and a mandate to train future classes.

“Instruments are expensive, but discipline is priceless,” he said. “Let this not be a one-time project.”

His closing line summed up why he came. “I came as the man who planted the seed,” he said. “I leave today as the proudest father of the harvest.”

World.title: 117,000 farmers collect FISP inputs in Central Province
World.content:
More than 117,000 farmers in Central Province have collected their agricultural inputs under the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP) ahead of the 2026/2027 farming season.

Provincial Permanent Secretary Milner Mwanakampwe says 117,141 out of the targeted 162,711 farmers have so far collected their inputs of choice.

Dr Mwanakampwe told the media in Kabwe that 125,517 farmers had deposited money to facilitate the collection of inputs, while 37,194 were yet to do so.

He observed that the government had continued to improve the implementation of FISP, with more than 60 percent of the targeted farmers collecting their inputs ahead of the farming season, unlike in previous years when inputs were accessed midway through the season.

Meanwhile, Dr Mwanakampwe has described the sale or sharing of subsidised farming inputs as sabotage of the government’s efforts to improve agricultural production and productivity under the Grow Zambia Agenda.

He warned that the practice would be treated as theft and urged beneficiary farmers to use the inputs for their intended purpose.

World.title: President Hichilema seeks parliamentary approval to restructure govt ministries
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has formally requested parliamentary approval to realign government ministries, targeting greater administrative efficiency and improved public service delivery.

In a press statement issued to the media, in Lusaka today, State House Chief Communications Specialist, Clayson Hamasaka, disclosed that Vice President Mutale-Nalumango will table a motion on the floor of the house seeking authorization to establish, merge and dissolve ministries.

Mr Hamasaka stated that the restructuring will align Government operations with the Grow Zambia Agenda, thereby strengthening implementation, and service delivery.

World.title: Ministry of Health working in partnership with the Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI) has signed and handed over the Results-Based Financing (RBF) Performance Agreements
World.content:
The Ministry of Health in Partnership with the Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI) has signed and handed over the Results-Based Financing (RBF) Performance Agreements and Registers to Health Facilities in Sinda District of Eastern Province.

The RBF agreement, involving the Provincial Health Office, the Local Authority and Health Facilities is a health financing approach that links funding directly to verified performance, the quantity of services delivered, and the quality with which they are delivered.

The initiative, being piloted in Sinda and Chadiza Districts in the Eastern Province aims to improve on key areas including looking at the number of women delivering with a skilled birth attendant, the number of children fully immunized, the number of women attending antenatal care early, and similar indicators that save lives by giving facilities and communities a direct stake in improving them.

Eastern Province Clinical Care Specialist Doctor Francis Mubanga who officiated at the signing ceremony held at Kwaela Lodge in Sinda District, described the undertaking as a solemn commitment to a shared vision of excellence, accountability, and measurable impact in health service delivery.

Dr Mubanga stated that the initiative further signifies collective resolve to move beyond aspirations and towards demonstrable results that tangibly improve the health and well-being of citizens rather than a procedural undertaking or the signing of contractual documents.

He also acknowledged the invaluable partnership and steadfast commitment of CHAI, whose support continues to advance the strengthening of health systems and the pursuit of improved health outcomes across districts.

“The Results-Based Financing is founded upon a powerful principle, that investments in health should be accompanied by measurable improvements in performance. It seeks to cultivate a culture where resources are utilised efficiently, interventions are implemented effectively, and achievements are objectively assessed against agreed targets,” Dr Mubanga noted.

He disclosed that under the arrangement, the grant provided serves as the foundational source of financing, enabling facilities to deliver essential health services and undertake planned interventions.

“The model goes a step further by introducing a performance-linked component, whereby supplementary financing is contingent upon the attainment of predefined targets and verifiable improvements in service delivery,” he indicated.

The Provincial Health Office has since pledged to provide strategic leadership, technical support, mentorship, monitoring, and oversight, as well as committing to strengthening governance, transparency, and accountability mechanisms through the stewardship of the Sinda Local Authority

Meanwhile, CHAI Representative Namakando Mukelabai, has reaffirmed the organisation’s commitment to supplementing the Zambian Government’s efforts to provide quality health service delivery.

“We are proud to support the Government of the Republic of Zambia, with funding from the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation, in implementing this programme, and we look forward to working with this district as you put these Agreements into practice,” Mr Mukelabai said.

And authorities at the health facilities have committed to making the pilot programme a success.

“We will be dedicated to ensure strengthened sensitization of the initiative to the community in order to achieve the desired outcomes,” Munendwe Health Facility Chairperson, Aaron Njobvu said.

World.title: Japan investors urged to tap into Zambia’s investment opportunities
World.content:
Zambia has urged Japanese investors to take advantage of investment opportunities in the country to accelerate economic growth, create jobs and promote value addition.

Zambia’s Ambassador to Japan, Tobias Mulimbika, says increased investment in mining, agriculture, energy, manufacturing, infrastructure and tourism will help advance the government’s Grow Zambia Agenda.

Dr Mulimbika was speaking during a reception in Tokyo marking Zambia’s 62nd Independence Anniversary under the theme, Zambia @62: Our Journey, Our Growth, Our Future.

He encouraged Japanese companies to go beyond traditional development cooperation by investing in local industries, transferring technology, developing skills and partnering with Zambian businesses.

Dr Mulimbika also highlighted Zambia’s ambition to increase power generation capacity to 10,000 megawatts and attract five million international visitors, noting that these targets present opportunities for Japanese investors.

He cited ongoing cooperation between the two countries, including collaboration with the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security, Zambia’s participation in the Tokyo International Conference on African Development and Expo 2025 Osaka, as well as the Japan–Zambia Investment Agreement, which came into force on 30th July 2026.

Meanwhile, Japan’s Director-General of the African Affairs Department at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Misako Takahashi, says the investment agreement is expected to improve Zambia’s investment climate and revitalise economic relations between the two countries.

Ambassador Takahashi reaffirmed Japan’s commitment to encouraging Japanese companies to invest in Zambia, citing the country’s copper and other mineral resources, agricultural potential and tourism opportunities.

She also emphasised the importance of human resource development and youth exchanges in strengthening bilateral relations.

Ambassador Takahashi disclosed that 45 young Zambians have studied in Japan under the ABE Initiative, while more than 5,000 Zambians have participated in short-term training programmes facilitated by the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA).

She added that 35 JICA volunteers are currently serving in Zambia, supporting sectors such as education and infectious disease control.

Ambassador Takahashi further highlighted youth exchange programmes between the two countries, including visits by Zambian and Japanese students aimed at promoting educational and cultural cooperation.

She also welcomed recent high-level engagements between the two countries, including President Hakainde Hichilema’s visit to Japan and the April 2026 visit to Zambia by Japan’s Foreign Minister, Motegi, which marked the first visit by a Japanese Foreign Minister to Zambia in 42 years.

This is according to a press statement issued to the media by First Secretary Press and Public Relations, at the Zambian Embassy in Tokyo, Japan, Faith Chilube.

World.title: Governance expert urges local participation in mining
World.content:
Governance expert and human rights advocate Wesley Miyanda has commended President Hakainde Hichilema for urging mining investors to prioritise Zambian citizens in employment and business opportunities.

Mr Miyanda says the call aligns with the Grow Zambia Agenda, which requires collective efforts to ensure citizens participate meaningfully in all sectors of the economy, particularly mining.

He said investors should ensure that Zambians benefit from the economic value generated by the mining sector beyond employment by participating fully in business activities.

Mr Miyanda said Zambians were ready to contribute to the country’s development agenda, particularly the target of producing three million tonnes of copper.

He urged local contractors to ensure their companies were properly registered and had all the necessary documentation to take advantage of business opportunities presented by mining investors.

Mr. Miyanda also advised local businesses to keep copies of contracts awarded to them, saying Zambians needed to be adequately prepared to benefit from government efforts to increase local participation in the economy.

He further welcomed the President’s call for holders of mining licences to avoid merely displaying or selling them to large mining companies, and instead explore partnerships with investors who had the financial capacity and technical expertise to support safer and more profitable mining operations.

“This country must move away from unsafe mining practices, which have resulted in the loss of lives, and therefore, the safety of Zambian citizens should remain a priority,” said Mr Miyanda.

He stressed that the government was making efforts to provide the necessary support to licensed miners.

Mr Miyanda also encouraged financial institutions, including the Citizens Economic Empowerment Commission (CEEC) and commercial banks, to help young people access financing for modern mining equipment.

He said meaningful local participation in mining was essential to achieving the objectives of the Grow Zambia Agenda and ensuring that the country’s mineral wealth benefited its citizens.

World.title: ZRA targets K185 billion in revenue collection
World.content:
Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) Commissioner General Dingani Banda says the authority has set a revenue collection target of K185 billion for this year.

Mr Banda says achieving the target requires effective tax administration and cooperation among taxpayers, government, businesses and other stakeholders.

He said this in a speech read on his behalf by Acting Director of Executive Support Laban Simbeye during the opening of a two-day ZRA media training for Lusaka Province at Legacy Resort in Chongwe District.

Mr Banda said the training had three objectives, the first being to strengthen the media’s ability to interpret financial and economic information and report accurately on taxation and business.

He said the second objective was to deepen journalists’ understanding of ZRA’s mandate, operations, tax administration procedures and emerging developments.

The third objective, he added, was to support informed scrutiny of the relationship between tax policy, business performance, the Grow Zambia Agenda and domestic resource mobilisation.

Mr Banda noted that domestic revenue enabled the government to finance education, healthcare, roads and other essential public services.

He said the media was an important partner in public education, helping to promote transparency, strengthen accountability and enable citizens to understand taxation matters affecting them.

“This workshop is timely as Zambia advances the Grow Zambia Agenda, with emphasis on expanding production, investment, exports and employment, and these ambitions give business journalists an important task to examine how national priorities translate into opportunities and results for firms, workers and households,” Mr Banda said.

He urged journalists to ensure they obtained accurate information to better inform the public.

Mr Banda explained that the Ministry of Finance and National Planning leads revenue policy, while ZRA administers the tax laws and contributes to operational evidence to reform.”

He further urged journalists to help audiences understand these responsibilities by distinguishing policy proposals from measures enacted into law.

World.title: ZRA sensitises Lavushimanda residents on Tax Compliance
World.content:
The Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) has embarked on a sensitisation programme in Lavushimanda District, Muchinga Province, to educate residents and business owners on its mandate and the importance of tax compliance.

ZRA Ndola Tax Consultant Officer Jacinta Banda said the programme was encouraging individuals and business owners to register their businesses and obtain individual Taxpayer Identification Numbers (TPINs) to comply with tax regulations.

Ms Banda said ZRA was extending its sensitisation activities to remote areas to ensure more people understood the importance of registering with the authority and meeting their tax obligations.

“Tax is not just about big companies registering and paying taxes. We aim to educate the country at large,” she said.

She disclosed that a permanent ZRA office had been established in Mpika District at the NAPSA building to serve residents of Mpika, Lavushimanda, Kanchibiya and Shiwang’andu districts.

Ms. Banda said the development was intended to improve access to ZRA services following complaints from taxpayers who had to travel long distances to access the authority’s services.

She urged individuals and business owners to visit the office to obtain TPINs and access other services, adding that ZRA would also educate them on the different types of taxes applicable to their activities.

Meanwhile, Lavushimanda District Commissioner Terries Kunda commended ZRA for visiting the district to educate residents on tax matters.

Mr Kunda said the sensitisation programme would help community members better understand their tax obligations and the services provided by the authority.

“It is important that you have come so that they learn something from you,” he said.

Mr Kunda observed that some residents mainly associated TPINs with accessing grants and loans under the Constituency Development Fund (CDF), noting that cooperatives seeking such support were required to provide TPINs as part of the registration process.

World.title: Six die in Chikankata Road accident
World.content:
Six people have died, while one other is receiving treatment at Mazabuka General Hospital following a road traffic accident in Chikankata District, Southern Province.

The accident occurred on October 25, 2026, around 11:10 hours opposite Lusitu Farm, approximately 15 kilometres south of Chikankata Police Station along the Great North Road between Chikankata and Mazabuka.

Southern Province Police Commanding Officer Moono Namalongo says the accident involved a Sinotruk, registration number AIH 1014, towing a trailer bearing registration number AIH 1253, driven by 62-year-old Mkhalipe Mwandu Mackson of Lusaka West, Lusaka, and a Toyota Wish, registration number AIH 9873, driven by 40-year-old Levy Mutope of ZESCO Compound, Victoria Falls, Livingstone.

Mr Namalongo says preliminary investigations indicate that the truck driver lost control while attempting to overtake improperly, resulting in a head-on collision with the Toyota Wish travelling in the opposite direction.

He says the Toyota Wish driver and five passengers sustained fatal injuries and were rushed to Mazabuka General Hospital, where they were pronounced dead upon arrival, while another passenger later died in hospital.

Mr Namalongo identified the deceased driver of a Toyota Wish as Levy Mutope, passengers Kabela Samba and Benjamin Kabamba, both males of Chirundu while Cresencia Kabazungu, a female of Chirundu; Nevious Moonga, a female of Kafue; and 25-year-old Soko Boyd, a male of Namwala, who died in the early hours of October 26, 2026.

He added that the surviving passenger, 30-year-old Rolf Namala of Garden Compound, Lusaka, sustained serious injuries and remains admitted to Mazabuka General Hospital, where his condition is reported to be stable.

Mr Namalongo says the bodies of the six deceased have been deposited in the hospital mortuary, awaiting postmortem examinations.

He says the truck driver escaped uninjured but left the scene before later reporting himself to the police.

World.title: Kenya: Police, Protesters Clash During Cost-of-Living, Fuel Demonstrations
World.content:
Cape Town — Nairobi police arrested several protesters on Monday as officers and demonstrators clashed in running battles across the CBD over rising fuel prices and the cost of living, The Eastleigh Voice reports.

Protesters gathered on Moi Avenue and Kimathi Street despite a heavy police deployment, carrying placards reading 'Remove taxes on fuel'. The protests followed the Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority's latest pricing review for the October-November cycle, which pushed petrol in Nairobi to Sh226.96 per litre, diesel to Sh227.76, and kerosene to Sh219.87.

In a letter dated October 22 and received at police headquarters the same day, the Coalition of Human Rights Defenders said the demonstration aimed to highlight the burden of fuel costs on households and businesses. Organisers estimated 500 to 900 participants, and pledged to keep the march orderly and respect the rights of other members of the public.

World.title: Ethiopia: At Least 48 Civilians Killed in Weekend Attacks in Ethiopia's Oromia Region, Once Again
World.content:
Ethiopia's regions, with Tigray and Amhara in the north, and Oromia further south.

Addis Abeba — At least 48 people have been killed and more than 31 others wounded, some severely, in attacks by armed men in Chole and Birbo kebeles of Shirka Woreda, Arsi Zone, in southeastern Oromia, residents who attended the victims' mass funeral told Addis Standard, describing door-to-door killings, looting and the use of heavy weapons.

The attacks began on Saturday, 24 October evening, and continued into Sunday morning, 25 October, according to the residents. They said the victims included women, elderly people and at least six children under the age of 15, with many of those killed reportedly followers of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.

"Armed men were going door to door shooting and stabbing civilians," one resident said, describing how local residents who had organized nighttime neighborhood watches were overwhelmed by heavily armed attackers carrying AK-47 rifles and other weapons.



The resident said the attacks lasted nearly six hours, leaving communities in the two localities devastated and many survivors too frightened to leave their homes.

The second resident said rumors had circulated in nearby towns, including Gobesa, Sire and Kula, two days before the attacks, alleging that "Tsimdo members", were using churches to organize themselves.

"No one tries to ask questions. Everyone is passing on information like wildfire," the resident said, adding that the allegations had heightened fear in an area that, according to the account, had not previously experienced comparable violence, even during earlier attacks against Orthodox Christians in nearby localities of Shirka Woreda.

The resident also said that local police supported the militias and said the attackers withdrew only after the federal army deployed to the area on Sunday evening.

Addis Standard could not independently verify the allegations concerning the rumors, the attackers' affiliations or the role of local security forces.

The resident said some people in Sire had prepared a letter on Friday to submit to the town administration, expressing fears about security and requesting protection, but their appeal was "not received in time".

"No one is interested to take us seriously," the resident said.

Mass burial as residents remain in hiding

The first 35 to 37 victims were buried in a mass grave on Sunday, according to the two residents. They said only a small number of people, "overcoming their fear", came out to participate in the burial, while many others remained in hiding.

The death toll had reached 48 by the time the residents spoke to Addis Standard earlier today, they said, adding that additional burials were still underway and that some of the wounded were in critical condition.

The injured were receiving treatment at hospitals in Gobesa and Shirka, while some had been referred to facilities as far away as Chanco, according to the accounts.

The residents also reported the looting of a church in Digelu town and the use of heavy weapons during the attacks.

Regional government blames 'Tsimdo'

The Oromia Regional Government had not issued a formal statement specifically detailing the weekend attacks at the time of publication. However, regional Communication Bureau head Hailu Adugna gave a brief remark to state media about the loss of life and property damage and attributing the violence to "Tsimdo."

Adugna claimed "Tsimdo, facing mounting losses, was attempting to divert the government's attention and expand internal conflict."

Hailu did not provide details of the killings, including the number of victims, the circumstances of the attacks or the response by security forces.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church had not issued an official statement on the latest attacks at the time of publication.

Several local reports have referred to a newly formed militia structure in the region which is said to operate alongside existing regional security formations.

Addis Standard could not independently verify the structure, mandate or chain of command of the reported formation.

Attempts to reach the regional government's peace and security and police offices for comment were unsuccessful.

Part of a wider pattern of killing in Oromia's Arsi

The latest killings add up to years of attacks against civilians, particularly Orthodox Christian communities, in Arsi Zone of Oromia. Previous attacks have resulted in dozens of deaths, displacement and the destruction or looting of religious properties.

Between 30 May and 1 June 2026, armed attacks in remote farming communities around Teleta Gebriel in Aseko Woreda killed civilians, displaced hundreds of residents into surrounding forests and resulted in the burning of the historic Teleta Saint Gabriel Church and the looting of Kara Kuftena Medhane Alem Church, according to previous reporting by Addis Standard.

On 15 June, Abayneh Tebeqe, a priest serving at Gado Saint Mary Church in Shirka Woreda, was kidnapped from his farm in Mitana Gado and subsequently killed, according to reports published at the time.

Close 

Earlier attacks have also targeted civilians in the area. On 13 August 2024, an attack in Tijo village, Aseko Woreda, left six civilians dead, including a local priest, and three others injured, according to previous Addis Standard reporting. In November and December 2023, separate attacks in Shirka and surrounding areas reportedly killed more than three dozen people, with Orthodox Christian families and worshippers among those targeted.

In July 2026, the Ethiopian Human Rights Council reported that at least 432 civilians and four local militia members had been killed in targeted attacks across East Arsi since 2021/2022. The rights group documented killings, kidnappings for ransom and forced displacement, with Orthodox Christian communities disproportionately affected, according to its report.

The repeated attacks have prompted condemnations from religious leaders and councils, including calls for independent investigations, accountability and measures to protect civilians. Responsibility for these killings has remained elusive, with government officials previously attributing some attacks to the armed group they refer to as "OLF/Shene".

World.title: Sudan: Sudan - One Year On From the Cataclysm of El Fasher
World.content:
press release

Takeover of North Darfur's Capital Marked by Wanton Abuses

"It is as if a tsunami had hit the city," said a resident who returned to Sudan's El Fasher only to find it destroyed and largely abandoned after the Rapid Support Forces' (RSF) October 2025 takeover.

For 18 months, the RSF laid siege to the city, digging a trench around it in its final months, forcing starving residents to survive on animal fodder, until even that ran out.

In the siege's final weeks, the RSF increasingly used drones to target government soldiers, aligned armed groups, and civilians who were ensnared in a tiny area, leaving many maimed or dead.



During the last days of the offensive, the RSF committed multiple massacres. The UN Human Rights Office estimates over 6,000 people were killed in just three days.

RSF fighters also committed widespread sexual violence against women and girls and ran a massive abduction-for-ransom racket, killing those who couldn't pay. Thousands of civilians may still languish in RSF dungeons.

Colombian private military contractors trained in UAE military bases were deployed alongside the RSF on the front lines, operating drones and artillery. Survivors' accounts confirm the contractors were present during some of the worst atrocities.

The UN fact-finding mission on Sudan concluded that the RSF campaign bore the "hallmarks of genocide," adding to an increasingly damning body of evidence of the RSF's serious crimes.

Governments did not act to prevent these atrocities. In the aftermath, several governments formed a coalition to prevent further atrocities and promote justice in Sudan, and they now need to act together to meet survivors' demands that those responsible be brought to justice.

One year on, RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo "Hemedti" has not even been sanctioned - bar previously by the President Biden administration - despite the crimes of his fighters. The Global Security Services Group (GSSG), the UAE-based company that apparently hired the Colombian fighters, has not faced sanctions, nor is the UAE being held accountable for its military support to the RSF, notwithstanding it violates the UN arms embargo on Darfur.

At the UN Security Council, the US is pushing for a countrywide extension of the arms embargo. Yet the existing UN arms and sanctions regime has only been renewed for a few months, and the publication of its Panel of Experts' latest report has been delayed.

Unlike tsunamis, the horrors of El Fasher were preventable. One year on, global actors should ensure it never happens again, take bold steps to protect civilians, and hold those responsible to account.

Laetitia Bader, Director, Horn of Africa

World.title: Ghana: Galamsey Now Threatens Ghana's Energy Security
World.content:
Illegal mining, popularly known as galamsey, has already caused extensive damage to Ghana's forests, polluted rivers and threatened the livelihoods of communities.

Now, reports that illegal miners are digging beneath gas pipelines operated by the Ghana National Gas Company Limited (Ghana Gas) present another worrying dimension to the menace.

This is a threat the country cannot afford to ignore.

The warning by the General Manager in charge of Engineering and Maintenance at Ghana Gas, Mr Maxwell Kwame Kelly, should serve as a wake-up call to the authorities, mining communities and the public.



Related Articles

He says illegal miners are encroaching on pipelines, particularly in the Western and Ashanti regions, exposing critical infrastructure to possible damage.

"Galamsey is not only damaging our environment, it is threatening energy production as well," he cautioned.

The implications are serious. Ghana depends on reliable gas supplies to support electricity generation and industrial activity.

Damage to a major gas pipeline could interrupt that supply, affect businesses and households, and impose significant costs on the economy.

Mr Kelly has warned that damaged infrastructure could take months to restore, with consequences for electricity generation across the country.

The Ghanaian Times is of the firm conviction that protecting gas pipelines must now become an integral part of the national fight against illegal mining.

The campaign cannot focus only on polluted rivers, destroyed forests and degraded farmland while critical energy infrastructure is left vulnerable.

The authorities must act before an avoidable incident plunges communities and businesses into further difficulties.

The Minerals Commission, the security agencies, local authorities and Ghana Gas must strengthen surveillance along pipeline corridors, identify areas where illegal mining is taking place and take decisive action against those responsible.

Where necessary, patrols and monitoring systems should be intensified, with clear arrangements for reporting suspicious activities.

Law enforcement must also be consistent. Those who mine dangerously close to gas infrastructure should face the full force of the law.

At the same time, investigations must establish whether landowners, financiers or other influential interests are facilitating such activities.

Enforcement should target all those involved, rather than only the workers at the mining sites.

Community participation is equally important. Residents living near pipeline corridors must understand the dangers of digging in restricted areas and know how to report encroachment. Ghana Gas should continue engaging traditional authorities, community leaders and residents, while making safety information accessible.

As the company's Principal Manager for Health, Safety and Environment, Mr Jaasu Yahaya, has indicated, community engagement and emergency preparedness are essential parts of protecting lives and infrastructure.

The government must also give serious attention to strengthening the country's gas supply network.

Ghana Gas is pursuing approval and financing for a proposed 278-kilometre, 20-inch high-pressure pipeline from the Western Region to Tema, with financing targeted for completion in the second quarter of 2027.

Close 

The project could support industrial development and job creation, but expansion must go hand in hand with effective protection of existing and future infrastructure.

The proposed pipeline is not a substitute for tackling illegal mining. Neither should the existing pipeline's capacity be taken for granted simply because it can currently serve the country.

The Ghanaian Times calls on the government and all relevant institutions to treat this warning with the urgency it deserves.

Protecting gas pipelines is not merely the responsibility of Ghana Gas; it is a national duty.

World.title: South Africa: Ready to Vote? Know What to Expect On Election Day
World.content:
South Africans will head to the polls on 4 November 2026 to elect local government representatives in the Local Government Elections.

According to the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC), special voting will take place on 2 and 3 November 2026 from 8am to 5pm.

On Election Day, voting stations will open from 7 am to 9pm.

Prior to Election Day, voters can check that their voter registration details are correct and confirm their voting station. According to the IEC website, for municipal elections, voters must vote at the voting station where they are registered.



Voters can check their details through the IEC website at www.elections.org.za, SMS their 13-digit ID number to 32810, or send "Hi" to the IEC WhatsApp number 060 088 0000.

Voters are reminded to take an acceptable identity document: a smart ID card, green barcoded ID book or valid temporary identity certificate.

The Electoral Commission cautioned South Africans not to bring driver's licenses, passports, student cards or photocopies of ID documents, as these are not accepted for voting purposes.

What happens at the voting station?

Upon arrival at a voting station, an election official will verify your identity and registration details. Your name will then be checked against the voters' roll.

Your thumbnail will be marked with indelible ink to prevent double voting. You will then receive your ballot papers.

Know your ballot papers

The number of ballot papers you receive depends on the municipality where you are registered.

If you are registered in a metropolitan municipality, you will receive two ballot papers.

These are:

- A ward ballot to choose a ward councillor.

- A proportional representation (PR) ballot to choose a political party for representation in the metropolitan council.

If you are registered in a local municipality, you will receive three ballot papers:

- A ward ballot to choose a ward councillor.

- A PR ballot to elect a political party for the local municipal council.

- A district PR ballot to elect a political party for representation on the district municipal council.

Take the time to understand each ballot before making your choice.

How to cast your vote:

- Take your ballot papers into the voting booth and vote in private.

- Make one clear X (cross) inside the box next to your chosen candidate or political party on each ballot paper.

Close 

- Do not write your name, sign the ballot or make unnecessary marks, as this could make your ballot invalid.

- If you make a mistake, do not place the ballot in the ballot box. Return it to the Presiding Officer and ask for assistance.

- After voting, fold your ballot papers to keep your choice private and place them in the ballot box as directed by election officials.

*This article first appeared in Vukuzenzele

World.title: Uganda: How Uganda's Sugarcane Boom Leaves Families Hungry
World.content:
opinion

What needs to change: First, the sugar mills should stop signing contracts with males only

Busoga, in eastern Uganda, is a low, fertile plateau surrounded on three sides by Lake Victoria, the River Nile and Lake Kyoga. Most of its 4.3 million people farm small, rain-fed plots. Yet hunger is common: in the 2024 census, about a third of Busoga households reported going whole days without food.

Sugarcane has been grown commercially here since the 1920s, when one family established a large sugar processing facility. New investors followed after the government stopped setting sugar prices and opened the industry to the private sector in 1991.



Seven mills now operate in and around the Busoga region, with the amount of sugar cane planted tripling in size between 2000 and 2024. Tens of thousands of families also grow cane on their own land as "outgrowers", selling this on contracts to the sugar mills.

I spent over 20 years working in Uganda's civil service before becoming an academic. For my doctoral research, I set out to understand why decades of sugarcane growth had not reduced hunger in Busoga. I visited two parts of Busoga - the Jinja and Buyende districts - and interviewed 27 officials, local leaders and farmer representatives. I also asked four groups of farmers for their views.

I asked who decides how land is used, who signs contracts, who receives the money, and how households eat while waiting for the harvest.

My research found that the hunger in Busoga isn't caused by farmers not growing enough sugarcane to sell. The prices of sugarcane are dropping, but my research found that the main problem is that sugar mills mainly sign contracts with men.

This means that decisions about what to use land and cash for are solely in the hands of the men. They don't always use the cash to feed their families. The work of feeding families falls mainly on women, who are left only with the option of planting what little land is left with food crops.

To solve the problem, the government and sugar companies all need to end the practice of only contracting with men, set up contracts with women farmers too and make sure that women from sugarcane farming families inherit contracts automatically when their husbands die.

One fifth of the land, all the responsibility

Only about 20% of the available farmland in the Jinja and Buyende districts of Busoga is available to grow food crops. Up to 80% of farmland owned by families is used to grow sugarcane to sell.

Mills recruit sugarcane farmers through male household heads, whose names appear on the contracts. In one focus group, women described husbands signing multi-year contracts covering the family's entire land without consulting them. When they questioned this, the women were told the decision was not theirs.

The payment, a lump sum at harvest, is made to whoever signed the contract. A political leader in Buyende, speaking anonymously, told me that many men now keep the cane money and don't use it to buy food for the home.

Uganda's Land Act says family land cannot be sold, leased, or mortgaged without a spouse's written consent. But cane deals rarely go through a land office, so no one checks if consent is being given.

A widow inherits the cane, but not the contract

Uganda's constitution recognises the right of women to inherit land. Yet my research found that when an outgrower dies, the contract usually remains in his name, and his widow has no standing with the mill.

The mill's recruitment agent, who signs up farmers, might decide not to allow her to take over her husband's contract. A clan meeting may instead hand the land to a male relative. A bank may refuse her credit without a man's signature. Although this is not legal, my research found that it is common practice and the government hasn't put in place any way of stopping it.

Government extension officers, who advise farmers, visit only registered contract holders, and don't advise the wives of contract holders. Researchers call this the gap between holding a right and being able to use it.

In some cases, young men inherit the family's land but then sell it to pay for a motorcycle, school fees, or a family obligation. With the land gone, many end up cutting and loading cane for daily wages. A technical officer in Buyende told me that most of those workers are children. Uganda's employment law bars this, but enforcement is weak: one study found that there were only 83 labour officers in Uganda, but that 1,344 were needed to make sure that labour laws were not being broken.

What needs to happen next?

All the different organisations in the sugar industry have a role to play in protecting the rights of women in sugarcane growing families.

Close 

First, the sugar mills should stop signing contracts with males only. Kidera Sugar, a new mill in Buyende that opened in 2026, is now recruiting outgrowers, and has not set its contracting rules yet, so there's an opportunity for at least this sugar mill to introduce practices where women benefit equally.

Second, the Sugar Industry Stakeholders Council, the sugar industry regulator, gives mills their licences. It could change the situation by refusing to approve contracts without both spouses' signatures in the case of married couples. It could also start a new practice of requiring that all contracts pass on to widows. It could even make a rule that widows should retain a share of each farm's food crops.

Third, district land offices could register cane agreements so the Land Act's consent rule applies. Fourth, the labour ministry should fund the jobs of more inspectors in cane-growing areas.

As contract farming spreads, who signs the contract can determine who controls the income and whether the family has enough to eat.

James Kintu Is the Postdoctoral Research Fellow, Centre for Governance and Sustainability, Umass Boston.

World.title: Kenya: Nubian Community Wins Kibos Land Dispute Against Kenya Railways
World.content:
Joshua Odiambo Nyamori, the advocate who represented the community, addressed residents on Monday, saying the Supreme Court decision left intact an Environment and Land Court ruling that recognised the communityâs claim to the land/CFM

Kisumu — The Nubian community in Kibos, Kisumu, has won a long-running land dispute against Kenya Railways after the Supreme Court upheld earlier court decisions recognising the community's rights to the contested settlement.

The ruling, delivered on Friday, October 23, marks a major milestone for families who have lived on the land for generations but lost their homes, a nursery school and a mosque during a demolition operation in 2021.

Joshua Odiambo Nyamori, the advocate who represented the community, addressed residents on Monday, saying the Supreme Court decision left intact an Environment and Land Court ruling that recognised the community's claim to the land.

Nyamori said the community had been allocated the settlement in 1937, decades before Kenya Railways was granted the land it claimed to own.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"We are here with excitement after the Supreme Court of Kenya pronounced itself on Friday that the land on which we stand belongs to the Nubian community living in Kibos," he said.

He explained that the community's settlement in Kisumu dates back to the colonial period, when the railway reached the lakeside town in the early 20th century.

According to Nyamori, Nubian elders met the colonial administration in 1937, leading to the allocation of the current settlement to the community.

He said the Environment and Land Court established that Kenya Railways was granted its land in 1963, after the community had already been allocated the settlement. The court also found that the boundary separating the community's settlement from railway land had been clearly marked.

The dispute escalated in 2021 when homes and community facilities were demolished in an eviction operation that Nyamori said was carried out at night during the COVID-19 pandemic.

"When the bulldozers started rolling over their houses, the nursery school and even the mosque, they reduced a thriving settlement to total ruins," he said.

Nyamori recalled meeting elderly residents who had been left without shelter after the demolitions, describing the destruction as a severe blow to their dignity and livelihoods.

He said the community subsequently moved to court seeking protection from eviction and recognition of its land rights.

The Environment and Land Court found that the manner in which the demolitions were conducted violated residents' constitutional rights, including the rights to housing, property and human dignity, according to Nyamori.

The court also allowed the community to pursue a separate case seeking compensation for property destroyed during the operation.

Close 

Kenya Railways challenged the decision at the Court of Appeal, which dismissed its appeal before the matter proceeded to the Supreme Court.

"The effect of that decision is that the Environment and Land Court decision that gave the land to the community stands as the valid decision," Nyamori said.

The ruling offers the community greater certainty over its claim to the settlement after years of legal uncertainty. However, residents are also seeking formal title documents to strengthen their tenure security.

Kisumu Muslim Association chairman Sheikh Musa Ismail Haji, who accompanied Nyamori, called on President William Ruto's administration to facilitate the issuance of title deeds to affected families.

"We are asking President William Ruto to help this community secure title deeds, just like other minority communities in the country," Haji said.

He said formal ownership documents would provide lasting security and help protect residents from future disputes over the land.

Haji also said he was engaging well-wishers to support the construction of decent houses for families whose homes were demolished in 2021.

He called for urgent assistance to help residents rebuild their homes and restore their dignity after years of hardship.

"We want the title deeds issued to the families before the 2027 General Election so that they can live here with security and peace," he said.

World.title: Nigeria: Nigeria Has No Ebola Cases After Patient's Evacuation to Switzerland - WHO
World.content:
Nigeriaâs Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has issued a public health advisory following the countryâs confirmed Ebola case.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) Regional Director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, says Nigeria currently has no Ebola cases following the medical evacuation of the patient and her husband to Switzerland.

Janabi disclosed this in a statement on his official X handle on Monday, adding that Nigeria would continue monitoring 52 contacts, while Switzerland would manage the patient and follow up with her husband.

He said the evacuation took place earlier in the morning, noting that both the patient and her husband were Swiss citizens.

According to him, the patient was clinically stable after Nigerian medical teams successfully managed her through the acute phase of the illness and stabilised her condition.

Janabi congratulated the Federal Government, health workers, clinicians, emergency responders and other partners involved in the Ebola response, describing the development as a remarkable achievement.

He said the successful management of the patient demonstrated Africa's expertise, resilience and leadership in public health, particularly when countries worked together to respond to health emergencies.

However, the WHO regional director stressed that vigilance remained critical despite the evacuation, urging continued attention to contact monitoring and other response measures.

He said Nigeria would maintain close follow-up of 52 contacts, while Switzerland would assume responsibility for the continued management of the patient and monitoring of contact number 53, her husband.

(NAN)

World.title: White House defends Trump after archbishop calls prayer moment 'manipulated' ahead of midterms
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The White House on Monday defended President Donald Trump after Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob publicly apologized for participating in an Oval Office prayer with the president, accusing the administration of using the religious gathering for political purposes less than two weeks before the midterm elections.

Grob issued a statement Sunday titled "A Public Apology," alleging that the White House distributed photographs and video of the Thursday prayer without the consent of the 12 participating bishops. He accused the administration of manipulating a sacred moment. The archbishop said he had received messages from Catholics concerned that the prayer appeared to constitute a political endorsement. Grob acknowledged having reservations before attending and apologized for the distress his participation caused.

"I feel a heavy sadness, not only over the pain I caused, but also for the fact that something so sacred to a group of religious leaders, prayer to our Heavenly Father, would be manipulated in that way," he said. "We came in good faith to try to work for the betterment of our fellow human beings, to ease their suffering, to build up the common good, and to pray with a president, not to pose for a political photo opportunity to benefit the few."

White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers defended Trump's record on religious liberty and Catholic priorities in a statement to Fox News Digital following the archbishop's public apology.

BISHOP ROBERT BARRON: MY YEAR WITH DOJ'S RELIGIOUS LIBERTY COMMISSION: WHY I SAID YES

"There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it: he stopped the weaponization of the federal government against Christians, proudly defended and expanded our religious rights, pardoned pro-life activists, stopped the chemical mutilation of our nation’s children, and protected parents’ rights," she said.

The meeting, which Grob said was arranged by the Heritage Foundation, was intended to address immigration enforcement, religious worker visas and other Catholic priorities. Following a 90-minute discussion with White House domestic policy staff and advisors, the bishops entered the Oval Office, where Trump presented commemorative tokens before they prayed together. Grob said the group was unaware that video was being recorded.

Des Moines Bishop William Joensen also criticized the gathering's subsequent publicity in a statement published Saturday, saying the bishops never intended to endorse a political candidate or party.

"None of us bishops were unaware that our meeting was on the cusp of a national election. Yet in no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate," he said. "That said, in retrospect, I would have done well to be more mindful of Jesus’ admonition: ‘Behold, I am sending you like sheep in the midst of wolves; so be shrewd as serpents and simple as doves’ (Matthew 10:16). I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes."

POPE LEO SLAMS THOSE WHO 'MANIPULATE RELIGION' FOR MILITARY OR POLITICAL GAIN, TRUMP RESPONDS

Denver Archbishop James Golka, who led the prayer, discussed his participation in an interview with the Denver Catholic. Golka acknowledged concerns about the video's political implications but emphasized that praying for elected officials remains a longstanding Catholic practice.

"I wasn’t sure what to do. On one hand, it was a great opportunity to raise important issues for the Church’s benefit," he said. "On the other hand, I knew people might be upset. Though I originally thought it would be a private meeting, I knew that it could be shared and that some might use it for political purposes.

"But as I prayed about it, I thought that this is what Catholics do," he continued. "We pray for people. No matter whether we agree or disagree on anything, we always pray for our country and leaders."

The controversy comes as Catholic leaders continue to disagree with the Trump administration over some of its policies, particularly immigration. The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops sued the administration in February 2025 over the suspension of refugee resettlement funding.

Other prominent Catholic leaders have encouraged continued engagement with the administration. In a May interview with Fox News Digital, Bishop Robert Barron, a member of Trump's Religious Liberty Commission, cautioned against demonizing the president despite disagreements over immigration and other policies.

"What I don't want from the church is a kind of demonization of the Trump administration," he said.

TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS
