World.title: Trump administration attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey again
World.content:
Trump administration attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey again

toggle caption i Alex Brandon/AP

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is attempting to prosecute James Comey for what it calls a decade-old leak of classified information, an effort the former FBI director's lawyers immediately dismissed as invalid and outside the legal time limit for when the Justice Department can file a criminal indictment.

The allegations from the Justice Department were revealed Monday in newly unsealed court documents that shed light on a closed-door fight that represents an unmistakable escalation in the administration's targeting of Comey, a longtime critic and foe of President Donald Trump who has faced two other criminal cases since the Republican returned to the White House last year. The effort to prosecute Comey is also part of a series of politically charged investigative actions the department has undertaken in the run-up to next week's midterm elections.

Sponsor Message

"Well, they're back — again," Comey said in a video statement Monday. "It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice – one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing's changed with me; I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people — and I still believe in an independent federal judiciary."

The Justice Department said it had filed what's known as a "criminal information" to extend the statute of limitations for when they can permissibly bring an indictment.

"Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals. This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further," a department spokesperson said.

An information can be filed without the approval of a judge or a grand jury's finding of probable cause to a court. Comey's lawyers made clear that they intend to fight the charges as invalid and barred by a 10-year statute of limitations.

"For the third time in little more than one year, the Department of Justice has attempted to charge Mr. Comey with a federal crime. Mr. Comey steadfastly maintains his innocence," his attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement.

The allegation was previously investigated

The latest allegation concerns an October 2016 New York Times story related to a secret court order that required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. The story cited two government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity about the order from a judge on the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court that Yahoo was barred from publicly disclosing.

Sponsor Message

Federal authorities, including prosecutor John Durham, began investigating the disclosure in early 2017. Durham, who later investigated the FBI's conduct as it scrutinized potential ties between Russia and Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, wrote a classified memo in December 2018 recommending no criminal charges against anyone in connection with the disclosure, Comey's attorneys said in a recent court filing.

In January 2019, the U.S. Attorney's office for the District of Columbia opened a second investigation of the same matter under the code name "Tropical Vortex." But that investigation was closed without any charges filed in February 2020.

"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone. Now, ten years after the article was published, the Government filed an "Information" against Mr. Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury. It purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit," Fitzgerald said.

Prosecutors in a newly unsealed filing said investigators found evidence that Comey "sought to correct misinformation which had appeared in the press by way of Reuters the day before" that New York Times story was published, directed his staff to speak to a journalist at the newspaper related to accuracy concerns "and thereby illegally transferred classified information."

The criminal information was filed under seal on Oct. 6, 2016, 10 years after the story was published. "But," Comey's lawyers said, "the applicable statute of limitations explicitly demands an indictment within 10 years of the offense; an information does not suffice."

They have asked a judge to dismiss the information, a request that is still pending.

Trump and Comey have a long and uneasy history

The first criminal case against Comey, filed in federal court in Virginia, accused him of having lied to Congress in 2020 but was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who brought the charges was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of "86 47," a case he has sought to dismiss and some legal experts have greeted with skepticism.

Sponsor Message

The cases are part of a Trump retribution campaign that has even extended to Comey's daughter, Maurene, who was fired from her job as a Justice Department prosecutor in New York last year in a termination that a federal judge on Monday ruled was illegal.

Comey was the FBI director when Trump took office in 2017, having been appointed by then-President Barack Obama, a Democrat, and serving before that as a senior Justice Department official in President George W. Bush's Republican administration.

But the relationship was strained from the start, including after Comey resisted a request by Trump at a private dinner to pledge his personal loyalty to the president -- an overture that so unnerved the FBI director that he documented it in a contemporaneous memorandum.

Trump fired Comey in May 2017 amid an FBI investigation into potential ties between Russia and Trump's campaign. That inquiry, later taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller, found that while Russia interfered in the 2016 election and the Trump team welcomed the help, there was insufficient evidence to prove a criminal collaboration.

The two men have been bitterly at odds ever since Comey's firing. Comey in 2018 published a memoir, "A Higher Loyalty," that painted Trump in deeply unflattering ways, likening him to a mafia don and characterizing him "untethered to truth." Trump, for his part, has repeatedly claimed that Comey should face charges for "treason" — an accusation Comey dismissed as "dumb lies" — and called him an "untruthful slime ball."

World.title: Trump administration pushes for food assistance card upgrade to fight fraud
World.content:
Trump administration pushes for food assistance card upgrade to fight fraud

toggle caption i Damian Dovarganes/AP

In a major step to combat a form of fraud that has robbed food stamp recipients of millions of dollars, the Trump administration is proposing a requirement for states to bolster the security features on their food assistance cards.

In recent years, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, has been the repeated target of card skimming, when thieves extract personal information from payment terminals and drain money from accounts. Most SNAP cards rely on a magnetic stripe for swipe payment – which tends to be vulnerable to skimming because it does a poor job of securing the data stored on cards.

Sponsor Message

Many banks in the U.S. took action against this issue over a decade ago by upgrading their cards to include microchips and tap-to-pay, which are considered more secure. But states have lagged in making such a transition for Electronic Benefits Transfer (EBT) cards, which are what SNAP recipients use to access food aid. Currently, fewer than a third of states have made the switch or are in process of doing so, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).

Now, under the proposed rule released by the USDA last week, all states would have to adopt chip-enabled EBT cards. It also requires retailers that accept SNAP benefits to have payment terminals that support tap-pay. The USDA's Food and Nutrition Administration, which administers SNAP, attributed card skimming as a reason behind the proposal.

"These proposed changes will protect SNAP benefits from thieves and ensure benefits are accessible by approved households," the Food and Nutrition Administration said in its summary of the rule.

Back in January, the USDA Office of Inspector General projected that SNAP theft could climb to $233 million between 2025 and 2026 — largely as a result of skimming. A recent ProPublica investigation found that last year, $470 million was stolen electronically from SNAP recipients. The total was calculated using data from Propel, an app that helps SNAP recipients check their food benefits.

Sponsor Message

In most states, stolen benefits are not replaced — leaving recipients to make difficult choices, such as skipping meals or borrowing money in order to pay for groceries, according to Propel.

Earlier this month, NPR reported that food assistance card modernization had widespread support from state officials and federal watchdogs, as well as Republicans and Democrats in Congress. But money has been a major barrier for states to make the switch. According to the Government Accountability Office, chip-enabled cards are about 10 times more expensive to produce than their magnetic strip counterparts.

The federal push for stronger card security features comes as state SNAP agencies are facing new budget pressures triggered by President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The proposed regulation recognized the financial barrier, adding that the USDA is interested in hearing from state agencies about the cost burden.

"As stewards of taxpayer dollars, the Department considers these administrative costs as a necessary investment to deter the loss of Federally-funded SNAP benefits," the proposed rule said.

The public has 60 days to submit comments on the proposal before the USDA publishes a final rule. The department is considering giving states a two-year deadline from that publication date to implement the rule, but it also welcomed input on whether that's enough time.

When asked if the department would consider providing funding to help states upgrade their card technology, the USDA said that "For years, States had access to administrative funds to stop this egregious abuse of taxpayer resources. Yet few acted."

The USDA added that the proposed rule has been in the works for nearly four years. It estimates that the changes will reduce stolen benefits by at least $1.5 billion over the next decade.

SNAP has been one of the focus areas in the Trump administration's war on fraud. Last week, the Justice Department announced that its fraud division helped uncover nearly $42 million in schemes targeting food benefits. The investigations ranged from identity theft to retailers illegally exchanging cash for food benefits.

World.title: Judge says DOJ illegally fired the daughter of former FBI director Comey
World.content:
Judge says DOJ illegally fired the daughter of former FBI director Comey

toggle caption i Win McNamee/Getty Images

A New York federal judge ruled Monday that the Justice Department unlawfully fired former prosecutor Maurene Comey, who is the daughter of ex-FBI Director James Comey.

Maurene Comey served as a federal prosecutor in Manhattan for around a decade, working on high-profile cases against defendants like Sean "Diddy" Combs, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell. The Trump Justice Department fired her in July 2025 despite her consistently receiving accolades from the department for her work.

In response, she sued the Justice Department and others, arguing that her dismissal was unlawful and unconstitutional. Her lawsuit said she was fired because her father is the former FBI director, a prominent critic of President Trump.

Sponsor Message

The Justice Department has twice indicted the elder Comey. The first case was dismissed. The second prosecution, which is still pending, accuses him of threatening the president in a photo of seashells posted on social media.

In his ruling Monday, U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman, a nominee of former President Barack Obama, wrote that the Department of Justice " invented a new and expansive theory of executive power " in dismissing Maurene Comey, and violated her constitutional right to due process.

"To accept Defendants' argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system," the judge wrote.

The opinion adds to concerns of politically motivated dismissals at the DOJ. Several federal prosecutors and former FBI agents have sued the DOJ under the Trump administration over their dismissals, alleging that they were fired for political reasons tied to their work.

Comey's lawyers praised Monday's ruling, and said it reaffirms that the president must comply with the law as part of the Constitution's checks and balances.

"This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law," her attorneys said in a statement.

The judge's ruling calls for Comey to receive back pay dating to when she was fired last year, and for her to return as a prosecutor to the Southern District of New York, if she so chooses.

Sponsor Message

The Justice Department said it disagreed with the decision, and would appeal in due course.

The court's order is not final. Judge Furman did yet not rule on Maurene Comey's First Amendment argument that she was fired for politically protected speech, and plans to hear further briefings on that claim.

—With assistance from NPR's Carrie Johnson.

World.title: AI giant Anthropic files for an IPO that could break records
World.content:
AI giant Anthropic files for an IPO that could break records

toggle caption i Patrick Sison/AP Photo



The artificial intelligence startup Anthropic, maker of the hugely popular Claude AI models, has taken a major step toward holding an initial public offering that analysts expect to be one of the biggest ever.

Anthropic filed final paperwork with regulators on Monday for an IPO under the ticker symbol ANT that reports have said could value the company at between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.

That would put it in league with Elon Musk's rocketry and AI company SpaceX, which was valued at around $1.8 trillion when it listed in June. Anthropic's listing prospectus did not say how many shares the company will offer or at what price range.

Sponsor Message

The filing of a public version of a registration statement called a Form S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission is a major milestone in Anthropic's meteoric rise. It was launched just five years ago by a breakaway group of OpenAI researchers, led by Dario Amodei, who were concerned that that company, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely.

Anthropic has since become a juggernaut, and OpenAI's biggest competitor, with some of the most widely used AI models on the market. But the company has faced controversy, including a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used and questions about Amodei's dire warnings on AI risks.

Still, the prospectus highlighted Anthropic's bullishness about the technology. "We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," it said.

In its prospectus, Anthropic highlighted breakneck growth — in revenue, income and losses. The company said its revenue in the first half of the year rose 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, vs. a loss of $1.8 billion the year before.

Sponsor Message

Anthropic has yet to turn an annual profit, and said it booked a loss of nearly $81 billion in the January to June period, up from $13 billion during the same six months last year.

In a statement emailed to NPR, Raj Joshi, senior vice president in the corporate finance group of Moody's, the ratings agency, called Anthropic's swing in adjusted operating income from negative to positive territory "a strong positive for the AI ecosystem."

U.S. stock indexes were up on Monday after Anthropic's early-morning announcement.

AI stocks have been hit by volatility

The filing comes at a volatile time in the stock market for AI-related companies, as investors waver between exuberance about the positive effects AI could have on the economy and concern about safety and the tsunami of investment in the technology.

The IPO, which could happen as soon as November, will be one of the most eagerly anticipated public share offerings in years. OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, is also planning an IPO, but those plans are temporarily on ice, with Altman ruling out a listing this year as "ill-advised" in the face of swirling AI safety concerns.

"Going public has a lot of advantages. It brings in capital for growth. It makes it easier for you to raise additional capital elsewhere. And it makes it possible for your existing investors to cash out," said Jim Angel, an associate professor and markets specialist at Georgetown University.

But, he added, "there's concern that we may be in an AI bubble. We're in a very dynamic industry, to say the least, and we can expect a lot of volatility in the markets." Still, Angel said, it makes sense for Anthropic to "strike while the iron is hot" and list shares now to get as high a valuation as possible.

With SpaceX already trading publicly, Anthropic's IPO could test investor appetite for AI businesses at a time when markets are jittery about whether they can be profitable enough to justify the mind-boggling sums of money being invested in AI. SpaceX's shares soared briefly after the listing, but have come back down to around $150, where they started trading.

In May, at its last private fundraising round, Anthropic had a post-money valuation of $965 billion.

Concerns remain about the AI sector

The balancing act for companies trying to ride the AI wave is real. The data center and infrastructure provider CoreWeave saw its share price plummet this month when investors got nervous about its ability to finance its expansion plans and its bond yields leaped. Other major players, including Intel, Meta and Nvidia, have also been buffeted by concerns and watched their share prices slide in recent weeks.

Sponsor Message

Debt financing has been a growing concern as AI-related companies scramble to raise money to meet demand at a time when interest rates are poised to keep rising as the Federal Reserve tries to douse stubborn inflation.

The S-1 filing that tees up the IPO flagged what Anthropic sees as the risks from AI — and to its business model. Among them are the risk that its AI models could develop faster than the company can keep them safe, or that they could be used to cause harm — or take harmful actions on their own. It also flagged the risk of heightened scrutiny or political backlash for the company's views on policy and regulation.

Amodei himself has issued some of the AI world's sharpest warnings about the possibility of AI spiraling out of control and causing harm, and urged AI companies to "pace the frontier," or to slow the development of their most capable models.

Anthropic has also clashed with the Pentagon this year over how the military can use its models. Amodei has drawn a line in the sand when it comes to using Anthropic's AI for autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans.

In response, the Pentagon blacklisted Anthropic and designated it a "supply chain risk" — a label previously reserved for entities affiliated with U.S. adversaries. Anthropic has sued the Pentagon in two federal district courts. Those legal battles remain ongoing.

World.title: Australian judge rejects prisoner's human rights challenge to Vegemite ban
World.content:
Australian judge rejects prisoner's human rights challenge to Vegemite ban

toggle caption i Rick Rycroft/AP

MELBOURNE, Australia — A prisoner on Monday lost his challenge to an Australian state's ban on inmates eating Vegemite after he argued in court that withholding the polarizing yeast-based spread breached his human right to "enjoy his culture as an Australian."

Andre McKechnie, 55, who is serving a life sentence for murder, took his battle for the salty, sticky, black-brown byproduct of brewing beer to the Supreme Court of the state of Victoria last year.

He had argued being refused Vegemite denied him his right under the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act to "enjoy his culture as an Australian in the community with other persons of Australian background," court documents showed.

Sponsor Message

Justice Claire Harris accepted prison authorities' refusal to allow McKechnie Vegemite "limited his cultural rights" under the charter.

But she found the ban was justified in meeting authorities' goals of removing illicit drugs and alcohol from the prison system.

"The limitation on Mr. McKechnie's ability to enjoy Vegemite in community with other persons of Australian background is primarily that he is a prisoner," Harris wrote in her 47-page judgment.

Prison officials testify Vegemite could impair drug sniffer dogs and be used to make alcohol

Prison officials testified at a trial in July that Vegemite had been banned throughout the state's 12 prisons for the past 20 years because it could potentially impair sniffer dogs' ability to detect narcotics and could be used to brew alcohol because of its yeast content.

McKechnie, who represented himself in court by video link from maximum security Barwon Prison west of Melbourne, argued that the fact that neighboring New South Wales state did not ban Vegemite from its prisons was evidence that there were "less restrictive means reasonably available" to achieve such drug and alcohol outcomes.

Most Australians revere Vegemite as an unfairly maligned culinary icon, and more than 80% of Australian households are estimated to have a jar in their pantries. Vegemite is typically considered an acquired taste at best by those who weren't raised on it.

Sponsor Message

The last U.S. president to visit Australia, Barack Obama, once said: "It's horrible."

Prisoner argues Vegemite ban contributed to vitamin deficiency

McKechnie had initially testified that the lack of Vegemite had contributed to his thiamine deficiency.

He said both Vegemite and pork were sources of thiamine, also known as vitamin B1. As a Jew who observed kosher law, he told the court he couldn't eat pork either and took daily doses of the vitamin.

Vegemite has long been marketed as a source of B vitamins thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3) and folate (B9) which are promoted as healthy additions to the diets of growing children.

But McKechnie dropped the thiamine issue as "not important," after lawyers for the prison authorities objected to his evidence.

Prisoner said Vegemite ban left him feeling 'deprived, sad and disconnected'

McKechnie said not eating Vegemite made him feel "deprived of being able to practice my Australian culture, sad and disconnected from my family and community."

The judge responded that "it is difficult to accept that the inability to consume Vegemite, rather than the fact of his imprisonment, is a material cause of his sadness and disconnection from his family and community."

McKechnie cited an article published in the food studies journal "Gastronomica" in 2003 that said, "Vegemite may be the best predictor of national identity of any food in the world."

The article, based on research by Australia's Queensland University in 1995, found that a "taste for the spread strongly correlates with early exposure and to Australian birth and ancestry."

McKechnie also referred to the Australian Olympic Committee overturning an Chinese import ban on Vegemite ahead of the 2008 Summer Olympics in Beijing.

He cited Australian band Men at Work's 1980s international hit "Down Under" that mentions a "Vegemite sandwich."

On the effectiveness of smearing contraband with Vegemite, McKechnie cited a Melbourne newspaper article from 2017 that reported a man's unsuccessful attempt to use the odor of the spread to conceal illicit drugs that he attempted to smuggle into a music festival in Victoria. The attempt was thwarted by police sniffer dogs.

Sponsor Message

Judge rejects evidence that Vegemite doesn't interfere with drug sniffer dogs

The judge upheld prison authorities' argument that McKechnie had failed to provide any proper foundations for his opinion that Vegemite does not interfere with drug sniffer dogs.

McKechnie also argued that Vegemite contained "no live yeast" and that any piece of fruit would be more useful in making alcohol than the spread.

A state prison department manager, Kevin White, cited publicly available research that said Vegemite helped home-brewed beer ferment more quickly.

Vegemite's owner, Bega Group, did not respond to a request for comment on Monday.

World.title: What to know about China's plenum as Xi seeks stronger party discipline
World.content:
What to know about China's plenum as Xi seeks stronger party discipline

toggle caption i Xie Huanchi/Xinhua via AP

HONG KONG — China's political leaders and elites began a four-day meeting Monday to discuss strengthening the ruling Communist Party's discipline, as Chinese President Xi Jinping pushes for greater loyalty and reliability from officials while deepening his yearslong campaign against corruption.

This week's closed-door gathering, known as the fifth plenum of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party, comes roughly a year before Xi is widely expected to secure his fourth five-year term as the party's leader and personnel changes to key leadership bodies.

Xi began the meeting by delivering a work report and speaking about a draft policy decision on advancing "full and rigorous party self-governance," according to China's official Xinhua News Agency. The policy aims to make cadres more disciplined, effective and less corrupt.

Sponsor Message

While Xi has consolidated his grip on power, analysts say the plenum will offer him an opportunity to further align what Chinese officials do with what Beijing wants.

"The plenum is a chance to ensure the new generations rising the ranks share Xi's assessment of the opportunities and risks China faces," said Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser at London's Tony Blair Institute for Global Change.

Here's what to know about one of Beijing's most significant political meetings this year.

Xi targets underperforming cadres and corruption

Xi's anti-graft drive has been a defining feature of his rule since he came to power in 2012. Purges of officials — including some viewed as his political rivals — have been carried out on a scale that led critics to argue the campaign was also used to consolidate his power.

But his focus has expanded to cracking down on underperforming cadres too. In recent years, the number of officials punished for "formalism" and "bureaucratism" — misconduct such as dereliction of duty, inaction and reckless acts that seriously hinder development — has surged.

Xi's policy proposals reflect his emphasis on the party's "self-revolution," a concept centered on the party reforming itself through efforts such as rooting out corruption and building ideological commitment, analysts say.

Sponsor Message

Osman said the disciplinary crackdowns are now aimed more at institutional longevity.

"It's less about purging elite rivals and more about building a disciplined system that can sustain Xi's political priorities across leadership cycles," she said.

Record-high disciplinary campaigns also do not necessarily mean a rebound in corruption, but rather that Xi has been steadily raising the bar for the party's expectations of officials, she added.

Mingda Qiu, senior analyst of Eurasia Group's China practice, said Beijing has been building its agenda for months.

"The message is clear: the anti-corruption campaign is not winding down. Officials are not only tested for loyalty, but also for compliance and action," he said.

Xi said in a January meeting that while decisions by the party's top leadership were smoothly implemented in general, inspections and audits found problems such as failures to comply and improper execution, according to an October article in the Qiushi Journal, a publication of the central committee.

Xi warned against "two-faced people" who might profess political loyalty while privately defying orders and doing as they please.

"During leadership transitions, we must keep our eyes sharp, elevate good cadres who are truly loyal and reliable, consistent in word and deed, and willing to take responsibility, and never allow 'two-faced people' or those driven by self-interest to slip through," Xi was quoted as saying.

Xi's purges of top army officials will be put on display

The number of empty seats in the conference hall this week will help observers gauge how widespread Xi's purges have been.

Neil Thomas, senior fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute, and his colleagues Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang noted that while Xi's civilian purges are record-breaking, 42 out of 44 officials affiliated with the military elected as full central committee members in 2022 have also been purged or disappeared.

Sponsor Message

The central committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 full and alternate members. Thomas and his colleagues estimated turnout this week could be less than 80%, potentially setting a record low at any plenum since the end of former leader Mao Zedong's rule in 1976.

Attention will also be on new demands on the officials who remain.

Thomas expects tighter scrutiny of public spending and major projects, more use of technology to uncover corruption, and tougher consequences for officials who fail to deliver on Xi's priorities.

New personnel appointments are possible, though Xi may wait until a once-in-five-years Communist Party Congress next year to anoint his picks, said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London. If he does fill any openings, it will be with loyalists, he added.

Hints at a Xi successor are unlikely

The underlying theme of the fifth plenum is that it will be another opportunity for Xi to position himself for an unprecedented fourth term in office.

Xi, who removed presidential term limits in 2018, is viewed by some as the most powerful Chinese leader since Mao. He is widely expected to be confirmed as party leader for the next term in the fall of 2027.

Ahead of that, Thomas said new ideological language reinforcing Xi's authority might emerge at this week's meeting.

He said the plenum should prepare the ground for Xi's fourth term and reinforce expectations of political and policy continuity.

"After Xi has purged so many of the people that he promoted at the last congress, watch for tougher scrutiny of the officials competing to join his next leadership team," he said.

World.title: Redistricting isn't playing out how the GOP hoped. And, Brazil's Lula wins 4th term
World.content:
Redistricting isn't playing out how the GOP hoped. And, Brazil's Lula wins 4th term

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

toggle caption i Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

Republicans had a plan to keep control of the House in the midterms: Redraw congressional district lines to favor the GOP and avoid the historical pattern of heavy midterm losses. President Trump began pressuring Republican-led states to do just that last year, but it isn't working out as expected. Republicans could now be spending millions of dollars on House seats that were supposed to be easy wins, and end up losing anyway. Of the 15 districts drawn specifically to favor Republicans, only five are rated by the Cook Political Report as either likely or solid Republican. Most are toss-ups or lean toward a Democratic win.



🎧 One reason the Republicans' redistricting push hasn't been as successful as expected is that some district lines were drawn based on the 2024 Trump electorate, NPR's Tamara Keith tells Up First. Since then, his support has weakened, particularly among young and Latino voters. Several Democratic incumbents targeted by redistricting have stuck it out to fight for their seats. A Republican strategist involved with midterm races, but who wasn't authorized to speak publicly, pushed back on the characterization that redistricting didn't work, saying that it "creates new battlefields" but doesn't "create outcomes."

Several Democratic incumbents targeted by redistricting have stuck it out to fight for their seats. A Republican strategist involved with midterm races, but who wasn't authorized to speak publicly, pushed back on the characterization that redistricting didn't work, saying that it "creates new battlefields" but doesn't "create outcomes." ➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.

Sponsor Message

In a stunning political comeback, leftist Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in the presidential runoff election in Brazil. Lula defeated Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, by more than 4 million votes. It's the first time since Brazil restored democracy in 1989 that a candidate who finished second in the first round has gone on to win the presidency.



🎧 Lula's win appears to have put the brake on a right-wing sweep in Latin America, NPR's Carrie Kahn says. Seven conservative presidents have been elected in the past 18 months. Kahn says one message helped rally voters in the final weeks of Lula's campaign: that the return of a Bolsonaro to power would be an existential threat to Brazilian democracy.

Large demonstrations against the government continued over the weekend in France, where more than 100,000 people showed up in Paris, and more than 400,000 came out nationwide. What started with students demanding better conditions has grown into a much bigger movement. Unions and public-sector workers have joined, calling for more public spending and protesting growing inequality. Similar protests have erupted across Europe, from Spain to Serbia.



🎧 The reasons behind the protests vary, from schools and housing costs to corruption, NPR's Eleanor Beardsley says. But they have something in common: most are leaderless movements by young people frustrated with the world they're being left to. In Serbia, crowds celebrated in the streets of Belgrade after a student-led movement known as the "student-list" defeated the party of longtime strongman Aleksandar Vucic in Sunday's parliamentary elections. The win followed two years of protests over government corruption and lack of accountability.

Sponsor Message

Healthcare helpline

Oona Zenda/KFF Health News

Out-of-pocket maternity expenses are difficult to predict. A federal requirement for insurers to provide personalized cost estimates under the No Surprises Act was supposed to take effect in 2022, but federal regulators haven't made it happen despite pressure from Congress. Until the cost of maternity care gets more transparent, here are some tips to help you budget for the cost of pregnancy:

👶 Enroll your baby in your insurance before your deadline. For most employer health plans, that's within 30 days of birth.

👶 Check what your maximum out-of-pocket expense is. That's the most you'll pay each year for covered, in-network expenses before your insurance pays 100% of the costs.

👶 Choose in-network providers whenever possible.

👶 Go over every bill, and don't be afraid to appeal errors.

👶 Ask your hospital or other providers about financial assistance.

Deep dive

toggle caption i National Oceanic and Atmospheric/National Oceanic and Atmospheric

When Hurricane Isaias made landfall in Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 storm, Google DeepMind's AI model outperformed the traditional model, correctly predicting it would hit the Florida Panhandle rather than head west toward Louisiana. Hurricane forecasters say they're increasingly relying on AI technology, and that it's rapidly transforming the field.



🌀 The National Hurricane Center first started incorporating Google DeepMind into its official forecasts last year. By the end of the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season, it was among the best at predicting a storm's strength and path.

🌀 Traditional physics-based prediction models use real-time atmospheric data like temperature, humidity, pressure and wind shear. AI models rely more on history and patterns from analyzing thousands of past storms.

🌀 AI models can feel like a black box; meteorologists depend on them but don't always know why their predictions are correct.

🌀 Humans still interpret the results of these models and translate them into clear guidance people can act on.

3 things to know before you go

The latest edition of NPR's Breakfast Around the World series takes us to the ancient city of Aleppo in northern Syria, where a sweet semolina pudding called mamounieh evokes memories both bitter and sweet. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported 4,588 confirmed measles cases across the U.S. this year through Oct. 22 — more than double the number for all of 2025. Cases are particularly high in Pennsylvania. The general fertility rate for U.S. women fell by 1% to a record low in 2025, according to the CDC. Birth rates declined among women in their 20s but rose among women ages 30 to 45.

Sponsor Message

This newsletter was edited by Majd Al-Waheidi.

World.title: Trump escalates anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed in Michigan
World.content:
Trump escalates anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed in Michigan

toggle caption i Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

PORT HURON, Mich. — President Donald Trump intensified his anti-Muslim rhetoric against Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday, portraying him as a threat to national security and questioning his loyalty to the United States in remarks that drew a sharp rebuke from a former top Arab American ally.

Trump called El-Sayed, a former Detroit health official, a "jihadist" who was "on the side of the terrorists" and would "have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate." He also repeatedly invoked the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, drawing a comparison between stopping El-Sayed from entering the Senate chamber and the passengers who fought back against the hijackers aboard United Flight 93.

El-Sayed, who would become the nation's first Muslim senator if elected, has called attacks on his loyalty to the country "shameful" and repeatedly denied any ties to extremist groups. The Republican president's remarks were condemned by Bishara Bahbah, a founder of Arab Americans for Trump, the group that helped lead the president's outreach to Arab American voters in 2024.

Sponsor Message

"The president's statements are out of line," he said in a phone interview. "They are crossing a red line. They are racist."

With Republicans on the defensive over inflation, soaring fuel prices and the Iran war, the president has been trying to generate turnout by claiming that El-Sayed and other Democrats are existential threats to America, instead of electoral rivals. Michigan's Senate race between El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers is among a handful of contests that could determine control of the chamber.

Trump made his remarks in Port Huron, a Canadian border city about an hour north of Detroit and near communities where he made significant gains among Arab American voters in 2024. He became the first Republican presidential candidate since 2000 to win Dearborn, a city with one of the nation's largest concentrations of Arab Americans.

Trump, who imposed a travel ban targeting several predominantly Muslim countries during his first term, has increasingly leaned into anti-Muslim rhetoric as Election Day approaches. He also attacked Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota at Sunday's rally, where he declared that he had come to Michigan "to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator."

Responding to Trump, who also regularly mocks his name, El-Sayed told supporters at a rally in Grand Rapids later Sunday that he doesn't care how Trump pronounces or misrepresents it.

Sponsor Message

"I don't even care that he remembers my whole name because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November," El-Sayed said, drawing cheers. "I will be Senator Muhammad to you, bro."

El-Sayed's faith, associations and past statements become campaign flashpoints

Central to Republicans' strategy against El-Sayed in the final weeks of the campaign has been an effort to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamic movement with branches that the U.S. government has designated as terrorist organizations.

There is no evidence that El-Sayed has any affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood. His half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, wrote on social media in 2012 that "my family has long been MB" and described a conversation with her mother about her involvement in the Muslim Brotherhood in the early 1970s.

El-Sayed was born in the United States to Egyptian immigrant parents who divorced when he was young. He was raised by his father, not his biological mother.

Trump on Sunday also targeted El-Sayed's ties to popular streamer Hasan Piker, who appeared alongside the Democrat multiple times during the primary campaign, including at his election night event.

Piker in the past has said that "Hamas is a thousand times better" than Israel, describing some Orthodox Jews as "inbred" and that "America deserved 9/11."

El-Sayed has faced criticism for his own rhetoric. He has repeatedly refused to answer questions about whether Iran or Israel poses a bigger threat to the country. Earlier this year, he said "hurt people hurt people" after an attack on a synagogue in the Detroit area. The attacker had lost four relatives in an Israeli airstrike on Lebanon the week earlier. El-Sayed later apologized, saying he was not trying to justify what happened.

"To anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful, I'm really sorry," he said. "That was not my intention."

Sponsor Message

Founder of Arab Americans for Trump calls the president 'racist'

Bahbah, whose organization has since changed its name to Arab Americans for Peace, said Trump's remarks were unacceptable to Arab and Muslim communities, including Christian Arabs.

"The remarks are out of line and crazy. I mean, no sane individual would say these things," Bahbah said.

Dearborn helped Trump win Michigan in 2024 after many voters in the city were outraged by the Biden administration's handling of the war in Gaza.

"The president of the United States saying that about a person because of his religion, that is just not acceptable," said Bahbah. "And people are going to remember that on Nov. 3."

Sen. Bernie Sanders, speaking at the Grand Rapids rally, said Trump and his allies were using Islamophobia because they have "nothing to say" about the issues most important to working people, such as health care, housing and income inequality.

"All they can do is foment hatred and divisiveness," Sanders said.

The campaign has been one of the most contentious this year

Rogers and El-Sayed have been locked in a bitter race to fill the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.

During their second and final general election campaign debate, Rogers questioned El-Sayed's loyalty to the United States.

"Are you for America, or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?" Rogers asked.

El-Sayed said that questioning was "shameful."

"I'm proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray," he said.

Speaking before Trump's appearance Sunday, Rogers repeated his allegations linking El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood.

"The Muslim Brotherhood celebrated exactly one victory in the United States in the primary this year," Rogers said on stage. "Abdul El-Sayed's."

toggle caption i Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

Rally doesn't deliver a new economic handout, but gets boost from Minaj

Trump has routinely announced new investments in factories at his campaign rallies, but he did not do so as part of his speech in Michigan, a state defined by the auto industry.

Sponsor Message

The president instead repeated investments already being made by domestic automakers. Those automakers could see their finances slump if the president expands his trade war with Canada, which has been an essential partner for the U.S. automotive sector.

While it lacked a fresh promise for Michigan's economy, Trump's rally did deliver a bit of star power.

Rapper Nicki Minaj appeared on stage and urged people to get out and vote for the state's Republican ticket. Her appearance followed an awkward moment from Trump, who has increasingly been fixated on commenting about other people's body parts.

After praising the body of Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican in a close election contest, Trump turned his eye toward Minaj and commented on her posterior.

The president then signaled for Minaj to stand for the crowd and she did, after which Trump said, "I hope Nicki wasn't insulted, but we love Nicki. She's been with us for a long time."

World.title: First Nations-first ministers' meeting brings funding announcements and mixed reviews
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The premiers said they were there to listen and the prime minister said he was there to act. But one chief said history will judge them by a different measure.

"History will not remember us for gathering in a room, taking photographs, making speeches," Chief Sheldon Sunshine of Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation in northern Alberta told Canada's premiers and prime minister on Monday morning.

He paused for dramatic effect before adding: "History will judge us by what we change."

And thus began the first Indigenous-focused first ministers' meeting in 21 years — and the first such meeting in 119 years to focus solely on First Nations issues.

The group convened not on opposing sides but in a circle behind closed doors in Ottawa at the John G. Diefenbaker Building on Sussex Drive, where there was no shortage of calls for change.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew surprised reporters by holding up his Indian status card as he called to abolish the Indian Act. Prairie chiefs joined former national chief Matthew Coon Come demanding Canada revisit the 1930 Natural Resource Transfer Acts that handed control over resource development from the federal to provincial governments.

WATCH | Prime minister addresses First Nations leaders: Carney seeks to 'commit to action' at historic First Nations-first ministers' meeting | Duration closed caption 0:50 Prime Minister Mark Carney said it was 'sobering' to realize first ministers and First Nation leaders have not met together in over two decades. 'Let's seize this opportunity,' Carney said, adding that the government 'will act' both today and in the upcoming budget.

"If this first ministers' meeting succeeds, it must come up with strong, concrete measures for next steps. If they don't do that, then this is another meeting of just talks," Coon Come told reporters.

Chiefs from Ontario called for constitutional amendments that would recognize First Nations as distinct orders of government. Grassroots activists protested outside, while inside Assembly of First Nations (AFN) leaders and Canada's first ministers debated the country's future.

As the meeting wrapped, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced both financial and political commitments. He said he shares Kinew's view that the time has come to reform or even abolish the Indian Act and would direct his ministers to work with First Nations on a path forward.

WATCH | Carney and Woodhouse Nepinak on future of the Indian Act: Carney 'very open' to abolishing Indian Act | Duration closed caption 3:35 Prime Minister Mark Carney said 'there's many reasons' to move on from the Indian Act, speaking after Monday's meeting between First Nations leaders and first ministers. Carney said the solution 'could be moving beyond, it could be reforming, it could be abolishing' the 1876 law in order to establish a modernized relationship.

He said he will instruct his finance minister to work with First Nations to develop new revenue-sharing mechanisms, including a potential sovereign wealth fund, which the AFN sought in one of its position papers circulated ahead of the meeting.

Carney also announced some proposed new spending, likely foreshadowing the Nov. 5 federal budget. This includes more than $2.5 billion over five years for emergency preparedness in First Nations communities across the country, and more than $630 million over four years for First Nations and Inuit policing.

In televised opening remarks earlier, Carney called it "sobering" that two decades have elapsed since the last such meeting, held when Paul Martin was prime minister in 2005. That meeting in Kelowna, B.C., yielded an agreement dubbed the Kelowna Accord.

"This is an important opportunity, yes, to share perspectives, to listen, to learn, but above all to commit to action," Carney said.

But the meeting unfolded under a cloud of skepticism, the absence of three premiers and concerns from some chiefs that the Carney government is using the meeting as political cover for its streamlining of major infrastructure projects.

The day included a blunt address from the Algonquin Nation on whose unsurrendered land Parliament Hill now sits.

"Our nation is still waiting for justice," Verna Polson, grand chief of the Algonquin Anishinabeg Nation Tribal Council, told the group.

In her opening remarks, AFN National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said nation-building "can't just be about ramming through major projects" as fast as possible.

"The national interests must also include the proposals, law and policy reforms that First Nations seek," she said. "We have been persistent and patient, but we cannot afford to wait many, many years for results and implementation."

WATCH | National chief opens meeting: 'Our rights must be taken seriously': AFN national chief | Duration closed caption 1:35 Speaking at the opening of a historic First Nations and Canadian first ministers' meeting, Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak says Indigenous rights 'can't be respected after the fact.'

Around 40 people gathered outside to protest AFN participating at all because it's a federally funded national advocacy body elected by chiefs and not rights-holding grassroots people.

Russ Diabo, spokesperson for the Truth Before Reconciliation Network, told CBC News the Carney government is on the wrong track.

"What [Carney] should be doing is changing the way he's interacting with First Nations and Canada and not using these administrative bodies that he controls like the Assembly First Nations," Diabo said.

Reviews were mixed coming out of the meeting.

Cody Diabo, grand chief of the Mohawk Council of Kahnawà:ke, left early, denouncing the meeting as all about "butterflies and rainbows" and not dealing with big-picture substantive issues. Hereditary Chief Na'Moks of the Wet'suwet'en Nation in B.C. felt the meeting was about finding "cheerleaders" for the federal agenda.

Others were more optimistic. Abram Benedict, AFN's Ontario regional chief, said he felt good about the investments and potential creation of a wealth fund, but there was no firm pledge to hold these meetings annually, as the AFN requested.

"There seems to be a willingness, but there was no commitment," Benedict said.

Carney said the right timeline for the next meeting is probably two years. Woodhouse Nepinak told reporters she was happy with the day and the tangible commitments secured.

World.title: Canada-U.S. trade talks intensifying but wide gap remains, sources say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With the U.S.-Canada trade war dominating the final days of the U.S. midterm campaign, trade discussions between the two countries have intensified. But sources tell CBC News and Radio-Canada that doesn't mean a deal is imminent.

A source familiar with the discussions told Radio-Canada that there are "substantive conversations, but there are still key elements that remain unresolved."

"We are not on the verge of an agreement just yet," the same source said.

Another Canadian government source told CBC News on Monday that while discussions between officials from both countries have become more frequent in recent days, the state of play is best understood by reviewing comments made last week by Janice Charette, Canada's chief trade negotiator.

"Pens are down, and the doors are open," Charette said at the Toronto Global Forum on Thursday. "Canada stands ready to continue discussions."

Charette said that while conversations are taking place at "multiple levels," they aren't happening at the negotiating table.

"We're having conversations to see whether or not we can come back to the table for a set of detailed negotiations," she said. "We don't know exactly when that's going to happen."

Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters on Monday that his government's position hasn't changed since talks fell apart in August and that he's only looking to sign a deal that's "in the interests of Canadians."

"We have very clear bottom lines, red lines, which meant that we were not willing to sign what was offered in August," the prime minister said.

"To the extent any progress has been made, it's because the U.S. is coming closer to our position."

According to several Canadian sources, the gap between the two sides has been too wide in recent days to reach an agreement.

"Canada remains in constructive dialogue with our U.S. counterparts on a range of priorities," a spokesperson from Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc's office said on Sunday.

"We stand ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada's interests."

A Canadian source told CBC News that LeBlanc had to stay in Ottawa this weekend because calls with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer increased in the past few days.

Some industry stakeholders received calls from senior members of the federal government over the weekend to discuss the current status of trade discussions, according to two industry sources.

U.S. trade spin and the midterms

U.S. President Donald Trump and other senior U.S. officials have suggested in recent days that progress is being made toward a deal with Canada.

"We'll have ​that settled pretty soon. They're willing to give us anything ​at this moment," Trump told a campaign rally in Port Huron, Mich., on Sunday.

And Kevin Hassett, the director of the National Economic Council and a key economic adviser to the White House, suggested on Fox News that trade talks had been hampered by the referendum vote in Alberta but since then "negotiations have picked up."

"They're gathering steam. Secretary Lutnick has been talking to his Canadian counterparts all week. I think it's very close to finally having a deal on that," Hassett said.

WATCH | More about Trump's stop in Michigan: Trump campaigns in battleground Michigan with trade talk swirling | Duration closed caption 2:55 U.S. President Donald Trump campaigned in Michigan with less than 10 days before the midterm elections. The U.S.-Canada trade war has become a key issue in several battleground states.

While the White House may want to send a political message that progress is being made on the trade front, it is far from clear whether the U.S. administration is prepared to make Canada an acceptable offer.

Polls show Trump's dispute with Canada is deeply unpopular among American voters in both major parties.

Canadian sources that have spoken with Radio-Canada caution it's in the Americans' interest to "spin" the narrative that a deal with Canada is possible — especially with the midterm elections a week away.

David Axelrod, a former chief strategist to U.S. president Barack Obama, suggested in a post on social media Monday that "an 11th-hour trade deal [with] Canada is an option [Trump] still might pursue to help his Senate candidates in northern states."

On Friday Trump removed some tariffs from some goods — while hitting other products with new tariffs — in order to help Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins whose campaign has been frustrated by the trade war's impact in her state.

Ford says 'we'll see what happens'

"They're going for an election down there and I don't think Trump's doing too well," Ontario Premier Doug Ford said on his way into a meeting between first ministers and First Nations leaders in Ottawa.

"I think the trade deal with Canada is affecting him."

The premier said he hopes talks are progressing, but for now it's a "we'll see what happens" situation.

Asked if Carney has asked him to reconsider the province's U.S. booze ban to move trade talks along, Ford said "not yet."

But he said a fair deal for steelworkers, autoworkers and manufacturing workers would have him put American booze back on LCBO shelves "in a heartbeat."

World.title: This 3-year-old scored 10 goals. Then police showed up at his soccer game
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In the viral video posted by his parents, a three-year-old central Florida boy dribbles the ball up the field, dodging the other pint-sized players and kicks it into the net as his parents cheer.

Then the boy, named Nevada, does it again. And again. And again.

Later in the same video, which has been viewed more than one million times on TikTok since it was posted Sunday, Nevada stands on the sidelines as his father says, "they called the police on a three-year-old because he was too good."

"Because he had the ball for too long, and nobody else could get the ball, so they called the police."

The reaction online was swift, with people equally enraged over the allegations and admiration for the preschooler's skills. In the TikTok comments, some called on the parents to sue, others alleged that calling the police was racist, and many commented on the "heartbreak" in the little boy's face when the police show up.

"I'm LIVID," children's entertainer and vocal children's rights advocate Ms. Rachel posted on Instagram Monday morning, calling on soccer stars and other athletes to support the child and his family.

" This is racist, sick, traumatizing and disgusting," she added.

Former NFL quarterback Robert Griffin III called the incident "crazy," writing on X that "punishing a 3 year old child for being too good at a sport is RIDICULOUS."

CBC News has reached out to Nevada's parents but has not yet heard back. The family already had a sizeable social media following on TikTok and Instagram, where they've documented Nevada's soccer skills over the years.

The Winter Park Police Department confirmed to CBC News Monday that officers were called to a children's soccer game Saturday after a league official "requested response to a disturbance between league officials and the parents of a player."

A screen shot of a post on Threads by children's entertainer Ms. Rachel on Monday. (@msrachelforlittles/Threads)

So, what actually happened?

The official called 911 at 9:53 a.m., according to the police incident report viewed by CBC News.

In a recording of the call provided by police, the official can be heard saying he has "an unruly parent here, calling me names and having me on Instagram."

He says the parent is being "really disruptive, like following me around and calling me names. I want her to be gone."

He describes her as a Black woman wearing pink.

The incident report says the official told police the parents were upset about their son's playing time, while the parents said their child "was being scorned for playing too well and was being taken out of [the] game."

The Winter Park Police Department said the league had asked the family to leave and offered to refund its fees. When police arrived, the official asked officers to communicate that to the family, the department said.

A screen grab of an Instagram post by illustrator and activist Nikkolas Smith, in support of 3-year-old soccer player Nevada, posted on Monday. (@nikkolas_smith/Instagram)

"The family stated the game was over and they were leaving," the police statement says, adding that the family was co-operative and no one was arrested, trespassed or forced to leave the park.

The video posted by Nevada's parents shows a Black woman wearing pink speaking with two police officers. One tells her the league office should be reaching out soon about a refund.

In a separate video, the parents claim the soccer officials repeatedly pulled Nevada from the 30-minute game after he scored and that, as a result, he played only about 12 minutes — but still scored 10 goals.

Boy is 'traumatized,' says mother

The soccer league, i9 Sports Maitland/Winter Park, told CBC News in a statement Monday that it was aware of concerns about "an incident at a local i9 Sports program" and takes them very seriously.

"We have reached out to the family and have begun a review that includes speaking with those involved," the league said.

In an interview with The Breakfast Club, Nevada's mother, identified as Martasia Griffin, said Nevada has been targeted all season because of his talent and that, at this particular game, some parents complained that no one else could get the ball.

She said the league director agreed it was unfair to other children and offered Griffin a refund.

"I cannot explain to my three year old son that he cannot play today because he's so good. I continued to let him play until the police walked in," Griffin said.

Nevada, she told HuffPost in another interview Monday, is "traumatized."

An Instagram post by former U.S. soccer player Eddie Johnson in which he supports 3-year-old Nevada. (Eddie_Johnson7/Instagram)

"He still wants to play soccer. He just doesn’t want to go back to that place. I don’t think that’s how he should be thinking, that as a 3-year-old he did something wrong."

Former U.S. professional soccer player Eddie Johnson posted about Nevada several times on social media Sunday and Monday, saying the boy would be joining his soccer program and criticizing how he was treated at the game.

"They wanna dim his light," Johnson posted to his Instagram stories.

"They thought they were taking your dreams away, but in reality (made) you the most famous three-year-old in the world right now."

World.title: Trump administration tries to prosecute former FBI director James Comey for 3rd time
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Trump administration is attempting to prosecute former FBI director James Comey for what it calls disclosing classified information, employing the unusual manoeuver of bypassing a grand jury — a move Comey's lawyers say makes the case legally invalid.

The allegations from the U.S. Justice Department came in documents unsealed Monday in federal court in Washington.

It would be the third criminal case that the Justice Department has brought against the longtime critic and foe of President Donald Trump since the Republican president's return to the White House last year.

"Well, they're back — again," Comey said in a video statement released after the documents dropped. "It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice — one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing's changed with me; I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people — and I still believe in an independent federal judiciary."

The Justice Department, for its part, said it had filed what's known as a criminal information to extend the 10-year statute of limitations for bringing a case.

"Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals. This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further," a department spokesperson said.

The new ‌case adds to the legal fights facing Comey, whom the Justice Department has already charged twice, accusing him of lying to Congress about media leaks and threatening Trump in ​a social media post.

A judge dismissed the false statements case, while the threats ⁠case remains pending.

Trump wanted pledge of loyalty

Comey was the FBI director when Trump took office in 2017, having been appointed by then-president Barack Obama, and serving before that as a senior Justice Department official in President George W. Bush's Republican administration.

A judge ruled Monday that Comey's daughter, Maurene Comey, seen here in May 2025, was illegally fired by the Trump administration from her position as assistant U.S. attorney. (Brendan McDermid/Reuters)

But the relationship was strained from the start, including after Comey resisted a request by Trump at a private dinner to pledge his personal loyalty to the president — an overture that so unnerved the FBI director that he documented it in a contemporaneous memorandum.

Trump fired Comey in May 2017 amid an FBI investigation into potential ties between Russia and Trump's campaign. That inquiry, later taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller, found that while Russia interfered in the 2016 election and the Trump team welcomed the help, there was insufficient evidence to prove a criminal collaboration.

News of the new case against Comey came the same day a judge ruled the Trump administration illegally fired Comey's daughter, Maurene, as a Justice Department prosecutor.

World.title: Police locate vehicle allegedly used by Toronto mother to abduct 3 children
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Toronto police say they have found a vehicle believed to have been used to abduct three children from Scarborough on Friday, but the children and their mother have not been found.

In a news release Monday, police said the mother of the three children, Somerda Miclescu, 22, was believed to be driving a 2017 White Ford Expedition vehicle with Ontario licence plate DJJS 875.

Police did not say where or when they found the vehicle.

Daniel, six, Irina, three, and Anastasia, four months, were having a semi-supervised visit with a relative on Friday, when polices say their mother took them and fled. Police say the children's mother does not have legal custody of them.

"Efforts to locate them remain ongoing," police said in the release.

Police described the mother as 5 feet 7 inches, about 180 pounds, with long, black hair. Police said she was last seen wearing a long black skirt and a dark-coloured top.

Somerda Miclescu is wanted by police for allegedly abducting her three children. (Toronto Police Service)

Police first responded to a call at about 11:30 a.m. Friday for an abduction in the Midland Avenue and Eglinton Avenue East area.

Ionut Stroe, 25, the owner of the vehicle that Miclescu allegedly used to abduct the children, has been named by police as a person of interest in the case.

Stroe is also wanted for four counts of failing to comply with a release order, unrelated to the abduction.

Police described him as being around 5 feet 11 inches, 235 pounds, with a tattoo on his right forearm.

World.title: Agent of author Steven Galloway says sex assault allegations derailed promising career
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The literary agent for Steven Galloway said it would have been "impossible" to sell any new work by his client in the years after a former student made unproven allegations of rape and sexual assault against the author a decade ago.

Henry Dunow described what he viewed as the detrimental impact of the claims on Galloway's "promising" career during a B.C. Supreme Court hearing in the author's defamation lawsuit against his accuser and other defendants.

Dunow said he thought of Galloway as a literary "star" with a bright future ahead.

But the allegations, which emerged in 2015, derailed that trajectory, he said.

Galloway has filed the lawsuit against a woman known only as A.B. and multiple others. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

An author's "social capital" and platform carry great importance in the industry, in a way more than the words on the page, Dunow told Monday's hearing.

Galloway, the former chair of creative writing at the University of B.C., denies the allegations, and he was never charged.

He is suing his accuser, known as A.B., whose claims of rape and assault were found unsubstantiated by a former judge hired by the university.

The lawsuit alleges A.B. and other defendants defamed Galloway by publishing the unproven allegations online and through other forums.

Several people originally named as defendants have settled with Galloway and offered public apologies.

WATCH | Defamation trial begins: Former UBC professor Steven Galloway’s defamation trial begins | Duration closed caption 1:14

The court learned earlier this month that A.B. was no longer asserting in her defence that Galloway assaulted her, rather that she reported he had done so.

The woman, whose name is under a publication ban, is not testifying in the case, citing mental health struggles.

Galloway, the author of The Cellist of Sarajevo and The Confabulist, was fired by the university and has said his career was destroyed by the allegations.

He testified earlier this month that he could no longer write, his income from book royalties had "cratered" and he was selling boats for a living.

Dunow told Monday's hearing that the allegations resulted in the cancellation of a $100,000 contract for a three-novel series Galloway pitched about a ventriloquist detective, meant to be a playful departure from his earlier, serious works.

He later agreed during cross-examination by A.B.'s lawyer Arden Beddoes that The Confabulist hadn't met expectations following the success of The Cellist of Sarajevo, though he said a so-called "sophomore slump" was not uncommon.

The New York-based agent said he believed A.B.'s allegations had also thwarted the realization of a film option of The Cellist of Sarajevo dating back to around 2011.

The case has drawn intense attention in the Canadian literary scene.

A group of authors, including Margaret Atwood, signed an open letter in November 2016 calling for an investigation into how the university handled Galloway's case.

The court has previously heard that Galloway and A.B. had a two-year affair, which he has said ended in 2013.

Galloway testified she was a former student who was older than him, whom he'd met sometime in 2011 when she took a writing course from a colleague of his.

"I remain ashamed of having had an affair, period, let alone an affair with a student at the university I was at," he told an earlier hearing. "I should not have been cheating on my wife, and I should have not been doing it with a student."

A.B.'s former husband testified last week, called as a witness by Galloway's lawyers.

Atwood has recently penned opinion articles supporting Galloway, writing in the Globe and Mail that testimony from A.B.'s ex-husband saying he was exchanging text messages with A.B. about a hockey game at the time of her alleged 2011 rape in Galloway's office, was like the "Aha!" moment in a Sherlock Holmes novel.

World.title: Microsoft gives voluntary buyout offer to about 60,000 employees
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Microsoft said on Monday it is offering voluntary buyouts to many staff members as the technology giant looks to contain costs and help fund its ‌massive AI investments.

The offer was extended to about 60,000 employees according to Microsoft. The company had 223,000 full-time employees ‌globally as of June 30, according to its annual filing, meaning more than a quarter of its global workforce would have received the buyout offer.

Staffers across the Windows maker would be eligible for the offers, including those working in AI experiences, Copilot, finance, human resources, Xbox and Windows + Devices, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters, requesting anonymity ​as the matter was private. Units such as marketing, ​commercial business and security will be excluded, the source added.

In a memo, Microsoft's executive vice-president and chief people officer Amy Coleman said the offer will be available to eligible employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Microsoft declined to tell CBC News how many Canadians were offered the buyout.

"This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company ​a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also ⁠gives participating organizations another ⁠way to adapt their workforce to changing needs," ‌chief people officer Amy Coleman said in a staff memo.

WATCH | Block CEO says AI tools behind cuts to nearly half its workforce: Block cuts nearly half its workforce, CEO cites AI tools | Duration closed caption 2:03 Tech company Block, which owns payment platform Square, announced it will lay off thousands of employees because of the potential of artificial intelligence. But some industry watchers say blaming AI can be an easy excuse.

The company said it was a time-limited, voluntary program and built on insights gained from a previous voluntary retirement program. The eligible employees will receive details within the next few hours, it added.

Like other tech giants, Microsoft is spending hundreds of billions of dollars on AI data centres and chips, drawing scrutiny from investors over whether the returns will ⁠justify the staggering cost. The company, slated to report first-quarter results after markets close on Wednesday, has forecast $175 billion US in capital expenditures for the 2026 calendar year.

Shares of Microsoft, which had risen about 10 per cent this year, were up about 1 per cent on Monday. The development was first reported by Business Insider.

The company earlier this year offered ​voluntary buyouts to about 7 per cent of its U.S. workforce, or about 9,000 employees.

In July, Microsoft announced it would ⁠cut 4,800 jobs, or about 2.1 per cent of its global workforce, overhauling its Xbox gaming business and ⁠divesting up to five studios as it looks to boost returns after years ⁠of ⁠heavy investment in the division.
