Para entonces parecía que no había manera de quitarle un premio al fútbol español (ocho de los trece premios se fueron para España). Pere Romeu se llevó el Trofeo Johan Cruyff al mejor entrenador del fútbol femenino, después de que su Barcelona hiciera pleno de títulos: Champions, Liga, Copa y Supercopa. “Claramente, el mérito es de unas grandísimas futbolistas y de un grandísimo staff”, destacó el técnico azulgrana. Como en el Kopa, el dominio español en los banquillos fue total, en el femenino y en el masculino. En este último parecía difícil que alguien se lo arrebatara a España, que tenía cuatro de los cinco candidatos: De la Fuente, Luis Enrique, Mikel Arteta y Unai Emery. El infiltrado era Kompany. El premio no fue para el campeón de la Premier (Arteta) ni para el de la Champions (Luis Enrique), pero tampoco salió de España: se lo llevó Luis de la Fuente, el seleccionador de la Roja campeona del mundo en Estados Unidos, México y Canadá. “Termino con una frase de Marco Aurelio: ‘El éxito individual nos hace visibles; el colectivo, invencibles”, cerró De la Fuente. Antes había dicho unas palabras en inglés y había sido fiel a su estilo: todos los que le rodean son los mejores. Rodri, Cucurella y Lamine Yamal lo escuchaban de pie.

Mejores jóvenes, mejores entrenadores y también mejores porteros. Siempre con España como protagonista. Cata Coll se llevó el Trofeo Yashin femenino, y Unai Simón, el masculino. “Es un orgullo ganar este premio y compartirlo con un español”, agradeció la portera del Barcelona. Un emocionado Unai Simón tomó el testigo: “Los porteros vivimos bajo presión. Hemos crecido con el error. Es muy gratificante estar aquí recogiendo este premio”.

El éxito de Laporta

El monopolio español en la gala lo rompió Bukayo Saka. El jugador del Arsenal recibió el Premio Sócrates, que reconoce la labor social de los futbolistas, de manos de Burna Boy, el artista nigeriano que interpretó con Shakira «Dai Dai», la canción oficial del Mundial 2026. La ausencia española en el escenario no duró mucho. Después de que Dembélé subiera a recoger el premio al mejor equipo masculino, que recayó en el PSG, el Barcelona se impuso en el femenino. “También quiero dar las gracias a las instituciones que organizan las competiciones: la UEFA, la Federación y LaLiga”, subrayó Laporta. Fue el discurso político de un político que, con la Superliga ya enterrada, se ha alejado del otro poder: el de Florentino Pérez y el Madrid.

No hubo apenas sorpresas en Londres, ni para el público ni para casi ninguno de los premiados, que sabían que iban a ser galardonados antes de aterrizar. Así ocurrió también con Charlyn Corral, exjugadora del Atlético y del Levante, y con Harry Kane, que se llevaron los premios a los mejores delanteros. “Esto no habría sido posible sin todos los que me han empujado a dar más”, destacó el inglés. La tensión, en cambio, llegó al final de la noche. Por la tarde, France Football había jugado al despiste. O alguien se equivocó al programar las publicaciones de su web. Hacia las 17.15, hora de Londres, apareció en la página de la revista un artículo que daba a Kane como ganador del Balón de Oro. Minutos después aparecieron otros dos, uno con Lamine y otro con Mbappé. El primero acertó. En el femenino no hubo misterio: todos sabían que era para Alexia.

“Recuerdo que la pierna me fallaba y aprendí a volver a andar y chutar”, se emocionó Putellas al recordar su lesión de 2022. Vestida de Dior, con un diseño inspirado en Atenea Niké, símbolo de la victoria, la fuerza y la sabiduría, se impuso a sus excompañeras Pajor y Guijarro. Lamine no pudo emularla. Fue tercero, por detrás de Mbappé. Se lo arrebató Kane, el quinto inglés en ganar el Balón de Oro, después de Stanley Matthews, Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan y Michael Owen, y el primero desde 2001, esta vez en casa. Pierde Lamine, pero gana Alexia. Y España. Ya tendrá tiempo Lamine.

World.title: Cabinet under pressure from both sides as budget talks resume
World.content:
The cabinet is resuming talks with seven opposition parties this week as it tries to secure the votes it needs to steer its budget for next year through parliament.

Prime minister Rob Jetten and finance minister Eelco Heinen still hope they can win support from both sides for a broad deal, despite warnings from party leaders that their demands are irreconcilable.

The largest opposition party, the left-wing Pro, is calling for the coalition parties to scrap plans to raise income tax to fill the gap created after it abandoned its welfare cuts, under pressure from Pro and the trade unions.

Pro and the pro-European party Volt say the money should be raised instead through higher taxes on savings and investments, but Heinen’s party, the liberal-conservative VVD, want to replace the wealth tax system with a capital gains tax.

The minority coalition of D66, VVD and CDA needs the support of at least two opposition parties to secure its legislation through parliament.

Pro and Volt have enough seats in the two houses of parliament to guarantee a majority, but the VVD fear that making too many concessions on the left will damage their already precarious standing in the opinion polls.

Asylum and nitrogen

Many VVD voters were dismayed by Heinen’s proposed reforms to the “box 3” wealth tax, which would have led to people with modest investment portfolios paying more, prompting the finance minister to go back to the drawing board.

Opposition parties on the right, such as JA21, are pressing the cabinet to tighten the rules on asylum further as the price for their support.

JA21 leader Joost Eerdmans wants the status of all 70,000 Syrian refugees in the Netherlands to be reviewed and asylum claims to be processed outside the EU. The party also wants to water down the so-called “spreading law” so that the government in The Hague cannot force municipalities to take in minimum numbers of asylum seekers.

Agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen is also expected to take part in the talks, suggesting the cabinet is prepared to compromise on its plans to cut nitrogen pollution, even though Pro has warned the reforms “must not be weakened”.

Another pivotal issue is likely to be the proposed surrogacy law, which the orthodox Protestant party SGP wants the cabinet to withdraw.

The bill was put in the spotlight last week when Jetten and his partner Nicolás Keenan announced they were having a baby next year with the help of a surrogate mother.

At the moment there is no law regulating surrogacy in the Netherlands. Couples who make their own arrangements must have the child adopted before they are legally recognised as parents.

The SGP have said they will not support the cabinet unless it withdraws a bill that would recognise the rights of parents who have children born through surrogacy immediately.

The party also wants the government to intervene to stop hospitals offering to perform abortions after 22 weeks without a compelling medical reason.

World.title: Indians in NL urge cabinet to speak out on “Cockroach” crackdown
World.content:
Indians living in the Netherlands are protesting for political solidarity and media attention to the ongoing “Cockroach” protests sweeping India, which are being met with a brutal crackdown by state forces.

The protests erupted in the summer over suspected corruption in the education system and have since turned to focus on changes in the voting system. Young Indians say they are being denied their democratic rights – something protesters say particularly affects minority groups and women.

Indians are a significant part of the Netherlands’ international community, with the statistics office CBS counting about 54,500 Indian nationals in the country – roughly 3.2% of all foreign nationals.

The Progressive Indians Europe group, based in Amsterdam, gathered in The Hague recently to call for recognition of the injustices they say Narendra Modi’s government is inflicting on its people.

A spokesperson for the group told Dutch News that it was asking the Dutch government to publicly stand up for the democratic principles and human rights commitments it recognises in its own foreign policy.

“These developments directly affect people in the Netherlands,” they said. “Our families, friends and communities remain connected to India. What happens there has real consequences for the people we care about, while the precedent set by the erosion of electoral safeguards matters to democracies everywhere.”

The suppression of the Cockroach movement, the group says, which has seen thousands arrested, journalists detained, and reports of widespread police brutality, means people in the Netherlands should “examine the reporting, listen to affected communities and recognise the importance of independent investigations, transparency and accountability.”

The group stressed that it was not asking people to accept every allegation without scrutiny.

“We hope it encourages the Dutch public, media and policymakers to engage seriously with these developments and recognise that defending democracy is a shared international responsibility.”

A spokesperson for the foreign affairs ministry told Dutch News: “The Netherlands follows the developments in India. As human rights and democracy are an important part of the Strategic Partnership between India and the Netherlands, the Netherlands and India discuss these topics regularly in diplomatic contacts and will continue to do so.”

Struck off

Some of the members said the situation abroad is significantly impacting their lives. Surabhi, from Amsterdam, said she takes her right to vote very seriously, both in India and in Dutch municipal elections.

“I am an Indian national and have always travelled back to India to vote,” she said. “Most recently, I voted in the national elections in 2024 and the municipality elections in Mumbai in January 2026.”

Her name, along with millions of others, has been removed during a revision of the electoral rolls by the Election Commission of India, which says it is improving the voting system by removing dead, duplicate and ineligible voters.

Another protester, Anubhav, described how he can only see the voting list on the Election Commission of India website by using a VPN. When he saw his name had been removed, he submitted a complaint, which was closed the very next day.

He says he is a “popular anti-BJP [the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party] guy on social media among my acquaintances. Is this just a coincidence? I don’t know.”

Cockroach movement

The Cockroach Janta Party, whose name plays on that of Modi’s BJP, started in May as an online satire account. It was a response to India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, describing some activists and unemployed young people as “cockroaches” and “parasites of society”. Kant later said his remarks had been misquoted and misrepresented.

In July, Modi’s education minister was forced to resign in the wake of street protests against leaked exam papers. Amnesty International found that police used pellet-firing shotguns, electric shock batons, tear gas and batons against demonstrators. Delhi police said more than 400 people, including officers, were injured.

The latest wave of protests that began on October 2 was a reaction to a nationwide revision of the voter rolls. According to reports, about 14% of the original names on the rolls – more than 133 million – have been removed since the process began last year. Protesters say eligible voters have been wrongly struck off in favour of the BJP.

The Indian electoral commission says voters removed in error can register again, and has said all its actions were lawful.

More than 2,000 protesters, including several opposition MPs, were detained in Delhi over the weekend of October 10 and 11. On October 13, Human Rights Watch said police had beaten protesters, dragged them through the streets, arbitrarily detained them and suspended mobile internet services.

Police have said protesters were uncooperative and that force was sometimes needed. The UN human rights office has called on the authorities to fully respect the right to peaceful assembly.

Dutch ties with India

Indians make up one of the largest groups of highly skilled migrants from outside the EU, according to statistics bureau CBS. Many work in IT, and more than 300 Indian companies now have a presence in the Netherlands.

The Netherlands is India’s third largest export destination worldwide, the largest in Europe, and the fourth largest investor in India. According to the Indian embassy, merchandise trade stood at $27.8 billion in 2024-2025.

In May this year, Modi visited the Netherlands and, at a roundtable with Dutch business leaders, spoke of a “new golden era in India–Europe relations”, following the conclusion of free trade talks with the bloc. The agreement “between the world’s two largest democratic and responsible powers will become a strong foundation for shared prosperity”, he said.

Before Modi arrived, prime minister Rob Jetten told reporters there were concerns in the Netherlands and other EU countries about developments in India. “It is not only about press freedom, but also about the rights of minorities, who are under severe pressure,” he said, according to de Volkskrant, adding that the concerns were “regularly raised” with India.

India’s foreign ministry later dismissed the remarks as showing a “lack of understanding”.

World.title: Protecting Frisian: trainee teacher numbers more than double
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The number of students electing to train as Frisian language teachers has doubled this year, amid a historic drive to strengthen and revive the Netherlands’ only officially recognised second language.

More than 34 students signed up to take a Frisian teacher training course at Leeuwarden’s hbo college NHL Stenden, either as a minor or part-time element of their studies, according to Omroep Fryslân.

The change signals a growing revival trend as Friesland, often ranked the Netherlands’ culturally proudest province, fights to protect its linguistic identity. Only 10 years ago, experts warned the language was on the verge of extinction.

Geert Driessen, of Radboud University in Nijmegen, said in a 2016 study that it was the “eleventh hour” for the province’s mother tongue – especially in urban areas, where Dutch speaking newcomers increasingly mix with locals.

Between 1994 and 2014, he found, Frisian spoken outside family homes had halved. This led to the founding of Taalplan Frysk 2030, a government-backed scheme to protect the language through education and social initiatives.

The plan has received millions of euros in funding, much of which has gone to NHL Stenden. Recent studies show Frisian comprehension is rising, and since this school year all primary and secondary school pupils in Friesland are actively taught the language.

In September, the University of Groningen also launched the first standalone Frisian language degree in 15 years.

World.title: Sugar rush: blood bank acts to stem flow of free iced biscuits
World.content:
Dutch blood bank Sanquin has had to lock away the iced biscuits it hands out to donors after discovering it was haemorrhaging money through the heartwarming gesture.

A volunteer at the donation point in Delft told Omroep West the organisation had taken the drastic step because some visitors were abusing its generosity. “People were going out of here with their bags full,” they said.

Sanquin’s Instagram page promotes the pink-topped biscuits as a “well-earned tradition” to thank blood donors and restore their blood sugar levels.

But according to volunteers, the gesture is costing it around €1,000 a month in Delft alone, forcing it to put the biscuits behind the counter.

Instead there are now laminated menus in the café telling people they can ask for a biscuit after they have given blood.

Not all Sanquin donation points have withdrawn the biscuits. NOS found they were still on display in Utrecht and at a football club in Utrecht.

A spokesman for Sanquin’s head office said it was up to individual branches to decide, but confirmed that at some locations there were problems with “people taking more than we would reasonably expect.”

A volunteer in The Hague said: “We see people taking more than they should, but if they say they’re taking them home, should we be forbidding that?”

World.title: Van der Burg plans to use more AI so government can cut payroll
World.content:
Deputy home affairs minister Eric van der Burg has set out plans to cut the number of civil servants by 16% by 2035 in a wide-ranging efficiency drive.

Van der Burg said he wanted to take 25,000 government officials off the payroll by standardising IT systems and using other tools to make government more efficient, including AI.

The VVD minister, whose official title is State Secretary for Decisive Government, also plans to reduce the number of advisory bodies and committees, currently 28 and 150 respectively, he wrote in a letter to parliament.

It is the first time Van der Burg has put a number on the civil service cuts, which the cabinet hopes will save €3.5 billion a year by 2035. The announcement confirms earlier reports in the Telegraaf that the cabinet plans to use AI technologies to streamline the apparatus of government.

The minister has not said which departments will have to bear the brunt of the savings, but the police and the defence budgets are expected to be excluded.

However, government agencies that are currently under strain such as the tax office and the employment benefits agency UWV are not likely to be spared.

Simpler regulation

Van der Burg said some of the savings could be made by having fewer regulations and “exceptions to exceptions”. The cabinet has committed to scrapping 500 rules a year under the coalition agreement drawn up by the D66, VVD and CDA parties.

But he admitted that not all the reductions could be compensated by more efficient methods. “Some choices will have to be made regarding what the government should be doing less or not at all,” Van der Burg said.

He also said the government wanted to tighten the rules around the freedom of information law Woo, which citizens and journalists rely on to access public information.

“The requests for information are frequently so broad that it is no longer clear what information we are supposed to provide,” he wrote.

World.title: International parcels drop by 32% after EU imposes surcharge
World.content:
The number of parcels sent from outside the EU dropped by one-third in the last three months, mainly as a result of tighter EU restrictions, postal service PostNL said in its latest quarterly report.

The company said the 32% drop mainly reflected a drop in packages being sent from Asia after the bloc imposed a €3 surcharge per product on July 1.

It follows a 15% dip in the second quarter of the year and PostNL expects the trend to continue after the import fees are raised by a further €2 from next month.

The impact was partly offset by a 40% increase in parcels within the EU compared to the third quarter last year as Asian websites lost trade to European rivals because of result of the new measures.

But PostNL said that growth was “more than wiped out” by the drop in deliveries from further afield.

Three-day deliveries

The company’s turnover increased in the third quarter by €6 million to €768 million after the government relaxed the rules on deliveries.

Since July PostNL has been required to deliver letters within two days rather than 24 hours and the deadline is due to be stretched to three days next July.

CEO Pim Berendsen said the move to three-day deliveries was an important “interim step” towards ensuring the postal service could survive in the long term, but also renewed his calls for the government to compensate the company’s losses in recent years.

“Until we have a future-proofed regulatory framework, the uncertainty for thousands of our postal workers, customers and consumers will continue,” he said. “This situation requires a structural solution.”

World.title: Study of revolutionary feminist wins Libris prize for history
World.content:
A biography of a radical feminist thinker who published a series of influential revolutionary tracts while raising a family of three children has won this year’s prestigious Libris history prize.

Dubbelleven (“Double Life”), a study of the life of the Dutch philosopher Geertruida Kapteyn-Muysken by historian Maite Karssenberg, was praised for “exposing the shockingly subordinate role of women in the 19th century”.

The jury also highlighted Karssenberg’s “completely original” approach to her work, using diaries and letters to recreate Kapteyn-Muysken’s life and lead the reader through the writer’s eight-year trawl through the archives.

Born in Hillegom in 1855 and raised in Haarlem, Kapteyn-Muysken spent 20 years in England with her husband and children before moving to Zürich, where she became known in radical intellectual circles.

She campaigned for votes for women, sexual ethics, pacifism and non-religious education in the early 20th century. After her return to the Netherlands in 1908 she held salons at her home in Scheveningen and counted progressive icons such as Clara Wichmann and Aletta Jacobs among her circle of friends.

“After her death she was praised as ‘one of the most free and unrestrained minds’ of the Dutch revolutionary movement, with an ‘almost universal knowledge of the intellectual and social movements of our time’,” Karssenberg wrote on her website.

Other nominees included Isabel Casteels for De kronieken van de dood; a study of torture and executions in the 16th century; Maarten van Ginderachter for Arm Vlaanderen, which focuses on poverty and famine in 19th-century Flanders; and Dik Verkuil for his biography of the former VVD party leader Frits Bolkestein.

The €20,000 prize is part of the Month of History, organised in collaboration with the magazine Historisch Nieuwsblad and the Dutch Open Air Museum (Nederlands Openluchtmuseum) in Arnhem.

World.title: Leopard attack leaves Beekse Bergen zookeeper critically injured
World.content:
A zookeeper was mauled by a leopard at Beekse Bergen safari park on Saturday, leaving her in critical condition. Medics say she is not expected to survive.

Two Persian panthers, which had been sheltering from the weather, attacked the woman in an enclosure, according to reports. There is no CCTV footage and investigations into what happened are ongoing.

The victim was highly experienced, according to Omroep Brabant, having spent around 25 years working at the park and caring for the animals. She sustained serious wounds to her head and neck from the attack, and her conditioned worsened over Sunday night.

She managed to call for help via a walkie-talkie and was rescued by colleagues before being almost immediately operated on. A trauma helicopter and large numbers of emergency workers rushed to the sight.

It is unclear why or how she was in the enclosure with the animals – something that is never normally allowed.

Wineke Schoo, director of the Dutch Association of Zoos, described the incident as a “worst case scenario” to Omroep Brabant, and said she has only ever experienced one such incident in 25 years of Dutch zookeeping, which was a lion attack in 2001.

Poland and Vietnam have upgraded their ties to a strategic partnership, pledging to deepen cooperation in trade and investment, security and defence, as well as education, science, technology and cultural exchanges. “Vietnam and Poland share a success story in terms of development,” declared Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a joint press conference with his Vietnamese counterpart Lê Minh Hưng in Hanoi on Monday. “The time has come to turn our successes into joint actions that will open up more opportunities.” The announcement comes amid a broader flurry of Polish diplomacy in Asia, with Tusk arriving in Hanoi following a visit to India and President Karol Nawrocki visiting the Philippines earlier this month. Poland also recently signed new strategic agreements with South Korea and Japan. 🇵🇱🤝🇻🇳 Polska i Wietnam wchodzą na poziom partnerstwa strategicznego! ✅ Podczas wizyty w Hanoi premier @donaldtusk oraz szef wietnamskiego rządu Lê Minh Hưng podjęli decyzję o podniesieniu wzajemnych relacji do rangi partnerstwa strategicznego, otwierając nowy rozdział we… pic.twitter.com/CCvHmc3eva — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 26, 2026 Tusk, who was making the first visit by a Polish prime minister to Vietnam in 16 years, pointed to the two countries’ rapid recent economic development. “Within a single generation, Vietnam achieved middle-income status”, while “Poland recently joined the ranks of the world’s 20 largest economies”. In fact, while Poland was forecast to join the world’s 20 largest economies last year, it eventually fell narrowly short. However, it is expected to soon overtake Switzerland, the current holder of 20th place. Tusk said that, during his visit, he had often heard people say that “Poland is the Vietnam of Europe and Vietnam is the Poland of Asia”. Last year, Hưng’s predecessor, Phạm Minh Chính, became the first Vietnamese prime minister in 15 years to visit Poland. The two countries first established diplomatic relations in 1950, and both leaders emphasised Poland’s large Vietnamese community, which dates back to students arriving around that time. Speaking on Monday, Hưng noted the two countries’ strong traditional ties, adding that Vietnam always remembers and is grateful for Polish support and assistance during his country’s struggle for independence and national reunification, reports the Vietnamese News Agency (VNA). The Vietnamese are Poland's largest non-European migrant group. Photographer Zula Rabikowska, through her images and interviews, offers an insight into their experiences, identities and the challenges they face https://t.co/tsRwHINapQ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 27, 2019 The new strategic partnership agreement signed by Tusk and Hưng pledges to “bring tangible benefits to both nations and contribute to peace, stability, cooperation and prosperity”. It contains commitments to “maintain regular high-level contacts”, reduce non-tariff barriers to trade, and strengthen cooperation on defence, including trade in military equipment. On Sunday, Poland’s deputy minister for state assets, Konrad Gołota, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that negotiations are already underway for Vietnam to buy Polish Krab howitzers and Rosomak armoured fighting vehicles, among other hardware. Polish arms firm Mesko has announced the best financial results in its 100-year history. Record revenues and profits were driven in large part by international demand for Mesko's flagship Piorun air-defence system, which has proved successful in Ukraine https://t.co/Dx1yY54qCP — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2026 Tusk, pointing to Poland’s current trade deficit with Vietnam, said that Warsaw’s “priority remains a better balance in trade”. “The sectors in which the Vietnamese side is most interested, and in which we really have something to offer, are the arms industry, satellite and space cooperation, pharmaceuticals and food, especially dairy products,” he added. Tusk also announced that the number of annual Polish-Vietnamese student exchanges would rise by 250% and noted that Poland’s national carrier, LOT, would resume direct Warsaw-Hanoi flights in the first quarter of 2027. Poland is taking steps to attract more foreign students as universities face lower enrollment due to demographic decline. Turkey, South Korea, Vietnam and Uzbekistan are among the countries with which the government is cultivating stronger academic ties https://t.co/r878KqS5OV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 25, 2026 The Polish prime minister acknowledged differences between Poland and Vietnam’s approach to Russia’s war in Ukraine. Vietnam, which has long maintained close ties with Moscow, has avoided condemning the Russian invasion. But he emphasised his belief that, “because of their history, wartime experience and international relations, both Vietnam and Poland can contribute a great deal to the peace process”. Tusk’s trip to Vietnam follows a three-day visit to India, where he and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a goal of doubling bilateral trade by 2030. Poland and India's PMs have, after meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies Polish-Indian relations are "gaining speed", said @narendramodi https://t.co/iIVIkCXnvr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 22, 2026 In April, Tusk visited South Korea, upgrading Poland’s relations with the country he described as Poland’s “most important ally after the United States”, and deepened Poland’s strategic partnership with Japan on the same tour. Earlier this month, Tusk also announced plans to visit China before the end of the year. Meanwhile, President Nawrocki visited the Philippines this month as part of a bid to secure backing from Asian nations for Poland’s hoped-for membership in the G20. World.title: Two thirds of Poles support liberalising abortion law, finds new poll
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Just over two thirds of Poles support liberalising the country’s abortion law, which is among the strictest in Europe, according to a new poll. However, most do not favour introducing abortion on demand, as protesters called for during demonstrations last week. The findings come shortly after parliament approved legislation intended to ease access to abortion. But the measures face a potential veto from right-wing, opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. 🔴 Sondaż dla @rzeczpospolita: Niemal 7 na 10 Polaków chce liberalizacji przepisów ws. aborcjihttps://t.co/f7mxwygIxz — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 25, 2026 In 2020, Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means pregnancies can now only be legally terminated in two cases: where they result from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if they threaten the mother’s life or health. In a new poll by SW Research for Rzeczpospolita, a leading newspaper, a total of 67.2% of respondents said that they want to liberalise that law. However, only 37.7% favoured introducing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. Meanwhile, 29.5% preferred the softer option of returning to the situation from before the 2020 TK ruling – often referred to the “abortion compromise” in Poland – in which terminations were only available in three cases. A further 16.2% supported maintaining the current abortion law; 6.0% wanted to make the rules even tougher (which would involve removing one or both justifications for abortion that currently exist); and 10.6% said they had no opinion. The poll found that support for liberalisation of abortion was stronger among women (73.8%) than men (60.3%). The latest findings are consistent with previous polling, which tends to show that a significant majority supports liberalising the abortion law but that there is not a majority in favour of abortion on demand (although some individual polls have narrowly found such a majority). One member of Poland's likely new ruling coalition, The Left, says polls show a majority in favour of abortion on demand. In fact, they do not. And this issue is likely to be one of the hardest for the incoming government to resolve, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/4Nze9wwEC3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 20, 2023 The issue has caused significant political disputes in Poland, not only between the right-wing opposition and the more liberal ruling coalition, but also within the coalition itself. Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and one of its partners, The Left (Lewica), favour introducing abortion on demand. However, more conservative elements of the government, especially the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), prefer a return to the pre-2020 “compromise”. Much of the right-wing opposition, meanwhile, favours maintaining the status quo. However, some more moderate elements of the opposition have suggested it would be best to reverse the TK ruling and return to the “compromise”. Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws https://t.co/q7eK7mV9zr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 23, 2026 In 2024, due to disputes within his coalition, Tusk declared that it was unlikely there would be any abortion reform during the current parliamentary term due to differences within his coalition. However, last week the issue was revived, with the government’s majority in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, approving a bill that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling (but not introduce abortion on demand). It also passed another bill decriminalising providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions. After both bills go through the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but not block them, they will pass to President Nawrocki, who can sign them, veto them, or send them to the TK for assessment. Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has declared his opposition to abortion, and has vetoed a record number of government bills, it is widely expected that he will seek to block efforts to liberalise the abortion law. World.title: Time is running out for Germany to pay Polish WWII victims the compensation they deserve [Opinion]
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Philipp Fritz, Warsaw correspondent for Die Welt (which first published this article in German here) Negotiations on compensation for the still-living victims of the German occupation of Poland have been going on for years. There are some 30,000 to 50,000 such survivors, but their number dwindles every week. Berlin should act now. No “humanitarian gesture” has emerged. “The draft budget currently reflects the fact that no decision has been made,” said Josef Hinterseher, a German foreign office spokesman, at a press conference in late September. He thereby confirmed what many observers had suspected: survivors of concentration camps, ghettos and death marches, former forced workers and participants in the Warsaw Uprising who are still living in Poland will not receive any compensation, one-off payment or monthly pension from the German government. The German chancellor has announced that his country will offer support to surviving Polish victims of WW2 and will help strengthen Poland’s eastern border. However, in both cases he did not provide details of what these measures will involve in practice https://t.co/gKX6142Alo — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2024 Just a few sentences later, Hinterseher moved onto the next subject – the fact that two Russian oligarchs were to be removed from the EU’s sanctions list. Or at least, that Berlin had not been successful in opposing this decision. The fact that these two issues were dealt with publicly one after the other shows that the German government is quicker to reach a decision that makes Putin’s supporters’ lives easier than it is with victims of the Nazi terror. It is a declaration of moral bankruptcy. Warsaw and Berlin have been negotiating compensation for the last remaining victims of the German occupation of Poland for years. There are between 30,000 and 50,000 of them – aged over 90, often living alone and in poor health. Their numbers are dwindling every week. The fact that talks are taking place in Berlin ministries but without any decision being taken is met with sadness and fury in Poland. Increasingly, Poles are getting the impression that, even if the Germans manage to put up memorials, they cannot offer survivors tangible help when it is asked for. It is a common view that in Berlin the descendants of the perpetrators are simply waiting for the victims to die so that this pesky issue will sort itself out. Should that happen, those left behind will not forget, and the Germans will hardly be able to forgive themselves. Warsaw is no longer demanding war reparations from Berlin. In December 2023, Donald Tusk’s government switched to talking about “making amends”. Polish foreign minister @sikorskiradek has called on Germany to “think creatively” about compensating Poland for WWII. On a visit to Berlin, he also said that the new government would "end the cold war" waged by the former ruling PiS party against Germany https://t.co/kZ62nUuqqO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 31, 2024 This is not just splitting hairs. In so doing, Tusk put the ball in the German government’s court, giving it the chance to take action and, through a gesture recognising suffering and providing a relatively small sum of money, to offer people tangible help and do a service to the German-Polish relationship. Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz is reported to have offered Tusk a one-off payment in 2024, but Poland’s prime minister turned the sum down as insufficient. Instead, Polish diplomats are demanding monthly pensions. In any case, we are talking about a few hundred million euro: a relatively small amount compared to the equivalent of €1.3 trillion that Poland’s former ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party once demanded from Germany, and also in comparison to many other budget items – and yet still there is nothing about compensation in the budget planning. Poland is seeking $1.3 trillion in war reparations from Germany, but Berlin says the issue was legally settled long ago. Legal scholar @MPiatkowski1 examines the arguments of both sides, explains the legal context, and looks at what could come next https://t.co/xsKAY2TukS — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2022 Rumour has it that, in return for compensation, German foreign ministry officials are asking for a kind of Polish guarantee that in future there will be no more demands for reparations, or at least that at least the German gesture will receive good press in Poland. If that is true, it would be thoroughly indecent, bringing to mind an image of a perpetrator trying to buy his victim’s silence. This reflects a belief in objectification, an ugly bureaucratic mentality stemming from a system in which “work” in a ghetto counts towards statutory pension contributions, but no one can bring themselves to pay compensation. This issue can be resolved at the very top. Chancellor Friedrich Merz would have to work with the relevant ministries – the foreign office and finance ministry – to provide for compensation for the victims in the budget. This would be a belated but major and morally right gesture. If politics is too slow – time really is of the essence – then civil society should take it upon itself to show where it stands. Donations for the still living victims of the German tyranny or a fund from which survivors would receive monthly payments can be created from within society. Business can also get involved. German corporations which were guilty of, for instance, exploiting forced labourers in occupied Poland, or those that emerged from them, such as BASF, Siemens, Volkswagen, BMW and Deutsche Bank, could contribute. Poland covers almost all the costs of maintaining former Nazi-German camps on its territory. It has spent more on this than Germany has paid in compensation to Polish war victims It's time for Germany to fund preservation of the sites, argues @W_Kononczuk https://t.co/08nf4c2jMz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 25, 2026 Right now, since its state elections in September, Germany gives the impression of a country whose compass for right and wrong is broken. As of 6 October, the state parliament of Sachsen-Anhalt has as its vice-president Hans-Thomas Tillschneider of the AfD, a man who wrote on X that “the Poles have been getting on my nerves for a long time now”. In Berlin, not only did the left-wing Die Linke celebrate their electoral success with Israel haters and antisemites, they even tolerate them in their ranks. It is shameful. But now Germany, and particularly its government, has the opportunity to show that the rhetoric of responsibility for the victims is not merely empty words. That, contrary to a mood that does not support it, they are doing what is morally right. Time is running out, Germany – it’s your last chance. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, the leader of a junior party in Poland’s ruling coalition, has announced her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party, the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), in protest over a parliamentary vote on Thursday. Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) is set to remain in the government, thereby maintaining Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s parliamentary majority. However, the dispute has highlighted tensions within the ruling coalition just a year ahead of parliamentary elections at which it will seek another term. Dwukadencyjność samorządów została utrzymana. Tak zdecydował dziś Sejm. Wygraliśmy! Zmiana, której chce 75% Polaków dojdzie do skutku! Stało się to jednak pomimo głosów K15X. Koalicja, w tym niestety znaczna część posłów Polski 2050, stanęła przeciw ludziom, a za politykierskimi… — Katarzyna Pełczyńska (@Kpelczynska) October 22, 2026 Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, who serves as minister for funds and regional policy, made her decision in the wake of an unusual voting result in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, on Thursday. Another junior partner in the ruling coalition, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), had proposed a bill abolishing two-term limits for mayors. Those limits had been introduced in 2018 with the aim of reducing corruption and cronyism by preventing local officials from becoming entrenched in power. However, PSL, which has a strong presence in local politics, argues that the limits prevent effective, popular mayors from being re-elected, thereby denying voters the right to decide who they want to represent them. Although the government has a majority in the Sejm, the bill was narrowly defeated, with 213 votes in favour and 215 against, after 15 MPs from the ruling coalition joined with the right-wing opposition in voting against it. Pełczyńska-Nałęcz herself is not a member of parliament, so did not vote. Her party was split, with six MPs voting for the bill, three against, three abstaining, and three not voting at all. Aftewards, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz made clear that she opposed the bill and celebrated the fact that it was blocked. She also announced her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party. “The coalition, unfortunately including a significant portion of MPs from Poland 2050, stood against the people and in favour of backroom political deals,” she wrote. “I am leaving Donald Tusk’s government because values are more important to me than positions.” “I am leaving the party in the hands of its founder, who stepped away but then returned,” she added, referring to Poland 2050’s founder, Szymon Hołownia. “I hope that he remembers what values he came to power in the name of.” Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s decision follows a year of turmoil for Poland 2050. In September 2025, Hołownia, who had led the party since founding it in 2021, announced that he was stepping down. However, a first attempt to choose a new leader was invalidated in January after technical problems with voting. Hołownia then hinted that he may reverse course and seek to continue leading the party, though in the end that did not happen. In February, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz was chosen as the new leader. That prompted her rival candidate, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, to quit the party, taking half of its MPs with her. They formed a new group called Centrum (Centre). Both Poland 2050 and Centrum remain in the ruling coalition. However, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz has had an uneasy relationship with Tusk. Around half the MPs from Poland 2050, a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition, have split from the party and formed a new parliamentary caucus. They expressed dissatisfaction with the actions of the party's recently elected new leader, @Kpelczynska https://t.co/IqU4vE1EEe — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 18, 2026 On Friday, Tusk, who is on a state visit to India, sarcastically responded to Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s resignation by saying, “I thought she’d at least call before she left”. He admitted that “cooperation [with her] has not been the easiest for a long time”. The prime minister, however, added that he “does not think [her resignation] will have any impact on the future work of the coalition…My intuition tells me that this is her individual decision”. Hołownia, who currently serves as head of Poland 2050’s parliamentary caucus, confirmed at a press conference on Friday alongside fellow MPs that the party intends to remain in Tusk’s coalition. But he also warned that, without Poland 2050, the government would not have a parliamentary majority. W @PL_2050 dowiedzieliśmy się o decyzji @Kpelczynska z mediów. Zaskakująca rezygnacja przewodniczącej z zaufania wyborców i odpowiedzialności powierzonej jej w bardzo trudnym momencie przez ludzi (w tym mnie) zaledwie po niespełna 1/3 kadencji – dla każdej organizacji byłaby… — Szymon Hołownia (@szymon_holownia) October 22, 2026 The episode highlights the tensions within the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right and contains parties that disagree on a number of issues. It also points to the pressure smaller coalition partners are feeling ahead of next autumn’s parliamentary elections. Only parties that win at least 5% of the vote nationally can enter parliament. But Poland 2050 has been polling at around 1% and PSL is on 3%. In the 2023 election, Poland 2050 and PSL in fact stood together as an alliance called the Third Way (Trzecia Droga), helping ensure that the two parties won enough votes to enter parliament. However, in 2025, they split from one another and confirmed that they would not stand together again. PSL and Poland 2050, the two parties that make up the Third Way alliance, have confirmed that they are splitting and will stand separately at the next elections. They will, however, remain part of @donaldtusk's ruling coalition https://t.co/NduEJY25eE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2025 The fact that the bill to end two-term limits for mayors was defeated has also caused tension between PSL and its coalition partners. In the wake of yesterday’s vote, PSL immediately announced that it would push for the introduction of two-term limits for members of parliament, arguing that the same rules should apply to national and local elected representatives. The right-wing opposition has long hoped that it could tempt PSL, the most conservative element of Tusk’s coalition, to quit the government. A recent report even claimed that US President Donald Trump had, at the behest of Poland’s opposition, suggested to PSL’s leader that he leave Tusk. World.title: Protesters return to Poland’s streets demanding liberalisation of abortion law
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws. However, the demonstrations, which took place on the sixth anniversary of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) ruling that introduced a near-total abortion ban, were nowhere near the scale of the massive protests that emerged back in 2020. Było deszczowo, ale nie brakowało ludzi i emocji. Rzeszów pokazał czerwoną kartkę za aborcję rządzącej koalicji. pic.twitter.com/oJo8BiWXxS — Paweł Preneta (@pawelpreneta) October 22, 2026 In Warsaw, a few hundred people gathered in the rain outside parliament, reported broadcaster RMF. Many held up red cards, a symbol used by the protesters to warn the government that it could be thrown out of power at next year’s parliamentary elections. When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, came to power in December 2023, it pledged to liberalise the abortion laws after eight years of rule by the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party. In particular, it wanted to reverse the 2020 TK ruling, which outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means abortions can now only take place in two cases: where the pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health. However, in the almost three years since, the government has failed to introduce any new legislation on abortion. One effort to do so in 2024 collapsed amid disagreements between more conservative and liberal elements of Tusk’s coalition. Finally, earlier this week, the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, approved two abortion bills: one that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling; the other that would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions. However, those measures do not go far enough for many of those attending Tuesday’s protests, who are seeking abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. In any case, both bills approved by the Sejm are likely to be blocked by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of government bills. Nawrocki has made his opposition to abortion clear. Parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland's abortion laws One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling that introduced a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise helping women in obtaining unlawful abortions https://t.co/nVj8SQVIsv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 21, 2026 In Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, around 1,000 people attended Thursday’s protest, according to police estimates cited by the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. Among the placards and banners was one showing Tusk with an extended, Pinocchio-style nose. “It’s sad that we have to engage in this fight again,” said one of the organisers. “For so long, they ignored us, only coming when they needed votes. Now let’s show that we can’t be ignored.” In Katowice, around 300 people gathered, according to the Polish Press Agency (PAP). In Poznań, around 400 or so protesters marched to the local headquarters of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, where they placed a symbolic red card and waved banners saying “You deceived Poland”. Czerwona kartka za aborcje. W #Lodz w proteście w strugach deszczu protestuje kilkadziesiąt osób @RadioZET_NEWS pic.twitter.com/okU7QjnhFw — Mateusz Szkudlarek (@m_szkudlarek) October 22, 2026 The 2020 TK abortion ruling triggered the largest protests seen in Poland since the communist era, with hundreds of thousands of people taking to the streets. That anger is seen as having played a major role in PiS losing power to Tusk’s coalition in 2023. Opinion polls consistently show that most Poles want the abortion law to be liberalised, though there remain divisions over whether there should be a return to the pre-2021 status quo or a move even further, to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. In autumn 2027, parliamentary elections will take place, deciding who governs Poland for the next four years. Opinion polls currently show a fairly even split in support between Tusk’s coalition and the right-wing opposition. World.title: Poland charges second Georgian man over murder of Russian dissident
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has charged a 22-year-old Georgian citizen with aiding and abetting the murder of Robert Kuzovkov (who went by the name of Semyon Skrepetsky), a Russian dissident killed near his home in Poland earlier this year. The suspect, who can be named only as Makhmud A. under Polish privacy law, was captured on Monday, a day after flying into Poland. Earlier this year, another Georgian citizen, Elnur A., was detained and charged with committing the murder itself. Warto przypomnieć: ▶️ Do egzekucji doszło w poniedziałek 15 czerwca 2026 roku rano na jednym z osiedli w Białej Podlaskiej, gdzie napastnik oddał do ofiary kilka strzałów z bliskiej odległości. ▶️ Zastrzelony to 44-letni obywatel Federacji Rosyjskiej, publicznie znany z… https://t.co/r1rZfsw1Bv — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) October 22, 2026 Kuzovkov was shot five times near his home in the eastern Polish town of Biała Podlaska on 15 June. He was an artist whose work, published under the name Skrepetsky, focused on creating satirical cartoons mocking Russian leader Vladimir Putin. He had fled Russia in 2021 due to fear of political prosecution. Before his death, Kuzovkov had reported on social media that he had received death threats from supporters of Chechen leader and Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov, who had also been the subject of the artist’s satirical cartoons. After the shooting, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “everything points to this being a political assassination”. He also revealed that Kuzavkov had previously been offered protection by the Polish authorities, but “for reasons unknown” had refused. On 18 June, the Polish authorities announced they had captured Elnur A. in a hostel near Warsaw. The following day, he was charged with the murder of Kuzovkov. He has remained in custody since then. Police have detained a man suspected of carrying out the murder of Russian dissident Semyon Skrepetsky, who was shot dead near his home in Poland this week. "Everything points to this being a political assassination," says Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/z37sBBxgJn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2026 On Thursday, Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office revealed that Makhmud A. had been detained on 19 October by the Internal Security Agency (ABW) in a car park along the A2 motorway. The ABW itself confirmed that it detained the suspect after he flew to Poland from Georgia on 18 October. He had been travelling with two other Georgians, who will now be expelled from Poland and handed a 10-year re-entry ban. Makhmud A. was subsequently charged with aiding and abetting the killing of Kuzovkov by “undertaking a number of actions in the period from 1 to 11 June 2026 that made it easier for Elnur A. to commit the murder”. He is additionally charged with illegal possession of firearms and ammunition. Makhmud A. is accused of providing the perpetrator with a weapon, means of transportation and a mobile phone with an application enabling monitoring of the victim’s vehicle, a spokeswoman for the district court in Lublin told broadcaster TVN. The court has approved a period of three months’ detention for Makhmud A., with prosecutors saying that they fear he could otherwise “flee, go into hiding, or unlawfully obstruct proceedings”. Under Polish law, someone found guilty of aiding and abetting a crime can face the same punishment as the person who committed the crime itself, meaning that both suspects face potential prison sentences of between 10 years and life if found guilty. They have pleaded not guilty. A Russian man has been shot dead in Poland, with reports indicating that he was an artist whose work ridiculed Putin and that his killing appeared to be an “execution”. However, the authorities have not yet officially identified the victim or any suspects https://t.co/Zd2u7IE0A0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 15, 2026 The Polish authorities have not yet revealed who they believe was ultimately behind the murder of Kuzovkov. However, in June, Tusk said that, if Russia’s involvement was confirmed, it would be a case of “state terrorism”. In recent years, Poland has become a primary target for Russia’s campaign of so-called “hybrid warfare”, which has involved acts of sabotage, disinformation, cyberattacks, and airspace violations. Most known on-the-ground activity has been carried out not by Russian operatives themselves, but by so-called “disposable agents” hired through messaging service Telegram and paid in cryptocurrency. In some cases, Russia has used existing criminal networks to carry out such tasks. Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 Earlier this month, a trial began in Warsaw of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. Shortly afterwards, Germany detained two Turkish men at the request of Poland, which believes they were responsible for the recent arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink. Poland believes that incident was also carried out on behalf of Russia. Last year, the interior ministry claimed that Poland is facing a growing wave of “imported crime”, committed in particular by immigrants from Georgia and other former Soviet states. World.title: Poland and India aim to double trade by 2030 as PMs meet in New Delhi
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The prime ministers of Poland and India have, after a meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies. Donald Tusk’s visit, the first by a Polish prime minister to India in 16 years, follows the upgrading of bilateral ties between the two countries to a strategic partnership during Narendra Modi’s trip to Poland two years ago, which was the first by an Indian prime minister in almost five decades. During a joint press conference with Tusk on Thursday, Modi said that his Warsaw visit had acted as a catalyst for the Polish-Indian relationship to “gain speed over the last two years”. Tusk added that the two leaders had now reviewed the results of their cooperation so far and outlined priorities for the coming years. They discussed, among other things, ways to deepen economic, investment and technological ties between the two fast-growing economies. Poland’s GDP is set to grow by 3.5% this year, the second-fastest rate in the European Union, while India will see economic growth of 7%. Poland’s economy is also on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to join the G20. “The economic strength of both countries offers a wealth of opportunities for strategic partnership,” Modi said. Tusk, meanwhile, underlined that “Poland and India are countries that have much in common and nothing that divides them…[with] no conflicting interests or historical grievances.” Poland hopes that the boost to bilateral trade will come from an EU-India trade deal expected to be signed in December. The agreement is designed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on goods accounting for 96.6% of the value of EU exports to the Indian market. Tusk said Poland wanted to capitalise on the opportunities created by the deal, with the ambition of becoming “India’s gateway to Europe”. Modi expressed confidence that Poland’s and India’s “shared goal” of doubling bilateral trade by 2030 “will certainly be achieved”. “Today, trade between Poland and India totals just over $6 billion,” said Poland’s finance minister Andrzej Domański, who joined Tusk on the trip to India. “We want this trade to grow, and the conditions for that are very favourable.” However, “it is no secret that we have a significant trade deficit with India”, Domański added. Last year, Poland exported goods worth €1.4 billion to India, with machinery, mineral products and metals the largest categories. Meanwhile, it imported €4.3 billion, in particular textiles, machinery and metals. The United States wants Poland to become a full member of the G20 "as soon as possible". "Poland’s economic growth, combined with its growing leadership position in the international arena, make it an ideal participant," says the @StateDept https://t.co/OjpWly4FTw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 According to the Polish prime minister’s office, the EU-India agreement could also help increase Polish investment in India, particularly in advanced manufacturing, food processing, biotechnology and mobility. To help facilitate such investments, Tusk travelled with almost 100 Polish business representatives, hoping the visit will help them to enter the large and rapidly growing Indian market. His office described the delegation as the largest of its kind in the history of Polish-Indian relations. Modi said he was “particularly happy” with Tusk’s decision to bring a business delegation and announced plans to strengthen links between startups in both countries, including through technology hackathons for young people. The countries plan to expand cooperation in critical minerals, raw materials and coal gasification, a process that converts coal into gas for energy and industrial use. Shipbuilding, defence, space and advanced technologies are also among the priority sectors. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 The leaders also highlighted historical ties and people-to-people exchanges as a foundation for closer relations. Modi recalled the role of Indian Maharaja Jam Saheb Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji, known in Poland as the “Good Maharaja”, who provided shelter and care to around 1,000 Polish children evacuated from the Soviet Union during the Second World War. “In 2022, Poland helped our Indian students, demonstrating that same spirit of humanity,” added Modi, referring to the support Poland provided to Indian students escaping from Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion. Modi said he hoped that the ongoing Jamsaheb Memorial Youth Exchange Programme, which recently took place for the second time, will “introduce the next generation to this Polish-Indian friendship”. The strengthening of bilateral relations has also come amid a rapid rise in Indian migration to Poland in recent years. This year Indians became the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, numbering around 25,500, up almost 5% in a year.
