World.title: How will recent scandals affect Polish politics?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Aleks Szczerbiak Political scandals generate intense media attention and public outrage but rarely produce dramatic shifts in party support that they once did. They are now more likely to affect electoral outcomes indirectly by demobilising softer, less committed voters and influencing turnout, particularly among supporters of the government disappointed by its apparent underperformance and broken election promises. The hospital scandal Two high-profile political scandals dominated the Polish news agenda for much of this summer. The first centred on irregularities at Warsaw’s Southern Hospital (Szpital Południowy) and involved a young and relatively inexperienced doctor, Dawid Kacprzyk. In spite of his lack of a specialist qualification, Kacprzyk coordinated the hospital’s emergency department and reportedly earned a staggering 1.6 million złoty (€366,000) in the previous year alone. He also served as a Warsaw district councilor for the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) grouping, Poland’s main governing party led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Public outrage intensified following reports that the hospital had operated a dedicated “VIP path” or special lounge where ruling-party-linked politicians and their families were allowed faster access and medical examinations without the usual queues faced by ordinary patients. Further claims emerged, including a whistleblower surgeon alleging that supervisory failures contributed to patient deaths and of improper private business activity in the hospital morgue. Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026 For its part, KO insisted that the scandal was the personal misconduct of one former party member rather than a general problem affecting the entire healthcare system. They noted that Kacprzyk quickly resigned his council seat and hospital role, and that party-aligned Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski had dismissed the hospital board and two of his deputy mayors overseeing the city’s health services. KO argued that no specific names of preferential VIP patients had been publicly confirmed, any irregularities were being fully investigated by prosecutors and independent bodies, and political and legal accountability would follow if ethical breaches or crimes were proven. The government also pledged systemic reforms including measures to curb excessive pay for doctors. Nonetheless, the scandal struck a deep chord with the Polish public, triggering massive negative media and political fallout that aligned perfectly with the right-wing opposition’s narrative painting KO as part of a “Warsaw elite” that enjoys special privileges at the expense of ordinary citizens. The cryptocurrency scandal The second major summer scandal centred on allegations of financial impropriety and political entanglement involving Zondacrypto, once Poland’s largest crypto trading platform, that claimed over a million users but earlier this year collapsed abruptly after thousands of retail investors were unable to access their funds. However, what began as a major financial scandal escalated into political warfare, providing the government with powerful ammunition to attack the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, party-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, and the broader conservative political eco-system over payments and donations made by the crypto firm. Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026 For example, Zondacrypto sponsored the 2025 Polish edition of the Conservative Political Action Committee (CPAC) conference attended by the then-presidential candidate Nawrocki, advertised heavily with conservative media outlets such as the TV Republika television network, and made donations to foundations linked to high-ranking PiS figures such as former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro. The government also tried to entangle Nawrocki, who repeatedly vetoed its cryptocurrency regulation laws, into the scandal, arguing that he was protecting the shady interests of the industry and its political beneficiaries at the expense of ordinary Poles (the Tusk administration lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority required to overturn a presidential veto). For their part, PiS and the broader Polish right dismissed the government’s accusations as a smear campaign and sought to shift blame for the scandal onto the Tusk administration for inadequate oversight to protect investors. Figures on the right, including those connected to foundations that received money, framed these dealings as legitimate sponsorships common across the media and other organisations. The president of the Polish Olympic Committee has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a crypto firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland's Olympic team https://t.co/QPG7ejAImD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 27, 2026 PiS rejected claims that the party or associated groups received funds from the firm and defended Nawrocki’s vetoes as necessary against flawed legislation. Nonetheless, opinion polls found that most respondents linked the scandal to PiS and the right-wing opposition, providing the government with numerous attack lines to force them onto the defensive. The diminishing impact of scandals It is worth recalling how an earlier era of post-communist politics scandals possessed much greater transformative, system-altering capacity and could act as catalysts for the restructuring of the electoral landscape. For example, at the beginning of the 2000s, the so-called “Rywin scandal” was widely seen as a decisive factor in the near-destruction as a political force of the previously powerful, and then-governing, communist-successor Democratic Left Alliance (SLD). The scandal erupted in late 2002 when film producer Lew Rywin allegedly solicited a large bribe from the Agora media group, publisher of the influential liberal-left Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper, in exchange for media legislation changes while claiming to act on behalf of a “group holding power” (grupa trzymająca władzę) linked to the ruling party. A high-profile parliamentary investigative commission, sustained media focus, and a series of follow-on scandals and accumulation of allegations of deep-seated influence peddling by post-communist networks created a powerful narrative of systemic bribery and corruption, completely discrediting the SLD as a competent governing force. Having won a substantial victory in the 2001 parliamentary election, securing 41% of the votes, its support collapsed to only 11% at the next 2005 poll. This helped clear the way for the rise of the KO (originally Civic Platform)-PiS duopoly that has structured the Polish party system ever since, thereby establishing a precedent that scandals were electorally fatal transgressions. The contrast with the recent hospital and cryptocurrency scandals is instructive and illustrates a broader transformation in the relationship between political misconduct and electoral politics in Poland. Whereas in the more fluid party system of the early post-communist period a cluster of major scandals or single-event shocks could rapidly destroy dominant parties and restructure competition, now – although they still generate intense, high-octane political and media outrage – such controversies appear to slide off the main political actors with remarkably little immediate consequence. Indeed, neither of these recent scandals produced the dramatic shift in headline polling numbers that some observers, drawing on historical precedent, might have anticipated given the intensity of the media coverage. Scandal-neutralising structural shifts This change stems from three interlocking shifts in the structural dynamics of Poland’s political system. Taken together, they have substantially diminished the capacity of scandals to move headline poll numbers and trigger the kind of large-scale systemic realignments seen in an earlier era of post-communist politics. Firstly, the sheer velocity of modern political communication prevents single-issue-based scandals from sustaining public focus. In the early 2000s, a major corruption scandal could dominate the news headlines for months through concentrated media attention. The Rywin scandal unfolded through prolonged televised parliamentary commission hearings, keeping the story alive and allowing public outrage to build into a sustained narrative that slowly drained the ruling party’s legitimacy. Today, digital algorithms and the 24-hour news cycle ensure that a major story, whether about healthcare management or cryptocurrency, moves at a breathtaking pace and is overtaken rapidly as public attention moves onto the next domestic controversy, international development, or strategic counter-narrative. Seven people have been charged in relation to alleged corruption in the issuing of Polish visas to foreign nationals The scandal has engulfed the government since last week, but officials say the opposition is exaggerating the scale and nature of the case https://t.co/iHnIShb1pQ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2023 This hyper-accelerated news cycle means that even a high-profile case that generates intense short-term media coverage does not remain the dominant story for long enough to produce cumulative, system-level damage by limiting the time window in which a scandal can convert temporary disapproval into lasting shifts in voting intentions. Scandals thereby become a form of ambient “background noise” in Polish public life rather than a singular focal point for popular outrage. Secondly, and perhaps most formidably, the protective shield of deep polarisation and socio-political division renders large segments of the electorate relatively impervious to allegations against “their” side. After 2005, the Polish party system crystallised around a durable “post-transition” socio-economic divide reinforced by cultural and geopolitical fault lines. In this deeply fractured and highly polarised landscape, with large segments of the electorate embedded within hostile camps, when a scandal like the hospital crisis or cryptocurrency controversy breaks, voters interpret allegations levelled against “their” party through a tribal filter as a politically motivated hit job or the work of hostile media. So even severe scandals are shaped by, and largely confirm, existing political loyalties and rarely trigger cross-camp voter defections. This is a sharp contrast with the early 2000s, when the party system was still fluid and electoral volatility high. Our essential guide to Poland's parliamentary elections, which will take place one year from now. How does voting work? What do polls suggest the outcome will be? Which issues may animate the campaign? And what role will President Nawrocki play? https://t.co/fmdoFpBaxz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026 Thirdly, the parties themselves have become far more professional at message discipline and crisis management. Today’s parties are centralised media machines staffed by sophisticated public relations strategists who view a scandal not as a moral crisis but a communication problem requiring aggressive damage containment. Rather than allowing a controversy to fester, they immediately launch counterattacks, accusing their opponents of far greater historical or concurrent corruption, and ruthlessly enforce internal party discipline and message conformity. They also deploy well-rehearsed crisis management playbooks including: personnel sanctions; framing the problem as local or individual responsibility, or residual rather than systemic failure; ordering visible audits, investigations, or reforms to demonstrate “taking action”; and co-ordinated messaging that seeks to close the story quickly and shift the focus back onto the other side’s weaknesses or broader policy issues. Differential mobilisation, not voter persuasion Yet while polarisation and professional crisis management allow parties to survive the immediate news cycle, this does not mean that scandals have become irrelevant. Rather, their effects are more subtle and delayed through the “slow-burn” mechanism of differential turnout by selectively demobilising specific voter segments. Although in a highly polarised polity the most committed hard-core partisans are relatively immune to negative information about “their” side, soft or conditional supporters may become disillusioned, or simply less motivated, when repeated scandals reinforce a narrative of self-interest or incompetence. The net result is a gradual, cumulative, asymmetric demobilisation of one camp that does not fully register in standard inter-election voting intention surveys, which generally show expressed party preferences among those willing to answer but not necessarily the intensity of that preference or the probability that a respondent will actually turn out to vote. In Poland’s deeply polarised political landscape, the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, is unlikely to be determined by persuading voters to cross the ideological divide. Rather differential levels of electoral turnout and mobilisation are likely to be the key, specifically: whichever side’s core base is more motivated to – and peripheral, less ideologically committed “softer” supporters are demotivated from – showing up on polling day. Young Poles are bucking the international trend by turning out at a higher rate than the oldest voters in recent elections. We spoke with experts and young voters to find out more about the growing frustrations that are driving this political engagement https://t.co/y1JpYYmbjb — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025 And in a context where the election is likely to be closely fought, and relatively small differences in participation rates could prove decisive, although they may not produce dramatic changes in headline party polling preferences, scandals can still play a significant role. However, we are only likely to see the full impact of any such scandals when voters eventually go to the polls and actual turnout patterns are revealed. Given the general disillusionment with the current government and growing narrative of its underperformance and failure to deliver on its electoral promises, scandals are more likely to contribute to the demobilisation of the governing camp. It is anyway inherently more difficult for incumbent parties to mobilise their disillusioned supporters to turn out and vote than it is for motivated oppositions to rally their base to oust them. Indeed, revealed voter preferences in the summer 2025 presidential election – when Nawrocki won an unexpected victory over Trzaskowski, the ruling party-backed favourite – and more recently the severe setback for KO in the Kraków mayoral by-election, suggest that government supporters are already showing greater reluctance to vote. So, while their effects are routinely neutralised by fast-moving news, tribal shielding and professional spin, scandals still matter in Polish politics, although the battleground has shifted from voter persuasion to differential mobilisation. World.title: Thirty Seconds to Mars to Play Prague in 2027 With Special Album Tour
World.content:
Thirty Seconds to Mars will return to Prague on May 18, 2027, for a concert at the O2 arena.

The Jared and Shannon Leto-led band will revisit two of its best-known albums, A Beautiful Lie and This Is War, as part of a special world tour.

The American rock band will perform without an opening act, with the show expected to last approximately two hours. Tickets start at CZK 1,500, excluding ticketing fees, and VIP packages will also be available.



The concert is part of the band’s A Beautiful Lie vs This Is War tour, which focuses on two records that helped establish Thirty Seconds to Mars as a major name in alternative rock.

Tickets will be available through Ticketmaster and Ticketportal from October 30, 2026, at 10 a.m. Fan club members will have access to a presale beginning October 27 at 10 a.m. Live Nation, Spotify and O2 presales will follow on October 29 at 10 a.m.

Two albums that defined the band’s sound

Released in 2005, A Beautiful Lie marked a turning point in the band’s career, bringing its music to a much wider international audience. The album features some of Thirty Seconds to Mars’ best-known songs, including The Kill, From Yesterday and the title track.

The follow-up, This Is War, arrived in 2009 and expanded that sound. Tracks such as Kings and Queens, This Is War and Closer to the Edge became signature songs, helping the band reach a broader audience.

From alternative rock to global tours

Led by brothers Jared Leto, the band’s vocalist, and Shannon Leto, its drummer, the group continued to develop its sound on Love, Lust, Faith and Dreams in 2013 and America in 2018. The latter included the singles Walk on Water and Rescue Me.

In 2023, the band released its sixth studio album, It’s the End of the World but It’s a Beautiful Day, exploring a different musical direction while maintaining its focus on melody and emotional themes.

The band has also received several MTV awards and a Billboard Music Award. Its touring history includes a Guinness World Records recognition for the longest concert tour.

The 2027 tour will take Thirty Seconds to Mars across Europe, the United Kingdom, South Africa and other destinations. Its Prague stop will bring the band’s anniversary celebrations and catalogue of established hits to the Czech capital for a show centred on two of its most influential albums.

World.title: Prague Tram Disruptions Will Affect Six Lines During Autumn School Break
World.content:
Prague tram passengers will face several service changes during the autumn school break, including a five-day suspension between I. P. Pavlova and Otakarova.

The changes come as Prague Public Transit Company adjusts services for the school holidays and carries out track repairs. Passengers travelling through Nusle, Vršovice and Žižkov should check their routes before setting off.

Six Tram Lines Affected by Track Repairs

Tram services between I. P. Pavlova and Otakarova will be suspended in both directions from approximately 4:30 a.m. on Wednesday, October 28, until midnight on Sunday, November 1.



Tram line 13 will be suspended entirely during this period. Lines 2 and 21 will be combined into one route, with trams running from Petřiny to Karlovo náměstí before continuing as line 21 to Slivenec. The same arrangement will apply in the opposite direction.

Other services will follow diverted routes. Tram line 6, travelling from Nádraží Holešovice, will run from Karlovo náměstí via Albertov, Ostrčilovo náměstí and Divadlo Na Fidlovačce to Otakarova, where it will rejoin its regular route.

Line 11 will be diverted from I. P. Pavlova via Náměstí Míru, Čechovo náměstí, Nádraží Vršovice and Otakarova. It will return to its usual route at Náměstí Bratří Synků and continue towards Spořilov.

Night tram line 96, which connects Petřiny with Spořilov, will also be diverted. It will run via Náměstí Míru, Čechovo náměstí, Nádraží Vršovice, Otakarova and Náměstí Bratří Synků.

A replacement bus service, X11, will operate during the day between Nádraží Vršovice and Sarajevská. It will also stop at Fričova, Divadlo Na Fidlovačce and Otakarova.

Žižkov Tram Restrictions to Last Until December 18

Separate restrictions in Žižkov have been in effect since October 11, with tram services suspended in both directions between Nákladové nádraží Žižkov and Ohrada. The disruption is scheduled to continue until December 18.

Tram lines 9 and 10 currently terminate at Nákladové nádraží Žižkov and are linked to each other. Lines 16 and 34 have been cancelled, while lines 5, 7, 11, 95 and 98 are operating on modified routes.

Three additional tram services have been introduced to help passengers travel through the affected area. Line 30 connects Sídliště Ďáblice with Spojovací via Palmovka and Ohrada. Line 37 runs from Lehovec to Spojovací, also serving Palmovka and Ohrada. Night line 90 connects Vozovna Kobylisy with Spojovací via the same two stops.

Replacement buses are running along the suspended section. Daytime services X9 and X95 connect Nákladové nádraží Žižkov, Biskupcova, Ohrada and Vozovna Žižkov. Night bus X98 serves Olšanské hřbitovy, Želivského, Nákladové nádraží Žižkov, Biskupcova, Ohrada and Vozovna Žižkov.

World.title: The Piano Bar Prague Combines Dining and Live Music at Savarin Palace
World.content:
Located inside Savarin Palace on Na Příkopě, The Piano Bar Prague brings together a restaurant, cocktail bar and live music venue under one roof.

The concept offers an alternative to an evening spent moving between different venues in the city centre.



The venue combines dinner, drinks and live performances, with separate spaces for dining, socialising and dancing.

Dining and Cocktails in One Venue

The restaurant is led by Executive Chef Ari Munandar, whose previous experience includes working at Mandarin Oriental, Hilton and SaSaZu. The menu focuses on contemporary cuisine, with an emphasis on ingredients, flavour and presentation.

Cocktails are also a central part of the offering, with the bar serving guests throughout the evening. The layout allows visitors to move from the dining room to the bar or lounge without leaving the venue.

Live Music and Dancing

Live music is another key element of The Piano Bar Prague. The program ranges from piano performances to live bands, depending on the evening.

While some guests may visit for dinner or drinks, the venue also caters to those looking for a later night out. The main bar and dance floor provide space for music and dancing, while the lounge offers a quieter setting for conversation.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Piano Bar Prague (@thepianobar_prague)

The different areas are designed to accommodate a range of occasions, from dinners for two and gatherings with friends to private celebrations and corporate events.

A Historic Setting in Prague 1

The Piano Bar Prague is located in Savarin Palace, a historic complex on Na Příkopě, one of Prague’s main shopping streets. Its central location makes it accessible to both residents and visitors staying in the city centre.

World.title: Smartwings Launches Direct Flights Between Prague and Lisbon
World.content:
Smartwings has launched a new direct route between Prague and Lisbon, with flights operating three times a week.

The first service departed on Friday, October 23, with every seat occupied, according to airline spokeswoman Vladimíra Dufková.

The new connection links Prague with the Portuguese capital on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays.



The route adds Lisbon to Smartwings’ existing scheduled services to Portugal, which already include Porto, Funchal on the island of Madeira, and Ponta Delgada in the Azores.

Flights are operated by Boeing 737 aircraft with a capacity of 189 passengers. The journey from Prague to Lisbon takes approximately three hours and 40 minutes, while the return flight takes three hours and 25 minutes.

One-way tickets start at CZK 2,940. The fare includes one piece of cabin baggage measuring up to 55 × 40 × 23 centimetres and weighing no more than eight kilograms.

Smartwings to Resume Prague–Bucharest Flights

Smartwings will also resume scheduled flights between Prague and Bucharest on November 26. The service will operate four times a week, on Tuesdays, Thursdays, Fridays and Sundays.

One-way fares for the Romanian capital start at CZK 2,470, including cabin baggage, Dufková said.

The two routes form part of Smartwings’ winter 2026–2027 flight schedule, which includes direct services from Czech airports to 39 destinations. The Smartwings Group will also operate flights from Poland, Slovakia and Hungary during the winter season.

World.title: Grand Jour de Champagne Returns to Prague With 30 French Producers
World.content:
Prague will host the 19th edition of Grand Jour de Champagne from November 5, bringing together French champagne producers, exclusive tastings and a gala dinner prepared by a two-Michelin-starred chef.

The festival’s main event, the Champagne Exhibition, will take place at Kaiserštejn Palace in Malá Strana, featuring around 50 cuvées from more than 18 champagne houses.

Visitors can sample different styles, meet producers and discover brands including Louis Roederer, Piper-Heidsieck, Philipponnat, Telmont and G. H. Mumm. Selected bottles will also be available to purchase at special festival prices.



The exhibition will run in two sessions, from 14:00 to 17:00 and 17:00 to 20:00. Tickets cost CZK 2,180.

Two-Michelin-Star Chef to Prepare Gala Dinner

Another highlight will be the Champagne Gala Banquet at Prague’s Municipal House, where French chef Valentin Loison will prepare a five-course tasting menu paired with champagnes from selected producers.

Loison, 32, earned two Michelin stars at his restaurant Bulle d’Osier in Langres, France, within approximately 18 months. The evening will also feature a musical performance by Czech violist Jitka Hosprová.

The gala begins at 20:00, with individual tickets priced at CZK 9,400.

Exclusive Tastings and Masterclasses

The festival programme also includes specialist tastings and masterclasses for champagne enthusiasts.

One session will focus on Louis Roederer’s Cristal, featuring vintages including 2006 and 2016, at the Zlatá Praha restaurant. Other events will explore the Meunier grape variety and pair foie gras with a rare 1996 de Venoge Blanc de Blancs Magnum.

Some masterclasses are limited to just 12 participants.

Tickets

Tickets and the full programme are available here. For additional information, contact [email protected].

Readers registering through Prague Morning can enter the code PM2026 in the designated field after their surname to help organisers identify their registration. Priority consideration is subject to ticket availability.

World.title: Beyond Tacos: Meet the Founders of La Casa Azteca in Prague
World.content:
La Casa Azteca brings traditional Mexican food and cultural celebrations to Prague.

Run by Miguel, originally from Mexico, and Modar, who comes from Syria, the restaurant draws on their experience in the city’s Mexican food scene while introducing customers to dishes and traditions from beyond the familiar.

Two routes to Prague

Modar arrived for work as a structural engineer. While learning Czech, he found himself working in a Mexican restaurant, where he became interested in the food and the business.

“I fell in love with the Mexican concept and the Mexican food, so I had to stay,” he says.



Miguel, meanwhile, had already spent years living abroad, including five years in Montreal and time in the United States. He had always wanted to experience different countries, and Prague was another step in that direction.

Still, the city felt unlike anywhere he had been before. He remembers seeing a tram when he first arrived and feeling as though he had landed in a fairy-tale country.

The two eventually met through Prague’s Mexican restaurant scene, around nine years ago. What started as a shared connection to Mexican food eventually grew into a business partnership.

Keeping Mexican food authentic — and introducing it to Prague

At La Casa Azteca, Miguel and Modar want to keep the food close to what customers would find in Mexico, combining street food with dishes more commonly associated with traditional restaurants. The menu includes mole, chiles, flautas and tacos, with each dish bringing its own flavours and character.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Azteca Cocina & Bar (@azteca_prague)

Keeping those flavours in Prague, however, sometimes means working with ingredients that are harder to find locally. Herbs commonly used in Mexico can be difficult to source, while ingredients such as tortillas and chillies can also be more expensive. Some elements therefore have to be substituted without losing the character of the dish.

They have also had to navigate some of the expectations Czech customers bring with them. Part of that process has been showing customers that Mexican cuisine goes well beyond the familiar image of tacos, enchiladas and very spicy dishes.

“People think that in Mexico we are always eating spicy food,” Miguel says. “It’s true, but not all our food is tacos and enchiladas. We eat normal food too — pasta, a piece of meat with rice.”

The same approach extends to drinks. Mezcal is still relatively unfamiliar to many Czech customers, so the team uses the restaurant as a place to explain where it comes from, how it is produced and how different varieties can taste.

“It’s something that people can explore,” Miguel says. “They appreciate the taste. They appreciate the liquor. It’s not just a party drink.”

Building a business abroad

Although Miguel and Modar have around nine years of experience in Prague’s Mexican restaurant scene, La Casa Azteca is a newer chapter. The current project, which combines a restaurant with a neighbouring service window, has been running for around six months.

Starting their own business required learning how to navigate the Czech system from scratch. “We had to learn so much about running a business in the Czech Republic,” Modar says. “Everything is very well organized and very well thought out, so you really need to be prepared. You have to pay attention to every detail and every small thing.”

There was also the risk that came with building something abroad, without the same safety net they might have had at home. “I think it’s harder to take risks when you’re living abroad because, if you fall, there’s no one to pick you up. The stress is greater. But at the same time, you know there’s no way back, so you have to make it work,” Modar says.

Celebrating Mexican culture in Prague

Beyond the menu, Miguel and Modar celebrate Mexican traditions through events at the restaurant. After marking Mexican Independence Day in September, they are now preparing for the Day of the Dead, with Mexican dancers, live mariachi music, decorations and special dishes planned for the end of October.

World.title: Turn a Sleepover Into a Special Memory With atelier stories
World.content:
A sleepover with friends can be one of those childhood moments that children remember for years.

But for parents, organising one often means buying decorations, preparing bedding, rearranging furniture and dealing with the cleanup afterwards.

Prague-based atelier stories takes care of everything, bringing a fully styled teepee sleepover directly to the family home. Parents choose the theme, date and number of children, while the company handles the delivery, setup, styling and collection.

Founded by Jana Hrochová, who has a background in event production, organisation and guest services, atelier stories was created around a simple idea: making special moments for children without turning them into another project for parents.



The concept works for birthdays, but it doesn’t have to be a special occasion. A weekend with friends, a school holiday or simply an evening when children want to do something different can become a small adventure at home.

Families can choose from three themes: Mermaid World, Wizard Academy and SPA Night. Each setup features coordinated colours, soft textiles, fairy lights and themed accessories. The result is a playful sleeping space designed to appeal to children while remaining stylish enough to fit comfortably into the family home.

Every booking includes the equipment and styling, with teepees assembled and individual sleeping spaces prepared with mattresses, bedding, pillows, blankets, decorative cushions and other details suited to the chosen theme. Optional extras include creative kits, themed activities, photography and Instax memories.

The service is designed to make the experience as easy as possible for parents. There is no need to buy decorations, assemble teepees, wash bedding or find storage space for the equipment afterwards. Once the sleepover is over, atelier stories returns to dismantle the setup, pack everything away and collect it.

Quality, comfort and hygiene are central to the service. The equipment and textiles are cleaned and prepared between bookings, and each sleeping space is carefully arranged to ensure children have a comfortable place to settle in for the night.

Families can book a sleepover for one night or an entire weekend. Prices start at CZK 3,490 for two children for one night, or CZK 4,900 for two children for a full weekend, from Friday to Monday. Both options include the equipment, styling, setup and collection, with delivery within Prague included free of charge.

The service can also make a thoughtful gift from grandparents. Instead of another toy or physical present, a gift voucher gives grandchildren an experience to look forward to.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by atelier stories | tématické přespávačky pro děti (@atelierstories.cz)

Vouchers can cover a complete sleepover or contribute towards one, allowing the family to choose the theme and date later. They are valid for one year and delivered by email within 24 hours of payment.

While at-home sleepovers remain the main focus, atelier stories also creates children’s lounges and play areas for weddings and other events, giving younger guests a dedicated space to play and relax while adults enjoy the occasion.

World.title: Czechia Has the EU’s Lowest Poverty Risk Rate, Eurostat Finds
World.content:
Czechia has the lowest share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion in the European Union, with 12% of its population affected, according to 2025 data from Eurostat.

The figure is well below the EU average of 21%, meaning that around one in five people across the bloc face the risk of poverty or social exclusion. Among children, the proportion rises to one in four.



The EU measure covers people whose incomes fall below the poverty-risk threshold, those experiencing severe material and social deprivation, and those living in households with very low work intensity.

Poland also records a relatively low rate, at 15%, followed by the Netherlands and Slovenia at 16%. Slovakia, Belgium, Finland and Cyprus each report 17%, while Austria stands at 19%.

At the other end of the scale, Bulgaria has the highest share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, at 29%. Greece follows at 28%, and Romania at 27%. Lithuania and Spain each report 26%, while Latvia stands at 25%. Italy records 23%, Estonia 22%, and Germany, France and Croatia each match the EU average of 21%.

EU Moves to Strengthen Anti-Poverty Measures

The figures come as European institutions seek to strengthen measures to reduce poverty and social exclusion across the bloc.

Earlier this year, the European Parliament called for more decisive action, stressing that poverty undermines human dignity and that everyone should have access to basic necessities.

In May, the European Commission adopted the EU’s first-ever anti-poverty strategy, setting out measures intended to prevent and reduce poverty across member states.

The strategy addresses several areas, including access to affordable housing, employment opportunities and support for families raising children. It also seeks to remove barriers to employment and tackle in-work poverty, which affects people who have jobs but still struggle to make ends meet.

Housing exclusion and the availability of social and affordable housing are among its priorities. The strategy also focuses on child poverty, support for older people through adequate pensions and opportunities to remain in employment, and efforts to combat discrimination and stigma.

World.title: Hungary signs EEA and Norway Grants deal after missing out on previous funding cycle
World.content:
Hungary has officially secured approximately HUF 92 billion (EUR 250.4 million) in funding through the European Economic Area (EEA) and Norway Grants for 2021–2028, following an agreement signed in Budapest with Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein.

Hungary to secure a huge amount of funds

The deal makes funding available for projects ranging from environmental initiatives and healthcare to local development, culture and Roma integration. The agreement was signed by Hungarian, Norwegian, Icelandic and Liechtenstein representatives at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Hungary’s Rural and Settlement Development Minister, Viktória Lőrincz, and Finance Minister András Kármán attended the signing alongside Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide, Icelandic Foreign Ministry state secretary Martin Eyjólfsson and Liechtenstein’s ambassador, Pascal Schafhauser. The agreement follows renewed negotiations initiated by Hungary’s new government. Foreign minister Anita Orbán helped restart discussions in September.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Where will the money go?

Of the EUR 254.1 million available, the largest allocation — EUR 80 million — is earmarked for the green transition. A further EUR 42 million will support local development, while EUR 25 million is allocated to healthcare. Culture and Roma integration programmes will each receive EUR 16 million.

Another EUR 20 million will fund institutional cooperation and capacity-building, while EUR 9.4 million is assigned to the Fund for Bilateral Relations. The Civil Fund will receive EUR 26 million, with EUR 19.7 million reserved for other tasks and administrative costs.

The Civil Fund will be administered, monitored and supervised under the responsibility of the donor countries. A consortium led by the Ökotárs Foundation, alongside the Autonómia Foundation and Carpathian Foundation–Hungary, was selected to manage the fund.

Finance Minister Kármán promised that spending procedures would be public and transparent, adding that not a single euro would be lost. He also said Hungary would contribute approximately HUF 12 billion (more than EUR 32.6 million) from its own budget to co-finance the programmes.

More on foreign affairs: Reuters report claims Hungary could drop Russia’s Rosatom from Paks nuclear project

Why Hungary missed out last time

The agreement is a significant step forward from the previous funding period, when Hungary received none of the nearly EUR 215 million allocated to it — approximately HUF 77 billion at the time. The dispute with the previous Fidesz government centred on the management of the Civil Fund.

The Hungarian authorities and donor countries failed to agree on an independent organisation to distribute grants to civil society groups, leaving the broader funding package unavailable. Kármán criticised the previous administration for allowing the funding to be lost rather than accepting independent oversight of the civil grants.

Norwegian Foreign Minister Eide welcomed the new agreement, saying cooperation, the rule of law and confidence in democracy were essential to Europe’s future. He said Norway had approached Hungary’s new government after the April election to restore relations and reach an agreement.

The funding is intended to support economic and social development across Hungary while strengthening cooperation between the participating countries. Its impact will now depend on transparent allocation and the effective delivery of projects over the coming years.

World.title: Ukraine mocks Orbán’s UN chief rumours, Tusk calls them ‘funny’
World.content:
Ukraine’s foreign minister has taken a swipe at former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán over reports that the US is backing him for the United Nations’ top job, while Poland’s Donald Tusk has also dismissed the rumours with a smile.

Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has mocked the possibility of Viktor Orbán becoming the next United Nations secretary-general, making a pointed reference to the former Hungarian leader’s record of blocking EU decisions. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has also reacted to the reports, describing them as amusing.

The comments followed a report by The Wall Street Journal that the Trump administration is encouraging Orbán to enter the race to replace António Guterres, whose second five-year term as UN secretary-general ends on 31 December.

Details: Could Viktor Orbán become UN Secretary-General? Trump administration reportedly wants him to

The UN was no friend of Orbán – So why is he now linked to its top job?

Ukraine’s foreign minister takes a swipe at Orbán

In a post on X, Sybiha sarcastically suggested that Orbán could put his political skills to good use on the international stage.

“I am certain that Viktor Orbán, as UN Secretary-General, would put to good use the masterful veto and blackmail skills he has developed over years of derailing major EU decisions,” the Ukrainian foreign minister wrote.

He added that Ukraine could share its experience with the rest of the world of taking Orbán out for coffee at the right moment.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha and Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán. Photo: X (Twitter) / Andrii Sybiha

The remark referred to an incident in December 2023, when Orbán left the European Council meeting room during a vote on opening EU accession negotiations with Ukraine. At the suggestion of then-German Chancellor Olaf Scholz, the Hungarian prime minister went for coffee while the other EU leaders approved the move.

I am certain that Viktor Orbán, as UN Secretary-General, would put to good use the masterful veto and blackmail skills he has developed over years of derailing major EU decisions. We can share with the rest of the world our great experience of taking him out for coffee at the right moment. — Andrii Sybiha 🇺🇦 (@andrii_sybiha) October 26, 2026

Tusk laughs off the reports

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also responded to the speculation when questioned by Politico on Monday. According to the outlet, Tusk smiled when asked about the possibility of Orbán becoming the next UN chief and said he had not heard about the proposal.

“Just a moment ago, he was a candidate for president of the European Commission. This seems to me just as funny as that first rumour,” Tusk said.

His remark referred to an earlier rumour about Orbán becoming president of the European Commission, which Tusk also treated with scepticism.

Donald Tusk. Photo: POLISH PRIME MINISTER’S OFFICE / HANDOUT

Could Orbán become the next UN secretary-general?

The speculation began after The Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration supports Orbán as a potential candidate for the UN’s top diplomatic position. According to the report, the former Hungarian leader could emerge as a compromise candidate with support from the United States, Russia and China.

Orbán was one of US President Donald Trump’s closest political allies in the European Union. Trump publicly endorsed him, calling him a “true friend”, while US Vice President JD Vance travelled to Hungary to campaign for him ahead of the April 2026 election.

However, Orbán suffered a decisive defeat in that election, losing power to Péter Magyar’s Tisza Party. His departure from office was welcomed in Brussels, where his repeated clashes with EU institutions had made him a controversial figure.

A potential UN candidacy would also mark a striking reversal of Orbán’s earlier position. In 2018, he criticised defeated politicians who took up positions at the United Nations, describing their ambitions as “aberrant”.

World.title: Russia says Viktor Orbán remains eligible for UN top job but rules out nominating him
World.content:
Former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán remains eligible to be nominated as the next United Nations secretary-general, according to a senior Russian diplomat, despite Moscow saying that neither Russia, the United States nor China will formally put his name forward.

Viktor Orbán to lead the United Nations?

Alexander Alimov, Russia’s deputy foreign minister, told reporters in Moscow on Monday that the nomination process remained open. His comments followed a report by The Wall Street Journal claiming that US President Donald Trump’s administration had proposed Viktor Orbán for the top UN position and encouraged him to consider running. “There are no restrictions; we do not rule out the emergence of other candidates,” Alimov said, according to Russian news agency Interfax.

However, he stressed that Viktor Orbán’s potential candidacy had not been discussed by the UN Security Council and that Russian officials had learnt of the reported initiative through the media. “Neither Russia, nor the United States, nor China will nominate Orbán, because we are permanent members of the UN Security Council and we do not nominate anyone for the post of UN secretary-general,” Alimov said. He added that those behind the reported proposal would need to find a country willing to submit the nomination. If that happened, Moscow would consider the possibility of discussions and consultations, he said.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Regional rotation could complicate Orbán’s chances

Alimov also pointed to the informal principle of geographical rotation in selecting the UN secretary-general. According to the diplomat, the next leader should come from Latin America or the Caribbean. He said Russia would consider the available options if candidates from that region could not be agreed upon. Alimov also noted that a country does not necessarily have to nominate one of its own citizens, meaning a Latin American or Caribbean state could theoretically put Orbán forward.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday, citing sources from three countries, that the Trump administration had raised the idea with Viktor Orbán. The report suggested that the proposal could have support from Russia and China, although Alimov’s subsequent remarks made clear that none of the three permanent Security Council members intended to nominate him directly. Orbán’s position on the reported offer remains unclear. The Hungarian politician did not respond to the newspaper’s request for comment, according to the reports.

Stay up-to-date: The UN was no friend of Viktor Orbán – So why is he now linked to its top job?

Standing in a big line to replace António Guterres

The current secretary-general, António Guterres, is due to complete his second five-year term on 31 December. Several figures are already being considered as potential successors, including International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi, former Ecuadorian foreign minister María Fernanda Espinosa Garcés and former Costa Rican vice-president Rebeca Grynspan.

Other reported contenders include Guyana’s UN ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett and Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh, who entered the race last week amid a deadlock in preliminary Security Council ballots. Any Orbán candidacy would therefore face both procedural and political hurdles. For now, his nomination remains a possibility reported in the media rather than a confirmed development in the UN selection process.

World.title: Former service villa of Hungary’s defence minister cost EUR 1 million more than previously estimated
World.content:
Renovation work on a luxury service villa formerly used by Hungary’s current Defence Minister, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, cost around HUF 650 million (EUR 1.77 million) despite the property already being largely complete, according to contracts obtained after more than a year of legal proceedings.

Defence minister’s former service villa cost millions more than estimated

The documents, reported by 24.hu on Monday, detail 19 construction contracts relating to the Dunakeszi property, which the minister resided in. They reveal substantial cost increases compared with initial estimates, with some individual items allegedly priced at up to 20 times their estimated market value.

The Ministry of Defence’s company, HM EI Zrt., commissioned the work. An architectural firm had reportedly assessed the building as being 75–80 per cent complete, estimating that finishing it would cost approximately HUF 250 million (EUR 680,000). Instead, the documented completion costs reached around HUF 640 million (EUR 1.74 million), while the total additional spending was reported at approximately HUF 650 million.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Millions spent on landscaping and construction

The contracts show that nearly HUF 500 million (EUR 1.36 million) was paid to contractors for construction work, including building services, electrical installations, roofing, terrace work and interior finishing. Material costs exceeded HUF 145 million (EUR 395,000). Among the largest individual items were HUF 39.6 million (almost EUR 108,000) for plants and HUF 35.5 million (EUR 96,700) for garden furnishings. The project also included HUF 25.6 million (almost EUR 70,000) for fence components and related materials, as well as HUF 17.3 million (more than EUR 47,000) for basalt panels.

One particularly striking example concerns the installation of glass-fibre mesh in the building’s exterior insulation. According to 24.hu, the agreed labour rate was HUF 38,790 (EUR 105.62) per square metre, excluding VAT, compared with an expert’s estimate of approximately HUF 1,600 (EUR 4.36) per square metre. The report said this item alone represented an alleged overpayment of HUF 18 million (EUR 49,000). The contracts do not indicate that Ruszin-Szendi personally directed the construction work. They were signed on behalf of the state by HM EI Zrt.’s chief executive or other company officials.

Stay up-to-date: The UN was no friend of Orbán – So why is he now linked to its top job?

Political controversy and unanswered questions

The property attracted public attention after minister Ruszin-Szendi, a former chief of the Hungarian Defence Staff, joined the opposition Tisza Party, which entered government in April and appointed him defence minister. The previous Fidesz government had highlighted the villa amid political disputes over luxury spending.

Hungary’s Government Control Office previously published a report identifying what it described as wasteful purchases for the property, including furnishings and equipment. That review did not examine the more expensive construction work now detailed in the contracts. A police investigation into suspected abuse of office was also reported to be ongoing following a complaint by former Fidesz MP Gyula Budai.

Defence minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi has previously said the ministry’s background institution handled the property’s purchase and management so it could serve as official accommodation for the chief of the defence staff. He said he was neither the buyer nor the owner. The newly disclosed contracts raise further questions about the cost of the project, but do not in themselves establish criminal wrongdoing.
