World.title: The UN was no friend of Orbán – So why is he now linked to its top job?
World.content:
Could Hungary’s former prime minister go from criticising the United Nations to leading it? A reported US-backed proposal involving Russia and China has raised questions about Orbán’s international ambitions, his past clashes with the UN and what such a move could mean for Hungarian politics.

Viktor Orbán becoming the next United Nations Secretary-General would be one of the most unexpected turns in his political career. According to The Wall Street Journal, the Trump administration has encouraged the former Hungarian prime minister to consider the position, with Russia and China reportedly open to supporting him. No formal nomination has been announced.

Political analyst Gábor Török described the prospect as a potential turning point for Hungarian politics, arguing that it could reshape Fidesz’s position, Orbán’s domestic role, the Tisza government’s strategy and the debate over accountability. He cautioned, however, that it was too early to draw firm conclusions.

Details: Could Viktor Orbán become UN Secretary-General? Trump administration reportedly wants him to

Why would Orbán be an interesting choice?

The most interesting aspect of the reported proposal is the suggestion that Washington, Moscow and Beijing could back the same candidate despite their competing interests.

The former Hungarian prime minister has cultivated relationships with both Donald Trump and Russia’s Vladimir Putin, while Hungary has also pursued closer economic ties with China. Support from all three powers would therefore be a remarkable diplomatic development, if confirmed.

Viktor Orbán and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

The Wall Street Journal portrays Orbán as an appealing figure for US conservatives because of his positions on immigration, liberal organisations and political power. Supporters of the idea could argue that his experience as a long-serving head of government would bring political authority to a role often associated with career diplomats.

Yet the same political record could make him a divisive choice, particularly among countries that have clashed with his government over democratic standards, the rule of law and relations with Russia.

Orbán once criticised politicians who sought UN jobs

There is a particularly striking contradiction in Orbán’s own words. According to 444.hu, in a July 2018 interview with Hungarian public radio, he criticised politicians who, having failed at home, sought to continue their careers at the UN. Discussing the UN’s Global Compact for Migration, Hungary’s withdrawal from negotiations and concerns about international influence over migration policy, he said the organisation was not designed to function as a world government.

Orbán argued that the UN’s purpose was to provide a place where countries with conflicting interests could communicate and resolve disputes. However, he warned against what he saw as attempts to use international agreements to shape national migration policies.

Those remarks would inevitably resurface if he were to pursue the organisation’s top job. The Secretary-General must work within the UN Charter and represent an institution whose purpose is international cooperation, including between governments with sharply different political systems.

Why the appointment might not happen

Even if the reported diplomatic initiative is genuine, support from the United States, Russia and China would not automatically secure Orbán the position.

The UK and France, which are also permanent members of the Security Council, could veto a candidate. The council must recommend a secretary-general before the General Assembly can appoint one.

Orbán’s political record could also prove an obstacle. A candidate perceived as too closely aligned with particular governments could struggle to gain broader confidence among UN member states. The role requires not only political leadership but also the ability to mediate international disputes and maintain the organisation’s credibility.

The selection process is already underway, and Orbán has not been formally nominated, according to the information currently available.

What would it mean for Hungarian politics?

A move to the UN would potentially transform Orbán’s role after his defeat in Hungary’s April 2026 parliamentary election. Rather than remaining the central figure of the opposition, he could take on an international position with a global profile.

As Török noted, the consequences could extend beyond Fidesz itself, affecting the Tisza government’s political messaging, the future of the Hungarian right and debates over accountability for decisions made during Orbán’s years in office.

World.title: River Danube contaminated by sewage water for days in Budapest
World.content:
Sewage-smelling water flowed into the Danube in northern Budapest for at least three days before the leak was stopped, raising concerns about water pollution and potential health risks. The cause of the discharge near Óbuda remains under investigation.

Sewage flowed into the Danube for days

The pollution was first noticed on 21 October near the K Bridge on Mozaik Street, close to the entrance to Hajógyári Island in Budapest’s third district. Witnesses reported cloudy water with a strong sewage odour pouring continuously from a drainage outlet into the river. Initial reports estimated that several tens of litres were entering the Danube every second, reports Blikk.

Local residents reported the incident to the Budapest Sewage Works (Fővárosi Csatornázási Művek), the company responsible for the capital’s sewerage network. The utility responded on Saturday, inspecting the area around the Mozaik Street sewage pumping station and successfully stopping the discharge. However, the precise cause has not yet been established. According to the company’s response, a substantially smaller quantity of treated water was flowing into the Danube following the intervention.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Investigators examine possible causes

Water management engineers have suggested that the discharge could have originated from a damaged sewer or a property not connected to the public sewerage network. Another possibility is that wastewater from buildings constructed after the area’s last major sewerage developments was never properly connected to the system.

No major public sewer construction or renovation project has taken place around Mozaik Street in recent years, according to the reports. Between 2013 and 2015, however, approximately 19 kilometres of sewerage infrastructure were renewed in Budapest’s third district as part of the Budapest Complex Integrated Wastewater Management Project.

The location of the discharge has prompted particular concern because the Danube supplies water to communities further downstream. Although the outlet was reportedly well below the capital’s drinking-water abstraction sites, residents warned that pollution entering the river could affect other settlements. It remains unclear whether the water contained untreated domestic sewage, and the investigation has yet to establish the source of the contamination.

More on the capital: Belgrade-Budapest trains to launch in December – Direct Vienna services also planned

Health risks from contaminated water

Untreated domestic wastewater can contain pathogens originating from human waste and contaminated household water. Exposure through swallowing polluted water or direct contact can cause gastrointestinal infections and other illnesses.

Zoltán Vincze, a specialist engineer in municipal wastewater management, warned that sewage can carry pathogens associated with diseases including hepatitis A and E, typhoid and cholera. The actual health risk from this particular incident, however, has not been established. While the immediate flow has reportedly been stopped, questions remain about what caused the leak, how long the contamination lasted and whether further action will be needed to prevent a similar incident.

Read also: Budapest’s Buda Castle could ban Airbnb rentals completely from 2028

World.title: New motorway connecting Hungary to southern neighbour is only one approval away
World.content:
A planned motorway extension in southern Hungary could create a new road connection with Croatia, potentially boosting regional trade and tourism. While preparations are reportedly advancing on the Croatian side, the Hungarian section of the proposed M60 motorway still depends on decisions by the government.

New motorway could connect Hungary to Croatia

Direct discussions have begun between Hungarian and Croatian representatives about extending the M60 towards the border near Barcs in southern Hungary and Virovitica in Croatia. However, while land acquisition and property preparations are reportedly under way in Croatia, similar progress has yet to become apparent on the Hungarian side.

Barcs mayor Erika Anderné Röszler outlined the latest developments at a local council meeting, stressing that better transport links are essential if the region is to attract investment and more visitors. “We cannot expect an economic recovery in our region as long as we have to travel on roads like these, whether towards Pécs or Kaposvár,” she said, adding that the municipality had sent its questions and concerns to Hungary’s Ministry of Transport and Investment, writes Sonline.hu.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

A new bridge across the Dráva

The proposed project would extend the M60 from Pécs towards Barcs and the Croatian border, where a new bridge across the Dráva River would connect the two countries’ road networks. According to the latest route plan cited by the Barcs mayor, the new border bridge would be built approximately 500 metres from the existing Dráva crossing. Croatian officials are aware of the proposed alignment and are reportedly planning accordingly.

One proposal under discussion is to invite Hungary’s foreign minister and transport minister to Virovitica for a joint site visit, with representatives from both countries involved. Local councillor Gábor Remes has also called for a high-level government meeting to help secure progress on the cross-border agreement.

The project could have implications beyond Barcs. Kaposvár is also seeking improved links to the national motorway network, with the city’s mayor, Károly Szita, describing better connections between the M7 and M6 motorways as a strategic economic priority.

More on transportation: Major roadworks to close lanes on 3 busy Hungarian motorways: Here’s what drivers need to know

What is the current status of the M60?

Planning for the Hungarian section is divided into three stages: a 37-kilometre stretch between Pécs and west of Szigetvár; a 28-kilometre section between Szigetvár and Barcs; and a final three-kilometre section linking Barcs to the border via the proposed Dráva bridge.

According to information from the ministry’s investment portal, environmental impact and feasibility studies have been completed for the first two sections, and an environmental permit has been issued. Authorisation plans are being prepared for the first section, while the location of the border crossing and its connection with main road 6 must be determined for the final section. Planning for the second section is expected to follow.

The motorway could offer a significant improvement in accessibility for southern Hungary and strengthen links with neighbouring Croatia. However, the project remains in the planning and preparation stages, and no construction timetable has been confirmed in the information provided. Its eventual delivery will depend on further decisions and coordination between the two countries.

Read also: Taxi driver clings to bonnet for more than 100 metres after crash in Budapest – Video

World.title: Could Viktor Orbán become UN Secretary-General? Trump administration reportedly wants him to
World.content:
The Wall Street Journal reports that Washington has encouraged former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán to enter the race for the United Nations’ top job, with Russia and China reportedly open to backing his candidacy. No final decision has been made, and Orbán has declined to comment.

The Trump administration is considering former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán for the post of United Nations Secretary-General, according to a Wall Street Journal (WSJ) opinion article published on Sunday, 25 October. The newspaper, citing sources from three countries, reports that Washington has raised the idea directly with Orbán and encouraged him to compete for the position.

According to the report, US officials believe Russia and China could also support the proposal, potentially making Orbán a joint candidate backed by three major powers. However, the plan has yet to receive final approval, and no formal nomination has been announced.

If you missed it: JD Vance refuses to endorse Benjamin Netanyahu, brings up Viktor Orbán’s election defeat as a reason

Why Washington is reportedly backing Orbán

A US State Department official quoted by the WSJ acknowledged that the idea might initially sound far-fetched. Nevertheless, the official suggested that Orbán could attract sufficient support in the UN Security Council.

The official estimated that eight of the council’s 15 members would support the former Hungarian prime minister, with backing from as many as 10 potentially within reach. Whether the United Kingdom and France would oppose his candidacy remains a key question, as both countries are permanent members with veto powers.

The newspaper reports that Orbán’s political outlook is a major attraction for the Trump administration. One US official described him as a “dream candidate for MAGA conservatives”, pointing to his positions on mass immigration and liberal non-governmental organisations, as well as his record of challenging the European Union.

The article also highlights Orbán’s close relations with Russia and his efforts to strengthen Hungary’s ties with China. While the WSJ notes that his perceived defence of leaders such as Vladimir Putin could count against him, the newspaper reports that US officials have continued to raise his name in discussions with Russian and Chinese counterparts.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Orbán is reportedly interested, but cautious

According to the WSJ, American officials initially approached Orbán to find out whether he would consider taking on an international role. The former prime minister reportedly appeared open to the idea but was reluctant to enter the race without a strong prospect of winning.

The report suggests that an announcement could come after the US midterm elections, with President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance expected to support Orbán’s candidacy if he decides to run. Orbán declined to comment on the newspaper’s claims.

The prospect of an international appointment is not entirely new. In May 2026, investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi reported that positions at the UN, including a deputy secretary-general role, had been discussed as possible options for Orbán. The latest report, however, concerns the organisation’s top leadership position.

Who will become the next UN Secretary-General?

The selection process for the next secretary-general is already under way. António Guterres’ term ends on 31 December 2026, and several potential candidates are being considered. Among them is Lana Nusseibeh, a diplomat from the United Arab Emirates, who announced her candidacy last week.

The appointment requires a recommendation from the UN Security Council, which has 15 members. A candidate needs at least nine votes and must avoid a veto from any of the five permanent members: the United States, Russia, China, the United Kingdom and France. The UN General Assembly then appoints the secretary-general following the council’s recommendation.

World.title: Czech Govt Faces Backlash Over Rushed Public Media Funding Reform
World.content:
Despite the cold and rainy weather that descended over the Czech capital, thousands of protesters filled Prague’s Old Town Square on Sunday afternoon, heeding the call of the Million Moments for Democracy movement with banners reading “Resign!”, “Hands off public media!”, “Shame!”, “We’ve had enough!”, and more colourful and explicit drawings and captions.

Other smaller demonstrations took place throughout the weekend across Czechia, including Brno, Liberec and Ceske Budejovice, hastily organised protests that testified to a sudden mood shift in society as fears of a government media grab intensify.

One of the governing coalition’s top campaign promises, the long-debated yet long-delayed reform to abolish license fees and fund both Czech TV (CT) and Czech Radio (CRo) directly from the state budget, appeared to have stalled in recent months.

But on Friday, the ruling three-party coalition of ANO, the ultraconservative Motorists for Themselves and the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD) party abruptly pushed through a priority reading of the bill.

This led to a swift and immediate response from citizens. Hundreds of protesters gathered on Malostranske Square in central Prague, and dozens were even blocked by the police from entering the lower house of parliament later that evening.

After a fast-track procedure that limited speaking time and set a fixed voting deadline, government MPs eventually approved the draft at around 04:30 in the early hours of Saturday morning, sending the bill to a second reading following hours of heated debate that saw personal attacks and vulgarities fly from both sides of the aisle.

According to the proposal, CT should receive an annual 5.7 billion crowns (234 million euros) from the state budget in 2027 (a billion crowns less than its 2026 license fee revenues), while CRo should also see its funding cut by 400 million crowns to a little over 2 billion crowns.

No ‘nationalisation’, Babis vows

Repeating the mantra pushed for the past year, government officials dismissed any concerns about the independence or the future of the public service broadcasters. “I reject the idea that changing the financing of public media is an attack on democracy or the end of the independence of public media,” insisted Culture Minister Oto Klempir, arguing that many other European countries fund their public broadcasters in a similar way.

A long-time critic of the public service media’s coverage and management, Prime Minister Andrej Babis accused the opposition of “lying, inciting hatred and dividing society”, while drawing a feeble comparison with protesters’ attempt to enter the Chamber of Deputies in Prague last Friday with the Capitol riots in Washington DC in January 2021.

He did, however, try to strike a reassuring tone as well. “Their funding will be guaranteed by law as a mandatory expenditure and linked to inflation,” he vowed. “No government will be able to arbitrarily cut [funding] based on whether it likes or dislikes a broadcast.”

This, however, did little to assuage widespread concerns that the government’s reform could put the two public service broadcasters under greater political control.

Warning that the reform threatens their editorial independence, undermines the stability of their funding and could lead to the nationalisation of both entities, staffers at CT and CRo have declared a day-long strike for November 3. “We ask everyone who is not indifferent to the fate of CT and CRo to make their position known publicly and loudly,” stated the Verejnopravne initiative, which is backed by about 3,200 of the 4,200 employees at the two broadcasters.

Addressing both the content of the bill and the fast-track legislative push, criticism has come from all corners, including the Czech Journalists’ Syndicate, the European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders, over a dozen other domestic and international media freedom groups, as well as President Petr Pavel – whose signature would be needed for the bill to come into force.

“I repeat that the media must have clear guarantees of independence in every respect, both in terms of content and funding,” Pavel said, additionally calling on politicians from both sides of the aisle to take it down a notch and work to deescalate tensions.

Experts also weighed in on the issue. “The way the rules of procedure [in the lower house of parliament] were handled in this case bears the features of a power grab, in which we can see inspiration from the rhetoric and tactics of leaders like Donald Trump and Viktor Orban,” argued political scientist Eva Klusova from the Czech Academy of Sciences.

Hypothesising that the reform could be a way for the government to cover up their earlier setback at this month’s recent municipal and senatorial elections, media expert Martina Urbanikova highlighted that the funding for public service media isn’t included in the 2027 state budget, and that the legislative agenda made it uncertain the reform could take effect from January.

But in the wake of Sunday’s street protests, Prime Minister Babis vowed not to back down, adding on Monday that specific provisions were still under consideration, including the option to allow for voluntary license fee payments.

Meanwhile, Million Moments for Democracy called for another mass demonstration, set to take place on Prague’s Letna plain on November 15, two days before commemorations marking the start of the 1989 Velvet Revolution.

World.title: Kosovo Woman Murdered Hours After Reporting Domestic Violence to Police
World.content:
The Basic Prosecution in Peja/Pec. Photo: Peja Basic Prosecution.

Arlinda Zekaj was murdered on Sunday evening in the village of Vitomirica, near Peja/Pec, shortly after returning from the police station where she reported domestic violence. Three days beforehand, she had asked the local prosecution to intervene to save her life.

“I hope the day never comes when you and the responsible institutions are forced to account for your actions only after my life has been taken,” Zekaj had written on October 22 in a letter to Lumturije Vucetaj, chief prosecutor of the Peja Basic Prosecution office. The letter called for urgent action against officials she accused of failing to protect her from domestic violence.

Three days later she was murdered with an axe, allegedly by her brother-in-law, who remains at large.

Zekaj is the seventh woman to be murdered by a family member in 2026 in Kosovo.

Kosovo police announced that they received a domestic violence report at around 7 p.m. on Sunday after which the police interviewed Zekaj and arrested her ex-husband for domestic violence. He was “placed in 48-hour detention. The victim was then taken to her home in the village of Vitomirica voluntarily,” the police statement reads.

“At around 9:10 pm, we were notified that she had been found dead”, the statement continues.

On Monday morning, Zekaj’s lawyer Adelina Shala contradicted the police statement, writing on Facebook that “it wasn’t the victim’s will” to return home. On Sunday evening, Shala accused Kosovo authorities of failing to protect her client, writing that “the state killed Arlinda”.

The prosecutor’s office in Peja/Pec stated in a late night press release that Vucetaj had ordered Zekaj’s letter to be registered for examination by the competent prosecutor, including “an assessment of potential criminal liability for abuse of official position or authority”.

Kosovo’s Chief State Prosecutor requested a detailed report and review on Monday to determine “whether there were institutional or individual failures” and how the victim’s letter was handled.

Kosovo President Justina Shiroka Pula called for “an urgent, comprehensive and impartial investigation. It must be clarified whether all necessary measures were taken to assess the risk and protect her.”

The Collective for Feminist Thought and Action, an activist group, called for a nationwide protest on Wednesday, “as an act of revolt and a final call to protect women’s lives”.

The Kosovo Women’s Network (KWN) said that “the case is particularly concerning given the challenges [Zekaj] had faced regarding custody and contact with her child, as well as the concerns raised about the institutional handling of her case”.

There have been a number of recent murders of women in Kosovo by family members.

On October 9, Nafije Bogujevci and her brother Egzon Bogujevci were shot dead. Nafije’s husband later turned himself in to the police. In late August, two women were allegedly killed by their husbands within days. The first victim was 25 years old and pregnant, the second aged 80. The first was shot, the second beaten to death.

On the last Friday in August, dozens of people marched through Pristina to demand justice for the victims of femicide and to call on authorities to treat gender-based violence in Kosovo as a national emergency.

World.title: Student List Wins Outright Majority in Serbian Parliamentary Polls
World.content:
The latest results issued by the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) on Monday show that the opposition Student List won an outright majority in Serbia’s snap parliamentary elections with 52.65 per cent of the vote, while the Serbian Progressive Party’s “United Serbia” electoral list, led by Aleksandar Vucic, won 39.2 per cent.

The results are based on vote counts from 8,135 polling stations out of a total of 8,392. Voter turnout was 68.8 per cent, according to RIK.

The results published by non-governmental election monitors vary only slightly.

The Centre for Free Elections and Democracy (CeSID) and Ipsos, which jointly monitored the elections, announced on Monday that, according to 96 per cent of their representative sample, the Student List received 52.9 per cent of the vote, while United Serbia won 38.8 per cent.

According to their projections, the Student List is expected to win 140 seats in the legislature, while United Serbia is projected to secure 103 seats. This means that the Student List could form a government independently without having to seek a coalition.

The remaining seats are expected to go to electoral lists representing national minorities. The Alliance of Vojvodina Hungarians is projected to win three seats and the Albanian Coalition is expected to win two seats.

The “Rasim Ljajic – The People (SDP–CDP)” list and “SDA Sandzak – Guardians of Sandzak” are each projected to win one seat. Both represent the Bosniak national minority.

The Student List was formed by the student movement, which led almost two years of protests following the Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse in November 2024 that killed 16 people.

Its candidate list was mostly made up of experts and professors chosen by students. They still haven’t presented their prime ministerial candidate, although the first name on the candidate list was Ilija Srdanovic, a professor at the Medical Faculty of Novi Sad University.

World.title: Monday Briefing from the Balkans: October 26, 2026
World.content:
Journalists protest for press freedom across Turkey

Journalists and rights groups staged simultaneous protests in 10 Turkish cities on Saturday against the detention and imprisonment of journalists, restrictions on media outlets and the appointment of state trustees to media companies.

Thousands of journalists and their supporters attended demonstrations in Istanbul and Ankara, while protests were also held in Izmir, Bursa, Eskisehir, Antalya, Adana, Kocaeli, Van and Diyarbakir.

The Journalists’ Union of Turkey said 11 journalists had been arrested over the past two months, while journalist Zafer Arapkirli in Istanbul said the demonstrations were also intended to defend the public’s right to access news and information.

Read BIRN’s latest report on press freedoms in Turkey.

Voters make headlines at elections in Serbia and Bulgaria

Parliamentary elections in Serbia and presidential polls in Bulgaria on Sunday delivered headline news for very different reasons at the weekend.

In Serbia, a strong turnout saw the opposition Student List defeat the “United Serbia” electoral list led by the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, ending its 14-year hold on power. The vote was hailed by European leaders and neighbouring states as a potential turning point for democracy, the rule of law and Serbia’s EU membership ambitions.

In Bulgaria, a runoff vote is now due on November 1 after a record low turnout in Sunday’s predidential polls failed to deliver the expected victory for acting President Iliana Iotova, who ran with the support of Prime Minister Rumen Radev. Her opponent in the runoff will be former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who was the runner-up.

Bulgarian politician slain on election weekend

Former Bulgarian MP, MEP, tycoon and former sportsman Slavi Binev was killed on Saturday morning. Within hours, three people were arrested.

A former taekwondo competitor and a coach of the national team, from the mid-1990s Binev was an integral part of a generation of sportsmen who entered business and politics. He was involved with several, now faded, nationalist parties.

Prime Minister Rumen Radev on Sunday linked the killing to turbulence caused by the election of his government, saying that “the oligarchy and the underground are losing control over public procurements and the financial flow in the country”. His words triggered accusations that his government is willfully abstaining from exercising control.

Binev had been supportive of Radev and his chosen presidential candidate Iliana Iotova. On September 9, Binev attended an event in Sofia at which Iotova kickstarted her presidential campaign.

Kosovo PM congratulates ethnic Albanians after Serbian election

Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti said on Sunday that ethnic Albanian parties joined in a single candidates’ list for Sunday’s Serbia’s parliamentary elections and reached an “extraordinary achievement” by securing two seats in parliament. “The political unification of Albanians is turning into a stronger parliamentary representation,” Kurti said.

A few weeks ago, Kurti convinced ethnic Albanian political leaders in southern Serbia to run in a single list. In the last term, Albanians living in three southern Serbia municipalities were represented with only one representative in parliament.

World.title: Bulgaria’s Presidential Election Heads to Runoff After Record Low Turnout
World.content:
The two main candidates in Bulgaria’s presidential elections on Sunday will face off against each other in a second round on November 1 after an unexpectedly close first round in which neither won an outright majority and voter turnout was extremely low.

Acting President Iliana Iotova, who ran with the support of Prime Minister Rumen Radev, won 34.8 per cent of the vote, coming in ahead of the reformist candidate and former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who won 31.9 per cent, according to the Central Election Committee after 99.94 per cent of ballots were processed.

Polls had Iotova and Gyurov as the two top candidates, but the final results strayed widely from some predictions that Iotova could win with a landslide.

On Sunday evening Iotova said her campaign was focused on “promoting peace” and, returning to a common theme across her campaign, added that she would “not let foreign flags be waved on our streets, I want to see only Bulgarian flags.”

Gyurov again challenged Iotova to an “honest and civilised” TV debate. Iotova has declined previous challenges to TV debates. “We owe it to all the citizens who voted for us but most importantly, those who decided to stay at home, still unconvinced,” Gyurov said.

The elections were notable for a record low turnout. According to Alpha Research, only 22.5 per cent of eligible voters cast their ballots. Voter turnout in elections in 2021 was 40.5 per cent, and in 2016, 56.28 per cent.

Low turnout appears linked to the fact that some major parties did not field candidates and so did not activate their core electorates.

According to Alpha Research, only around 30 per cent of the people regularly voting for GERB, the dominant party for much of the period from 2008 to 2025, voted on Sunday.

The political party Movement for Rights and Freedom – New Beginning, which is tied to the sanctioned tycoon Delyan Peevski and favoured by many Bulgarian Turks, also did not participate in the elections. Local media noted record low turnout in the regions where Bulgarian Turks live as well as fewer diaspora votes coming from Turkey.

One of the major campaign issues was increasing security concerns over the shaky government response to drone attacks in the Black Sea amid the ongoing Russian war against Ukraine – an issue that highlighted an East-West divide between candidates.

On Monday, Prime Minister Radev raised the topic again, saying that in the runoff, people will have to choose between “peace and war” – suggesting Iotova will be able to ease the situation with Russia while comparing Gyurov’s pro-EU and pro-Ukraine positions to warmongering.

World.title: European Leaders Welcome Victory for Serbia’s Opposition Student List
World.content:
European leaders and officials in neighbouring countries congratulated Serbia’s Student List on its victory in Sunday’s snap parliamentary elections, expressing hopes for democratic reforms, a new era in regional cooperation in the Balkans, and renewed progress towards European Union membership.

Serbia’s former President Aleksandar Vucic has acknowledged the Student List win, while preliminary results published by Serbia’s Republic Electoral Commission on Monday morning showed the opposition had taken 52.54 per cent of the vote, compared to 39.29 per cent for Vucic’s ruling coalition.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated the Student List, expressing the EU’s readiness to support Serbia’s European integration.

“We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union,” von der Leyen wrote on X.

European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos described the election as a turning point that followed student-led protests for democracy, the rule of law and political accountability, which erupted in 2024 after the Novi Sad railway station disaster.

“Dear Serbia, you have made your voice heard! After nearly two years of protests for democracy, the rule of law and the fight against corruption, Serbians turned out in historic numbers. Congratulations to the Student List on your victory!” Kos wrote on X.

Kos added that now “a new chapter can begin for Serbia. The door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together.”

Council of Europe Secretary General Alain Berset, also writing on X, welcomed Vucic’s acceptance of the election result and his commitment to a peaceful democratic transition and hailed the student movement “perseverance, energy and commitment to European principles and Serbia’s future”.

Congratulations also came from neighbouring counties, with which Serbia under Vucic’s leadership has sometimes had difficult relationships.

Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajic expressed hope that the change of government would prove to be a turning point in relations between Montenegro and Serbia.

“I congratulate the representatives of the Student List and firmly believe that a new chapter lies ahead for Montenegro and Serbia, based on respect and open dialogue, without unnecessary escalation of tensions,” Spajic wrote on X.

Montenegrin President Jakov Milatovic also hailed the result as a possible new beginning.

“I am convinced that this electoral result will open a new chapter in the relations between Montenegro and the Republic of Serbia, based on friendship, sincere dialogue and commitment to a shared European future,” Milatovic said.

In Croatia, there were warm words from the government and the opposition.

“I think the message from the citizens of Serbia was very clear – they wanted change,” Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic told reporters in Zagreb on Monday.

Plenkovic said that he expected “better relations” with Serbia after the election. He added that he had congratulated Ilija Srdanovic, the lead candidate of the Student List, and that he had heard “very moderate, rational and reasonable messages” from the winning camp.

Sinisa Hajdas Doncic, president of Croatia’s largest opposition party, the Social Democratic Party (SDP), said on Monday the result presented an opportunity for political change and the opening of a new chapter in Serbia’s relations with Croatia and the European Union.

In a Facebook post, Hajdas Doncic expressed his respect for the Student List and citizens of Serbia who had persistently demanded government accountability and a fairer society. “Citizens’ trust carries a great responsibility,” he said.

The opposition party Mozemo! (We Can!) described the election result as a “major democratic victory” that opened the door to restoring independent institutions, strengthening the rule of law, ensuring media freedom and combatting corruption.

Vucic’s longtime ally in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Serb-led entity Republika Srpska, Milorad Dodik, also congratulated the Student List on its victory, writing on X that “Republika Srpska and Serbia will continue forward together, maintaining the closest and best possible relations, with cooperation and mutual support on all regional and international issues.”

In Serbia’s northern neighbour Hungary, where strongman leader Viktor Orban was voted out of office earlier this year, Prime Minister Peter Magyar voiced his congratulations for the Student List, saying he had spoken by phone with its leaders and assured them of Hungary’s support.

“I was delighted to hear how much strength our victory in April had given them during this difficult struggle,” Magyar wrote on X.

NOTE: This article was updated on October 26, 2026 to add comment from Croatia’s prime minister.

World.title: Serbia Erupts in Celebration as Aleksandar Vucic’s Long Rule Ends
World.content:
Supporters of the opposition Student List began celebrating soon after the polls closed on Sunday night, thronging city centres across Serbia in an emotional response to their defeat of the Serbian Progressive Party’s “United Serbia” electoral slate and its leader Aleksandar Vucic.

After his long political dominance of Serbia was ended by a surge of opposition support at the parliamentary election, Vucic acknowledged around 9.30 p.m. that “it is clear that we have lost this election”.

According to the latest figures from the Republic Electoral Commission, Student List won 52.6 per cent of the vote and “United Serbia” 39.2 per cent.

World.title: Albanian Prime Minister Announces New Anti-Protest Legislation
World.content:
Violent protest in Albania’s capital, Tirana on October 24, 2026. Photo: Xhemali Moku/BIRN.

Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama on Sunday announced new legislation intended to tackle violence at street protests after several weeks of clashes between anti-government protesters and police, which continued to flare over the weekend.

Rama described the legislation as “a new package against violence and urban anarchy”.

He again blamed the head of the opposition, Democratic Party leader Sali Berisha, for the violence at the protests. He also blamed “Antifa [anti-fascist] extremists who glorify violence throughout Europe, and foreign actors who do not want Albania in the European Union”.

Rama said that the legislation will include measures to compensate small businesses for damage caused by protests and measures that will allow police to limit protests at several public institutions.

It will also include measures that allow police to demand that social media posts be delete by the user if they incite violence, “while also offering psychological support when needed”.

Rama said the legislation will bring in fines for “participation in an unauthorised gathering and failure to comply with calls to disperse” ranging from 100 to 1,000 euros for each participant”, as well as fines for people who hide their identities using masks.

“Failure to comply with an order to disperse and the concealment of one’s identity shall be punishable by a fine of up to 5,000 euros for each participant. Meanwhile, the obstruction of traffic shall be punishable by a fine of euros for each participant,” he announced.

A “special electronic register” will be established for people under suspicion of committing criminal offences against the state, public order, and public security, Rama continued, but without giving specific details.

There will also be a new code of ethics for pre-university teachers; the current wave of protests has seen school-age teenagers participating.

“Schools must remain a safe space for children; the Code of Ethics stipulates that no teacher may use their authority to take children under the age of 18 to gatherings of any kind, actions that would be contrary to the children’s best interests and the expectations of their parents,” Rama said.

Rama added that “remaining at the scene of violence following police warnings” will become a criminal offence” as will “organising a gathering that has been prohibited by a lawful decision”, while “calls for violence on social media” will also be classified as criminal violence.

Activists immediately raised concerns about how the new legislation will affect the freedom of assembly and freedom of speech.

Violent clashes on Saturday continued for several hours and saw the police use tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets in attempts to disperse protesters. Protesters chanted “Revolution” and “Rama in prison, Berisha in prison”.

One protester, named as Erjon Vishkulli, was injured in the eye with a rubber bullet and sent to Italy for emergent medical treatment. Another protester, who was not resisting police, was seen being beaten by a group of officers on Saturday night.

On Sunday, police said that an “administrative investigation” has been launched for both cases and the officer seen beating the protester has been suspended.

The weekend demonstrations were a continuation of anti-government protests that first began peacefully on May 31, initially in opposition to a proposed luxury tourist resort in a protected environmental area in ​​Zvernec, a project linked to Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

In October, the protests took a violent turn, with daily clashes between police and young demonstrators who are demanding that Rama and his government step down, accusing them of corrupt governance and economic mismanagement. Rama has repeatedly refused to quit.

World.title: Marble Torso of Roman Emperor From Salona Sold in New York for Over $34 Million
World.content:
October the 26th, 2026 – A stunning marble torso of a Roman Emperor that originated from Salona in Croatia was sold in New York for over $34 million. The head is likely still buried somewhere in Croatian soil.

Croatian cultural heritage is breaking records. Ana Vela reports for Dnevnik that a remarkable marble torso of a Roman emperor originating from Salona was sold across the pond in New York for over $34 million. With that, it set the record for the highest price a Roman antiquity has ever achieved at any auction. At the same time, a painting by Croatian artist Vlaho Bukovac also set a record with its sale in Vienna. This is the story of artworks whose value has skyrocketed.

After 15 minutes of bidding, the fall of the hammer marked a sale at a price almost three times higher than the starting estimate for the Salona torso. “When I heard how much it was sold for and that it was more than $34 million, I was shocked because in 2010, it was sold for seven million, and at that time, it was estimated at one to one and a half million dollars. Perhaps then there was a realistic chance of participating in the auction. However, this amount is, in my opinion, beyond all reason,” said Dražen Maršić from the Department of Archaeology at the University of Zadar.

croatia could unfortunately do nothing but watch the sale…

“We even considered whether it would be possible to find some funds, but an amount of $34 million is truly enormous and exceeds the budget for the construction and equipping of an entire new museum,” said Nina Obuljen Koržinek, Minister of Culture and Media.

The torso is otherwise part of a collection put up for sale by an anonymous collector. “It’s the most significant item at the auction. It is a Roman torso from the first half of the first century,” said Calvine Harvey, the auction specialist. Croatian experts had long been convinced that it was lost forever. New information arrived in 2010 when it first appeared at auction. “Around 1857, an ancestor of the then owners, Aloys Maximilian Neumann, bought the torso from a collector in Split,” said Maršić. There were no legal obstacles and therefore no basis for a restitution claim. “It’s a legally sold work of art that left the territory of Croatia a long time ago,” the Croatian minister explained.

The new owner is unknown. “If we find out who now owns it, whether a collector or a museum, then we will try to have it come to an exhibition in Croatia,” the minister added. Hope remains that the head of the Roman emperor is still somewhere in Salona. “There is a realistic possibility that the head is still buried somewhere, either in an archaeological context or buried as was done with similar objects of Roman art during the early years of Christianity,” said Maršić.

vlaho bukovac also wows in vienna

From Vienna comes another record auction news. Vlaho Bukovac’s “Pink Dream” was sold for almost half a million euros, becoming the most expensive Croatian painting ever sold at an official auction. “The moment when we can reach for restitution is when we can establish that the artwork was illegally taken out,” concluded Obuljen Koržinek.

World.title: Drivers in Croatia Could Have to Pay 3X Higher Fines
World.content:
October the 26th, 2026 – Drivers in Croatia could need to pay 3X higher fines for driving offences as stricter traffic rules loom.

Last year, out of a total of 320,046 recorded speeding offences, cameras detected 200,137 of them, or 62 percent. Poslovni reports that a new Rulebook (Pravilnik) proposes a reduction of the so-called safety margin, which means that speed exceedances recorded by cameras will be tolerated significantly less than until now. Under the current rules, 3 km/h is deducted from the measured speed up to 50 km/h. For speeds from 51 to 100 km/h the tolerance is 10 km/h, and above 100 km/h 10 percent of the measured speed is deducted, rounded up to the higher value.

With the new rulebook, for example, a driver travelling at 86 km/h in a built-up area with a 50 km/h limit would be granted a tolerance of only five instead of the current 10 km/h. The relevant speed would be 81 km/h, which is 31 km/h above the limit, and the fine would amount to €390 instead of €130.

cameras record the vast majority of driving offences

If current trends continue, such a change would also significantly increase revenues from fines. Data from the Ministry of the Interior show that fixed speed monitoring devices recorded the majority of such offences. Last year, out of a total of 320,046 established speeding offences, cameras recorded 200,137 of them, or 62 percent. In the first eight months of this year, out of a total of 226,302 speeding offences, fixed devices recorded 145,129 of them, which is 64 percent. Data for last year also show that the most numerous were those exceeding 10 to 20 kilometres per hour above the permitted speed in built-up areas, with a total of 124,611 such cases.

more locations than cameras

Croatia currently has 206 fixed cameras that are distributed across a total of 807 locations. The Ministry of the Interior explains that the cameras are relocated at different time intervals, depending on the assessment of the competent police administration. The highest number of locations for installing cameras is in the area of the Split-Dalmatia Police Administration and the Zagreb Police Administration, with 86 in each, followed by the Međimurje Police Administration with 62 locations. The fewest are in the area of the Karlovac Police Administration, with 12, and the Požega-Slavonia Police Administration, where there are 13.

Although fixed cameras primarily serve to determine speeding, they can also record other traffic offences. “If, for example, the offence of using a mobile phone while driving, not wearing a seat belt or some other unlawful behaviour is visible on the recording, the driver or passenger can also be fined for such offences,” the Ministry of the Interior explains.

revenue from fines is increasing

The Ministry of the Interior states that it does not keep separate statistics on the amounts collected by type of offence, but collectively for all monetary fines under the Road Traffic Safety Act. Nevertheless, the Annual Report on the Execution of the State Budget shows that last year, 2025, €80.77 million was collected from fines for traffic and other offences under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior. That is €11.6 million more than in 2024.

World.title: Croatia is the Leading Charter Power, But Earns Less Than Greece – Why?
World.content:
October the 26th, 2026 – Croatia is the world’s leading charter power, yet it earns less than Greece does from the same sector. The big questions is why?

Croatia is the number one charter power in the world with nearly five thousand vessels in its fleet. In the first eight months of this year, more than 431 thousand charter guest arrivals and more than 2.7 million overnight stays were recorded. However, market saturation has led to charter prices, especially for sailing yachts, falling by 50 percent or more during the peak season. As Alenka Juricic Bukarica reports for Glas Istre, this is not only the case this year. At the same time, competition in other Mediterranean countries is growing, especially in Greece, which last year had just over 3,000 vessels in charter. That is still fewer than Croatia, but with a clear upward trend.

Rising operating costs in recent years have also significantly changed conditions on the Croatian charter market, particularly for smaller vessels, and have negatively affected the return on investment and, consequently, the interest of new investors. Croatia is no longer perceived as a cheap destination, and there has also been a change in the structure of guests: instead of professionals, charter is increasingly chosen by people who are not normally involved in sailing, which increases demand for skippers and hostesses. Ultimately, people from the industry say that in some cases better prices can be achieved on the market in September than in the peak season…

in typical croatian style, there’s a paradox…

The current situation on the Croatian charter market was recently analysed by Ani Trstenjak, head of the Yacht Rent charter agency, and Daniela Gračan from the Faculty of Tourism and Hospitality Management (FMTU) in Opatija. Nautical charter has become, they emphasise, an important part of the tourism economy. It has attracted domestic and foreign capital and created a business ecosystem that includes vessel owners, charter companies, marinas, service providers, intermediaries and numerous providers of supporting services.

However, the success that for decades was measured by fleet growth, number of bookings and total revenue is opening an increasingly uncomfortable question – can Croatian charter continue to grow in the same way without endangering its own profitability.

“Market analysis by the vessel rental platform Yacht-Rent.com for 2026 points to an interesting paradox. Namely, Croatian sailing yachts and catamarans are among the cheapest compared to competing markets, while at the same time achieving high occupancy. Croatian charter does not primarily suffer from a lack of demand, but from a structural problem where demand is increasingly difficult to convert into revenue and profit. At the same time, it is clear that revenue is necessary to cover operating costs, financing, maintenance, depreciation and fleet renewal,” Trstenjak explained.

She clarified that Yacht-Rent’s market analysis for this year compares prices and bookings of vessels across six Mediterranean markets. It covers the operating season from 1 April to 2 November 2026, and expresses prices per person (berth) per week so that different vessel sizes can be compared on a comparable basis. According to that analysis, Croatia has the lowest average weekly price per berth among the compared markets for both sailing yachts and catamarans.

an exceptionally demanding market

Specifically speaking, sailing yachts in Croatia achieve an average weekly price per berth of €355, compared to €454 in Greece and €494 in Turkey. The price in Croatia is 22 percent lower than for a sailing yacht in Greece and 28 percent lower than in Turkey. At the same time, Croatian sailing yachts have an average of 19.4 booked weeks, slightly more than 19 weeks in Greece and significantly more than 17 weeks in Turkey. The estimated gross seasonal revenue per berth in Croatia amounts to €6,887, compared to €8,626 in Greece and €8,398 in Turkey.

The situation with catamarans is similar to that of sailing yachts. The average price of €706 per berth per week in Croatia is 16 percent lower than in Greece and 14 percent lower than in Turkey. Catamarans in Croatia are on average booked for 18.8 weeks during the season, which is close to 19.2 weeks in Greece, but significantly more than 15.4 weeks in Turkey. Despite this, the estimated gross seasonal revenue per berth in Croatia amounts to €13,273, while in Greece it reaches €16,147. Turkey achieves €12,659 in seasonal revenue per vessel.

“These data shows that Greece in the observed sample manages to combine high utilisation with a higher price. Croatia, on the other hand, achieves high capacity utilisation with a significantly lower price,” pointed out the head of the Yacht Rent agency. Adding that Croatian charter today operates on a highly competitive Mediterranean market, she also recalled that a guest can today easily compare prices, year of construction, equipment and capacity of vessels, rental conditions, additional costs and available destinations. And when vessels are very similar to each other, price becomes one of the most important decision criteria. However, she stresses, price is not the cause of the crisis, but its symptom.

higher and higher costs

Although not all segments of charter are equally price-sensitive, Trstenjak explains that luxury crewed vessels, differentiated service, special routes and a top customer experience can have greater pricing power. A standard sailing yacht comparable to dozens of other vessels at the same destination has significantly less room to raise its price independently. Charter companies today face high costs for berths, servicing, spare parts, insurance, labour, cleaning, administration, sales and distribution. Financing, depreciation and the need for fleet renewal, berth prices and insurance also play a significant role. All of this leads charter firms to accept a lower price in order to still rent out the vessel. In the short term such a decision can be rational, our interlocutor says, if the booking covers the additional costs of the rental and contributes to covering fixed costs. However, in the medium or long term, such a decision can be disastrous.

“When discounts become a permanent way of doing business, a serious problem arises that Croatian charter has been facing since 2023. Revenue may cover part of the costs, but it very likely no longer leaves enough funds for equipment renewal, major services, vessel replacement and return on capital. A company can therefore have high turnover, positive operating profit and at the same time an insufficient return on the capital invested in charter management. Every charter company wants to have enough vessels to attract guests, expand its offer and increase turnover.

But when a large number of investors make similar decisions, total supply can grow faster than demand. The number of available vessels increases, but the number of guests and attractive periods does not necessarily grow at the same speed. Therefore, an individual discount may be rational, but collective reliance on discounts can reduce the profitability of the entire market because supply does not adjust quickly enough,” Trstenjak says.

capital investment

She also addressed the problem of charter management, i.e. the fact that many Croatian citizens or companies, as well as foreigners, have in recent years seen the purchase of a sailing yacht or catamaran as a profitable form of capital investment. For the vessel buyer, the charter company handles the rental business, while the owner can use it for part of the year and collects income from the rental. Maintenance costs of the boat are borne by the owner. In such a model, the vessel owner expects a return on capital, the charter company wants to achieve the highest possible margin, while the guest wants the best price-quality ratio.

“If the vessel was purchased with excessively high expectations regarding rental price and number of booked weeks, a change in market conditions can seriously endanger the profitability of the investment. The owner expects a return, while the charter company has to choose between a lower price and the risk of unfilled periods,” our interlocutor warned. She concludes that the Croatian charter market has matured and that it is actually very important to make better use of the season and develop the offer outside the main summer months. At the same time, marinas, anchorages and the preservation of the sea must not be neglected, because it is precisely the quality of the destination that attracts guests. “The future of the charter sector does not depend only on further growth, but on how sustainable and profitable that growth will be,” concluded Ani Trstenjak.

a charter loss of €35 million…

The HUP Nautical Sector Association presented the Blue Book of Croatian Nautics and an initiative for the establishment of a National Nautical Council that should define a common development vision until 2040 at the Biograd Boat Show.

According to HUP’s analysis, entrepreneurs in nautics last year achieved €2.8 billion in business revenue and €1 billion in export revenue, employing 18,323 people. Business revenues rose 9.4 percent and exports 14.8 percent compared to the previous year. The analysis is based on HUP’s register of more than 3,200 mapped economic entities in activities related to nautics. In the period from 2021 to 2025, exports grew 70.8 percent, from €597.1 million to more than €1 billion. The share of gross investments in fixed assets in business revenues simultaneously increased from 11.7 to 18 percent. In the Blue Book, however, a warning was issued about pressure on the profitability of charter, which last year recorded a net loss of €34.7 million. “For the further growth of Croatian nautics, safer investment conditions, faster procedures and the availability of qualified workers are needed.

The Blue Book shows that revenue per employee in the sector from 2021 to 2025 rose by 43 percent, from €108.5 thousand to €155.1 thousand, which confirms the potential for creating greater added value. We want more design, production and servicing to take place in Croatia and for a larger part of the value created to remain in the domestic economy, while preserving the sea and the coast,” said Irena Weber, Director General of HUP. Luciano Beg, president of the HUP Nautical Sector Association, also pointed out that in addition to counting berths and overnight stays, the success of nautics should be measured by the production of vessels and equipment, overhauls, innovations, exports and quality jobs, and that this requires a long-term vision and better coordination between the economy, state institutions and the scientific community.

World.title: “I Won’t Shoot My Own People” – How Perišin Escaped the JNA in a MiG
World.content:
October the 26th, 2026 – Rudolf Perešin refused to shoot at his own people, instead escaping the JNA and flying to Austria.

On the 25th of October 1991, pilot Rudolf Perešin, then a member of the Yugoslav Air Force, defected in a Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21 fighter from the JNA base in Bihać to Klagenfurt, Austria. Index writes that with that act, he became one of the symbols of resistance and the struggle for Croatia’s independence. After landing in Austria, the public forever remembered his statement: “I am a Croat and I won’t shoot at my own people.”

His MiG-21 was never returned to the Yugoslav People’s Army. It remained in Austria, and Perešin soon joined the Croatian Army and the Croatian Air Force. He became commander of the 1st Fighter Squadron and took part in numerous combat missions during the Homeland War.

During the military-police operation Flash, which took place on the 2nd of May 1995, Perešin’s aircraft was hit in the sky above western Slavonia. He managed to eject, but landed in territory controlled by enemy forces and was killed. His remains were found only two years later – on the 4th of August 1997. He was buried with full military honours on 15 September 1997 at Mirogoj Cemetery in Zagreb. Rudolf Perešin has remained a lasting symbol of courage, patriotism and professional honour of Croatian pilots. His legendary MiG-21 is today exhibited in Zagreb as a reminder of one of the most important moments in the history of the Croatian Air Force.

The aircraft in which Perišin defected was displayed in a museum in Klagenfurt until 2019, when it was returned to Croatia.

World.title: He Survived a Shipwreck and Built a Church – 900 Years Later, Croatia Officially Protected it
World.content:
October the 25th, 2026 – A merchant surviving a shipwreck and then building a church in gratitude that Croatia officially chose to protect almost 1,000 years later is the story behind a construction on an island few know about.

It’s believed that the Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian (Crvka sv. Kuzme i Damjana) on the island of Ugljan dates from the 11th or 12th century. It is located in a peaceful cove, right by the sea, not far from the hamlet of Guduće. Olive groves, dense pine forests, beautiful coves, old fishing villages, crystal-clear sea and views of the Zadar archipelago are what await visitors to Ugljan.

As Ivana Vasarevic writes for Putni Kofer, it’s widely known as one of Croatia’s greenest islands, which also carries the flattering nickname “the garden of Zadar.” It’s just 22 kilometres long, has a little over 5,600 inhabitants, is separated from the mainland by the Zadar Channel, and is connected to the neighbouring island of Pašman by a bridge across the Ždrelac passage. Among Ugljan’s main attractions is the fortress of St. Michael above Preko; nearby is also the islet of Galevac, known for its Franciscan monastery, while in Muline you can visit the remains of an ancient oil mill where the Liburnian olive oil was once produced.

TODAY IT IS CONSIDERED THE OLDEST PRESERVED CHURCH IN THE SETTLEMENT OF UGLJAN

The island’s special charm comes from its small stone churches. One of them was recently declared a cultural asset by the Ministry of Culture and Media of the Republic of Croatia. It is the Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, located in Ljokine Cove, not far from the hamlet of Guduće, on the southwestern side of the island. This modest stone building stands right on the shore and is the oldest preserved church in the settlement of Ugljan: it is believed to date from the 11th or 12th century.

Besides its exceptional historical value, the Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian is also interesting because of the unusual legend that has accompanied it for centuries. According to the story, a merchant and sailor named Toricella was shipwrecked in the waters around Ugljan. He managed to save himself and swim to the shore in Ljokine Cove, and on that spot he decided to build a votive church. He dedicated it to Saints Cosmas and Damian, early Christian martyrs and physicians, in gratitude for his rescue.

THE ROOF OF THE SIMPLE LITTLE CHURCH WAS COVERED WITH BROKEN STONE SLABS

Although the shipwreck story cannot be historically confirmed, the name Toricella also appears in old documents. The little church is first mentioned on 6 August 1512 in the will of F. Toricella from Bergamo in Italy. In it he stipulated that a piece of land should be given for use to the priest who celebrates a sung Mass in the little church on the feast of Saints Cosmas and Damian. According to the interpretation of don Marko Dokoza, a priest who for years led tours of Ugljan’s little churches as part of Open Doors Days, Toricella was only later identified with the seafarer from the shipwreck legend.

The original church was a very simple, square stone building, 4.8 metres long and 2.8 metres wide. Its walls were about 80 centimetres thick, and at the rear it had a lowered semicircular apse. The roof was covered with broken stone slabs, and there were two small windows in the side walls. The interior had a half-barrel vault, while the simple architectural details reflected the modesty and age of the building.

PAINTINGS DEPICTING SAINTS COSMAS AND DAMIAN AND THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY WITH THE CHILD

At the beginning of the 20th century the little church was significantly enlarged. A new nave, ten metres long and 3.8 metres wide, intended for gatherings of the faithful, was added to its front part. Today its interior contains an altar, pews and paintings depicting Saints Cosmas and Damian as well as the Blessed Virgin Mary with the Child. On the façade a small round window stands out, and above it a stone bell-gable with a bell made in the workshop of Jakov Cukrov in Split.

Saints Cosmas and Damian, to whom the church is dedicated, were twin brothers and physicians who helped the sick free of charge. Their feast day is celebrated on the 26th of September. For centuries that date held special significance for the inhabitants of Ugljan: according to records in the parish chronicle, numerous pilgrims from all the settlements on the island, as well as from the neighbouring areas, used to come to the little church on that day.

IN THE NEARBY HAMLET OF GUDUĆE YOU CAN ALSO SEE A UNIQUE MOSAIC BENCH

The tradition, of course, lives on today. Mass is still celebrated in the little church, during which blessings are invoked upon Ugljan sailors and ships all over the world. Thus this small place of worship has remained connected with the sea and seafarers, just as in the legend of its origin. The Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian on the island of Ugljan is also interesting as an excursion destination.

It is located in a peaceful cove, and a gravel road through a pine forest leads to it. In the nearby hamlet of Guduće you can also see an unusual mosaic bench created back in 2019 by the retired Božica Kliman, known as Boška. On its front side is a depiction of the Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian itself, along with a magical sunset, a squid and a lighthouse — colourful reminders of the islanders’ unbreakable connection with the sea and fishing.

World.title: The 3,500 Year Old Settlement Found Near Split
World.content:
October the 25th, 2026 – There is a fascinating 3,500 year old settlement in the suburbs of Split, with archaeologists coming upon the remains of houses, ovens and ancient graves.

Split is well known as the second largest city in Croatia and one of the best-known tourist destinations. It boasts an exceptionally long and proud history, but many don’t know that in its suburbs lies a settlement that is even older than this Dalmatian gem. As Lana Mindoljevic writes for Putni Kofer, over more recent years, archaeologists visiting the settlement of Stobreč have been discovering remains of life from the Bronze Age, long before the arrival of the Greeks and the Romans. Stobreč is formally a suburban settlement of Split and a popular tourist area, but it has its own exciting history that many people simply overlook.

the remains of an ancient epetium

Stobreč has long been known to archaeologists as the site of ancient Epetium, or Epetion. However, extensive protective research that began back in 2024, the largest so far conducted at this site, has also opened a much older chapter of its history. According to the information available so far, the earliest finds date approximately to 1500 BC, and detailed processing of the material is still ongoing.

over 10,000 fragments have been found

In a scientific paper written by Marina Ugarković and Niko Romac, published on the Hrčak website, parts of Hellenistic defensive walls and a tower, a Roman road and drainage system, and late antique buildings are described. Among these layers, the remains of an earlier prehistoric settlement have for the first time been unequivocally confirmed. Already in the research covered by that paper, more than 100,000 fragments of objects and other movable finds from different periods were documented. The soil under Stobreč has proven to be a vast archive of life that changed and built upon itself here for centuries.

ancient homes and grave sites

Archaeologist Niko Romac also described finds of ovens, possibly intended for food preparation, and complete ceramic vessels: trays, cups and jugs. Precisely such objects bring the ancient inhabitants of Stobreč closer to us. Someone made them, took them in their hands and used them in everyday life. Based on traces of burning and the arrangement of the remains, researchers assume that the house was destroyed by fire. Among the particularly sensitive finds, the grave of a newborn in its floor was also recorded.

an archaeological park is being considered

These remarkable discoveries have also opened the question of the future of the very special site. According to the response of the Ministry of Culture and Media, a zone of approximately 3,000 square metres is currently being planned for the presentation of the archaeological heritage. On an additional around 2,500 square metres construction is possible, but it depends on the results of further research. The sensitive Bronze Age finds require special protection. The Ministry states that the ovens and the find interpreted as a threshing floor should be moved to the Archaeological Museum in Split, while the appearance of the settlement could be presented with three-dimensional models and virtual reconstructions. An archaeological park currently exists only as an idea, and time will show whether it will be realised.

Stobreč is located on a peninsula east of Split, near the mouth of the Žrnovnica. In the central part of the place there are sandy and pebble beaches, while towards the southwest the coast becomes rockier. Because of the beautiful beaches and the proximity of Split it is a popular summer destination, and the proximity of Perun and Mosor also opens possibilities for trips into nature. Interestingly, even the name of Stobreč itself preserves the memory of its long past. As the Croatian Encyclopaedia notes, archaeologist Frane Bulić etymologically linked the present-day name of the place with the name of Saint Lawrence, i.e. the Roman martyr Laurentius, to whom the local early Christian basilica was dedicated. In its apse a small church of Saint Lawrence was later arranged, later dedicated to Our Lady of Carmel. Along with the preserved remains of the ancient walls, this is another reminder that in Stobreč different periods of history can be encountered during a completely ordinary walk.

World.title: Croatia is Introducing a New Digital Customs System
World.content:
October the 25th, 2026 – Croatia is set to introduce a brand new digital customs system as of November the 1st this year, with the hope of making crossing the border more efficient.

As of the 1st of November 2026, the Customs Administration is introducing a new digital service called eObračun of customs duties in passenger traffic (eODPP). Index reports that this brand new service is intended for passengers who bring goods into Croatia, i.e. the EU, on which import duties are payable, and its aim is to facilitate and speed up border crossing.

how it works…

Via the new application, passengers will be able to check in advance whether there is an obligation to pay duties on the goods they are bringing in their personal luggage. The service also enables them to declare goods whose value or quantity exceeds the permitted limits and to pay online the customs duties and taxes calculated on the basis of the declaration. Goods can be declared up to five days, i.e. 120 hours, before the planned arrival at one of the international border crossings within the territory of Croatia.

Upon arrival at the border, a customs officer will check the declaration and the goods in a short procedure. If no irregularities are found, the import procedure will be quickly completed. The Customs Administration states that the application is designed to be intuitive, and the data-entry procedure for calculating duties has five steps.

no registration required

The brand new Croatian digital customs service will be available to all passengers entering the EU via Croatian road, railway, air and maritime border crossings. No registration is required to use it. The system is adapted for computers, smartphones and tablets, and will be available from the 1st of November 2026 here.
