World.title: Why are Abkhazia residents with dual citizenship asked to show Russian passports at Moscow airports?
World.content:
Abkhazia‘s Foreign Ministry has said that some residents of the breakaway republic who hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship are experiencing difficulties crossing the Russian border at Moscow airports.

Russian border guards have reportedly been refusing to allow dual nationals to enter or leave the country using their Abkhaz passports, instead demanding Russian documents.

As Abkhazia is a largely unrecognised republic, its passports are also not widely recognised internationally. Travelling on an Abkhaz passport is virtually impossible, except to a handful of countries, including Russia. For Abkhazians, obtaining a Russian passport is therefore practically the only way to travel internationally. However, this generally means a Russian international passport rather than a domestic identity document. Most do not hold Russian internal passports because they permanently reside in Abkhazia, where Russian passport holders account for around 70% of the population.

The ministry added that people holding only Abkhaz citizenship do not encounter such problems at airports. Similar incidents have not been reported at other border crossing points either.

Russia explains its position by saying that, for dual nationals, a Russian passport is not merely the primary document required to cross the border, but the only acceptable one. However, the explanation has been met with scepticism in Abkhazia, where some suspect the border guards may have other motives.

The issue was discussed by Abkhaz and Russian foreign ministers Oleg Bartsits and Sergei Lavrov during a recent meeting in Moscow. However, no solution has yet been found. According to Abkhazia’s Foreign Ministry, the matter remains subject to “consultations with the competent authorities of the Russian Federation, taking into account the provisions of existing bilateral agreements”.

In the meantime, the ministry has advised Abkhaz citizens experiencing difficulties at border crossings to formally report the incidents to the ministry, providing detailed accounts of what happened.

From the perspective of international practice, border guards at Moscow airports are not doing anything unlawful.

As a general rule, people holding two or more citizenships are required to present the passport of the country whose border they are crossing, if they are citizens of that country. This requirement is enshrined in national legislation and strictly enforced in countries including Georgia, the United States and many others.

This raises the question: what exactly is the problem, why are Abkhaz citizens unhappy, and why are they reluctant to present their Russian passports at the border if they have them?

For some Abkhazians with dual citizenship, the right to use an Abkhaz passport is a matter of principle and national pride. While this argument carries little legal weight, it is highly significant in Abkhazia.

Others simply want the option of crossing the border using their Abkhaz documents in certain circumstances, such as when their Russian passport has expired and they have not yet received a replacement.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: England forward Harry Kane wins Ballon d’Or
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane has won the Ballon d’Or as the world’s best footballer of the 2025/26 season, according to French magazine France Football. The award ceremony was held in London.

Last season, Kane scored 61 goals and provided seven assists in 51 appearances for Bayern Munich. He won the German Bundesliga and the DFB-Pokal with the club, finished as the Bundesliga’s top scorer and claimed the European Golden Shoe.

Representing England, the forward won bronze at the World Cup, scoring six goals and providing one assist in seven matches at the tournament.

World.title: Azerbaijan-banned Turkish media representative detained in Istanbul
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 26. Muhammed Emin Yıldırım, the Istanbul representative of the Köklü Değişim magazine and media group, who was declared persona non grata by Azerbaijan and banned from entering the country, has been detained.

The media group announced this on the social media platform X.

It was reported that he was detained by Istanbul police over his social media posts.

“We are closely monitoring the legal proceedings through his lawyer,” the media group added.

It should be noted that 31 Turkish citizens have been declared persona non grata in connection with statements made on various social media platforms and online outlets that were directed against Azerbaijan’s sovereignty, national security, constitutional order, people and leadership, as well as calls for the violent seizure of power and the incitement of violence on the grounds of religious radicalism, religious hatred and hostility. Muhammed Emin Yıldırım is also on the list.

World.title: Azerbaijan, UNESCO discuss prospects for developing cooperation (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. On October 26, Azerbaijani Deputy Foreign Minister Elnur Mammadov met with UNESCO Deputy Director-General Asa Regner, who is visiting the country.

This was reported by the Press Service Department of Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

According to the report, the meeting addressed the current state and prospects for developing cooperation between Azerbaijan and UNESCO, as well as intercultural dialogue, education, science, artificial intelligence, cultural heritage, sustainable tourism, the Man and the Biosphere Programme, and support for African countries and small island states.

It was noted that the Framework Agreement signed in 2013 and the Azerbaijan–UNESCO Trust Fund established that year play an important role in advancing cooperation. Azerbaijan’s interest in continuing to support UNESCO programmes and projects in line with the country’s national priorities was also emphasized.

Satisfaction was expressed with UNESCO’s active participation in the 7th World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue. It was noted that the organization had hosted three panel discussions as part of the forum.

Elnur Mammadov provided information on the Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Republic of Azerbaijan for 2025–2028 and the Digital Development Council. It was noted that artificial intelligence technologies are being applied to promote the country’s development and digitalize public services.

Asa Regner thanked Azerbaijan for the successful organization of the 7th World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue and for its cooperation. She highly appreciated Azerbaijan’s support for African countries, gender equality, girls’ education and small island states, which are among UNESCO’s priority areas.

The meeting also included an exchange of views on other issues of mutual interest.

World.title: Six years pass since Armenia's rocket attack on Azerbaijan's Barda district
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. Six years have passed since Azerbaijan's Barda district was once again subjected to rocket attack by the Armenian armed forces during the Second Karabakh War.

The Armenian forces once again shelled Garayusifli village in Barda, located outside the frontline zone, with Smerch rockets on October 27, 2020.

As a result, civilians Ofeliya Jafarova, Aybaniz Ahmadova, Ehtiram Ismayilov, Aysu Isgandarova and Almaz Aliyeva (born in 2013) became martyrs, and 13 more people were injured.

The rocket fire completely destroyed several residential houses and caused significant damage to the villagers.

During the Second Karabakh War, Barda district and city center were subjected to rocket and artillery fire by Armenian armed forces three times (October 5, 27, and 28). As a result, 29 people became martyrs, 112 were wounded, and vehicles and civilian infrastructure facilities located in the area were significantly damaged.

In light of this fact, the General Prosecutor's Office of Azerbaijan initiated criminal proceedings under articles 120.2.1 (premeditated murder by an organized criminal community), 120.2.4 (premeditated murder with particular cruelty or in a generally dangerous way), 120.2.12 (premeditated murder with intent to incite national, racial, religious enmity, or hatred), 100.2 (waging a war of aggression), and other articles of the Criminal Code of Azerbaijan.

A preliminary investigation was entrusted to the Investigation Department of the Prosecutor's Office.

In total, during the war that began on September 27, 2020 and lasted 44 days, as a result of the military aggression of the armed forces and illegal armed groups of Armenia against Azerbaijan, 93 civilians were killed (including 54 men, 27 women and 12 children), and 444 people were injured (including 268 men, 109 women and 67 children).

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 27, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Chronicle of the 31-st day of the second Karabakh war:

- First Vice President of Azerbaijan Mehriban Aliyeva shared a post on her Instagram account.

- The Azerbaijani Defense Ministry has released information on the latest situation on the front.

- The chief of staff of the Armenian motorized infantry division was killed. The list of destroyed military equipment of the Armenian armed forces has been announced.

- Tartar city and the villages of the Tartar district were shelled.

- The Azerbaijani army liberated four cities, four settlements and 165 villages in just one month.

- The territories of Goranboy, Tartar and Barda districts were shelled. The death toll from Armenian missile attack in Barda has reached four. One of the dead in Barda was an 8-year-old child.

- The Defense Ministry said that over the past day, Armenian armed forces repeatedly violated the humanitarian ceasefire.

World.title: Leyla Aliyeva and Alena Aliyeva visit Capybara Azerbaijan farm in Shamakhi (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 26. On October 26, Leyla Aliyeva, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, and Alena Aliyeva visited the Nasimi Gardens complex in Shamakhi.

Leyla Aliyeva and Alena Aliyeva first viewed the artworks displayed in the area. The guests then visited the Capybara Cafe, which was created based on the capybara concept.

Capybara Cafe offers visitors a unique and relaxing atmosphere. The cafe's interior and offered products are designed in line with a unified concept, where every detail resembles capybaras. Even the desserts on the menu are presented in the shape of capybaras.

For guests wishing to purchase souvenir gifts, a souvenir shop operates inside the cafe.

Subsequently, Leyla Aliyeva and Alena Aliyeva visited the Capybara Azerbaijan farm and were briefed on the conditions created there, while also feeding the capybaras. Recognized as the first capybara farm ever established in Azerbaijan, the Capybara Azerbaijan aims to introduce visitors more closely to these unique animals, contribute to the development of ecotourism, and support the formation of a responsible and caring attitude toward animals. The farm has quickly turned into a top destination for numerous visitors in a short span of time.

Considered the world's largest rodents native to Central and South America, capybaras have gained immense popularity in various countries in recent years. Being incredibly friendly animals, capybaras attract people's attention with their unusual appearance and social characteristics, fostering greater love for animals and nature in general. Taking into account the above-mentioned factors, the Capybara Azerbaijan farm was constructed using advanced technologies.

The existing infrastructure at the farm was designed to create conditions matching capybara’s natural habitat as closely as possible. Both indoor and outdoor pools, as well as individual baths, have been built for capybaras. The farm is equipped with a modern water filtration system, an automatic humidification system ensuring optimal humidity, and special UV lamps simulating natural sunlight.

At this venue, which garners great interest from both children and adults, it is possible to get in touch with a piece of exotic nature. Visitors can feed capybaras and gain interesting information about their lifestyle, behavior, and natural habitat.

The guests also visited the Magic Village section, another popular project consisting of themed houses built in the style of hobbit homes.

World.title: Should we replace controversial colonial statues? Hobart just did
World.content:
The divisive statue of a colonial figure, which was toppled in a Tasmanian park, has been replaced with a native garden surrounded by a "ring of truth telling", in a project believed to be the first of its kind in Australia.

Vandals cut down the statue of William Crowther at Hobart's Franklin Square in mid-2024, hours before the Tasmanian Civil and Administrative Tribunal upheld a council's decision to organise its removal.

The statue of William Crowther was cut down at the ankles in Franklin Square in Hobart in 2024. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Crowther was a surgeon and politician during the 1800s, who most historians agree broke into a morgue and stole the skull of deceased Aboriginal man William Lanne for pseudoscience.

The permanent replacement for his statue, unveiled by the City of Hobart today, incorporates a native garden and circle of bronze around the vacant plinth which once held the statue.

A bronze ring surrounding the plinth garden is inscribed with three stories. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

The bronze ring has been inscribed with contributions from three writers: one on Crowther and colonial life, one on Lanne and Palawa history, and one offering social commentary about statues.

Despite the vandalism, the project is believed to be the first example of an Australian council deciding to remove a colonial statue through a democratic process.

The permanent replacement for the statue incorporates a native garden and circle of bronze. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

In a statement, Hobart's Lord Mayor Anna Reynolds said the installation was the result of more than five years of consultation with the community and it provided a "more honest and complete" understanding of the city's history.

"It's not about erasing history, but rather providing even more information, context and a broader range of perspectives that have often been absent from public spaces," Cr Reynolds said.

"This new installation demonstrates how complex — and at times controversial — issues can be addressed through respectful engagement, thoughtful design, democratic decision-making and proper legal processes."

Design invites people to walk 'meditatively' around garden

Mat Hinds, the architect commissioned to design the reinterpretation, said the native garden was a reference to the area's past as an "open flowering field" before colonisation.

The project is believed to be the first example of an Australian council deciding to remove a colonial statue through a democratic process. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

He said the bronze ring was a reference to the material of the original statue and to Lanne's work on whaling ships, on which bronze was an essential material.

"It's been repurposed as a ring of truth telling, effectively like a halo of light, and the three narratives run in that," Mr Hinds said.

"What it requires is that people walk in a circular way, almost meditatively, around the perimeter of the garden and take in the messaging of what's been written."

The new artwork is made of bronze (ABC News: Jake Grant)

The architect said the decision to keep the original plinth in place was an "echo" of the decision to remove the original statue.

Mr Hinds said the reinterpretation was a "sophisticated" approach to sharing local history, as statues were a "really dumb way of retaining communal memory".

"For what they show, in equal measure, they hide, and more often than not, statues are out of proportion with the actual person," he said.

Mat Hinds says the bronze ring is a reference to the original statue and to William Lanne's work on whaling ships. (ABC News: Dane Meale)

Aboriginal experience 'reflected in this space'

One of those who contributed to the inscription was Nunami Sculthorpe-Green, a Palawa and Warlpiri woman, who wrote about William Lanne and life for Aboriginal people in Tasmania during the 1800s.

Ms Sculthorpe-Green said the project gave her a chance to "re-centre" the life of Lanne within this story.

"After decades of calling for change, the Tasmanian Aboriginal community can now see our experience and humanity reflected in this space," she said.

Nunami Sculthorpe-Green contributed to the inscription. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

History writer Alison Alexander contributed to the ring with some words about Crowther, which she said was important as the city "can't pretend the story didn't happen".

"There was a statue there, it's been taken down in this more enlightened age, and so I think it's important to tell that story and to say, right, we are putting the past behind us," Dr Alexander said.

Alison Alexander says it is important to still tell William Crowther's story, as we "can't pretend" it didn't happen. (ABC News: Dane Meale)

The final contribution was from arts writer Andrew Harper, who wrote about the history of statues being toppled and how "history is action and not objects".

Mr Harper had tried to find another city-led project where Aboriginal artists were asked to respond to a colonial statue with a "problematic" history, but he could not find one.

"That's a huge achievement for this city and for the people that drove the project and for the artists that took part in it and even for the people who objected to it," he said.

" We did something that might be new, something we can share with the entire world, because there are people all over the world asking, 'What do we do about this?' "

Each writer had to limit their contribution for the ring to just 250 words, however a longer piece of text is available on the City of Hobart website and accessible through a QR code on the site.

Andrew Harper says the project is something the entire world can look at when dealing with similarly controversial public artworks. (ABC News: Dane Meale)

Statues at centre of global debate

Statues have become a major point of public debate, protest and political action in Australia and across the world, as modern communities question who should be honoured in public spaces.

Protesters in the United Kingdom pulled down a bronze statue of merchant and slave trader Edward Colston, before throwing it into Bristol's harbour during a Black Lives Matter demonstration in 2020.

The statue of late 17th century slave trader Edward Colston was pushed into the river during protests in Bristol, England. (Getty Images / NurPhoto)

A statue of British explorer James Cook in the Melbourne suburb of St Kilda was sawn off at the ankles by vandals on the eve of Australia Day in 2024.

Other statues of Australian colonial figures, including Melbourne founder John Batman and New South Wales governor Lachlan Macquarie, have been the subject of fierce debate.

A statue of James Cook in St Kilda, Melbourne was defaced on the eve of Australia Day in 2024. (ABC News)

While some believe they should be removed, others have argued this would be silencing, erasing or rewriting the nation's history.

A small group gathered to protest the removal of the original statue. (ABC News: Jake Grant )

The reinterpretation of the Crowther statue in Hobart was the culmination of a multi-year public arts project, which involved temporary artworks by Palawa artists and community consultation.

The original bronze statue of William Crowther has been restored, with the ankles re-welded to the main body, though it was still being kept in storage by the City of Hobart.

World.title: Blind woman says smart glasses replaced her guide dog
World.content:
Victorian woman Heidi Biggin has been legally blind since she was 22.

For the past 16 years, Ms Biggin, who lives in Ballarat, has not been able to do regular things like cross a road or get groceries without the help of a guide dog.

Heidi Biggin has been legally blind for 16 years. (ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes)

But everything changed for the mother of three when she got her first pair of smart glasses.

She said she did not think she would ever get a guide dog again.

'Regular person in a regular shop'

Ms Biggin said AI glasses had given her independence she never imagined she could have.

"I've had [the glasses] for about six months now and I've had my [current] guide dog for about four years," Ms Biggin said.

" I'd go as far as to say I wouldn't get another guide dog because of these AI glasses. "

She said she felt like a "regular person in a regular shop" because of the glasses.

"I say, 'Hey Meta, look and tell what section of Kmart I'm in,'" Ms Biggin explained.

"And it'll come back straight into my ear, 'You seem to be in the women's section. To the left of you is the register and behind you seems to be the entrance.'"

She said when she was in public with her guide dog and three young children, she felt like she stood out, often being hounded with questions.

"But when I've got my glasses, I can just blend in," she said.

"My twin nine-year-old boys have their athletics carnival next week and I'm going to the shops to buy them a blue top for their athletics day.

"I'll be able to do that completely myself."

Heidi Biggin says when she is wearing her smart glasses she can finally blend in with the crowd. (ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes )

Accused of filming

But the glasses are not without their problems.

Ms Biggin said she got stopped at least three times a week by people accusing her of filming them.

"Halfway through the walk I'll have somebody grab me on the arm and say, 'Oi, you just filmed me,' because [the glasses] light up when they're in use," she said.

"People automatically assume I'm recording them. It gets exhausting having to explain every time."

She said people should educate themselves about how smart glasses could work to de-stigmatise wearers amid all the "pervert glasses" rhetoric.

"I don't look blind … [but] I also don't want to wear a big badge that says, 'I'm blind please be nice to me,'" she said.

Heidi Biggin says she often gets stopped by people accusing her of filming them. (ABC News: Scott Preston)

She also expressed concern over a ban on smart glasses in Victorian schools, starting from term one next year.

Ms Biggin, who is an inclusion coach who often works in schools, said there was not enough information on how an exemption could be obtained.

"They said there's exemptions but they haven't listed what and how you get exemptions," she said.

"Whether it's a doctor's certificate, a working with children's check or a letter from your employee, we don't know what it looks like.

"As of now, I cannot perform my job wearing AI glasses within schools as of term one.

"I don't think they've taken into account that people are using them for legitimate reasons."

Will guide dogs become redundant?

While covered by government schemes for clients, guide dogs cost more than $50,000 to produce. (Supplied: Guide Dogs Australia)

In Victoria, it takes nearly two years and more than $50,000 to breed, raise, and train a guide dog — a cost that is covered by government schemes for clients.

Waitlists in the state can be anywhere from three months to nearly two years.

While smart glasses are proving helpful for people like Ms Biggin, Guide Dogs Victoria state partnership coordinator Erin Goedhart says seeing eye dogs are irreplaceable.

"Your primary mobility aid as someone who is blind or low vision should always be a guide dog or white cane," she said.

Ms Goedhart is vision-impaired herself and has used both guide dogs and smart glasses.

"I'm in-between dogs at the moment, so I'm using a cane as my primary mobility aid at the moment," Ms Goedhart said.

"There is absolutely no way I could get from A to B, with the glasses and not a mobility aid as well.

"At this stage I can't see guide dogs or white canes being replaced anytime soon.

"In 50 years' time when technology is doing who knows what, let's have another conversation."

World.title: Meghan Markle will return to Australia to co-host Junior MasterChef
World.content:
The Duchess of Sussex, Meghan Markle, will return to Australia to be a host on Junior MasterChef Australia.

In a statement, Ms Markle, who is married to Prince Harry, said she was thrilled to return to the cooking show's team, after joining as a guest judge on MasterChef Australia in April this year during the couple's visit.

"When they approached me to come back and work with this young group of talent, it was an easy yes," she said.

" I love cooking with my own kids, so seeing what these young stars create in the kitchen is going to be a lot of fun. "

Meghan Markle visited a women's shelter in Melbourne during her April visit. (AP: Jonathan Brady)

A Network 10 spokesperson said the junior version of the program is returning after a six-year hiatus, and Ms Markle will judge the program alongside Poh Ling Yeow.

"I had a lovely time filming with Meghan earlier this year, and being reunited will be a real treat," Ms Ling Yeow said.

"I can't wait to meet our pint-sized culinary adventurers — I'm expecting plenty of delicious surprises and a little mischief, too."

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle visited Sydney in April. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

In August, the couple relocated back to the UK after living in the US for six years.

They gave up their royal duties at the start of 2020 and moved to the exclusive seaside area of Montecito, near Santa Barbara, as relations with the royal family soured.

Filming will take place at the MasterChef Australia Kitchen in Melbourne for a few weeks in 2027.

World.title: Police who pull over speeding driver find themselves delivering baby
World.content:
When two Warrnambool police officers pulled over a car for speeding last week, they didn't expect to be asked if they were "any good at catching babies?"

What began as a normal night shift for Sergeant Liam Cook and Constable Angus Hill quickly became one they will "never forget".

They were patrolling the Princes Highway near Dennington, near Warrnambool, just after 2am on Monday, October 19, when they pulled over a blue SUV going slightly above the speed limit.

"Both the driver and passenger side door flew open, which to us as police officers is a bit of a red flag," Sergeant Cook said.

But when the officers approached the car, the driver, Joel, asked them if he could settle any fines later as his wife was in labour.

That's when Joel turned to them and asked, "Are you any good at catching babies?"

"To which I think I had some expletives in my reply," Sergeant Cook said.

The officer calmly called for an ambulance, but the baby was not going to wait.

The expectant mother, Jamie-Lee, said Constable Hill offered to hold her hand while Sergeant Cook helped her partner deliver their second child.

Within two minutes, baby Ashlee was born.

Baby Ashlee has been a calm and "cruisy" baby since her birth a week ago. (ABC News: Tamsyn Buckle)

"We've got the little girl all wrapped up, nice and warm," Sergeant Cook called over the radio.

He then informed Jamie-Lee that it was a girl.

"It was a really special moment for us to be involved in as well, to share the news that they had a daughter," he said.

Constable Angus Hill and Sergeant Liam Cook say the roadside birth is something they will never forget. (ABC News: Tamsyn Buckle)

Once the ambulance arrived, the healthy baby and parents were taken to hospital "just to be safe".

Jamie-Lee and Joel were reunited with the two officers yesterday for the first time since the roadside birth.

"We're lucky we had such great fellas to experience it with us," Jamie-Lee said.

Little Ashlee has an 18-month-old sister, who Jamie-Lee said took a "lot longer" to enter the world.

Joel and Jamie-Lee gave chocolates to the two police officers when they reunited in Warrnambool. (ABC News: Tamsyn Buckle)

"You hear the stories and you never think it's going to be you, but unfortunately it was us," she said.

The family lives about 50 kilometres outside of Warrnambool and made it within 4 kilometres of Warrnambool Base Hospital.

Joel said he was focused on getting to the hospital until he heard the sirens.

"We were going to get there as far as I was concerned," he said.

Dennington is a dairy farming town near Warrnambool. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

"Until they said the ambulance was coming, that was the first time I thought, 'Well, it's happening.'"

Warrnambool's two makeshift midwives, Sergeant Cook and Constable Hill, received a warm reception back at the station.

"Everyone was ecstatic. It was such a good energy in the police station," Sergeant Cook said.

It was a similar reaction when Sergeant Cook called his wife, who happens to be a midwife.

"She was just in disbelief that if it was going to happen to anyone, it happened to me," he said.

"She said we did a good job. She said everything that we did [was] almost textbook."

While delivering a baby isn't part of police training, both officers agreed it highlighted just how varied policing could be.

"Nine times out of 10, we're dealing with people on their worst day, so it was lovely to deal with someone on their best day," Constable Hill said.

"[It was] certainly a career highlight that I don't think Angus and I, we won't top it," Sergeant Cook said.

While Joel and Jamie-Lee don't have any plans for a third child right away, they said things would be different if there was a next time.

"If there is, we'll be staying in town," Joel said.

World.title: Collingwood crisis deepens with coach to leave struggling club
World.content:
Collingwood's AFLW crisis has deepened, with coach Sam Wright another casualty in a horror season.

Wright will leave his position after the Magpies' final-round match against Essendon at Windy Hill on Sunday, ending a three-season campaign.

The Magpies have managed just one win from 11 games to anchor the AFLW ladder alongside the Bombers and St Kilda.

Collingwood's woeful AFLW season Former AFLW player and coach Lauren Arnell has criticised the standard of Collingwood, while emphasising the responsibility of coaches to "put on a show" to grow the game.

The match will also be the last for Essendon coach Natalie Wood, while St Kilda is already looking for a replacement for Nick Dal Santo.

Wright's news comes after skipper Ruby Schleicher announced last week she would leave the Magpies to head home to Western Australia, with other players believed to be also planning a departure.

Tarni White, Lauren Butler, Bri Davey, Sarah Rowe and Mattea Breed are all out of contract, while vice-captain Jordyn Allen is contracted but is expected to seek other opportunities.

Players and staff are reportedly frustrated with list management, development coaching, and medical treatment at the powerhouse AFL club.

Wright backed Collingwood's commitment to the women's football program.

"I look forward to coaching the group this Sunday and I wish them all the very best for the future — I leave knowing Collingwood is committed to driving its AFLW program forward," he said in a statement on Tuesday.

"It has been a privilege to serve the AFLW program at Collingwood.

"I will always look back on my time at the Pies with gratitude, and I want to thank every player, coach, staff member and supporter I've shared this journey with.

"While these decisions are never easy, I know it is the right one for my family and the football program as we move forward."

The Magpies haven't made the AFLW finals since 2022 when they were semifinalists, after ending the regular season sixth.

Despite their resources, they have finished outside the top 10 in each of the following seasons.

AAP

World.title: Randa Abdel-Fattah to appear at Adelaide Writers' Week
World.content:
Palestinian-Australian author Randa Abdel-Fattah has accepted an invitation to appear at next year's Adelaide Writers' Week, the Adelaide Festival has confirmed, as it unveils its program for next year.

The 2027 festival will include West End play Oedipus starring Richard Roxburgh and Heather Mitchell, Bela Bartok's opera Bluebeard's Castle, TAO Dance Theater from Beijing and a "provocative, daring theatre work" from Brazil entitled The Brotherhood.

Highlights from the line-up for Adelaide Writers' Week — which is part of the greater Adelaide Festival program — have been unveiled today.

In January, the Adelaide Festival board decided to remove Abdel-Fattah from the 2026 Adelaide Writers' Week program, citing her "past statements", but did not specify which ones.

"Whilst we do not suggest in any way that Dr Randa Abdel-Fattah's or her writings have any connection with the tragedy at Bondi, given her past statements we have formed the view that it would not be culturally sensitive to continue to program her at this unprecedented time so soon after Bondi," the board's statement read.

At the time, Abdel-Fattah has said it was "outrageous" to be linked to the incident at Bondi in December last year.

Abdel-Fattah was later the subject of an apology from the Festival Corporation, which invited her back for 2027.

Abdel-Fattah appeared at an alternative literary festival, Constellations, which was organised in the wake of the cancellation of Adelaide Writers' Week.

Palestinian author's axing triggered 'coercive behaviour' warning An extraordinary series of emails sheds light on the reservations that preceded, and internal fallout that followed, the decision to scrap Randa Abdel-Fattah's Writers' Week appearance.

It was reported in April, by the Australian Financial Review, that Abdel-Fattah had accepted that invitation — an outcome confirmed by Adelaide Festival Artistic Director Matthew Lutton.

"The board offered an invitation to her earlier in the year and she's accepted," Mr Lutton said.

"That was a decision that the board made and I support their decision."

Mr Lutton said Writers' Week's new director Rosemarie Milsom — the successor to Louise Adler, who resigned as director in January in solidarity with Abdel-Fattah — would be unveiling highlights on Tuesday.

"Then the full Adelaide Writers' Week program will be announced in January," he said.

Mr Lutton said affordability had been a consideration for the broader festival, which would be making some $40 tickets available across the program to people under the age of 40.

"There's free events across the festival. We have an expanded visual arts program across seven different galleries where six of them are free exhibitions," he said.

Adelaide Writers' Week is an annual event held as part of the Adelaide Festival's program. (ABC News)

He said performing artists were keen to join the line-up of the festival, which will run from February 25 to March 14.

"I think they see it as a place where they know national audiences from around Australia will be gathering and they know that there's a really daring and engaged audience at Adelaide Festival," Mr Lutton said.

World.title: Brisbane hospital boards lack Indigenous voices despite legal requirements
World.content:
Prominent medical leader and former Liberal National Party candidate Bill Glasson says the Queensland government is flouting its own laws, branding the lack of Indigenous representation on Brisbane's major hospital boards a direct breach of state legislation.

For six months, the state government has failed to fill mandatory Indigenous board positions at two major Hospital and Health Services in Brisbane, despite the Hospital and Health Boards Act.

Bill Glasson says it is a violation of state law. (ABC News: Lexy Hamilton-Smith)

Metro South has the largest absolute Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population of any Hospital and Health Service in the state, serving 30,000 Indigenous Queenslanders.

Brisbane's Metro North catchment has the second-largest Indigenous population, according to Queensland Health figures.

Dr Glasson, a longtime advocate for Indigenous health and former state and federal president of the Australian Medical Association, called on Health Minister Tim Nicholls to use his powers under the act to make urgent, temporary appointments to both boards.

"Unless the boards reflect the people [they] serve, then we will get nowhere in terms of improving health outcomes," he said.

No shortage of talent

Dr Glasson, who serves on the board of the Institute for Urban Indigenous Health, said plenty of qualified candidates were available.

"I was at an [Indigenous Health] conference last week, and there was a room full of people with the credibility and experience to fill those roles and make a difference to what is happening on the ground," he said.

Mr Nicholls can make urgent temporary appointments if he "reasonably believes it is necessary" because a board lacks the "skills, knowledge or experience to perform the board's functions effectively".

The legislated Indigenous board positions at Metro North and Metro South have been vacant since March 31.

In the meantime, cabinet has appointed or reappointed 91 other board members to hospital boards across Queensland. Half of the eight board members at both Metro North and Metro South Health are new appointments.

Tim Nicholls says recruitment efforts are ongoing. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

While Mr Nicholls boasted about delivering on a key election commitment to legislate that a local clinician serve on each area hospital board, the existing legal requirement to fill the First Nations seats in Brisbane was not addressed during that wave of appointments.

Legislation mandating Indigenous board roles was designed to improve Aboriginal and Torres Strait health outcomes, following a damning 2017 report that found extreme levels of racism inside Queensland Health.

At the time, a leaked copy of the report named Brisbane's Metro South Hospital and Health Services as the worst in the state.

"I can only surmise that they are not interested in having Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander representation," said Tom Calma, a Kungarakan and Iwaidja man, whose work highlighting deep health disparities between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians as social justice commissioner in 2005 laid the foundation for the Close the Gap campaign.

Professor Calma said it was "critically important" the roles be filled, given the substantial Indigenous population in South-East Queensland.

Mr Nicholls did not respond to questions about whether the government was in breach of the legislation.

However, Dr Glasson said it was.

"Absolutely, it's in breach, " he said.

Tom Calma says these roles are "critical" for cracking down on institutional racism in hospitals. (Supplied)

Gaps left unfilled

Official Closing the Gap statistics show the rate of potentially preventable hospitalisations for First Nations peoples in Queensland remains 2.4 times higher than for other Queenslanders.

Progress on healthy birth weights has stalled. First Nations men and women die an average of 7.4 and 7.0 years younger than non-Indigenous Queenslanders.

Professor Calma said institutional racism and a lack of cultural safety routinely caused patients to avoid hospitals or abandon treatments altogether.

"We know ​people are discharging from hospitals against medical orders, people are not fronting up to clinics because they might have had a poor experience," Professor Calma said.​

"Therefore, they're not getting the level of service every citizen is entitled to from the state. ​

"The board of any institution sets the tone and culture of the whole organisation. They're the safeguards at a governance level."

In a statement, Mr Nicholls said, "Recruitment and selection processes are underway to fill existing First Nations vacancies in South East Queensland."

Earlier this year, he acknowledged that efforts to recruit suitable candidates for the roles only began on March 27, just four days before the roles were to become vacant.

Metro South Indigenous director Donisha Duff was given five days' notice to vacate her role on March 31, halfway through her appointed term.

Ms Duff, who has more than 20 years' experience in health and Indigenous affairs, ran as an ALP candidate during the 2022 federal election.

Long-time Metro North Indigenous director Adrian Carson left his role to pursue private healthcare consulting.

Interviews to replace them were conducted as far back as June.

Metro North and Metro South Health did not respond to a series of questions from 612 ABC Brisbane about whether they were concerned that they were operating in breach of state law. They also did not respond to questions about whether they had followed up with the minister or urged him to make temporary Indigenous appointments.

According to Metro South's annual report, the board subcommittee advising on improving Indigenous health outcomes was inoperative.

As at August 31, the First Nations Health Equity Board Committee was currently "awaiting appointment" for both its chair and members.

However, despite the absence of an Indigenous director at Metro North, the board has appointed a guest advisor to its Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples Equity Advisory Committee.

Both boards say they are committed to improving health outcomes for First Nations people.

The Crisafulli government has also faced criticism over a series of decisions, including scrapping the Truth Telling and Healing Inquiry, abandoning the path to treaty, and removing senior and experienced Indigenous leaders from government boards, including major cultural centre boards.

World.title: Queensland youth advocate claims government cut budget in retaliation
World.content:
A leading advocacy group says its funding has been slashed for criticising the Queensland government's strong-handed youth justice measures.

The Youth Advocacy Centre (YAC) provides legal services and support to young people in and around Brisbane who are in contact with the judicial system, child safety, or are homeless or at risk.

Chief executive Katherine Hayes said her organisation had applied for a swathe of tenders after their contract, set to expire in 2028, was cut short.

None were awarded to YAC.

"That's $3 million, that's 19 frontline workers, that's 350 kids per year [who won't receive] training courses, counselling, medical assessments, housing, food, clothing, family therapy," Ms Hayes said.

'Hard not to be angry'

Ms Hayes believes the only reason her funding has been cut is because she has been critical of the government and its approach to dealing with youth crime.

She said her organisation has "unprecedented experience" in the sector, and YAC's program had been independently reviewed by the government and shown to reduce offending "more than any other program that was in place at the time". She said YAC's performance benchmarks had always been met.

"It's hard not to be angry, particularly when you see the distress that it's caused to the young people who have long-standing relationships with our workers, and we've had kids say that without YAC, they wouldn't be here today."

Youth Justice Minister Laura Gerber says reoffending on bail remains above 60 per cent. (ABC News)

Asked by Greens MP Michael Berkman if YAC funding had been cut because of its criticism, asked Youth Justice Minister Laura Gerber said the claims were a "complete falsehood".

She said the contracts were awarded through an independent tender process and that the centre did not meet its KPIs.

In a statement earlier today, Ms Gerber said the program "was not renewed because it was not delivering on the Crisafulli Government’s KPIs to not offend while on bail, and reoffending remained higher than 60 per cent".

Community groups had anonymously spoken to the ABC earlier this year, saying they were effectively gagged from speaking out in fear of retribution.

The head of Queensland Council of Social Service Aimee McVeigh earlier accused the government of "making laws in an echo chamber," after the social service body was not invited to speak at public hearings to discuss proposed breach bail, go to jail laws.

Aimee McVeigh accused the government of making laws "in an echo chamber" earlier this year. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

The legislation is expected to pass parliament this week with bilateral support.

Ms Hayes said it something she has also observed.

"Because in every tranche of new youth justice law that comes through, the government has received an avalanche of reliable, evidence-based submissions which show why the laws won't reduce re-offending. And they never consider those submissions."

The committee overseeing the bail law overhaul made no recommendations for change to the legislation.

'Chilling' effect

Opposition leader Steven Miles said the YAC had been "LNP'd" and the funding cut was designed to send a message to other frontline services.

"They want to send a chill through other organisations and scare them off from talking to Queenslanders," he said.

"Their bail support program has been evaluated in detail and proven to work.

"The only reason to remove their funding is if you do not want an advocacy service speaking out against your government, and that's precisely why David Crisafulli has made this decision, which will affect 19 hardworking staff."

World.title: ‘Bold, but sane’? The future of AI is riding on Anthropic’s float
World.content:
BusinessMarketsAI Opinion ‘Bold, but sane’? The future of AI is riding on Anthropic’s float Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist October 27, 2026 — 12:21pm

October 27, 2026 — 12:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Anthropic has launched the prospectus for what may be the biggest-ever initial public offering – and the fate of the entire US artificial intelligence complex may rest on it. The float of the leading frontier model entity, which is expected to raise about $US100 billion, is critical to the continuing ability of a sector that has a voracious and open-ended appetite for capital. It has to succeed and be seen as successful if the access to the trillions of dollars of new funding the industry will seek over coming years is to remain open. The Anthropic float is a make-it-or-break-it moment for the AI sector. Bloomberg If it were to fail, or to be regarded as less than very successful, the highly interconnected and interdependent sector that relies on that continuing access to equity and debt – from those at the pointy end like Anthropic and OpenAI to hyperscalers like Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Meta to neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius – would be at risk.



And for all but the hyperscalers, the risk would be existential. The scale of the access to cash required was underscored by the Anthropic’s prospectus. The company -- which is about to raise $US100 billion or so, already has $US112.4 billion of cash and recently increased the size of its revolving credit facility from $US3 billion to $US15 billion -- warns in it that it may need to raise even more funding sooner than it had previously anticipated. Anthropic’s IPO has to succeed and be seen as successful if the access to the trillions of dollars of new funding the industry will be seeking over the next few years is to remain open. To maintain access to funding, AI companies have to be able to boast ever-increasing valuations. Anthropic was widely expected to raise its $US100 billion at a company valuation of about $US2 trillion, although recent reports suggest its bankers have brought that back to a range of $US1.5 trillion to $US1.75 trillion because of the recent pullback in the prices of listed technology stocks.



About a year ago, Anthropic raised $US13 billion at a valuation of $US183 billion. In February, it raised another $US30 billion at a $US380 billion valuation. In May, it got another $US65 billion at a $US965 billion. Overall, since its first capital raising in 2021, it has raised more than $US140 billion at ever-increasing valuations of its business. That escalation in perceived value cannot slow or - horror! - stop if the boom in AI investment and development is to continue. As the leading frontier lab, Anthropic’s performance is critical to the rest of the sector. It has to be able to demonstrate a dazzling sales trajectory and the quasi-realistic hope of an eventual earnings explosion. Related Article Wall Street This brother and sister co-founded Anthropic five years ago. Now they are worth $19 billion each It does have explosive growth, with revenue in the first half of this year of $US16.3 billion, up 1300 per cent from the $1.16 billion generated in the same half last year. Its third-quarter revenue growth was, however, a ‘mere’ 45 per cent, so the rate of growth (on a vastly larger base) has been slowing. Anthropic had a net loss of $US80.7 billion, but most of that ($US72.4 billion) was a non-cash charge relating to the increased value of convertible notes it has on issue. At an operating level, the loss was $US693 million.



Its filing shows it spent almost $US9 billion in the half year on computing power and infrastructure ($US1.1 billion in the same period last year) and has commitments of about $US417 billion to buy compute – chips, data centre capacity and cloud services – in the future, although it has foreshadowed spending more than $US750 billion over the next decade. Anthropic’s founders conceded in the share sale documents that their investment in compute “may seem irresponsibly large at first glance,” but described it as “bold, but sane.” More bang for bucks The encouraging aspect of the company’s numbers is that the revenue growth has been outstripping its growth in spending. Moreover, Anthropic is getting more bang for its bucks.



In the first quarter of last year, it spent a little more than $US2.50 on compute and infrastructure for each dollar of revenue it generated. In the June quarter, it spent less than US50¢. If it can maintain that trajectory, the daunting scale of its future capital expenditures might start to make economic sense. The 355-page prospectus was notable, as was the prospectus for Elon Musk’s SpaceX earlier this year, for its dire warnings of the risks of AI, with 94 pages outlining the potential pitfalls. Anthropic and its chief executive Dario Amodei have been more vocal than others in the industry in warning of the potentially “catastrophic” and even existential risks associated with the development of AI. The filing also outlined, however, that the technology could cure diseases and grow economies and “revolutionise every area of human endeavour.” The other unusual element of the document was its disclosure of the company’s proposed governance model which is, to put it mildly, novel.



Within the governance structure is a “Long-Term Benefits Trust,” which has the power to nominate (or remove) four of the company’s seven-member board, although it doesn’t have the power to remove either Dario Amodei or his sister and co-founder Daniela. It appoints its own members, one of whom is former US Federal Reserve Board chair Ben Bernanke. Shareholders can elect the remaining directors. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and his backers will be watching the fate of the Anthropic IPO nervously. Bloomberg There are seven co-founders of Anthropic, including the Amodeis, who will receive a special class of stock that confers no economic interests, but grants them 50.1 per cent of the voting interests, cementing their control. Ordinary shareholders will effectively have no say in the way the company is run, which is a breach of corporate governance norms, but fits with the vision the founders had when they left OpenAI to develop their own AI venture that the technology should be developed responsibly and for the long-term benefit of humanity. That mission wouldn’t necessarily sit easily within a more conventional profit-maximising listed company.



OpenAI’s Sam Altman and his backers will be watching the fate of the Anthropic IPO nervously. OpenAI was also scheduled to float this year, also targeting a valuation of about $US1.5 trillion, but appears to have deferred its listing into 2027. If Anthropic’s float stutters, OpenAI’s access to funding – its viability – would be threatened. Related Article Opinion

World markets The ‘death spiral’ that could destroy this Wall Street boom In fact, Anthropic will provide a test for the entire industry. There have been signs recently, in sliding share prices and spiking bond yields, that the equity and debt markets’ willingness and ability to meet the AI sector’s demands for capital is being stressed. These are massive lumps of capital that are being sought. SpaceX raised more than $US86 billion of equity in its IPO, then promptly hit the debt market and is now raising another $US40 billion via a deal backed by Broadcom chips. Meta has announced plans for a $US95 billion equity raising. Most of the hyperscalers’ AI spending is outstripping their cashflows, forcing them to tap debt markets to keep up with the capital expenditures.



At some point – and the process might have started, given the battering the neoclouds have been getting on Wall Street in recent weeks – the sector needs to be rationalised and consolidated to enable the markets to back a smaller and stronger cohort of AI aspirants. If Anthropic drains the market of available capital, even a successful float might have some unintended but very unpleasant consequences for those AI players that carry too much debt as interest rates are rising and their access to equity is more limited than that of AI heavyweights like Anthropic. Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner has pitched a multibillion-dollar expansion of Brisbane’s busways, proposing new bridges, tunnels and transit ways for dedicated routes for Metro vehicles.

Almost 30 years ago, the state government’s South East Queensland Integrated Regional Transport Plan proposed 75 kilometres of busways, but only about one-third was built, including the South East Busway.

Schrinner wants to revive the unfinished 1990s plan, which proposed busway links to the north and east.

A Brisbane Metro vehicle departing The University of Queensland. Courtney Kruk

Those routes are similar to the ones he announced for the Metro expansion in 2024, with 22 new stops and stations, although the council’s proposal added a link to the airport.

Politicians will receive a security boost after the attack on independent MP Helen Haines, which the prime minister has described as a turning point.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told the Labor caucus on Tuesday morning that the government would speed up an existing security review that was due to report next year.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese during question time at Parliament House in Canberra on Monday. Alex Ellinghausen

Albanese said last week’s attack on Haines had been a “turning point”, and while there had been greater investment in safety and security for MPs, more “can and should be done”.

He said the government was looking at all options, and he had requested the recommendations of the security review be expedited.

World.title: This episode was the best romcom of the year. I wish TV had more like it
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I can recall certain TV kisses the way sports fans remember iconic plays. I know where I was and how it felt, holding my breath in the building anticipation. I can still hear the squeal that involuntarily left my body as the moment finally arrived. The best ones are those that really make you wait. It took Nick (Jake Johnson) and Jess (Zooey Deschanel) 39 episodes of New Girl to passionately kiss – drunk but more clear-headed than ever – in the hallway of their shared loft, her then-boyfriend waiting on the other side of the bedroom door. We waited 28 episodes for Jim (John Krasinski) to work up the courage to confess his love to Pam (Jenna Fisher) at Dunder Mifflin’s casino night in The Office. The show may be the world’s favourite comfort watch but that stolen glimpse of their first kiss, through the blinds of an empty office before the season-two finale cut to black, was TV at its most electric. Related Article Streaming In the mood for love? New rom-coms (and wrong-coms and dom-coms) to watch now There are plenty of great kisses on TV these days. Netflix romcom Nobody Wants This burst onto the scene in 2024 with one of the best. It was in the show’s second episode that hot rabbi Noah (Adam Brody) and sex podcaster Joanne (Kristen Bell) locked lips on the street after rationalising they were “just friends”, her face cupped in his hand as bubblegum electro-pop swelled in the background. But 25 episodes later, it’s a different couple that has my attention. In its just-released third season, this fun and fizzy series has landed something you don’t see so much any more: a proper slow burn. (Warning: spoilers below!) Justine Lupe as Morgan and Timothy Simons as Sasha in Nobody Wants This. Netflix Noah’s brother Sasha (Timothy Simons, Veep) and Joanne’s sister Morgan (Justine Lupe, Succession) have had a strange intimacy since the start. Sure, Morgan was literally repulsed by him (“The brother is brutal. Ogre emoji. Vomit emoji” she immediately texted Joanne in season one). But her barbs were always taken with jest and understanding. The next time they met they bonded over being the “loser siblings”, and by the finale of season one they were hiding their blossoming but awkward friendship from Sasha’s wife, Esther. There was undeniable chemistry. But it wasn’t clear – to the audience or the characters themselves – if that was platonic, weirdly familial or something more.



I love that it took us more than another full season, and the respectful dissolution of Sasha and Esther’s marriage, to find out the answer. And the resulting episode, well-earned after years of tension, stands alone as one of the best romcoms of the year. Netflix had a hit romcom with Voicemails for Isabelle. Nobody Wants This, pictured, was better. Emily V. Aragones/Netflix Timothy Simons and Justine Lupe in season three of Nobody Wants This. Katrina Marcinowski/Netflix Directed by Richard Shepard and written by Jenni Konner and Megan Mazer, the episode, titled Watch What Happens, ends with Sasha and Morgan’s Nick-and-Jess/Jim-and-Pam moment – an almost missed kiss at a bedroom door, landed on the crescendo of LCD Soundsystem’s iconically melancholic power ballad New York, I Love You but You’re Bringing Me Down. But the entire episode is a triumph. Editor's pick Streaming Everything we should (and shouldn’t) expect from the Girls reboot By picking up these characters from the most definitively LA show on television and dropping them in a New York hotel (visiting the city for Morgan’s appearance on Watch What Happens Live), it allows for a more surreal and intimate dynamic to flourish. Noah and Joanne’s phones are turned off back home – perfect sitcom high jinks in itself – and these supporting characters are free to be the leads, playing out whatever fantasy they have of themselves separately and as a potential couple (Pretty Woman-style dress montage included). In the episode’s 25-minute run time they have reckoned with their feelings for each other, flirted with taking it further, decided against it and turned back with ease. And if that sounds like too much to handle in a 25-minute run time, you’re probably not familiar with the director’s previous work.



Editor's pick Streaming The 14 most anticipated TV shows still to come this year Shepard is the same man who helmed Lena Dunham’s iconic and impressively load-bearing standalone episodes on Girls including One Man’s Trash, American Bitch and The Panic in Central Park – that last one another romantic, surreal adventure through New York, featuring a would-be couple weighed down by the heaviness of their real lives. That same magic is present here, no doubt also thanks to Konner. A co-writer of this episode, and Nobody Wants This co-showrunner since season two, Konner was also Dunham’s key collaborator on Girls. Watch What Happens may not go down in TV history as a “perfect episode” in the same way as The Panic in Central Park (though it might for romcom diehards who delight in seeing new spins on old tropes) but it is testament to how powerful it is when a series can cash in on long-term character growth and well-nourished relationship dynamics. And that’s something increasingly rare in a TV landscape where so many of our favourite shows drop only a handful of episodes every couple of years and sometimes disappear without a trace. Nobody Wants This has reliably released three seasons in three years – the way it should be. Katrina Marcinowski/Netflix Almost every great TV romance was built in the pre-streaming era, when network and cable shows were given more than 20 episodes to play with each season – enough room to craft a full story arc without fear of cancellation – and audiences would spend almost half a year with these characters as new instalments rolled out each week. Cheers fans tuned in to watch Sam and Diane flirt for six months before they kissed in the season-one finale. Ross and Rachel took 31 episodes to kiss in Friends, and audiences were still hanging off the drama of whether they would or wouldn’t end up together in the series finale nine years later. These are impossible standards to live up to in an environment where the longest season-run you can hope for is generally 10 episodes – all of which will probably drop on the same day and be largely forgotten the next. (Shout-out to Abbott Elementary, a rare show keeping the network dream alive.) But that makes it all the more impressive when something special and truly squeal-worthy slips through the cracks. Nobody Wants This is now streaming on Netflix.

World.title: ‘Make friends, not profit’: Valley workers mourn looming closure of cult sandwich bar
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In a dimly lit food court in an aged Fortitude Valley building largely abandoned by businesses, office workers form a long line for a humble sandwich. And now, after 30 years of feeding the Valley, Fresh to Go is closing up shop as the owners prepare to retire. The concept is simple yet classic, and it keeps cult-like customers queueing day after day for more. Choose your bread, meat and salads from the bain-marie, all lovingly prepared by couple He Ming Wang and Li Hua Ma. He Ming Wang and Li Hua Ma have been feeding Brisbane’s Fortitude Valley for 30 years. Dean Swindell Fresh to Go is a far cry from the trending, “Insta-worthy”, chef-led sandwich shops this masthead typically features. It feels like stepping back in time, from the decor to the prices. A salad sandwich starts at just $4.40. A blueberry muffin? Just $2.50. They have been doing this for decades, originally in the Valley Metro station and for the past 13 years at this spot in McWhirters.



Fresh to Go’s sandwiches are stacked with salad. Dean Swindell The McWhirters building in Fortitude Valley is quiet before Fresh to Go’s lunchtime rush. Dean Swindell The store doesn’t have a Google listing let alone a social media following, yet every day the line stretches out the door. The couple serves about 100 customers each day and the most popular offering – roast pork and crackling – almost always sells out before midday. Fresh to Go’s signature roast pork that keeps Brisbane customers coming back for more. Dean Swindell They remember nearly every customer’s order, down to whether they like butter and their salad preferences. “They come in every day, and they never change [their order]. Every day [is] the same, that’s the way I know,” He Ming said.



Fresh to Go has been in Fortitude Valley’s McWhirters building for more than 13 years. Dean Swindell The pair begin every day at their Valley store before 5am to prepare and cook 14 kilograms of pork. They finish about 3pm, but the work doesn’t end there. After they close, they go shopping for ingredients to prepare for the next day’s rush. Justin Phillips, who works at nearby Duncan Street, has been getting a sandwich from Fresh to Go three to four times a week for the past three years. The couple remember every detail of their regular customers’ sandwich orders. Dean Swindell “They remember everyone’s order to the point where if I’m on a phone call, I show up, and they’ll just make my sandwich, hand the eftpos machine for me to pay, and hand it to me without saying a single word. “It’s phenomenal.”



Much to Phillips’ joy, the couple refer to him as “handsome man”, but he says it’s definitely the sandwich that keeps him coming back. His usual order of Turkish bread with butter, roast pork, gravy, crackling, carrot, lettuce, cheese, tomato, salt and pepper, sets him back about $9. The Valley’s main drag is well known for colourful characters and He Ming has seen it all. The McWhirters building in Brisbane’s Fortitude Valley. Dean Swindell “Before the Valley was very good. I remember before we had [the] Optus [shop] over there and the Brisbane City Council teaching building – now, everything move. “The Valley situation is getting worse … It makes people feel scared but we’re not. We know everyone, we even know some drug dealers.”



This week they told Phillips they would close for good on November 19, and while he’s glad the couple are getting some well-deserved rest, he doesn’t know what he will do without his lunch ritual. Regulars at Fresh to Go will miss the couple’s friendly faces and fresh sandwiches. Dean Swindell “It’s extremely sad. I don’t know where I’m going to eat now in the Valley,” he said. Duncan Street worker and loyal Fresh to Go diner Alec McFadden shares that sentiment. “I was very sad [to hear of the shop’s closure] but I’m happy for them to retire. “The sandwiches are so good, and they’re so cheap,” he said. “I won’t be able to find anywhere in the Valley for under $10 for lunch.”

Not going as well this year. Will be grateful they pay back to last.
