World.title: ‘I feel betrayed’: Is the heartland about to turn on Trump and the Republicans?
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Caleb Renner, a young corn and soybean farmer from north-central Iowa, has voted for Donald Trump twice. A fifth-generation farmer, he comes from a state that has been fiercely loyal to the president, backing him with a growing margin at each election. But on November 3, Renner will vote for Democrats for the first time. He doesn’t believe he’s alone in breaking from the president and the Republicans. “I feel very betrayed”: Iowa farmer Caleb Renner, 25, is voting for Democrats for the first time at this election. “I would say Liberation Day was the beginning,” he says, referring to Trump’s announcement of sweeping tariffs on most US trading partners, including Australia. “How he handles foreign trade is extremely damaging to farmers. It all comes to a critical point with the Iran war. That’s the most in-our-face, anti-campaign promise policy action that he could have taken … I feel very betrayed.” ‘It’s putting a Band-Aid on a bullet hole.’ Farmer Caleb Renner on Trump’s $US8 billion relief package If there is a blue wave at these midterm elections, it will show up here in the American heartland – farmers and small-town folk hit particularly hard by rising fuel prices, tariffs and trade wars.



Polls suggest something is afoot, but the extent is difficult to gauge, and their record of accuracy is patchy. The Cook Political Report rates four Midwest Senate races as toss-ups: Iowa, Kansas, Michigan and Ohio, along with Alaska, Texas and Maine. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to control the chamber. Farmers have been one of Donald Trump’s most loyal constituencies, but they are feeling the pinch from his policies. Bloomberg The 25-year-old Renner was never a diehard Republican. He grew up in an area where people instinctively voted conservative; in 2024, he supported Trump “with hesitancy”, mostly because Trump was endorsed by Robert F. Kennedy Jr, whom he liked at the time. But now the president’s policies are having a material impact on his life. Disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has spiked the cost of fertiliser. Trade disputes with China slowed down soybean sales. The price of diesel has risen from below $US4 a gallon to more than $US6 ($8.55). ‘One news cycle, one tweet, one social media post, and it affects the markets greatly … There’s no way to plan what’s going to happen.’ Glenn Brunkow, Kansas Farm Bureau president “Every single step of the harvest process relies on diesel. We’re not running EVs or gas-powered tractors,” Renner says. “You’re basically 2x-ing one of our inputs, which is going to show up on our balance sheets at the end of the year after harvest. Our margins are getting tighter, and the markets are not getting any more favourable.” At a campaign rally in Kansas last week, Trump announced a $US8 billion aid package for farmers hit by fuel prices. It followed a $US12 billion relief effort late last year to combat the impact of trade disputes. But the money won’t flow until after the election.



President Donald Trump has held several rallies in Kansas and Iowa during his midterm campaign blitz. AP Photo/Alex Brandon Renner scoffs at the idea. “It’s putting a Band-Aid on a bullet hole,” he says. Nor does it work, he argues – the money just ends up with the banks and suppliers. “Then what happens next year is the input companies are going to say, well, farmers afforded that last year, so we can continue rolling out these outrageous prices for fertiliser, for seed, for chemicals. All this does is inflate the farm economy.” The $US8 billion lifeline was welcomed by the American Farm Bureau Federation, a national agriculture lobby group. But to Renner, the ploy smells of election desperation. “I think he’s under the impression he’s going to buy back farmers’ votes if he throws money at us. It’s honestly disrespectful.” Renner says he will vote for the Democratic candidate for the US Senate in Iowa, Josh Turek, and Democratic gubernatorial hopeful Rob Sand. But he plans to vote Republican in some local races – “ticket splitting”, as it’s known in the US. “If you are beholden to one party, then you’re not really a voter,” he says. “You’re more just a rubber stamp.” Glenn Brunkow, president of the Kansas Farm Bureau, predicts many farmers will voice their frustration by staying home. Michael Koziol It’s one thing for a young farmer who is still figuring out their politics to switch sides. But convincing lifelong Republicans to turn blue is another matter. The more likely outcome is that people disappointed by the president and the Republican Party simply stay home. That’s precisely what Glenn Brunkow, the president of the Kansas Farm Bureau, predicts will happen. The fifth-generation farmer of sheep, cattle, soybeans and corn is also feeling the pinch from higher prices. He meets this masthead at his office in Manhattan, Kansas – a city north of Wichita fondly known as The Little Apple.



“I think there’s some frustration,” he says of the agriculture community. “The volatility is more the frustration than anything. One news cycle, one tweet, one social media post, and it affects the markets greatly … There’s no way to plan what’s going to happen.” Related Article Analysis

US midterms Trump’s election rallies are getting weirder and looser – and more racist Trump recently tried to settle the consumer price of beef by importing more meat from Argentina, a move that did not go down well with farmers. “It really had no effect on the ground beef price,” says Brunkow. “But it did affect the price we receive for calves.” The Trump administration doesn’t seem to understand the agriculture business, Brunkow says. He won’t reveal his own voting intentions, but says there is rising apathy in the agriculture community that is likely to result in people choosing not to vote. Trump meeting with farmers in the White House Rose Garden in June. AP “I’ve heard from producers, ‘DC doesn’t get me, they don’t understand, and there’s no point in voting’. Most agriculture producers are staunch Republicans. There probably are some that have changed. But for the most part, I think if there’s a change in the party dynamics in Kansas, it’s because Democrats showed up and Republicans didn’t.” Many ranchers are not thrilled to vote Republican this year, but will do it anyway. Landrey McGahuey owns a cattle farm on 2000 acres in south-west Iowa, just outside Mount Ayr. He has signs outside his home for several Republican candidates and is clearing dirt with his excavator when this masthead randomly stops by.



McGahuey says he votes Republican because “it’s more logical, their way of thinking”. He has a distaste for liberal politics, although he doesn’t specify the problem. And although he’s hurting from the higher cost of diesel, he doesn’t blame Trump or the Republicans. “I really just don’t blame anybody for it,” he says. “I don’t follow politics a lot because it just seems like you got two groups of people that are so far apart, and they become further apart every day. Nothing gets accomplished, and it’s tit-for-tat.” Landrey McGahuey on his farm in southwest Iowa. Michael Koziol The 44-year-old sometimes sounds like a disgruntled citizen who won’t vote for either side. He knows a few of those people – locals, customers, other farmers – who will stay home rather than show up for the Republicans. Related Article Opinion

US midterms Obama has never mocked Trump so personally. That comes with a big risk Bruce Wolpe Senior fellow at the US Studies Centre and former political staffer “They’re starting to question what [Trump] is capable of doing or maybe what he said he was gonna do that he hasn’t done,” he says. “But I think … every time he tries to get something done, there’s a roadblock. He has so many people working against him that he doesn’t get to do the things that he wants to do. He has contradicted his timeline on certain things a few times. But I don’t know that it’s his fault.” That is a common sentiment in this part of the world. Such is the distaste for Democrats and the so-called Washington elite that Trump – who promised 10 years ago to “drain the swamp” – is given a long leash and afforded the benefit of the doubt.

World.title: Why Trump suing the BBC could become the biggest TACO of all
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaDonald Trump Opinion Why Trump suing the BBC could become the biggest TACO of all Stuart Littlemore Barrister and former ABC journalist. October 27, 2026 — 11:48am

October 27, 2026 — 11:48am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A $US10 billion (AU$14.2 billion) defamation case brought by Donald Trump against the BBC over a program broadcast after the January 6, 2021 riots reached a make-or-break point this week when the judge ordered the US president to turn up and be examined before December 11. Trump is suing the UK broadcaster over an episode of current affairs program Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol. The lawsuit accuses the BBC of “deceptively doctoring” the speech. The broadcaster has already apologised for the error, admitting that it gave “the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action”. Supporters of Donald Trump, including Jake Angeli, aka Yellowstone Wolf (centre), enter the Capitol on January 6, 2021. AFP In commencing this action, perhaps Trump was misled by the $US86.5 million ($123 million) paid to him by Paramount Global and other media and tech companies, including ABC, CBS and Facebook, pretending the vast amounts were genuine defamation settlements, and believed the BBC would fall into line. So far as I know, Australia has had only one such case, in 1986 – when businessman Alan Bond, having acquired Kerry Packer’s Channel 9, paid then-Queensland premier Joh Bjelke-Petersen a $400,000 bribe, successfully passing it off as an out-of-court defamation case settlement from the Packer days. Even the barristers’ chambers cat knew the case was worth $50,000 tops, and it was no more or less than a bribe for Joh’s protection of his business operations in Queensland.



The judge here – Enjolique Lett – ruled that Trump’s persistent failure to meet her case management orders will no longer be tolerated, and that he must give sworn evidence even before the trial starts, in a deposition by the BBC’s legal team. It appears, then, that Trump must either attend and answer their questions, or drop the matter. Related Article Trump diplomacy Trump ordered to sit for deposition in defamation case against BBC Which might just be the biggest TACO (Trump Always Chickens Out) of them all. Defamation lawyers in London and New York were nonplussed from the very beginning of the litigation, seeing it as always doomed to fail. And it was. A man whose name is mud takes on a revered titan of British journalism that courteously said “Sorry!” for a bit of a blunder – one that cost the CEO his job. It has loomed as the biggest such case ever litigated, despite it looking unwinnable, and why did he even start it? Does he really need damages from the court? Getting the edit wrong on his calls for the insurrectionists to “fight” surely pales against his insouciant embrace of obscenity and his defiant boasting of sexual assaults. He didn’t sue over those. Why didn’t Trump sue in London? This was a foreign television show never broadcast in the US, making it seem impossible for his lawyers to gather evidence making the BBC liable for any extraterritorial publication of the single Panorama program. And as to vindication: in the UK, damages for defamation causing reputational injury would not exceed a piddling £300,000, although they are not capped. Hence it has to be a Florida judge and jury. The choice of venue most inconveniently leaves the plaintiff with the apparently insurmountable onus of proving not just that the BBC published the show in Florida (when it didn’t), but also persuading the judge not to apply the UK libel law to a publication made in Britain for a British audience, by a British corporation. At its strongest, the gist of the Trump case is that the editing of the speech he made on January 6 was actionable because it carried the charge that he called on the MAGA crowd to take violent action at the Capitol. Further, if that imputation is established on the balance of probabilities, he’ll have to defeat the defence that he is so notoriously a person of bad character (courts have judged him a fraud and a sexual offender to a civil standard) that the imputed words didn’t further damage his standing in the estimation of right-thinking people. In other words, the president of the US of A would be wasting his time trying to prove that his good name needs vindication. Defamation encompasses slander and libel, although libel is published in permanent form.



Back to Florida, and a judge he didn’t appoint. If Trump meets all his pre-trial obligations, and the case proceeds on February 15 next year as set down, he will have to overcome a full suite of defences, perhaps under British law, perhaps American, rebutting everything from the “public figure” test created in NY Times v Sullivan (certainly not British law, and requires actual malice motivating the libel, not sloppy journalism), substantial truth, and very complex free speech arguments of the “fair comment” kind. And triviality. He may well be advised to retain two teams of specialist counsel. Talk about a lawyers’ picnic. Related Article US midterms ‘I feel betrayed’: Is the heartland about to turn on Trump and the Republicans? To lawyers, the riveting denouement of the litigation will be its eventual disposal by Trump’s Supreme Court lickspittles, although – to be fair – some seem to be working to assuage their shame, now that his character is unquestionably indefensible. Because the US Supreme Court is where this will end if it is ever started. To this lawyer, the hard thing to understand is how the BBC’s American lawyers are fighting the matter. US lawyers are the ones who take 45 per cent of the verdict moneys as their fee. But the parties’ strategy and legal tactics? The BBC’s early application to strike the case out for lack of jurisdiction failed when the judge ordered that it should continue at least through its discovery stages, including Trump’s deposition. Puzzling, when it can’t have been in genuine dispute that no BBC publication took place within any American jurisdiction. The BBC’s smartest tactic resulted in Trump dropping his economic loss claims – his own and his companies’ – rather than open the books. So he’s left seeking damages for only his reputational injuries. And obviously, the defendant will call evidence not so much as to Trump’s character, but of what people think of him. His reputation. And the only people whose evidence on reputation can be received are those proved to have watched the program. It gets sillier. Stuart Littlemore, KC, is a barrister and former ABC journalist. He was the founding host of Media Watch.

World.title: ‘Bold, but sane’? The future of AI is riding on Anthropic’s float
World.content:
BusinessMarketsAI Opinion ‘Bold, but sane’? The future of AI is riding on Anthropic’s float Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist October 27, 2026 — 12:21pm

October 27, 2026 — 12:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Anthropic has launched the prospectus for what may be the biggest-ever initial public offering – and the fate of the entire US artificial intelligence complex may rest on it. The float of the leading frontier model entity, which is expected to raise about $US100 billion, is critical to the continuing ability of a sector that has a voracious and open-ended appetite for capital. It has to succeed and be seen as successful if the access to the trillions of dollars of new funding the industry will seek over coming years is to remain open. The Anthropic float is a make-it-or-break-it moment for the AI sector. Bloomberg If it were to fail, or to be regarded as less than very successful, the highly interconnected and interdependent sector that relies on that continuing access to equity and debt – from those at the pointy end like Anthropic and OpenAI to hyperscalers like Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Meta to neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius – would be at risk.



And for all but the hyperscalers, the risk would be existential. The scale of the access to cash required was underscored by the Anthropic’s prospectus. The company -- which is about to raise $US100 billion or so, already has $US112.4 billion of cash and recently increased the size of its revolving credit facility from $US3 billion to $US15 billion -- warns in it that it may need to raise even more funding sooner than it had previously anticipated. Anthropic’s IPO has to succeed and be seen as successful if the access to the trillions of dollars of new funding the industry will be seeking over the next few years is to remain open. To maintain access to funding, AI companies have to be able to boast ever-increasing valuations. Anthropic was widely expected to raise its $US100 billion at a company valuation of about $US2 trillion, although recent reports suggest its bankers have brought that back to a range of $US1.5 trillion to $US1.75 trillion because of the recent pullback in the prices of listed technology stocks.



About a year ago, Anthropic raised $US13 billion at a valuation of $US183 billion. In February, it raised another $US30 billion at a $US380 billion valuation. In May, it got another $US65 billion at a $US965 billion. Overall, since its first capital raising in 2021, it has raised more than $US140 billion at ever-increasing valuations of its business. That escalation in perceived value cannot slow or - horror! - stop if the boom in AI investment and development is to continue. As the leading frontier lab, Anthropic’s performance is critical to the rest of the sector. It has to be able to demonstrate a dazzling sales trajectory and the quasi-realistic hope of an eventual earnings explosion. Related Article Wall Street This brother and sister co-founded Anthropic five years ago. Now they are worth $19 billion each It does have explosive growth, with revenue in the first half of this year of $US16.3 billion, up 1300 per cent from the $1.16 billion generated in the same half last year. Its third-quarter revenue growth was, however, a ‘mere’ 45 per cent, so the rate of growth (on a vastly larger base) has been slowing. Anthropic had a net loss of $US80.7 billion, but most of that ($US72.4 billion) was a non-cash charge relating to the increased value of convertible notes it has on issue. At an operating level, the loss was $US693 million.



Its filing shows it spent almost $US9 billion in the half year on computing power and infrastructure ($US1.1 billion in the same period last year) and has commitments of about $US417 billion to buy compute – chips, data centre capacity and cloud services – in the future, although it has foreshadowed spending more than $US750 billion over the next decade. Anthropic’s founders conceded in the share sale documents that their investment in compute “may seem irresponsibly large at first glance,” but described it as “bold, but sane.” More bang for bucks The encouraging aspect of the company’s numbers is that the revenue growth has been outstripping its growth in spending. Moreover, Anthropic is getting more bang for its bucks.



In the first quarter of last year, it spent a little more than $US2.50 on compute and infrastructure for each dollar of revenue it generated. In the June quarter, it spent less than US50¢. If it can maintain that trajectory, the daunting scale of its future capital expenditures might start to make economic sense. The 355-page prospectus was notable, as was the prospectus for Elon Musk’s SpaceX earlier this year, for its dire warnings of the risks of AI, with 94 pages outlining the potential pitfalls. Anthropic and its chief executive Dario Amodei have been more vocal than others in the industry in warning of the potentially “catastrophic” and even existential risks associated with the development of AI. The filing also outlined, however, that the technology could cure diseases and grow economies and “revolutionise every area of human endeavour.” The other unusual element of the document was its disclosure of the company’s proposed governance model which is, to put it mildly, novel.



Within the governance structure is a “Long-Term Benefits Trust,” which has the power to nominate (or remove) four of the company’s seven-member board, although it doesn’t have the power to remove either Dario Amodei or his sister and co-founder Daniela. It appoints its own members, one of whom is former US Federal Reserve Board chair Ben Bernanke. Shareholders can elect the remaining directors. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and his backers will be watching the fate of the Anthropic IPO nervously. Bloomberg There are seven co-founders of Anthropic, including the Amodeis, who will receive a special class of stock that confers no economic interests, but grants them 50.1 per cent of the voting interests, cementing their control. Ordinary shareholders will effectively have no say in the way the company is run, which is a breach of corporate governance norms, but fits with the vision the founders had when they left OpenAI to develop their own AI venture that the technology should be developed responsibly and for the long-term benefit of humanity. That mission wouldn’t necessarily sit easily within a more conventional profit-maximising listed company.



OpenAI’s Sam Altman and his backers will be watching the fate of the Anthropic IPO nervously. OpenAI was also scheduled to float this year, also targeting a valuation of about $US1.5 trillion, but appears to have deferred its listing into 2027. If Anthropic’s float stutters, OpenAI’s access to funding – its viability – would be threatened. Related Article Opinion

World markets The ‘death spiral’ that could destroy this Wall Street boom In fact, Anthropic will provide a test for the entire industry. There have been signs recently, in sliding share prices and spiking bond yields, that the equity and debt markets’ willingness and ability to meet the AI sector’s demands for capital is being stressed. These are massive lumps of capital that are being sought. SpaceX raised more than $US86 billion of equity in its IPO, then promptly hit the debt market and is now raising another $US40 billion via a deal backed by Broadcom chips. Meta has announced plans for a $US95 billion equity raising. Most of the hyperscalers’ AI spending is outstripping their cashflows, forcing them to tap debt markets to keep up with the capital expenditures.



At some point – and the process might have started, given the battering the neoclouds have been getting on Wall Street in recent weeks – the sector needs to be rationalised and consolidated to enable the markets to back a smaller and stronger cohort of AI aspirants. If Anthropic drains the market of available capital, even a successful float might have some unintended but very unpleasant consequences for those AI players that carry too much debt as interest rates are rising and their access to equity is more limited than that of AI heavyweights like Anthropic. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner has pitched a multibillion-dollar expansion of Brisbane’s busways, proposing new bridges, tunnels and transit ways for dedicated routes for Metro vehicles.

Almost 30 years ago, the state government’s South East Queensland Integrated Regional Transport Plan proposed 75 kilometres of busways, but only about one-third was built, including the South East Busway.

Schrinner wants to revive the unfinished 1990s plan, which proposed busway links to the north and east.

A Brisbane Metro vehicle departing The University of Queensland. Courtney Kruk

Those routes are similar to the ones he announced for the Metro expansion in 2024, with 22 new stops and stations, although the council’s proposal added a link to the airport.

World.title: Albanese confirms bolstered security for MPs after Haines attack

Politicians will receive a security boost after the attack on independent MP Helen Haines, which the prime minister has described as a turning point.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told the Labor caucus on Tuesday morning that the government would speed up an existing security review that was due to report next year.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese during question time at Parliament House in Canberra on Monday. Alex Ellinghausen

Albanese said last week’s attack on Haines had been a “turning point”, and while there had been greater investment in safety and security for MPs, more “can and should be done”.

He said the government was looking at all options, and he had requested the recommendations of the security review be expedited.

World.title: This episode was the best romcom of the year. I wish TV had more like it
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I can recall certain TV kisses the way sports fans remember iconic plays. I know where I was and how it felt, holding my breath in the building anticipation. I can still hear the squeal that involuntarily left my body as the moment finally arrived. The best ones are those that really make you wait. It took Nick (Jake Johnson) and Jess (Zooey Deschanel) 39 episodes of New Girl to passionately kiss – drunk but more clear-headed than ever – in the hallway of their shared loft, her then-boyfriend waiting on the other side of the bedroom door. We waited 28 episodes for Jim (John Krasinski) to work up the courage to confess his love to Pam (Jenna Fisher) at Dunder Mifflin’s casino night in The Office. The show may be the world’s favourite comfort watch but that stolen glimpse of their first kiss, through the blinds of an empty office before the season-two finale cut to black, was TV at its most electric. Related Article Streaming In the mood for love? New rom-coms (and wrong-coms and dom-coms) to watch now There are plenty of great kisses on TV these days. Netflix romcom Nobody Wants This burst onto the scene in 2024 with one of the best. It was in the show’s second episode that hot rabbi Noah (Adam Brody) and sex podcaster Joanne (Kristen Bell) locked lips on the street after rationalising they were “just friends”, her face cupped in his hand as bubblegum electro-pop swelled in the background. But 25 episodes later, it’s a different couple that has my attention. In its just-released third season, this fun and fizzy series has landed something you don’t see so much any more: a proper slow burn. (Warning: spoilers below!) Justine Lupe as Morgan and Timothy Simons as Sasha in Nobody Wants This. Netflix Noah’s brother Sasha (Timothy Simons, Veep) and Joanne’s sister Morgan (Justine Lupe, Succession) have had a strange intimacy since the start. Sure, Morgan was literally repulsed by him (“The brother is brutal. Ogre emoji. Vomit emoji” she immediately texted Joanne in season one). But her barbs were always taken with jest and understanding. The next time they met they bonded over being the “loser siblings”, and by the finale of season one they were hiding their blossoming but awkward friendship from Sasha’s wife, Esther. There was undeniable chemistry. But it wasn’t clear – to the audience or the characters themselves – if that was platonic, weirdly familial or something more.



I love that it took us more than another full season, and the respectful dissolution of Sasha and Esther’s marriage, to find out the answer. And the resulting episode, well-earned after years of tension, stands alone as one of the best romcoms of the year. Netflix had a hit romcom with Voicemails for Isabelle. Nobody Wants This, pictured, was better. Emily V. Aragones/Netflix Timothy Simons and Justine Lupe in season three of Nobody Wants This. Katrina Marcinowski/Netflix Directed by Richard Shepard and written by Jenni Konner and Megan Mazer, the episode, titled Watch What Happens, ends with Sasha and Morgan’s Nick-and-Jess/Jim-and-Pam moment – an almost missed kiss at a bedroom door, landed on the crescendo of LCD Soundsystem’s iconically melancholic power ballad New York, I Love You but You’re Bringing Me Down. But the entire episode is a triumph. Editor's pick Streaming Everything we should (and shouldn’t) expect from the Girls reboot By picking up these characters from the most definitively LA show on television and dropping them in a New York hotel (visiting the city for Morgan’s appearance on Watch What Happens Live), it allows for a more surreal and intimate dynamic to flourish. Noah and Joanne’s phones are turned off back home – perfect sitcom high jinks in itself – and these supporting characters are free to be the leads, playing out whatever fantasy they have of themselves separately and as a potential couple (Pretty Woman-style dress montage included). In the episode’s 25-minute run time they have reckoned with their feelings for each other, flirted with taking it further, decided against it and turned back with ease. And if that sounds like too much to handle in a 25-minute run time, you’re probably not familiar with the director’s previous work.



Editor's pick Streaming The 14 most anticipated TV shows still to come this year Shepard is the same man who helmed Lena Dunham’s iconic and impressively load-bearing standalone episodes on Girls including One Man’s Trash, American Bitch and The Panic in Central Park – that last one another romantic, surreal adventure through New York, featuring a would-be couple weighed down by the heaviness of their real lives. That same magic is present here, no doubt also thanks to Konner. A co-writer of this episode, and Nobody Wants This co-showrunner since season two, Konner was also Dunham’s key collaborator on Girls. Watch What Happens may not go down in TV history as a “perfect episode” in the same way as The Panic in Central Park (though it might for romcom diehards who delight in seeing new spins on old tropes) but it is testament to how powerful it is when a series can cash in on long-term character growth and well-nourished relationship dynamics. And that’s something increasingly rare in a TV landscape where so many of our favourite shows drop only a handful of episodes every couple of years and sometimes disappear without a trace. Nobody Wants This has reliably released three seasons in three years – the way it should be. Katrina Marcinowski/Netflix Almost every great TV romance was built in the pre-streaming era, when network and cable shows were given more than 20 episodes to play with each season – enough room to craft a full story arc without fear of cancellation – and audiences would spend almost half a year with these characters as new instalments rolled out each week. Cheers fans tuned in to watch Sam and Diane flirt for six months before they kissed in the season-one finale. Ross and Rachel took 31 episodes to kiss in Friends, and audiences were still hanging off the drama of whether they would or wouldn’t end up together in the series finale nine years later. These are impossible standards to live up to in an environment where the longest season-run you can hope for is generally 10 episodes – all of which will probably drop on the same day and be largely forgotten the next. (Shout-out to Abbott Elementary, a rare show keeping the network dream alive.) But that makes it all the more impressive when something special and truly squeal-worthy slips through the cracks. Nobody Wants This is now streaming on Netflix.

World.title: ‘Make friends, not profit’: Valley workers mourn looming closure of cult sandwich bar
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In a dimly lit food court in an aged Fortitude Valley building largely abandoned by businesses, office workers form a long line for a humble sandwich. And now, after 30 years of feeding the Valley, Fresh to Go is closing up shop as the owners prepare to retire. The concept is simple yet classic, and it keeps cult-like customers queueing day after day for more. Choose your bread, meat and salads from the bain-marie, all lovingly prepared by couple He Ming Wang and Li Hua Ma. He Ming Wang and Li Hua Ma have been feeding Brisbane’s Fortitude Valley for 30 years. Dean Swindell Fresh to Go is a far cry from the trending, “Insta-worthy”, chef-led sandwich shops this masthead typically features. It feels like stepping back in time, from the decor to the prices. A salad sandwich starts at just $4.40. A blueberry muffin? Just $2.50. They have been doing this for decades, originally in the Valley Metro station and for the past 13 years at this spot in McWhirters.



Fresh to Go’s sandwiches are stacked with salad. Dean Swindell The McWhirters building in Fortitude Valley is quiet before Fresh to Go’s lunchtime rush. Dean Swindell The store doesn’t have a Google listing let alone a social media following, yet every day the line stretches out the door. The couple serves about 100 customers each day and the most popular offering – roast pork and crackling – almost always sells out before midday. Fresh to Go’s signature roast pork that keeps Brisbane customers coming back for more. Dean Swindell They remember nearly every customer’s order, down to whether they like butter and their salad preferences. “They come in every day, and they never change [their order]. Every day [is] the same, that’s the way I know,” He Ming said.



Fresh to Go has been in Fortitude Valley’s McWhirters building for more than 13 years. Dean Swindell The pair begin every day at their Valley store before 5am to prepare and cook 14 kilograms of pork. They finish about 3pm, but the work doesn’t end there. After they close, they go shopping for ingredients to prepare for the next day’s rush. Justin Phillips, who works at nearby Duncan Street, has been getting a sandwich from Fresh to Go three to four times a week for the past three years. The couple remember every detail of their regular customers’ sandwich orders. Dean Swindell “They remember everyone’s order to the point where if I’m on a phone call, I show up, and they’ll just make my sandwich, hand the eftpos machine for me to pay, and hand it to me without saying a single word. “It’s phenomenal.”



Much to Phillips’ joy, the couple refer to him as “handsome man”, but he says it’s definitely the sandwich that keeps him coming back. His usual order of Turkish bread with butter, roast pork, gravy, crackling, carrot, lettuce, cheese, tomato, salt and pepper, sets him back about $9. The Valley’s main drag is well known for colourful characters and He Ming has seen it all. The McWhirters building in Brisbane’s Fortitude Valley. Dean Swindell “Before the Valley was very good. I remember before we had [the] Optus [shop] over there and the Brisbane City Council teaching building – now, everything move. “The Valley situation is getting worse … It makes people feel scared but we’re not. We know everyone, we even know some drug dealers.”



This week they told Phillips they would close for good on November 19, and while he’s glad the couple are getting some well-deserved rest, he doesn’t know what he will do without his lunch ritual. Regulars at Fresh to Go will miss the couple’s friendly faces and fresh sandwiches. Dean Swindell “It’s extremely sad. I don’t know where I’m going to eat now in the Valley,” he said. Duncan Street worker and loyal Fresh to Go diner Alec McFadden shares that sentiment. “I was very sad [to hear of the shop’s closure] but I’m happy for them to retire. “The sandwiches are so good, and they’re so cheap,” he said. “I won’t be able to find anywhere in the Valley for under $10 for lunch.”

World.title: First look at the Melbourne Cup form - we rate the top 24 horses
World.content:
SportRacingMelbourne Cup First look at the Melbourne Cup form - we rate the top 24 horses Danny Russell October 27, 2026 — 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This guide will be updated when the field is set with comments from Melbourne Cup-winning jockey Michelle Payne assessing each runner’s chances. If the early bird catches the worm, then we are giving you every chance to pick the winner of this year’s Melbourne Cup. We have burned the midnight oil a week out from the race that stops the nation to provide a comprehensive runner-by-runner guide to the top 31 chances in this year’s event – the field of 24 will be finalised on Saturday night. Point of Law rockets into Melbourne Cup favouritism after winning the Geelong Cup. Getty Images The top 24 have been ordered in most likely saddle cloth numbers – from top weight down to bottom weight.



Sons and Lovers (GB) 6yoG (gelding) 57.5kg

Trainer: Joseph O’Brien. Jockey: Ryan Moore

Career: 23: 6-2-6 Last start: Second of 11 G3 Kilternan Stakes Leopardstown Russell says: A dual group 2 winner from Ireland who sounds more like a midday soapie than a racehorse. That being said, in our view he has more chance of winning an Emmy than the Melbourne Cup, considering he has to lug 57.5kg to victory first-up in Australia. Stinger Glass (JPN) 6yoH (stallion) 57kg

Trainer: Yasuo Tomomichi. Jockey: Christophe Lemaire

Career: 12: 6-2-0 Last start: 13th of 18 G1 Takarazuka Kinen 2200m



Russell says: Japanese horses generally get the shivers at the hint of rain, so a big watch on the weather forecast. If we have a dry track, go on his win two starts back in a group 3 over 3401m. That puts him right in the mix. Jockey Christophe Lemaire won the 2011 Cup on Dunaden. If dry, can win. If wet, could finish last. Stinger Glass doing track work at Werribee earlier this month. Getty Images Trustyourinstinct (IRE) 7yoG 57kg

Trainer: Joseph O’Brien. Jockey: James McDonald

Career: 30: 9-7-4 Last start: 4th of 7 G1 Irish St Leger 2816m Russell says: If you believe in the saying, ‘follow the money’, this is the horse for you. He’s owned by Irish billionaire JP McManus, who used to be a bookmaker. That’s a good lead right there. He is also a group 2 winner with a serious chance. Watch to see if McManus bets up big on Cup eve. Top five hope.



Defiantly (FRA) Related Article Cox Plate No October joy for Carlton stars on Cox Plate’s sojourn to Flemington 5yoG 56.5kg

Trainer: Joseph O’Brien. Jockey: Dylan Browne McMonagle

Career: 9: 3-1-1 Last start: First of six G2 Prix Kergorlay Deauville 2999m Russell says: The UK’s version of Pride Of Jenni who will turn this year’s race into a war of attrition. Capable of leading from start to finish in the same manner as O’Brien’s 2020 Cup winner Twilight Payment. The Kergorlay is a good form guide, having thrown up Cup winners Americain (2010) and Protectionist (2014), but a 24-horse Cup field might cause him agoraphobia. Middle Earth (GB)



7yoG 56.5kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Mark Zahra

Career: 26: 6-2-3 Last start: Eighth of 12 G1 Cox Plate 2040m Russell says: If this galloper’s name has been plucked from JRR Tolkien mythology, then surely his trainer, Ciaron Maher, qualifies as some sort of modern-day wizard. Maher is on fire and has given this fellow the old-fashioned Cup preparation. Bart Cummings’ rule was 10km – he has racked up 9.94km in five lead-up races. He looked good late in the Cox Plate. A winning chance. Robbie Dolan rides Knight’s Choice to a famous win in the 2024 Melbourne Cup. Getty Knight’s Choice 7yoG 56.5kg

Trainer: John Symons & Sheila Laxon. Jockey: Robbie Dolan

Career: 31: 6-3-3 Last start: 14th of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m



Russell says: The shock 2024 winner was robbed of the chance to defend his crown in 2025 because of the equine equivalent of a lockdown. Not COVID-19, but strangles – a contagious bacterial disease – that was detected at Macedon Lodge on the eve of last year’s spring. Great run in the Herbert Power two starts back, might have copped interference in Caulfield Cup. Can’t win. Loading Vauban (FR) 9yoG 56.5kg

Trainer: Gai Waterhouse & Adrian Bott. Jockey: TBC

Career: 33: 10-5-6 Last start: Ninth of 13 G3 Geelong Cup 2400m Russell says: The veteran is lining up for his fourth Melbourne Cup – the first two for Irish trainer Willie Mullins before he was sold to Australian connections to be trained by Waterhouse and Bott. He finished sixth last year, but might not be going as well. Although he was first-up in the Geelong Cup, so hard to tell.



Royal Supremacy (IRE) 6yoG 56kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: TBC

Career: 22: 7-3-4 Last start: 15th of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Russell says: Cooked in the Caulfield Cup by a head-scratching ride from visiting hoop Jamie Spencer. He bolted to the front, whacked on the handbrakes and then looked confused when the pressure went back on from the 800m. He was flying before that. Outside the top 10. Enfjaar (IRE) 7yoG 56kg

Trainer: Roger Varian. Jockey: Ray Dawson (TBC)

Career: 17: 5-2-3 Last start: Third of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m



Russell says: Best of internationals in the Caulfield Cup, and in my view, internationals need an impressive lead-up run in Australia if they are to win the Melbourne Cup. He ticks that box. And for those struggling to pronounce his name, Google says Enfjaar means “burst” in Arabic. Top 10. Wine Dark Sea (GB) 5yoG 56kg

Trainer: Harry Charlton. Jockey: Damien Lane

Career: 11: 4-2-0 Last start: 11th of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Russell says: Purchased abroad by Australian Bloodstock, who have won the Cup with Protectionist and Gold Trip, and was a massive spruik horse leading into the Caulfield Cup. Sadly for punters, he didn’t live up to expectations. Needs a gigantic turnaround. Goodie Two Shoes, left in the green-and-yellow silks, finishes second behind Half Yours in the 2025 Melbourne Cup. Joe Armao



Goodie Two Shoes (IRE) 8yoM (mare) 55kg

Trainer: Joseph O’Brien. Jockey: Wayne Lordan

Career: 31: 14-2-7 Last start: Tenth of 11 G3 Kilternan Stakes 2414m Russell says: A former hurdler who ran a surprise second in the Melbourne Cup last year. Trained by Joseph O’Brien, who has already won the race twice, and owned by Irish billionaire JP McManus. Slightly disappointing last start, but that might have been a pipe owner. Top 10 finish. Juja Kibo (IRE) 6yoG 55kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Sam Clipperton

Career: 20: 6-3-6 Last start: First of 16 G2 MV Gold Cup 2500m



Russell says: In hot form, having won its past two starts, including a big win in the group 2 Metropolitan at Randwick on October 3. Didn’t make the cut for the Caulfield Cup, but many believed he could have won the race. Copped a 1.5kg for the MV Gold Cup win. Still think he brings the B-grade form. Top 10. Trainer Ciaron Maher will have a number of horses running in the Melbourne Cup. Getty Images Asterix (NZ) 8yoG 55kg

Trainer: Chris Waller. Jockey: TBC

Career: 33: 8-1-2 Last start: 12th of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Russell says: Caught up in the backwash of the tragic fall in the Caulfield Cup. A group 1-winning stayer from New Zealand owned by former Kiwi cricket great Mark Greatbatch and now in the Chris Waller barn. An outsider, but any rain will help.



Saint George (GB) 7yoG 55kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Blake Shinn

Career: 24: 6-5-2 Last start: Fifth of 12 G1 Cox Plate 2040m Russell says: Aiming to become the first grey to win the Cup since Efficient in 2007, and has had the perfect preparation – second in the Caulfield Cup followed by an absolute flashing light run in the Cox Plate. Traditionally, that is a winning formula. Top three pick. Hopewell Rock (IRE) 5yoG 54.5kg

Trainer: George Boughey. Jockey: Zac Lloyd

Career: 10: 3-3-2 Last start: Second of 22 Ebor Handicap 2787m



Russell says: Another international with decent credentials, but will have to defy history to win this year’s Cup. No runner has come out of York’s Ebor Handicap and saluted on the first Tuesday in November. But a few have been close – Heartbreak City ran second in 2017, while Purple Moon was a runner-up in 2007. Sits 24th in order of entry, so still not guaranteed a start. Onesmoothoperator wins the Geelong Cup in 2024. Getty Images Onesmoothoperator (US) 9yoG 54.4kg

Trainer: Tim Fitzsimmons. Jockey: Declan Bates

Career: 51: 6-11-6 Last start: 11th of 13 G3 Geelong Cup 2400m Russell says: Has gone off the boil. The veteran started second favourite and ran 12th in the 2024 Melbourne Cup after winning the Geelong Cup in the lead-up. Won the MV Gold Cup last year before finishing 16th in the Cup. Not going as well this year. Will be grateful they pay back to last.



Soul Of Spain (IRE) 6yoG 54.5kg

Trainer: Chris Waller. Jockey: Tommy Berry

Career: 26: 5-5-6 Last start: Eight of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m Russell says: Ran second in the Sydney Cup over 3200m but has been slightly disappointing at his past two starts, including a seventh in The Metropolitan. Might have been ridden upside down in the Caulfield Cup. Needs to improve. Zahrann (IRE) 5yoH 54.5kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Ben Melham

Career: 12: 4-2-1 Last start: Sixth of 18 G1 Caulfield Cup 2400m



Russell says: This year’s smoky, considering he started second favourite in the Caulfield Cup and was clearly disadvantaged after being caught up in the tragic mid-race fall. Has not raced over 2400m, but being Irish-bred should relish the two miles. Top five chance. James J Braddock (GB) 4yoH 53.5kg

Trainer: Joseph O’Brien. Jockey: Craig Williams

Career: 8: 2-1-2 Last start: 6th of 11 G3 Kilternan Stakes 2414m Russell says: Another northern hemisphere three-year-old bought by a big group of Aussies. Three things to consider here: He is still trained by O’Brien. Tick. He was sourced by big Melbourne buyer Ozzie Kheir. Tick. Craig Williams sought the ride. Double tick. He is a group 3 winner, lightly raced, and will carry a light weight. First-up in Australia the only concern. A first-four pick. Ethan Brown salutes his Geelong Cup win on Point of Law. Getty Images



Point Of Law (GB) 4yoH 53kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Ethan Brown (TBC)

Career: 5: 3-1-0 Last start: First of 13 G3 Geelong Cup 2400m Russell says: Point to the winner’s circle more like it. This striking specimen’s Geelong Cup victory was the greatest Melbourne Cup audition since Dunaden did the Geelong-Melbourne double in 2011. A northern hemisphere three-year-old who supposedly cost his Aussie owners $3.5 million, and might be worth every cent. Maher did caution about him being inexperienced. Top three. Strictly Business 4yoM 53kg

Trainer: Thomas Carberry. Jockey: TBC

Career: 11: 2-2-0 Last start: 16th of 16 G2 MV Gold Cup 2500m



Russell says: One of the stories of last spring when she won the VRC Oaks for a big group of Irish expats and small-time Ballarat trainer Carberry. Ballarat’s Miners Rest Tavern has never been the same since. But she has struggled to make the transition from three-year-old to open company. Not going well enough. Related Article Updated

Spring racing carnival Viva Via: Champion mare wins back-to-back Cox Plates before punters tear up the track Mr Monaco (GB) 6yoG 52.5kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Jabez Johnstone

Career: 20: 6-2-2 Last start: Third of 16 G2 Moonee Valley Gold Cup 2500m Russell says: Flopped in this year’s Sydney Cup despite starting second favourite, which is a bit of a concern. Qualified for the race by winning the group 3 Bart Cummings (2500m) on a heavy Flemington track on October 3. Maybe a rung below the top-liners, but any rain will help.



Zakouma 6yoG 52kg

Trainer: Grahame Begg. Jockey: William Pike

Career: 18: 5-2-1 Last start: 11th of 11 G2 Crystal Mile 1600m Russell says: Booked a golden ticket in May by winning the Andrew Ramsden Stakes (2800m). That form looks like an egg-and-spoon race compared to other Cup form lines. But Begg is an astute old-school trainer and jockey-of-the-moment Willie Pike takes the ride. Last start was merely a warm-up lap. Shockletz (NZ) 5yoM 51kg

Trainer: Ciaron Maher. Jockey: Harry Coffey

Career: 20: 7-3-1 Last start: Second of 15 G3 Tesio Stakes 2040m



Russell says: Another golden ticket winner, having saluted in the group 3 Archer Stakes at Flemington in September, but looms as a contender for Caulfield Cup-winning jockey Harry Coffey. Dusted off the cobwebs with a strong second in the group 3 Tessio Stakes on Cox Plate day. The Euphrates stretches out late in his Kingston Town Stakes win. Getty Images OUTSIDE THE TOP 24 The Euphrates (GB) – Twenty-fifth on the order of entry. Entered in Wednesday’s Bendigo Cup. World.title: ‘I feel betrayed’: Is the heartland about to turn on Trump and the Republicans?
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Caleb Renner, a young corn and soybean farmer from north-central Iowa, has voted for Donald Trump twice. A fifth-generation farmer, he comes from a state that has been fiercely loyal to the president, backing him with a growing margin at each election. But on November 3, Renner will vote for Democrats for the first time. He doesn’t believe he’s alone in breaking from the president and the Republicans. “I feel very betrayed”: Iowa farmer Caleb Renner, 25, is voting for Democrats for the first time at this election. “I would say Liberation Day was the beginning,” he says, referring to Trump’s announcement of sweeping tariffs on most US trading partners, including Australia. “How he handles foreign trade is extremely damaging to farmers. It all comes to a critical point with the Iran war. That’s the most in-our-face, anti-campaign promise policy action that he could have taken … I feel very betrayed.” ‘It’s putting a Band-Aid on a bullet hole.’ Farmer Caleb Renner on Trump’s $US8 billion relief package If there is a blue wave at these midterm elections, it will show up here in the American heartland – farmers and small-town folk hit particularly hard by rising fuel prices, tariffs and trade wars.



Polls suggest something is afoot, but the extent is difficult to gauge, and their record of accuracy is patchy. The Cook Political Report rates four Midwest Senate races as toss-ups: Iowa, Kansas, Michigan and Ohio, along with Alaska, Texas and Maine. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to control the chamber. Farmers have been one of Donald Trump’s most loyal constituencies, but they are feeling the pinch from his policies. Bloomberg The 25-year-old Renner was never a diehard Republican. He grew up in an area where people instinctively voted conservative; in 2024, he supported Trump “with hesitancy”, mostly because Trump was endorsed by Robert F. Kennedy Jr, whom he liked at the time. But now the president’s policies are having a material impact on his life. Disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has spiked the cost of fertiliser. Trade disputes with China slowed down soybean sales. The price of diesel has risen from below $US4 a gallon to more than $US6 ($8.55). ‘One news cycle, one tweet, one social media post, and it affects the markets greatly … There’s no way to plan what’s going to happen.’ Glenn Brunkow, Kansas Farm Bureau president “Every single step of the harvest process relies on diesel. We’re not running EVs or gas-powered tractors,” Renner says. “You’re basically 2x-ing one of our inputs, which is going to show up on our balance sheets at the end of the year after harvest. Our margins are getting tighter, and the markets are not getting any more favourable.” At a campaign rally in Kansas last week, Trump announced a $US8 billion aid package for farmers hit by fuel prices. It followed a $US12 billion relief effort late last year to combat the impact of trade disputes. But the money won’t flow until after the election.



President Donald Trump has held several rallies in Kansas and Iowa during his midterm campaign blitz. AP Photo/Alex Brandon Renner scoffs at the idea. “It’s putting a Band-Aid on a bullet hole,” he says. Nor does it work, he argues – the money just ends up with the banks and suppliers. “Then what happens next year is the input companies are going to say, well, farmers afforded that last year, so we can continue rolling out these outrageous prices for fertiliser, for seed, for chemicals. All this does is inflate the farm economy.” The $US8 billion lifeline was welcomed by the American Farm Bureau Federation, a national agriculture lobby group. But to Renner, the ploy smells of election desperation. “I think he’s under the impression he’s going to buy back farmers’ votes if he throws money at us. It’s honestly disrespectful.” Renner says he will vote for the Democratic candidate for the US Senate in Iowa, Josh Turek, and Democratic gubernatorial hopeful Rob Sand. But he plans to vote Republican in some local races – “ticket splitting”, as it’s known in the US. “If you are beholden to one party, then you’re not really a voter,” he says. “You’re more just a rubber stamp.” Glenn Brunkow, president of the Kansas Farm Bureau, predicts many farmers will voice their frustration by staying home. Michael Koziol It’s one thing for a young farmer who is still figuring out their politics to switch sides. But convincing lifelong Republicans to turn blue is another matter. The more likely outcome is that people disappointed by the president and the Republican Party simply stay home. That’s precisely what Glenn Brunkow, the president of the Kansas Farm Bureau, predicts will happen. The fifth-generation farmer of sheep, cattle, soybeans and corn is also feeling the pinch from higher prices. He meets this masthead at his office in Manhattan, Kansas – a city north of Wichita fondly known as The Little Apple.



“I think there’s some frustration,” he says of the agriculture community. “The volatility is more the frustration than anything. One news cycle, one tweet, one social media post, and it affects the markets greatly … There’s no way to plan what’s going to happen.” Related Article Analysis

US midterms Trump’s election rallies are getting weirder and looser – and more racist Trump recently tried to settle the consumer price of beef by importing more meat from Argentina, a move that did not go down well with farmers. “It really had no effect on the ground beef price,” says Brunkow. “But it did affect the price we receive for calves.” The Trump administration doesn’t seem to understand the agriculture business, Brunkow says. He won’t reveal his own voting intentions, but says there is rising apathy in the agriculture community that is likely to result in people choosing not to vote. Trump meeting with farmers in the White House Rose Garden in June. AP “I’ve heard from producers, ‘DC doesn’t get me, they don’t understand, and there’s no point in voting’. Most agriculture producers are staunch Republicans. There probably are some that have changed. But for the most part, I think if there’s a change in the party dynamics in Kansas, it’s because Democrats showed up and Republicans didn’t.” Many ranchers are not thrilled to vote Republican this year, but will do it anyway. Landrey McGahuey owns a cattle farm on 2000 acres in south-west Iowa, just outside Mount Ayr. He has signs outside his home for several Republican candidates and is clearing dirt with his excavator when this masthead randomly stops by.



McGahuey says he votes Republican because “it’s more logical, their way of thinking”. He has a distaste for liberal politics, although he doesn’t specify the problem. And although he’s hurting from the higher cost of diesel, he doesn’t blame Trump or the Republicans. “I really just don’t blame anybody for it,” he says. “I don’t follow politics a lot because it just seems like you got two groups of people that are so far apart, and they become further apart every day. Nothing gets accomplished, and it’s tit-for-tat.” Landrey McGahuey on his farm in southwest Iowa. Michael Koziol The 44-year-old sometimes sounds like a disgruntled citizen who won’t vote for either side. He knows a few of those people – locals, customers, other farmers – who will stay home rather than show up for the Republicans. Related Article Opinion

US midterms Obama has never mocked Trump so personally. That comes with a big risk Bruce Wolpe Senior fellow at the US Studies Centre and former political staffer “They’re starting to question what [Trump] is capable of doing or maybe what he said he was gonna do that he hasn’t done,” he says. “But I think … every time he tries to get something done, there’s a roadblock. He has so many people working against him that he doesn’t get to do the things that he wants to do. He has contradicted his timeline on certain things a few times. But I don’t know that it’s his fault.” That is a common sentiment in this part of the world. Such is the distaste for Democrats and the so-called Washington elite that Trump – who promised 10 years ago to “drain the swamp” – is given a long leash and afforded the benefit of the doubt.

World.title: Why Trump suing the BBC could become the biggest TACO of all
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaDonald Trump Opinion Why Trump suing the BBC could become the biggest TACO of all Stuart Littlemore Barrister and former ABC journalist. October 27, 2026 — 11:48am

October 27, 2026 — 11:48am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A $US10 billion (AU$14.2 billion) defamation case brought by Donald Trump against the BBC over a program broadcast after the January 6, 2021 riots reached a make-or-break point this week when the judge ordered the US president to turn up and be examined before December 11. Trump is suing the UK broadcaster over an episode of current affairs program Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol. The lawsuit accuses the BBC of “deceptively doctoring” the speech. The broadcaster has already apologised for the error, admitting that it gave “the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action”. Supporters of Donald Trump, including Jake Angeli, aka Yellowstone Wolf (centre), enter the Capitol on January 6, 2021. AFP In commencing this action, perhaps Trump was misled by the $US86.5 million ($123 million) paid to him by Paramount Global and other media and tech companies, including ABC, CBS and Facebook, pretending the vast amounts were genuine defamation settlements, and believed the BBC would fall into line. So far as I know, Australia has had only one such case, in 1986 – when businessman Alan Bond, having acquired Kerry Packer’s Channel 9, paid then-Queensland premier Joh Bjelke-Petersen a $400,000 bribe, successfully passing it off as an out-of-court defamation case settlement from the Packer days. Even the barristers’ chambers cat knew the case was worth $50,000 tops, and it was no more or less than a bribe for Joh’s protection of his business operations in Queensland.



The judge here – Enjolique Lett – ruled that Trump’s persistent failure to meet her case management orders will no longer be tolerated, and that he must give sworn evidence even before the trial starts, in a deposition by the BBC’s legal team. It appears, then, that Trump must either attend and answer their questions, or drop the matter. Related Article Trump diplomacy Trump ordered to sit for deposition in defamation case against BBC Which might just be the biggest TACO (Trump Always Chickens Out) of them all. Defamation lawyers in London and New York were nonplussed from the very beginning of the litigation, seeing it as always doomed to fail. And it was. A man whose name is mud takes on a revered titan of British journalism that courteously said “Sorry!” for a bit of a blunder – one that cost the CEO his job. It has loomed as the biggest such case ever litigated, despite it looking unwinnable, and why did he even start it? Does he really need damages from the court? Getting the edit wrong on his calls for the insurrectionists to “fight” surely pales against his insouciant embrace of obscenity and his defiant boasting of sexual assaults. He didn’t sue over those. Why didn’t Trump sue in London? This was a foreign television show never broadcast in the US, making it seem impossible for his lawyers to gather evidence making the BBC liable for any extraterritorial publication of the single Panorama program. And as to vindication: in the UK, damages for defamation causing reputational injury would not exceed a piddling £300,000, although they are not capped. Hence it has to be a Florida judge and jury. The choice of venue most inconveniently leaves the plaintiff with the apparently insurmountable onus of proving not just that the BBC published the show in Florida (when it didn’t), but also persuading the judge not to apply the UK libel law to a publication made in Britain for a British audience, by a British corporation. At its strongest, the gist of the Trump case is that the editing of the speech he made on January 6 was actionable because it carried the charge that he called on the MAGA crowd to take violent action at the Capitol. Further, if that imputation is established on the balance of probabilities, he’ll have to defeat the defence that he is so notoriously a person of bad character (courts have judged him a fraud and a sexual offender to a civil standard) that the imputed words didn’t further damage his standing in the estimation of right-thinking people. In other words, the president of the US of A would be wasting his time trying to prove that his good name needs vindication. Defamation encompasses slander and libel, although libel is published in permanent form.



Back to Florida, and a judge he didn’t appoint. If Trump meets all his pre-trial obligations, and the case proceeds on February 15 next year as set down, he will have to overcome a full suite of defences, perhaps under British law, perhaps American, rebutting everything from the “public figure” test created in NY Times v Sullivan (certainly not British law, and requires actual malice motivating the libel, not sloppy journalism), substantial truth, and very complex free speech arguments of the “fair comment” kind. And triviality. He may well be advised to retain two teams of specialist counsel. Talk about a lawyers’ picnic. Related Article US midterms ‘I feel betrayed’: Is the heartland about to turn on Trump and the Republicans? To lawyers, the riveting denouement of the litigation will be its eventual disposal by Trump’s Supreme Court lickspittles, although – to be fair – some seem to be working to assuage their shame, now that his character is unquestionably indefensible. Because the US Supreme Court is where this will end if it is ever started. To this lawyer, the hard thing to understand is how the BBC’s American lawyers are fighting the matter. US lawyers are the ones who take 45 per cent of the verdict moneys as their fee. But the parties’ strategy and legal tactics? The BBC’s early application to strike the case out for lack of jurisdiction failed when the judge ordered that it should continue at least through its discovery stages, including Trump’s deposition. Puzzling, when it can’t have been in genuine dispute that no BBC publication took place within any American jurisdiction. The BBC’s smartest tactic resulted in Trump dropping his economic loss claims – his own and his companies’ – rather than open the books. So he’s left seeking damages for only his reputational injuries. And obviously, the defendant will call evidence not so much as to Trump’s character, but of what people think of him. His reputation. And the only people whose evidence on reputation can be received are those proved to have watched the program. It gets sillier. Stuart Littlemore, KC, is a barrister and former ABC journalist. He was the founding host of Media Watch.

World.title: 'The green cow': World's Jersey breeders coming to New Zealand
World.content:
Dozens of dairy farmers from across the world are set to visit New Zealand next year as part of the World Jersey Conference 2027.

The conference will bring together Jersey breeders, farmers, scientists, and industry leaders for a three week tour across Aotearoa showcasing our industry, farms, people and genetics.

The theme of next year's conference is 'The Next Generation', looking at where the Jersey breed is heading, and exploring how genetics, technology, sustainability, efficiency and innovation are shaping dairy farms of tomorrow.

The president of the World Jersey Cattle Bureau and event organiser described Jerseys as a "green cow".

"She's a lighter weight, so there's a lower footprint. She's very, very efficient. It's not unusual for a 450 kilogram Jersey to produce 450 kilograms of milk solids.

"Her calving ease is well noted. Her ability to be heat tolerant is a well-known fact and that's why places like in Africa the Jersey is a favoured breed because of her ability for heat tolerance."

The timing of the conference comes as the dairy industry is increasingly focused on producing more from less, and improving farm efficiency while responding to environmental, economic and animal performance challenges.

Genetic progress is another key part of the conversation.

DairyNZ's latest national animal evaluation data showed Jersey cows continuing to sit strongly for breeding worth and production worth, while current Jersey genetics are being selected for a combination of production, fertility, functional survival, conformation and efficiency traits.

Gibb said more than 80 delegates from up to 39 World Jersey Bureau member countries are expected to take part.

It also marked a significant milestone for JerseyNZ, with 2027 being the organisation's 125th anniversary.

"New Zealand has always been seen as having the highest Jersey population and I believe we still do but sadly Jerseys are diminishing in New Zealand.

"But on a world scale we still I believe have the highest population of Jerseys."

The conference will be held over six days in February next year, followed by option tours across both the North and South Island.

World.title: US suspends visa-free travel for Chinese visitors to Northern Marianas
World.content:
The United States has suspended a special visa-free travel programme for Chinese nationals visiting the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), citing national security concerns, human smuggling and other criminal activities.

The Department of Homeland Security announced the suspension of the CNMI Economic Vitality and Security Travel Authorisation Program (EVS-TAP) in a Federal Register notice published on Tuesday.

The suspension takes effect on 31 October.

The EVS-TAP, introduced in February 2025, allows eligible Chinese nationals to visit the Northern Marianas without a US visa for up to 14 days.

Chinese visitors are prohibited from travelling onward to Guam or other parts of the United States under the arrangement.

The department said more than 3000 Chinese nationals entered the Northern Marianas under EVS-TAP during fiscal year 2025.

However, Homeland Security officials determined that the program presented unacceptable security and law enforcement risks, including the possibility of espionage targeting US military installations in the region.

The department cited previous cases involving Chinese nationals being smuggled from Saipan to Guam, some of whom were subsequently encountered near sensitive military facilities.

It also raised concerns about birth tourism, money laundering, and labour abuses associated with Chinese-linked businesses, including the former Imperial Pacific casino operation on Saipan.

The department acknowledged that suspending the program could affect businesses in the Northern Marianas that depend on Chinese tourists but said national security concerns outweighed the potential economic impact.

The suspension applies to new applicants and travelers who already have approved EVS-TAP authorisations.

Chinese nationals already legally in the Northern Marianas under the program may remain until their authorised stay expires.

Future visitors from China will need to obtain an appropriate US visa unless another lawful exception applies.

The department said it would review the program in consultation with the US departments of State and the Interior.

World.title: Sand-related toys will need to tested for asbestos before being sold in New Zealand
World.content:
Any toys containing sand will soon require testing to prove they are asbestos-free before they can be sold in New Zealand.

It follows a recall on Kmart coloured sand products from November last year, after it was discovered they contained asbestos.

In a statement, the Commerce Commission said it - alongside New Zealand Customs - would enforce the new safety check as part of an Unsafe Goods (Consumer Sand Products) Notice from 1 February 2027.

The commission's principal compliance adviser Grant McIntosh said the new rules were designed to reduce the risk of asbestos exposure from products containing sand.

"Parents and caregivers should be able to feel confident that the products they buy for their children are safe. These new testing requirements will help prevent sand products containing asbestos from reaching New Zealand shelves and homes."

The new rules only cover certain sand products - but all toys for children under the age of 14.

As of October 2026, the commission said 23 products have been recalled after finding traces of asbestos - affecting more than 45,000 items. News first broke of the situation in November 2025.

It said the testing requirements would apply to:

toys and other consumer products containing accessible sand;

or sand within a coating that can be penetrated during normal use

decorative, art and craft products containing accessible sand.

The commission said asbestos cannot be identified without testing - "making it hard for consumers to know whether a product poses a risk simply by looking at it".

Anyone who has purchased sand-related products is advised to

check whether the product has been recalled;

stop using recalled products immediately;

follow the instructions provided in the recall notice;

keep up to date with product safety alerts and recalls.

The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment said the notice would be in place for 18 months.

Keren Lee - a Lower Hutt mum whose two young children were exposed to the contaminated sand - asked why it was not permanent.

"We all believe this should be a permanent thing put in place, but we have to start somewhere so it's great news."

"It's validated that this should have been in place already."

Before news broke in November last year, Lee said many parents assumed products they purchased in New Zealand had been checked.

"Why would these checks ever not be in place? So many of us families assumed that they were," she said.

"I genuinely thought if you purchased something in New Zealand, even if it had been made overseas, that it had been through some kind of check to know that it wasn't toxic."

She said the entire saga had been "sickening".

"I've focused on the things I could do something about, getting rid of everything and getting reimbursed, but this uncertainty about our children's health is going to hang over us for a lifetime."

Lee hoped the safety conversation would continue beyond sand.

"It's not just sand, there's been lots of products with questionable materials in them," she said.

World.title: Child assaulted at Myers Park in stable condition, accused gets name suppression
World.content:
A child who was assaulted at a central Auckland park over the weekend is in a stable condition.

The assault happened at Myers Park, near Queen Street, at about 4.45pm on Sunday.

On Tuesday, police said the child, who was taken to Starship Hospital with critical injuries after the attack, was doing well and remained in a stable condition.

Police confirmed that a 20-year-old man had been charged with attempted murder and was in custody.

He had been taken to hospital in serious condition following the attack as a result of self-inflicted injuries.

Defence lawyer Jason Yang said the man would not be appearing in court on Tuesday, as planned, because he was still in hospital.

He said his client, who has name suppression, has had his first appearance rescheduled to 9 November.

World.title: Labour pledges to help public housing tenants buy their homes
World.content:
Labour is promising to help public housing tenants buy their own homes, putting $100 a week towards their deposits under a new rent-to-buy scheme.

Under the election policy, working tenants in Kāinga Ora homes and participating community housing properties would be able to build up a deposit while paying rent.

They would receive a $100 weekly credit, adding up to $5200 a year, with the money held in a trust account.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407446768112

Tenants could then buy the house they were renting, at a price set by an independent valuation.

Labour would also expand the existing First Home Loan scheme, lifting the income limit to $300,000 and allowing more people to buy a house with a deposit of just five percent.

Tenants could use both schemes together to buy their homes with a five percent deposit.

Labour says it would build three new public homes for every Kāinga Ora property sold through rent-to-buy, using the money from sales to help fund construction.

World.title: What will Prada closure mean for Queen Street?
World.content:
Luxury retail brand Prada will close its Queen Street outlet on Wednesday, but one retail consultant isn't expecting it to have a big impact on the street.

The two-storey retail outlet covers about 350 square metres and opened more than 10 years ago.

Auckland's Queen Street has changed significantly in recent years, with stores Smith & Caughey's and Yoyoso having shut their doors over the past 18 months.

Retail consultant Chris Wilkinson, of First Retail Group, said he did not think the exit would have an impact because others were likely to take the opportunity to use the space to grow their footprint, or another brand could enter the market.

Audio player for " Should you buy a house from your mother-in-law? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2186354%2Fwhat-will-prada-closure-mean-for-queen-street

"Even within the Prada group there are brands that may be better suited to the audience here.

"The fundamentals of Queen Street are strong as are the future indicators with Britomart's announced redevelopment, Te Waharoa, the city's new international cruise terminal and the revitalisation driven by CRL. Luxury brands typically play the long-game and know that opportunities in tightly held areas rarely come along.

"While other luxury brands have steadily increased presence and rarely exit markets, Prada has had a history of adaptation. In 2012, the company pulled back retail presence to heighten its 'scarcity value' and more recently it has been right-sizing representation in regions as part of its broader moves to bring the Versace stable into its fold."

Retailers generally have been under pressure lately.

Stats NZ's latest Electronic Card Transaction data for September shows actual core retail spending rose just 0.1 percent compared to the same month last year, including food and fuel. Apparel spending was down more than 5 percent.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said the luxury market had been hit globally, "especially because the aspiring middle classes have pulled back on luxury purchases. So the uber-wealthy market remains as it always was. But the growth via aspiring middle is currently less so".

Gareth Kiernan, chief forecaster at Infometrics, said he thought underlying economic conditions were likely to have had a limited influence on the decision to close.

"That luxury precinct at the bottom of Queen Street is like another world, and it has remained highly sought after in recent years, despite the lingering effects of Covid, CRL and other cityscape construction, and the drift away from physical retailing that have been more evident on the retail sector further up Queen Street.

"I expect there are broader business strategy reasons behind the decision, and Auckland isn't seen as enough of a growth market compared to other opportunities internationally."

World.title: Start-up companies attracting larger investments amid record growth
World.content:
More established start-up companies are attracting larger investments with the first half of the year seeing record growth.

The Young Company Finance report issued by NZ Growth Capital Partners and The Angel Association indicates there was also a rebound in new deals at proof-of-concept and pre-seed stages.

A total of 68 funded deals were recorded in the six months ended June, with $775.7 million invested.

"While the number of deals fell slightly by 6.8 percent on the same period last year, total funding took another leap forward, growing by 114.5 percent and representing a greater amount invested than in all of last year, reflecting the global funding trend," the report says.

Angel Association executive director Bridget Unsworth said early-stage investment was making a comeback.

"The first half of 2026 tells the story of an ecosystem that is scaling quickly while also beginning to rebuild its foundations. Both trends matter, and both deserve attention."

She said more capital was invested in the first six months of this year than in the whole of 2025.

"Larger rounds are no longer the exception. They are becoming a defining feature of the market."

Unsworth said New Zealand companies were making progress in attracting the capital needed to compete internationally, and doing so in sectors with genuine global reach.
