The sectors included agtech and space technology, software and other deeptech.

"The growing role of venture capital in leading rounds shows a capital stack that is maturing and gaining sophistication."

She said record funding was allowing NZ companies to go global.

"It shows that a New Zealand company can raise at a scale that would have been hard to imagine a few years ago.

"The large rounds we celebrate today rest on early backing that angels provided years ago, and a renewed flow of new companies is the best indicator that this pattern can continue."

World.title: Electorates to watch: Te Tai Tokerau
World.content:
Of Aotearoa's seven Māori seats, Te Tai Tokerau is probably the most contested and the hardest to call.

This sprawling electorate stretches 400km from Te Rerenga Wairua/Cape Reinga to the North Shore and even reaches deep into West Auckland, encompassing areas of deprivation and social malaise through to the well-heeled boom towns of the east coast.

One in three of its roughly 45,000 enrolled voters is aged under 35, making it one of the youngest electorates in the motu.

Why is it interesting?

The seat has switched hands regularly in the past, but the current contest is unlike any other before - so the past is no guide to what will happen on November 7.

The seat is currently held by Mariameno Kapa-Kingi, who set up her own Te Tai Tokerau party after an acrimonious split with Te Pāti Māori last year. She faces three strong challengers, all of whom have high profiles and leadership positions outside Parliament.

Also, Te Tai Tokerau voters are a savvy lot who know how to use their votes strategically. The outcome could have an outsize effect on the overall result due to the potential for overhang, whereby a party ends up with more seats in Parliament than its proportion of the vote would allow.

Recent polling suggests Hūhana Lyndon could - if the poll result is replicated on election day - make history by becoming the first Green candidate to win a Māori seat.

Who's standing?

Hūhana Lyndon (from left), Mariameno Kapa-Kingi, Willow-Jean Prime and Aperahama Edwards are running for Te Tai Tokerau. RNZ / VPN

Current MP Mariameno Kapa-Kingi, standing for her own Te Tai Tokerau Party, is hoping to hold onto the seat. She is a former chief executive of Te Aupōuri iwi who has strong support in the very Far North, but also in West Auckland where many votes are concentrated. She wrestled the seat off Labour's Kelvin Davis in 2023.

Willow-Jean Prime (Labour) is a sitting list MP who has previously contested the Northland general electorate, which she won in the "red tide" of 2020. This is her third term in Parliament but will be her first tilt at a Māori electorate. She is number seven on the Labour list, making her the party's highest-ranked wahine Māori.

Hūhana Lyndon (Green) is a first-term list MP and former chief executive of Ngātiwai Trust Board and Ngāti Hine Forestry Trust. She is known in the North as "Hui-hana" because she has a reputation for being everywhere and turning up at almost every kaupapa.

Aperahama Edwards (Te Pāti Māori) is the chairman of Ngātiwai Trust Board and co-chair of Te Kahu o Taonui, Northland's iwi leaders forum. He had a prominent role in last year's Hīkoi mō Te Tiriti and has been endorsed by former MP Hone Harawira, who briefly considered seeking the party's candidacy himself.

Also standing are Maki Herbert of the Aotearoa Legalise Cannabis Party and Karl Barkley of Your Pic Party.

National, New Zealand First and Act are not contesting the seat.

What do the people say?

Audio player for " What matters most to voters in Te Tai Tokerau " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2186332%2Felectorates-to-watch-te-tai-tokerau

What matters most to voters in Te Tai Tokerau Morning Report Download MP3 3m

RNZ took to the streets in Kaikohe, Whangārei and the North Shore to ask voters on the Māori roll about the issues that mattered most to them, and who was likely to get their vote.

Gina-Maree Makiha, of Kaikohe, said her top issue was "absolutely" the cost of living, followed by homelessness and alcohol and drugs.

Gina-Maree Makiha just hopes the people of Te Tai Tokerau get out and vote - and she even wears her message on a hand-stitched ribbon. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

She said politicians had largely bypassed Kaikohe on the campaign trail so far, so she was doing her best to drum up some interest in the town.

"I'm really hoping that the whānau here in Tai Tokerau get to the polling booths. I just feel that there hasn't been so much presence around here in Tai Tokerau. I mean we see it on screen, we see it on social media, but I want to see the politicians out on the streets talking to the people, face to face. I haven't seen much of that at all, to be honest."

Like many people spoken to by RNZ, Makiha was thinking about splitting her vote.

"I'm looking possibly at Aperahama Edwards [Te Pāti Māori] and the Greens. I like what they're doing. They're proactive, they're out there talking to the people."

Just down the street at Bouquets on Broadway, the top issues for florist Karla Tawhai were the environment and the cost of living.

"Also, being in business, you're always looking for something that's going to help businesses improve or even be able to afford to hire somebody because at this stage, the way that everything is going with the economy, I can't even afford to hire someone. I can hardly even pay myself sometimes."

Bouquets on Broadway owner Karla Tawhai, of Kaikohe, says the environment and the high cost of running a business are her two biggest concerns. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Tawhai not yet decided who to vote for.

"I am a bit worried about that because normally I have it in my head and already planned, but I'm really still unsure. There's too many other things on my mind just to do with being able to stay afloat. Plus I'm over all the palaver that happens in government, unfortunately."

Whangārei's Josh Ambler had a similar list of priorities.

"For me, the biggest issues are the cost of living, housing, and the environment. The impacts of how we develop the whenua and what that looks like for future generations is really important for me."

Ambler said he also planned to be strategic, splitting his vote between Te Pati Māori and the Greens - in the hope of creating an overhang and bringing about the change of government he wanted.

"The current government has really disenfranchised Māori on a range of things. And the impacts that they've had on Te Tiriti and the partnerships with Māori and all of that stuff has been quite devastating. I think they've done some real harm."

Kaikohe's Hilton Harris, owner of Māori apparel store Cuzy T Aotea Collective, was concerned about high unemployment and wanted more support for small businesses.

Cuzy T Aotea Collective owner Hilton Harris, with Wairua Davis, wants the government to support small businesses rather than big corporates. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

He believed the government focussed too much of its attention on the large corporates.

"I'd like to see more private enterprise in this town. How it was back in the late 80s, early 90s, when this town was thriving. Once you have private enterprise, you bring wealth back into the community, and that money circulates within the town."

Further south, on Auckland's North Shore, Sophie Farrell was pursuing a degree in engineering and Māori studies.

She was concerned about the coalition's approach to race issues and what that would mean for the future.

Student Sophie Farrell worries about what she sees as racism in government and the axing of fees-free tertiary education. RNZ / Erin Johnson

"Also with university funding from the government and cutting the fees-free, I think that's pretty bad. I think it's pushing people towards more manual labour jobs instead of high-level skill jobs, which are better in the long term for the country."

Roofer Dillon Coyle, who grew up speaking te reo in isolated Panguru, wanted to see more Māori in government.

He had supported Winston Peters in the past but with no NZ First candidate contesting Te Tai Tokerau, he was considering giving his electorate vote to the Greens' Hūhana Lyndon.

For him, the key thing was for Māori to "have each other's backs and uplift each other".

Roofer Dillon Coyle, originally from Panguru, wants to see more Māori in Parliament. RNZ / Erin Johnson

Also on the North Shore, Teri Samuel said she planned to vote for the first time in more than a decade.

With unemployment nudging record levels in the North, she said the government's top priority should be jobs.

"Give people a job so they can get a home, because it's all about the money right now. We need the money to move on. There's too many of us that are unemployed, and some of them [employers] won't take us because they need experience. But what about those that haven't got experience and need a chance to grow?"

Teri Samuel believes unemployment is the single biggest issue facing Māori in the North. RNZ / Erin Johnson

Samuel said she was tossing up between Labour and the Greens, parties she said stood up for the poor.

"We really need somebody that focuses on us, our land, our country, especially for our future, our mokopunas, so we can leave something behind for them."

What do the polls say?

A Whakaata Māori-Curia poll released last week showed Green candidate Hūhana Lyndon on 24 percent support, ahead of Labour's Willow-Jean Prime (18 percent), Te Pāti Māori candidate Aperahama Edwards (17 percent), and Te Tai Tokerau Party's Mariameno Kapa-Kingi (12 percent).

However, it also showed 20 percent were still unsure who to vote for.

The poll surveyed 500 enrolled Te Tai Tokerau voters and had a margin of error of 4.5 percent.

Labour held the biggest share of the party vote (27 percent) with the Greens close behind on 25 percent. Te Pāti Māori registered 11 percent, NZ First 6 percent and National 4 percent.

World.title: Kane breaks 25-year English drought to claim top football award
World.content:
Harry Kane won the Ballon d'Or on Monday, local time in London, becoming the first Englishman to receive the prestigious prize in 25 years.

The Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals for club and country last season, smashing scoring records in Germany and leading England to a third-place finish at the World Cup this past summer.

Kane was the top vote-getter among nominees who included Lamine Yamal, Kylian Mbappe and Lionel Messi.

Earlier, Spain star Alexia Putellas won her third women's Ballon d'Or after leading her former club Barcelona to multiple trophies last season, including the Women's Champions League.

Putellas, who joined London City Lionesses in the off-season, also helped Spain win the Women's Nations League in December.

The 32-year-old midfielder ended Spain teammate Aitana Bonmati's three-year reign.

Putellas won the prestigious award in back-to-back seasons — 2021 and 2022 — before tearing her ACL and watching Bonmati rise to stardom.

Bonmati, who completed her women's Ballon d'Or three-peat in 2025, was not on this year's shortlist after breaking her leg in December.

AP

World.title: Veteran rugby prop cited for allegedly grabbing opponent's genitals
World.content:
Veteran Ireland prop Leinster's Tadhg Furlong has been cited for allegedly grabbing the genitals of Munster's Gavin Coombes during their United Rugby Championship match last weekend.

Coombes alleged during the game on Saturday that his testicles had been grabbed, but an immediate television review ordered by referee Andrew Brace was inconclusive, with no evidence of the incident.

However, since the incident was noted in the referee's report, it can be reviewed by the citing commissioner Peter Ferguson.

"Leinster Rugby's Tadhg Furlong has been cited for an incident that occurred in the 37th minute of the United Rugby Championship [URC] Round 4 fixture at the Aviva Stadium against Munster Rugby on Saturday, 24 October," a statement from the URC said on Monday.

"The Citing Commissioner in charge has made a complaint about an act of foul play by the Player [Tadhg Furlong No. 3] against opponent Gavin Coombes [No. 8].

"The Player has been cited under Law 9.27 — A player must not do anything that is against the spirit of good sportsmanship, including but not limited to grabbing, twisting or squeezing the genitals.

"Arrangements for the disciplinary process are currently in progress and will be announced in due course."

Coombes has been backed in his allegation by Munster coach Clayton McMillan.

"All I know is that I back our players 100 per cent — that if they make an allegation like that, they wouldn't do it lightly — and that's not the sort of person Gavin is, so we'll see where that goes," McMillan said.

Furlong faces the possibility of a lengthy ban if found guilty. The 33-year-old is a British & Irish Lion and key member of the Ireland team, approaching 100 test caps. He is in the squad for November's Nations Championship fixtures, and a ban would be a blow to his personal reputation as well as to the Irish team.

Leinster head coach Leo Cullen said: "Obviously, once that accusation is made, it becomes a serious matter for the citing commissioner. So my comment is not going to help in any way here. But from what I've seen, I can't see anything."

In the URC last season, Bulls hooker Jan-Hendrik Wessels was handed a nine-week suspension for grabbing the testicles of Connacht's Josh Murphy.

Reuters

World.title: De Minaur pulls off massive comeback to improve ATP Finals hopes
World.content:
It had looked like goodnight Vienna for Alex de Minaur as he trailed Tomas Machac by a set, a break and 0-30 on his own misfiring serve.

Machac, a top 20 player last year, was fizzing winners onto the lines and Australia's number one seemed to have no answer to his excellence.

The Czech was six points from victory and de Minaur's chances of making the end-of-season ATP Finals were receding rapidly as a first-round exit loomed in the Austrian capital.

But Demon never quits. He won the next four points to hold, then broke Machac in a three-deuce game. He then survived a break point on his next service game, which lasted nearly nine minutes, then broke again to take the set.

Machac broke immediately in the third set but it was a last hurrah. De Minaur took the next five games before completing a near-two-hour 1-6, 6-4, 6-3 win with an ace.

De Minaur greeted Monday's victory with a roar of delight, relief and vindication. The 27-year-old has made a career out of comebacks but few have been such a turnaround as this.

"For three-quarters of that match it was very tough for me," he said. "I have dug deep, found a way to get a crucial break when I needed it, and the momentum changed."

Referring to his recent run to the final in Beijing, and a narrow quarterfinal loss to Alexander Zverev in Shanghai, he added: "The last couple of tournaments I've learned a lot about myself and was able to draw on those situations and come out with some big serves when I needed it."

De Minaur began Vienna's ATP 500 event tenth in the standings for the season's Turin finale and, with Jannik Sinner's competitive season over, needs to be in the top nine to qualify.

AAP

World.title: Roosters stunningly withdraw contract offer to halfback Sam Walker
World.content:
Sam Walker's future at the Sydney Roosters is uncertain after the club pulled a contract extension offer to the premiership-winning halfback.

The 24-year-old Walker, a Roosters fan as a child, has stated on several occasions in the past month that he wanted to get an extension beyond 2027 sorted at the club.

This year he represented Queensland with distinction on his State of Origin series debut.

He then debuted for Australia at halfback in a 36-22 win over Fiji on Sunday after winning the NRL premiership with the Roosters, returning a week before the grand final in record-equalling time from a syndesmosis injury.

Walker said before his Kangaroos bow against the Bati that he wanted to get through the match before considering his extension talks.

"My preference is obviously to stay at the Roosters," he said.

That aspiration is now in considerable doubt after the Roosters last night dropped a bombshell statement

"The Sydney Roosters have this evening advised the management of Sam Walker that the club's offer for a contract extension beyond the 2027 season has been withdrawn after the parties were unable to reach an agreement on terms," the statement said.

"The club remains focused on maintaining a premiership-winning roster, with all recruitment and retention decisions made to support the strength, balance and long-term success of the playing squad."

The bottom line is that Walker's management and the Roosters have not been able to reach an agreement on his long-term value.

Walker, who has played 109 NRL games for the Roosters since his NRL debut in 2021, is contracted to the Tricolours in 2027.

If he is unable to revisit contract talks with the Roosters, he will be the most sought-after half in the game after November 1.

AAP

World.title: Labuschagne must beat mental block to overcome the 30s in third Test
World.content:
Australia are set to favour Marnus Labuschagne's ability to soak up pressure against the new ball and help the batters around him, and to give him one more chance for the third Test in South Africa.

Labuschagne's selection has remained the key talking point ahead of the third Test against the Proteas, after his run of innings without a century extended to 47.

Matt Renshaw is expected to open in place of the dropped Nic Maddinson in Cape Town, with Cameron Green to bat in the middle order.

Steve Smith's neck injury could also affect the final team, but Labuschagne is expected to hold his spot regardless, ahead of the fit-again Josh Inglis.

The Queenslander has scored between 30 and 49 in six of his past nine innings, while his career average over the past 37 Tests is half what it was in his first 30.

Marnus Labuschagne (left) has failed to score a century in his past 47 Test match innings. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Australia have made no secret of their frustration with that, with Pat Cummins last week admitting 30s "aren't going to win too many matches",

By the same token, Australia do believe Labuschagne is getting through the hard period and batting well, before a psychological issue around the 30s.

"The focus is on hundreds. I don't think I'm in a position to defend the performance," chief selector George Bailey said.

"But in terms of the collective, there's been times when that's helped. And that's the question we keep asking ourselves.

Smith will be 'fine' as Australia returns to Cape Town Australia returns to the scene of Sandpapergate for the third Test in Cape Town, with the series on a knife edge.

"We're seeing some good things, yes. Is there a block at the moment around 30s? Yes.

"He's still contributing in terms of his ability to get through a number of balls. So it's a decision around what does that look like if it gets through there.

"And what does it look like for the collective around and how everyone else, is it helping others around him. Is it helping the team get a result?"

Labuschagne's long-time teammate Usman Khawaja also raised similar questions around a potential mental block on Monday.

"He has obviously struggled for a while, and I find when things are going that long it is usually mental more than technical," Khawaja said.

"It is very hard to score in this game even if you are slightly clouded in the mind. I don't envy Marnus.

"He has played some terrific innings over the years for Queensland and Australia. It is hard. It has always been hard.

"I remember this feeling, and it is tough. He has obviously struggled of late, and that is what cricket does. It is a great leveller."

Asked on Monday whether Labuschagne's crease occupation against Inglis' scoring rates were being weighed up, Cummins suggested it may be a factor.

"Both have positives to it," he said.

"I think anywhere in the world, batting in the top three is really tough and Marnus is doing the hard work. He is facing quite a lot of balls and getting himself in."

AAP

World.title: Wheelaroos out to 'send a message' in pursuit of breakthrough World Cup title
World.content:
Australian wheelchair rugby league is poised for a breakthrough moment this week, with Wollongong, south of Sydney, hosting the nation's first World Cup since 2008.

Bundled in as part of the larger Rugby League World Cup, which also includes the men's, women's and physical disability tournaments, the wheelchair competition will benefit from free-to-air coverage in prime-time slots.

It is the kind of exposure most non-mainstream sports could only dream of, and Australia's Wheelaroos are well aware of the gravity of the moment.

"I think it's going to bring a whole different experience for wheelchair rugby league in Australia," Australia captain Bayley McKenna told ABC Sport.

"It's gonna bring people together, it's gonna bring people in to support our sport."

Australian wheelchair rugby league will be hoping for a breakthrough moment at the upcoming World Cup in Wollongong. (RLWC26 Media: Mark Nolan)

The Wheelaroos are currently ranked fourth in the world and are yet to claim a world title, with their game generally taking a back seat to the likes of wheelchair basketball and wheelchair rugby at a grassroots level in Australia.

But coach Brett Clark has told ABC Sport his charges are ready to take the rough-and-tumble sport into living rooms across the country.

"We know this is a quality game for all to play and this is the opportunity for us to show it at its top level," Clark said.

A unique kind of inclusion

Wheelchair rugby league, not to be confused with Paralympic favourite wheelchair rugby, is played on a basketball-sized court and with five athletes per side.

The sport replaces tackles with tagging like in Oztag and uses AFL-style handballing instead of kicking, but otherwise, remains relatively faithful to the running game.

Played across full-length 40-minute halves, it is a game filled with exhilarating chair skills, hair-raising collisions and retains much of rugby league's trademark physicality.

For Wheelaroos captain McKenna — who played the running game for years before joining the wheelchair sport — wheelchair rugby league's physicality is one of its biggest drawcards.

"In hindsight, I've had more injuries playing wheelchair rugby league than I did in the running game," McKenna said.

"You can hit people as hard as you want as long as you're going for the tag."

At 26, McKenna is a Wheelaroos trailblazer, being both the youngest and first non-disabled national team skipper.

Wheelchair rugby league is unique among international wheelchair sports in allowing teams to field up to two non-disabled players at any given time.

Bayley McKenna is his country's first non-disabled and youngest-ever skipper. (Getty Images: Richard Sellars)

This policy ensures that teams at every level of the sport can attract enough players to compete, while also fostering a unique kind of inclusion that flows from the grassroots all the way to elite competition, allowing for both non-disabled and disabled friends and family to share the same court.

McKenna, who began playing wheelchair sports alongside his disabled father, has seen the benefits of that inclusiveness firsthand.

"Being a non-disabled athlete in this sport is one of the most unreal things you can ever be a part of," McKenna said.

"The sport's so big, it's so broad, you can travel all across the world … it's so inclusive, because for me it gave me an opportunity to play a sport underneath my dad as a coach."

Luff believes that the inclusion of non-disabled players only adds to the sport. (Getty Images for RLWC: Henry Browne)

Wheelaroos squad member Liam Luff, living with hereditary spastic paraplegia, told ABC Sport the policy was an "incredible benefit".

"It just opens the doors to more and more people in our sport, which is what we need to grow awareness, get more people in chairs and show how special wheelchair rugby league is," Luff said.

The importance of the moment

Beginning on Friday, the 2026 World Cup will be just the fifth edition of the wheelchair tournament, with France and England having split the first four titles evenly.

With the sport having been first designed in France in the early 2000s, the two northern hemisphere titans have benefited from close contact and regular meetings.

In England, the sport experienced an explosion in popularity after the nation hosted the 2022 World Cup, which was also held alongside the men's and women's competitions. Grassroots participation saw a sharp uptick in the year after the event, while standalone international games have attracted audiences in the thousands since.

The Wheelaroos are now optimistic the 2026 tournament will have a similar impact in Australia, and Luff believes the sport is well and truly ready for it.

"I think more people are going to stumble across the game and find out about how special wheelchair rugby league is," Luff said.

Finding a way past France and England will undoubtedly be an almighty task for the Wheelaroos, who will play three group-stage games before the knockouts.

But the team is bullish on its chances in the Illawarra, and Luff is convinced the Wheelaroos are finally ready to take a seat amongst the world's elite.

"This is our biggest opportunity to really prove where the Australian Wheelaroos are in wheelchair rugby league," Luff said.

"We are gonna make sure we can prove ourselves taking on those top dogs … I think we're gonna really send a message about where we stand."

World.title: Sports commission urges kids not to specialise in sports
World.content:
Prior to becoming arguably the greatest tennis player in history, Roger Federer sampled a huge range of other sports.

"I had a flair for all different kinds of sports and tried skateboarding, basketball, table-tennis, badminton, football, wrestling, skiing, swimming," he said in a 2004 letter to his fans.

In a 2019 TV interview he urged kids to do other sports for fun.

"Go play squash, go ride your bike, go play basketball, go ski whatever it is," Federer said.

"If you only start focusing on just one sport only, I feel like you can get burned out."

A bleach-blond Roger Federer in 1998 at the age of 17, after winning the boys junior tennis event in Miami. (Getty Images: Ron C. Angle)

The tennis great's words are echoed in an Australian Sports Commission (ASC) position statement.

The report said specialisation for children younger than 12 could result in reduced motivation, burnout, injury and psychological stress.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

"What we don't want is kids specialising really early and losing their love for it and not partaking in sport at all in the future," Australian Institute of Sport director Matti Clements said.

"That's the worst thing we could hope for.

"There's got to be the enjoyment, the motivation to do it."

AIS director Matti Clements says many female coaches still face key barriers. (ABC News: Peter Healy)

The ASC said there had been a trend towards youth athletes specialising at an early age.

The statement said specialisation had been viewed as a way to increase opportunities for selection, scholarships and progression to elite or professional sport.

"Often, unfortunately, mum and dads [are] getting misinformation around the value of early specialisation," Clements said.

"If you have someone saying you need to specialise early in this sport if you're going to make it … then of course you're going to listen to that."

She highlighted the the proliferation of private academies for certain sports, including soccer.

Queensland families are being encouraged to apply for FairPlay vouchers to help with the cost of junior sport. (ABC News: Jonathon Gul )

"I think that the establishment of academies that are a business model academy, they can often present a compelling message to a parent that their child should be in there early," Clements said.

"We all know an individual who was physically quite developed at a young age and therefore was absolutely smashing it out of the out of the park in a particular sport but, by just doing that sport, lost the enthusiasm for doing it."

That "burnout" can be seen in the figures provided the ASC's most recent survey into sport in Australia.

Participation in Australia's most-played sport, soccer, peaks for girls and boys between nine and 11 and then quickly declines.

That teenage dropout trend is evident in all the popular sports played in Australia, netball, cricket, Australian Rules, basketball, tennis and rugby league.

"Athletes who maintain broader sport participation until after age 12 and then specialise are more likely to succeed in their chosen sport," the statement said.

That rang true for Australian fast bowler Kim Garth, who played multiple sports when she was a kid.

"I played football in the winter, cricket in the summer, and then I played a fair bit of Gaelic football as well," the Irish-born cricketer said.

Kim Garth (left) and Ellyse Perry played multiple sports when they were kids. (Getty Images: ICC/Alex Davidson)

Garth chose Gaelic football over cricket in her final year of school, but cricket won out as she progressed to the Irish national team before transferring her allegiance to Australia in 2022.

"I couldn't speak more highly of trying to play as many sports as you can when you're younger," she said.

Clements said specialisation in and of itself was not necessarily bad, but depended on the individual and their development.

She hoped the position statement would help young athletes, their parents, coaches and organisations make considered choices about when children started to specialise.

World.title: Dr Redmayne aims to lift Brisbane Heat's WBBL fortunes
World.content:
New Brisbane Heat captain Georgie Redmayne returned to work as a doctor this year and will now help improve the side's form after last season.

The wicketkeeper-batter takes over from all-rounder Jess Jonassen, who led the side for the past six WBBL seasons.

In 2025, the Heat finished last and did not win a match. The Queensland Fire, with many Heat players, then won the 2025-26 WNCL final with Redmayne captaining the 50-over side and scoring a century in the decider.

Strikers pip winless Heat The Adelaide Strikers pull off a tense WBBL victory over the struggling Brisbane Heat.

She said the form in the 20-over format was achievable for the Heat.

"If we win one game we are on the up," Redmayne said, grinning.

"To be more serious, pre-season has been really good and winning the WNCL was massive for us with a lot of the same core group, so we know we are still a winning team.

"We just have to tweak a few things to be successful in that T20 format. We have got our first game at home (on Friday night) against the Sixers, which is always a good rivalry.

"Last year we didn't really turn up in the high-pressure moments … but hopefully we go back to the winning ways which we were known for in the past"

Redmayne said she got a lot out of returning to work as a doctor after a few years where cricket took centre stage.

"I actually came back to it this year. It was really nice," she said.

"I did a bit of a stint in April and another stint in August/September this year at Greenslopes Private Hospital in Brisbane.

"It helps provide a great bit of grounding for me, especially when you go away playing cricket.

"You can think it is the be-all and end-all playing professional sport, but it is literally grounding seeing some real world problems."

Redmayne has been a great success at the top of the order for the Brisbane Heat and was the leading run scorer in three consecutive seasons from 2020-2022.

Grace Harris, her opening partner much of the time, topped the aggregates in 2023 and 2024. The Heat made the finals in all five of those years and were runners-up twice.

The Heat moved Redmayne down the order last season, but it did not work, so a return to opening with Harris would be a good place to start for the side to turn their form around.

"(Opening) is somewhere I really enjoy batting and where I would like to bat," Redmayne said.

"My favourite time playing cricket was always opening the batting with Grace. We had a couple of very successful seasons.

"Last year our order was very changeable. I started at number eight and ended up at number four.

"I don't mind where I bat, so long as we are winning games."

AAP

Tech.title: OpenAI announces three big science discoveries and a new way to work with academics
Tech.content:
OpenAI results added to GitHub today:

Local smoothing for the Euclidean wave equation. The proof uses an auxiliary partial differential equation to establish Sogge’s local smoothing for waves in every spatial dimension at least two. It also yields the Kakeya maximal and dimension conjectures and Stein’s spherical restriction estimates throughout the interior of the conjectured range. We are releasing the model output directly, as we did in our October 6 release.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False. The paper gives a deterministic algorithm that exactly counts satisfying assignments of fixed-width CNF formulas in subexponential time and polynomial space. The case of 3-SAT refutes the Exponential Time Hypothesis. An independent working group of computer scientists led by Russell Impagliazzo, Ramamohan Paturi, and Ryan Williams will examine and explain the proof. At the group’s request, we are making the materials public immediately so others can examine them as well.

Tech.title: Samsung’s Switch 2-ready MicroSD Express card is on sale for less than $50
Tech.content:
Running out of space on your Nintendo Switch 2? Thankfully, Samsung’s P9 MicroSD Express card is discounted at multiple retailers, with the 256GB version going for $47.99 ( Amazon , B&H Photo ) and the 512GB version $99 ( Amazon , B&H Photo ). The smaller card typically sells for around $80, and the larger option usually sells between $150 and $200, though both are higher than their original launch prices, likely because of the ongoing memory shortage.

The P9 is great if you need more storage for your Nintendo Switch 2. The microSD Express card offers sequential read speeds of up to 800MB/s, but only gadgets with a microSD Express card slot can take full advantage of the highest speeds. That includes certain cameras, tablets, and drones with a microSD USH-I slot.

First-party Switch 2 games generally run between 10 and 30 gigabytes each — the upcoming The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is 27GB, for example — while third-party games can take up even more space (Cyberpunk 2077 is 60GB). Until recently, the Switch 2 was one of the few devices that could take advantage of the faster MicroSD Express standard, but this year’s Asus ROG Ally X20 also added support for MicroSD Express. While expensive, the latter is an impressive gaming handheld that runs Windows 11, giving it a versatility that’s hard to find elsewhere.

Tech.title: Anthropic is burning gas to feed the AI boom
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

As it prepares to go public, Anthropic’s S-1 filing makes generative AI’s methane dependency glaringly obvious.

“Competition for access to electrical supply and data center locations with adequate power availability is intense.”

In documents filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission Monday, Anthropic acknowledges that data centers are becoming increasingly reliant on “natural gas” — the fossil fuel industry’s marketing term for what is primarily methane — leaving the company’s AI data center buildout vulnerable to rising fuel costs and existing supply chain constraints. And in a possible catch-22, Anthropic admits that rising global temperatures — a symptom of burning fossil fuels — will increase the company’s operating costs.

“Competition for access to electrical supply and data center locations with adequate power availability is intense,” Anthropic says, adding that some of its planned data centers rely on electricity generated by natural gas turbines on-site. Anthropic leases capacity from hyperscalers, but it announced a $50 billion dollar plan last year to expand data centers in Texas and New York.

Now, a shortage of gas turbines is slowing data center construction. Some developers are installing gas engines on-site as a way to avoid long wait times to connect to power grids. Developers are also turning to more simple turbine technology at these sites as they face backlogs from turbine manufacturers, making on-site power generation less efficient and more polluting as a result.

Data center electricity demand could wipe out decades of gains in air quality over the next five years, one recent Texas-based study found — raising levels of soot, smog-forming pollutants, and planet-heating carbon dioxide. Even as data centers create more greenhouse gas pollution, Anthropic’s S-1 points to climate change as a risk to its bottom line. It will have to pay more for electricity and water to cool servers at data centers as temperatures climb.

Nevertheless, Anthropic expects increased competition for natural gas and pipeline capacity from hyperscalers and cloud service providers rushing to build their own data centers. “This competition could drive up the price of natural gas,” the company notes.

Gas makes up the biggest chunk of the US electricity mix, 40 percent of the nation’s power generation. And Americans are already feeling the pain of rising costs as utilities scramble to upgrade energy infrastructure and meet rising power demand.

Pissed-off residents have successfully blocked dozens of proposed data centers across the US. Anthropic acknowledges that the specter of ballooning utility bills is enough to interfere with a data center project. “If our efforts to secure electrical power are perceived to affect other utility customers and the broader grid, regulators may impose conditions, standby charges, or other requirements intended to address such impacts,” it says.

If regulators push data center developers to shoulder more of the costs for new energy infrastructure, Anthropic says that could also raise its operating costs. And without a secure gas supply and the pipelines to transport the fuel, the company says, it might need to delay or abandon planned data center projects altogether.

Ultimately, these challenges could stunt Anthropic’s growth:

Any failure to secure access to adequate electrical power, any legal, regulatory, or other administrative action or change limiting the availability of electricity, or any significant increase in energy or compliance costs, could adversely affect our cost structure and limit our ability to scale our compute infrastructure, develop and deploy our models, and service our customers.

Tech.title: iPhone Duo now supports Apple Pencil with iOS 27.2
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple has just released iOS 27.2, bringing Apple Pencil support to the iPhone Duo. The software update also includes an “Edge Light” feature for the iPhone Duo that’s intended to illuminate your face during video calls.

The iOS 27.2 update also allows Siri AI to take suggested actions in Messages, while adding support for Siri AI in more languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. Apple is rolling out support for Google’s SynthID AI watermark in Photos and Image Playground, too, according to 9to5Mac.

Other smaller but notable updates include user profiles on the Apple TV app on iPhone. The Apple Podcasts app is also replacing its “Up Next” queue with a list of “New Episodes,” along with a “Continue Playing” section just beneath it. You’ll also see the new Apple Music logo. And group calls on FaceTime now support dual capture so you can show both what’s visible from your selfie cam and your back cameras.

Tech.title: The NBA’s response to gambling scandals is to add more gambling partnerships
Tech.content:
is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment. He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget.

From the bright minds that brought you FTX Arena and NBA Top Shot NFT maketplace (where sales last month dropped to $762,781, which is a 99.66 percent decrease compared to the February 2021 peak of $226,350,843), the NBA announced Monday that it has new “preferred” prediction market deals for Kalshi and Polymarket, as well as a memorandum of understanding with the US CFTC about how to manage the relationships. It also announced an expansion of its DraftKings deal to include prediction markets, and says that more expansions will be announced with others soon.

The NBA is already facing scandals after Jontay Porter pleaded guilty to conspiracy over a gambling and manipulation scheme in 2024, Malik Beasley is reportedly in negotiations over a plea deal on similar charges, while former player Terry Rozier and coach Chauncey Billups are under indictment on charges of allegedly rigging prop bets and participating in rigged poker games, respectively.

NBA Head of Media Distribution & Partnerships Scott Kaufman-Ross proclaims that “Protecting the integrity of the game is our top priority,” as it establishes its integrity framework for the Kalshi and Polymarket deal. Under the new arrangements, prediction markets will be able to use official league data and IP, while promising limitations on “permissible markets” and information-sharing on suspicious trades and investigations.

Tech.title: The RealReal won’t let AI agents hog designer clothing
Tech.content:
is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools.

The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion consignment retailer, said it’s updating its bot defense system, effectively making it harder for AI agents to shop on its site.

The change comes days after The Verge reported that an AI agent could be used to take advantage of The RealReal’s item reserve system. On the retailer’s website, an item goes “on hold” and is unavailable for other customers to buy for 20 minutes once it’s placed in a user’s shopping cart. Using Meta’s Muse, The Verge was able to instruct the AI agent to continuously re-add The RealReal listings in a shopping cart as soon as the 20-minute hold had expired, effectively blocking other shoppers from purchasing products for hours or longer.

After publication, chief technology officer Luke Friang said in an email that the company had addressed the Muse use case flagged by The Verge’s story. The RealReal’s bot defense configuration now makes it much more difficult for all agents to log in, add items to cart, and check out, Friang said. Agents will still be able to surface listings from The RealReal and direct Muse users to product pages, Friang said, adding that the company will continue to strengthen protections as AI-powered online shopping evolves.

Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Technology companies are selling agents as personalized assistants for billions of people — always-on, compliant entities that will schedule meetings, throw parties, and purchase things for human users. So far, agents and shopping seem to go hand in hand; Meta said in its Q3 earnings call this month that it was the most common use case for Muse so far, and that purchases were over $200 on average. Muse has been a hit for Meta and could signal a turning point for AI agents: The company said 10 million people in the US had downloaded the app in 40 days.

But robots shopping for things instead of humans has the potential to upend the balance of the web as we know it. For one, if humans stop visiting websites directly and instead access the web through chatbots, businesses become one step removed from their customers. Retailers — most notably Amazon — have recognized that reality could disrupt their bottom line, especially advertising revenue, and have blocked agents from shopping on their sites.

An influx of AI agents accessing consumer platforms could also break or complicate even the most unexpected things shoppers take for granted, like the reserve system of a used clothing website. There is, of course, a realistic limit to how long a person is willing to spend adding and re-adding designer clothing to their shopping cart if they’re indecisive. An agent in contrast does not care. It is perhaps precisely the type of busywork a fashion-forward person might pay an actual personal assistant to do on their behalf. Now, a capability like this is at the fingertips of millions of consumers, and they are just beginning to learn how to take advantage of it. Retailers, too, are playing catch-up.

Tech.title: Apple acknowledges iPhone Duo display ‘issue’ after reports of cracked screens
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Following reports of iPhone Duos with cracked and broken inside screens, often showing a bright line running from the center to the right side, Apple says in a statement to Bloomberg and 9to5Mac that it’s aware of “an issue impacting the inner display” on a “small number of iPhone Duo units.” If your iPhone Duo is affected, Apple says to contact AppleCare for a replacement.

Here is the full statement, which Apple’s Alex Kirschner shared with The Verge:

The response to iPhone Duo from early users has been incredibly positive, and we are seeing exciting things from developers who are rapidly updating their apps to take advantage of its unique form factor. We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement.

Kirshner says most units aren’t susceptible and that the issues appear quickly on units with the defect.

Shortly after launch, iPhone Duo users started reporting similar issues where the hinge would tighten, and opening the device caused a crack and the distinctive bright lines on the display. One user in Australia said that an Apple Store replaced their unit “on the spot.”

This weekend, iFixit published its teardown of the phone and gave its perspective on why some phones might be cracking. Where the damage has been happening, iFixit shows how the foldable screen might be pushing against a center bar.

The Verge has contacted Apple about the reports, but has not received an on-the-record response about the issues with these new phones. They’re some of the first devices to launch after new CEO John Ternus took over from Tim Cook.

Updates, October 26th: Added Apple’s statement and additional context.

Tech.title: Nothing’s eye-catching Ear 3A earbuds are matching their best price to date
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If you want a decent pair of noise-canceling earbuds without spending a fortune, Nothing’s Ear 3A are worth considering. The wireless earbuds offer a lot of features for the price, and they’re an even better value now that all four colors are on sale at Amazon, Walmart, and Best Buy for $79 ($20 off), matching their all-time low price.

The Ear 3A deliver great performance for the price, with extensive EQ options that let you fine-tune the sound to your liking. My colleague John Higgins found the default sound a little too bass-heavy, but appreciated how easy it was to adjust — which is great, since that level of customization is unusual for earbuds at this price. While they won’t completely drown out chatter of your local coffee shop, the ANC does a good job of quieting low drones, including air conditioners and airplane cabin noise. We did encounter some bugs in testing, however, including abrupt changes in noise cancellation levels when using adaptive ANC, as well as occasional issues with voice calls in noisy environments.

Still, they’re relatively minor drawbacks given what you get for the price. The Ear 3A also come in some fun colors — including a striking pink shade — and each pair includes extra-small ear tips for a more comfortable fit. They even offer a shortcut to access ChatGPT and include 32MB of built-in storage, letting you record up to two hours of a phone call and transfer the recording through the companion app.

Tech.title: Databricks co-founder shares his secrets for winning big enterprise customers
Tech.content:
Startups have never been under more pressure to grow quickly. To do that, many of them must land large enterprises, the deep pockets of the IT world, as customers. But as any company that sells to enterprises will tell you, it’s not easy to win such contracts.

One critical mistake most younger startups make is believing that their tech will practically sell itself, says Arsalan Tavakoli-Shiraji, co-founder and senior vice president of field engineering at Databricks, which helps businesses store and analyze huge amounts of data.

Yes. The tech must work well. But that’s not enough, he warns. Databricks today is an AI and big data storage giant, valued at $190 billion, with more than 70% of the Fortune 500 as customers. But it was once a tiny startup, and Tavakoli-Shiraji was responsible for helping bring in its first big deals.

“Everybody when they’re selling to enterprises at startups … we think it’s all about the tech and having the best tech,” Tavakoli-Shiraji told attendees at TechCrunch Disrupt last week. But he learned the hard way that “people and processes matter the most.”

He remembers securing a meeting with a prospect in the early days, only to discover that it was the same person who signed a mega-deal with his major competitor. “He has no interest in listening to me because he bet his career on that competitor,” Tavakoli-Shiraji said. He also remembers early deals fizzling because the startup wasn’t prepared for legal, contractual, or security questions.

He offered his top tips for startups to win big customers:

Sell under a bigger tech company’s umbrella

When Databricks was young, it tried and failed to score a meeting with UBS, the large Swiss bank. Then it did “a partnership with Microsoft,” becoming an Azure cloud partner. That meant sales agreements would be covered under Microsoft’s terms.

But it also meant that Microsoft’s sales folks actually booked the meetings and advocated for the startup. “All of a sudden, that meeting wasn’t hard to get,” the founder recalled. “It was a huge boon to us that we were able to partner with somebody who had that access and distribution.”

With Microsoft’s sales team helping, “we started getting pulled everywhere.” That created new problems, like prospects wanting features for countries Databricks hadn’t expanded to, but they were good problems to have.

Today, Databricks is the big company that works with startups, selling their products under Databricks’ own terms and cybersecurity setup. Examples include Hightouch, which provides AI-powered marketing and customer-data tools (Databricks has also invested in it); Addepar, which offers data tools for investment professionals; and Tecton, a machine learning startup that Databricks later acquired.

When selling AI, address the “four Cs”

Tavakoli-Shiraji groups enterprises’ main concerns and objections into four categories he calls the four Cs: context, choice, cost, and control. Context means an AI that can be trained “like bringing on a new employee,” he says, learning the company’s terminology, processes, priorities, and so on.

Choice is the freedom to switch AI models rather than be tied to a single provider. Cost is about controlling how much the AI product will cost to run. Control involves the safeguards that govern the AI’s behavior and protecting sensitive information.

Attack the expensive legacy systems enterprises think they’re stuck with

Tavakoli-Shiraji jokingly asks CIOs where they stand with AI on a scale of one to five. A one means employees merely have access to ChatGPT, and a five means the company has adopted new AI capabilities that have changed its business processes.

“And everybody loves picking, ‘I’m three leaning towards four.’ But 99% of the ones I talk to are in bucket one and two.” Enterprises still haven’t figured out how to deploy AI agents in ways that create value beyond allowing engineering teams to write code. “It’s going to take many, many years before people can actually properly deploy AI in a very meaningful way in the enterprise.”

One big opportunity for startups to bring that value is to modernize expensive legacy systems. “If you go to any bank today, they still have [an IBM] AS/400 and mainframes,” he described. “Nobody wanted to touch it because nobody knew what that code did.”

But today, AI agents “can go in and understand and actually decompose what that code does.” That, he says, opens the door to products that do everything from adding modern interfaces for those ancient systems to replacing them altogether.

Tavakoli-Shiraji also shared his predictions for the future of enterprise AI adoption, along with an anecdote of what happened when the company was young and he pretended to be a lawyer to land a big enterprise contract. See the full interview below.

Tech.title: Watch out, YouTube — Instagram goes from short-form to 90-minute videos
Tech.content:
If you could have 1 million followers on any social media platform, which would you choose? There is a correct answer, and it’s YouTube, assuming you’d like to get paid for your work. But Instagram’s latest update could upend YouTube’s long-held position as the most lucrative platform for creators, if only Instagram plays its cards right.

Instagram announced on Monday that it’s testing a new type of video upload that will allow creators to share “Features,” videos up to 90 minutes long. After years in which every social platform (even LinkedIn!) aggressively pursued short-form video, this is a notable shift in strategy for Instagram.

Short-form, vertical video content has defined the internet of the 2020s, but the creators behind these clips don’t actually make much money directly from platforms like Instagram — the Meta-owned platform has some monetization tools like subscriptions, but it doesn’t typically pay creators on a per-view basis.

“You can get paid by the platform directly, you can get paid by a fan, and you can get paid by a brand,” Instagram head Adam Mosseri explained on the Colin and Samir Show, an interview show about the creator economy. “And right now, the way that it works on Instagram primarily is you primarily get paid by brands. Some people get paid by fans. We have still a small performance-based program, but … we spend more money than we make back by a long shot, and so it doesn’t really make sense to scale up because we’re just burning capital.”

YouTube’s payment model is more straightforward: There are ads on videos, and creators enrolled in YouTube’s Partner Program get 55% of the ad revenue YouTube earns from their videos. That adds up. The platform said last year that it paid more than $100 billion to creators, artists, and media companies in the previous four years.

Instagram and TikTok haven’t been able to replicate YouTube’s model with short-form content, which is inherently trickier to monetize than longer videos because there’s less room to place ads. Many creators see those accounts more like promotional arms for their YouTube channels than meaningful drivers of revenue.

Image Credits:Instagram

Instagram is encouraging creators to upload longer videos, as it already did eight years ago with the now-defunct IGTV. It’s possible that its parent company, Meta, which makes its billions on advertising, will put ads in those long-form videos, too.

If Meta does add ads, could Instagram meaningfully compete with the YouTube Partner Program for the first time?

“It’s too early to share a long-term monetization model, but we’re exploring ways for creators to earn from brands, fans, and Instagram, including performance-based incentives,” a Meta spokesperson told TechCrunch. “Over time, we think there will be compounding benefits for creators to tell new stories, reach new audiences, and find new partners, which should lead to many monetization opportunities.”

It’s not a particularly promising answer, but it’s also not a no.

Mosseri explained in a video announcement why the platform is suddenly embracing long-form content after scrapping its old video product, IGTV.

“For a long time, I have been against doing long-form video on Instagram,” Mosseri said, noting that shorter content like Reels drives more shares and DMs among users. Instagram VP of Product Tessa Lyons, who has been advocating for this change, finally convinced Mosseri to give long form another shot.

“Reels is still going to be a core part of Instagram. But when you want to go deeper with the creators you love and the content that they’re creating, you should be able to do that on Instagram,” Lyons said in the video.

In other words, Instagram would rather keep fans on its own platform to enjoy both short- and long-form content from a creator than lose them to YouTube. Instagram is testing a feature called “Clips as Reels,” which lets creators make Reels out of their long-form content. The Reels link viewers to the longer video. Viewers can also save the longer video to send to the Instagram app on their TV.

Instagram is currently testing “Features” and “Clips as Reels” in Brazil and will now expand to the U.S. in a small test. The platform is also working on improved discovery features for Live video and a hub on a creator’s profile for episodic Reels, meaning a series of connected Reels similar to TikTok’s playlist feature.

“The thing that the team has been working on that we’re excited to share with you is trying to make it so that the short-form and the long-form video can be symbiotic,” Mosseri said. “We’re going to try to support these different types of formats, both in the mobile app, but also on the TV app, which I think is … going to take some time to get right. But I’m actually very excited about it, and we’re very committed to it long term.”

Tech.title: Uh-oh, it sounds like the iPhone Duo keeps cracking and users aren’t happy about it
Tech.content:
In Brief

The launch of the iPhone Duo, Apple’s hotly anticipated foldable phone, is off to a rough start. The phone was announced at this year’s Surprise and Shine event, with Apple promising that it had finally gotten a notoriously tricky form factor right.

Now, however, Bloomberg reports that early Duo users have been complaining about screens cracking “after just hours or days of use.” Some users have reported hearing a loud crunching noise, followed by the appearance of a crack. Others have reported display malfunctions.

404 Media has also reported that early adopters are dealing with “big fat creases down the middle of the [$2,000] folding screen.”

TechCrunch reached out to Apple for comment and will update this story if it responds. The company told Bloomberg that it was “aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units.”

Creating a functional foldable phone has long been an ambition in Silicon Valley, but many of the models released so far have suffered from similar maladies. Apple promised that it had cracked the code, but these early complaints suggest it may not have solved the problem after all.

Tech.title: Fusion startups are giving the government shares in exchange for awards. Is it worth it?
Tech.content:
The U.S. government has long had an on-again, off-again relationship with the fusion power sector. As of last week, it’s definitely back on.

Helion and Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS) received awards totaling $260 million from the Department of Commerce under the CHIPS and Science Act, the 2022 law that funds domestic semiconductor development, to develop advanced semiconductors used to help power and control their reactors. Helion landed $175 million, while CFS reeled in $85 million.

But as with many recent government awards, these come with strings attached. Helion and CFS have agreed to give the government nonvoting shares in return. With these awards, the fusion industry is finally getting the government’s attention, though maybe not the sort it envisioned.

In the past, government support for a startup meant nondilutive capital, meaning money that doesn’t shrink existing investors’ ownership percentages, while giving the company a bigger war chest. Investors loved the deals because it meant their startups got more money without them having to pony up. The government doled out the cash to boost American innovation, though it also meant that, in most cases, the government didn’t directly benefit when it picked a winner.

The Trump administration has been pushing to change that calculus.

Small awards with big consequences?

For both companies, the total dollar amount pales in comparison to how much each has raised. CFS has raised about $4 billion, while Helion is close behind with $3.2 billion in committed capital. The awards are perhaps more important as signals that, after years of cutting and then trickling out fusion funding, the U.S. government is back in the game.

Fusion, which generates power by fusing atoms together as the sun does, is an expensive endeavor, requiring exotic materials, sophisticated computer modeling, and complex manufacturing. Progress over the last decade has attracted private investors who have bet more than $14 billion that one or more companies will be able to put a power plant on the grid.

Yet according to the Fusion Industry Association, the sector’s trade group, that’s still not enough to beat other countries in the race. Last year, the trade group called on the federal government to inject a one-time infusion of $10 billion into the sector, with $5.4 billion intended for fusion startups.

“Other nations are moving aggressively to accelerate their commercial fusion industries, pouring billions in state-backed efforts to win the race to fusion power,” a spokesperson for CFS told TechCrunch. CFS is a member of the Fusion Industry Association. “The $10 billion ask is designed to build out the research infrastructure in the DOE’s Fusion Roadmap and be catalytic for the U.S. domestic fusion industry to compete with China.”

Until recently, the federal government had been dribbling out dollars for fusion. The Biden administration introduced the Milestone-Based Fusion Development Program, a Department of Energy program that pays companies as they hit technical goals, but the dollar amounts were paltry; less than $50 million was distributed in the first couple years. More recent awards were a little bigger, but still well shy of money the Fusion Industry Association has called for.

Now, with two companies getting $260 million, it looks like the lobbying may be starting to pay off, though not quite as planned as it comes from Commerce rather than the research budget the Fusion Industry Association sought, and it carries equity strings.

The Fusion Industry Association’s lobbying campaign did not include conversations about equity stakes in exchange for awards, a person familiar with the matter told TechCrunch. Yet Helion said the government will receive $175 million in nonvoting equity based on its Series G round, which valued the company at $15.5 billion. That works out to a stake of roughly 1%. The government’s stake in CFS will also be nonvoting and based on the company’s most recent valuation, which CFS has not shared publicly. That means the size of the government’s stake in CFS is not known.

“This type of structure has become more common in large U.S. government investments in recent years,” David Kirtley, co-founder and CEO of Helion, told TechCrunch in a statement. “This approach aligns the interests of Helion and the U.S. taxpayer around our commercial success.”

The CFS spokesperson echoed those comments. “This U.S. equity stake will enable the U.S. taxpayer to participate in the upside of our commercial success in exchange for investing in important research and development that supports the growth of an American commercial fusion industry.”

Not alone

Helion and CFS are the latest in a series of companies that have seen the government take a stake in exchange for federal dollars.

Last year, critical minerals supplier MP Materials gave the government a 15% stake in exchange for a $400 million investment coupled with a $150 million loan, offtake agreements (which are guaranteed purchases of its output), and profit sharing. Another critical minerals company, USA Rare Earth, gave up a 10% stake for a $277 million award and a $1.3 billion loan. And Intel set an even more awkward precedent. The Biden administration had already awarded the company $8.9 billion that hadn’t yet been paid out. Last year, the Trump administration turned that money into a roughly 10% stake in Intel. The list goes on.

Outside the U.S., Germany-based fusion startup Proxima Fusion confirmed to TechCrunch that the German government and the European Union are on its cap table. It also has received equity investments from German government-backed funds, including SPRIND (Germany’s federal agency for disruptive innovation) and DCTF (Deutsche Climate Tech Fonds).

Not every fusion startup that has worked with the government has given up equity. Thea Energy and Avalanche Energy, which have received federal awards and contracts, and Pacific Fusion, which has partnered with federal labs, confirmed to TechCrunch that they have not given the government a stake. Inertia Enterprises also told TechCrunch that it had not given the government any equity; the startup has a public-private partnership with the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory to commercialize the fusion technology developed there.

So far, it’s just a handful of startups that have agreed to government stakes in exchange for awards. Still, it could set the tone for the industry.

By directly investing in fusion startups, the Trump administration is signaling that fusion power is a strategic priority for the U.S. Such backing could boost investor confidence, though it could just as easily have a chilling effect on private investment. VCs will now have to weigh whether the dilution from a government stake is worth the trade-off. And what happens to cap tables in case of pay-to-play rounds or wind-downs? Who gets priority?

The fusion industry may have raised billions of dollars in recent years, but it will need billions more to deliver on its promises. Federal awards used to be no-brainers when it came time to scale up. Now they’ve grown more complicated. Will the new bargains be worth it?

Tech.title: This startup’s self-driving excavators help dig up $600M in new funding
Tech.content:
Bedrock Robotics has raised $600 million in a funding round that values the autonomous vehicle technology startup at $4.1 billion, marking a speedy ascent for the two-year-old company.

The Series C round, co-led by CapitalG and Emergence Capital, comes two months after the startup reached a key milestone: moving its autonomous excavators beyond testing and pilot programs and putting them to work on active construction sites.

Bedrock Robotics has developed a self-driving kit that can be retrofitted onto construction and other worksite vehicles. Excavators outfitted with Bedrock’s autonomous-driving tech are now commercially operating at a Nevada-based water treatment facility, an earthwork site run by Champion Site Prep in Texas , and a 1.2 million-cubic-yard civil sitework project with Zachry Construction Corporation.

Bedrock has raised nearly $1 billion since it was founded in 2024 by a group of autonomous vehicle and robotics industry veterans. Co-founder and CEO Boris Sofman previously led Waymo’s now-shuttered self-driving trucks program. Sofman also co-founded and led Anki Robotics, the maker of the popular Cozmo consumer robot, which shut down in 2019.

Other co-founders include Waymo veterans Kevin Peterson, Bedrock’s chief technology officer, and Ajay Gummalla, who serves as Bedrock’s vice president of engineering and infrastructure. Tom Eliaz, who previously worked at Segment and Twilio, is also a co-founder and VP of engineering and hardware.

The fresh capital will help Bedrock accelerate its transition to commercial work. The company plans to deploy its technology at more construction sites, while expanding the teams and infrastructure needed to support customers in the field.

“We have proven that fully autonomous excavators can perform real work of value alongside the crews and workflows already in place on job sites. The next challenge is delivering that capability to more contractors as a dependable part of how projects get built,” Sofman said in a statement.

Bedrock is particularly focused on autonomous excavators, in part because of a growing shortage of skilled operators. It takes five years or more to master operating an excavator, according to Bedrock. Meanwhile, a growing number of construction workers are approaching retirement age. The Associated Builders and Contractors, a national construction industry trade association, estimates that more than 40% of construction workers will retire in the next five years.

Bedrock is betting that the industry will increasingly turn to autonomous driving tech to help close that labor gap.

The startup’s newest partner is Haydon, an Arizona-based general contractor that plans to use Bedrock-equipped machines across a range of projects, including advanced manufacturing facilities, water and wastewater plants, data centers, and healthcare facilities.

New investors US Innovative Technology Fund (USIT), Bessemer Venture Partners, and Temasek participated in the round, alongside existing investors 8VC, Georgian, Valor Equity Partners, Xora, Eclipse, Perry Creek Capital, and Nvidia.

The startup also announced two executive hires as it scales commercial operations. Amy Jones Satrom, a veteran of Amazon, Nuro, and Uber, has joined Bedrock as its vice president of operations. Lando Juarez, formerly head of legal for Uber’s autonomous mobility and delivery business, was hired as general counsel.

Tech.title: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals its strategy for keeping enterprise customers hooked
Tech.content:
Anthropic is building the same kind of cross-product ecosystem that helped make tech companies like Amazon and Uber enormously sticky, and its S-1 suggests the strategy is working. More than half of customers spending at least $100,000 annually now use both the Claude platform and a first-party app like Claude Code or Cowork, up from about 30% at the end of last year.

“The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI,” the S-1, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, reads.

As of September 30, Anthropic recorded more than 11,900 customers spending at least $100,000; more than 1,900 customers spending upward of $1 million; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more annually.

Anthropic attributes customer momentum to a “significant usage expansion as customers realize the value of deploying Claude across their organizations,” which drove net revenue retention of about 900% as of the end of the third quarter.

Throwing shade at the entire legacy SaaS industry, Anthropic pitches Claude as not a “static product that serves a single use case,” but rather “frontier AI with rapidly advancing capabilities” spanning the models, the developer platform, and the applications users interact with directly.

“An advance at any layer compounds across all three layers, accelerating the pace at which we can deliver more capable intelligence,” the filing reads, calling this “integrated approach” the reason more customers use both the Claude Platform and first-party apps.

The playbook is familiar. Uber began by selling rides but has expanded into food delivery and freight. With AWS, Amazon drew in customers with cloud computing services before expanding those relationships into storage, databases, and other offerings, making the ecosystem increasingly hard to leave. Like those companies, Anthropic doesn’t have to sell each product to a brand-new buyer: A business that starts with the API can deploy Claude Code to their engineers and then Cowork to their broader workforce.

Those app users become far more valuable. In the third quarter, the highest-spending 5% of Claude Enterprise customers who used Claude Code spent about 20x as much per month as the average enterprise user who didn’t use the coding tool, per the filing. The finding demonstrates how much room there is for per-user spend to grow, and illustrates why Anthropic is keen to get its applications into the accounts that start with the API.

Anthropic said it amplifies that organic diffusion by investing in Applied AI teams. An internal Applied AI team works with startups and enterprises to help place Claude inside customers’ existing technology stacks, and the company recently launched a separate venture with Blackstone and other private equity firms, dubbed Ode with Anthropic, to embed forward-deployed engineers into businesses to build bespoke AI tools with Claude.

Anthropic also leans on its third-party distribution partnerships with hyperscalers AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Under what the filing calls a “joint go-to-market approach,” Anthropic holds the direct contractual relationship with customers and pays each cloud provider a fee, which the company says lets it “avoid channel conflict” and “set pricing.”

Anthropic’s budding stickiness strategy may become essential as the AI giant seeks to constantly “reinvent our business” by releasing “new classes of products whose aim is to dwarf the economic value of our existing ones.” The company says it will devote less effort than a typical business to “entrenching our current products and business models, and more effort to defining new ones.”

The filing also flags headwinds, despite impressive revenue growth of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. The cloud partnerships that help sell Claude are increasingly seeing Anthropic as a competitor, which Anthropic says could lead to difficulties securing the compute it needs from them. The filing states that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft may prioritize their own requirements or rivals they’ve invested in.

Customer concentration is another risk.

“Any adverse change in demand from our largest customers … could adversely affect our business and prospects,” reads part of the risk factors section. “As a result, a significant reduction in spending by, or the loss of, one or more of our largest customers, if not offset by new customer relationships or increased business from our other existing customers, could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.”

Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

Tech.title: SpaceX locks in $40B GPU financing deal with Apollo
Tech.content:
SpaceX has reached a binding commitment for roughly $40 billion in financing for AI chips and related data center equipment, the company disclosed in a regulatory filing Monday. In a statement, SpaceX called the deal the “largest committed GPU financing”.

Under the agreement, an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, the New York-based private equity giant, will buy the chips and related server hardware, then lease the equipment to SpaceX. The leases will last about five to five-and-a-quarter years, beginning when each tranche of equipment is delivered, according to the filing.

SpaceX expects the deal to close by year-end, subject to closing conditions, with leases starting in the first half of 2027 as the GPUs and related equipment arrive.

The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.

“This lease diversifies our funding sources and addresses a notable portion of the funding required to deliver on our growth plans,” SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said in a statement Monday, noting it is seeing “less than one-year payback periods” on its AI infrastructure investments as it scales compute to power Grok and its cloud services.

Apollo said the financing will help deliver Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX’s “terrestrial compute buildout.”

The financing comes as SpaceX ramps spending to expand its AI infrastructure, alongside its Starlink and launch businesses.

The financing follows a blockbuster third quarter for SpaceX’s AI business. SpaceX’s AI segment, which includes the Grok chatbot, the Cursor coding tool, and its cloud compute business, outperformed investor expectations in the third quarter and brought in $7.6 billion of SpaceX’s $14.6 billion in revenue, more than Starlink and rocket launches combined.

Capital expenditures also surged to nearly $20 billion, up from $6.9 billion a year earlier, as SpaceX races to expand its compute footprint. CFO Bret Johnsen said on the company’s October 20 earnings call that SpaceX expects to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter alone.

The massive lease comes after a tumultuous stretch in the debt markets for AI infrastructure players, as investors grow squeamish over runaway capital expenditures and limited profits.

While SpaceX had no trouble tapping Wall Street, Musk used the $40 billion announcement to take a victory lap over pure-play AI compute rivals.

Pointing to SpaceX’s “investment-grade” status and steady cash flow from Starlink and rocket launches, Musk argued on Sunday that debt markets have largely closed the door on companies without major revenue streams outside of AI data centers — spelling trouble for the more than 200 neocloud companies built solely to rent out GPUs for AI workloads.

“That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” Musk wrote on X. “Some will make it through, but not many.”

Tech.title: Microsoft offers buyouts to around 60,000 employees
Tech.content:
Microsoft is offering buyouts to around 60,000 employees, the company confirmed to TechCrunch on Monday. The move marks Microsoft’s latest efforts to cut costs and rework its workforce for the AI age.

Microsoft’s chief people officer, Amy Coleman, sent employees a note about the buyouts, which was also published on the company’s website.

Employees at the vice president level and below on select teams in the United States, Canada, India, and the United Kingdom will be eligible, according to the note. Bloomberg reports that divisions including Xbox, Windows, Copilot, and Finance are participating in the buyout offer. Some employees, including those working in data centers, sales and marketing, are excluded.

The news was first reported by Business Insider.
